articles.title: Zelenskyy says Ukraine behind drone attacks on Russian ships near Libya
articles.excerpt: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Ukrainian forces sank ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠a Russian warship in Benghazi and also hit a cargo ship used to transport weapons off the coast of Libya, hailing an “exemplary Ukraini...
articles.body_text:
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Ukrainian forces sank ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠a Russian warship in Benghazi and also hit a cargo ship used to transport weapons off the coast of Libya, hailing an “exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia’s war”.

Ukraine’s president said  in a statement on Monday that the Merkury, one of Russia’s newest warships, sank after Ukrainian forces launched seven naval drones on Sunday. A KA-27 combat helicopter was also destroyed in the attack.

He confirmed that Ukraine’s forces also attacked the cargo ship Angara. Libya’s eastern health ministry in Benghazi said all crew members from the cargo ship had been rescued and were receiving treatment after Sunday’s attack.

Authorities in eastern Libya said the warship was docked in the port of Benghazi when the explosion occurred.

“We firmly reject the use of our territory or territorial waters as an arena for settling scores or as an extension of external conflicts,” Saddam Haftar, the deputy commander-in-chief of the eastern Libyan administration’s forces said.

“The security and sovereignty of Libya are a national responsibility that leaves no room for political posturing or the exploitation of incidents to propagate accusations and incite fear,” he said.

Reporting from Moscow, Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova said that Russian authorities have not yet made an official comment on the drone attack on the warship.

“According to the Libyan side, the ship was returning to Russia from its mission and stopped in Benghazi for refuelling,” our correspondent said. She said it was not clear if there were any casualties.

“Russian military infrastructure is Ukraine’s target, not just in Russia, but pretty much throughout the world,” she said.

The United Nations Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) expressed “serious concern” over the drone attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”.

“Libya cannot afford and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts,” UNSMIL wrote on X.

The eastern administration did not identify who was behind Sunday’s attack but said Libya was “not a party to the Russian-Ukrainian war”.

The oil-rich nation of Libya has been divided between the government in Tripoli and a rival administration in the east since the overthrow of longtime ruler Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.

articles.title: Boy, 7, pulled alive from rubble hours after Russian strike on Ukraine, rescuers say
articles.excerpt:
'Danger seems greater all the time': Ukrainians search for missing after Russian strikes hit Kyiv

A seven-year-old boy has been rescued from the rubble of a residential building in Dymer, in the Kyiv...
articles.body_text:
'Danger seems greater all the time': Ukrainians search for missing after Russian strikes hit Kyiv

A seven-year-old boy has been rescued from the rubble of a residential building in Dymer, in the Kyiv region, after 14 hours. Overnight Russian strikes on the village killed 11 people, Ukrainian officials have said.

The attack occurred in the early hours of Sunday. A 79-year-old woman was also rescued alive from the collapsed building, Kyiv's regional head Tymur Tkachenko said.

A strike on a private home in Bila Tserkva killed one more person and set the building ablaze, he added.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also said three people were killed and 13 wounded in a separate strike on Vyshneve, also in the Kyiv region, that hit a grocery store on Sunday.

Ukrainian authorities said the boy in Dymer is in stable condition and was taken to hospital, and have thanked everyone involved in saving his life.

Zelensky and Ukraine's national police also confirmed the rescue of the boy.

In a Telegram post, Tkachenko said the 79-year-old woman rescued from the rubble was receiving treatment in hospital.

Earlier he said six people were injured in the attack, while others were still missing.

The attack on the residential building occurred in the early hours of the morning while people were asleep

Zelensky said more than 130 people are involved in emergency operations at the scene, and that they will continue until they have "complete information about every single person".

Sending his condolences to the families and loved ones of those killed, he said the strike struck the residential building, "practically blowing a section of it to smithereens".

Zelensky added that "rescue efforts are complicated by constant new air raid alerts and renewed threats".

The strike hit the building at 05:00 local time, when families were still asleep, Ukraine's minister of internal affairs Ivan Vyhivskyi said.

More than 70 strikes have been launched across 10 Ukrainian regions as of Sunday evening, Vyhivskyi added.

Emergency workers continue to search for those missing after Russian drone and missile attacks in Dymer.

In his video address posted online, Zelensky also said three people were killed and 13 injured in a strike on an "ordinary grocery store" in Vyshneve.

Mayor Illya Dikov wrote on social media that three children were among the injured.

Russia also struck a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Ukraine's Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said in a post on X., external

articles.title: Belgium’s airports set to shut down due to anti-austerity strike
articles.excerpt:
Nearly all flights are set to be cancelled in Belgium on Monday after the country’s air traffic controller said its staff would take part in a national strike against government austerity measures.

S...
articles.body_text:
Nearly all flights are set to be cancelled in Belgium on Monday after the country’s air traffic controller said its staff would take part in a national strike against government austerity measures.

Skeyes, the company responsible for Belgium’s air traffic control, said it would be unable to provide regular services at the country’s airports and in its airspace between 7am (06:00 GMT) and 9pm (20:00 GMT) on Monday.

“The anticipated staffing levels will not allow the safe handling of regular air traffic to be guaranteed during this period,” the company said. “Skeyes is therefore obliged to temporarily suspend the services concerned.”

It added that only essential services for emergencies and other safety-critical flights would continue.

The Brussels-Charleroi airport, a major European hub for low-cost airline Ryanair, said the strike would result in the “complete shutdown of all the country’s airports for an entire day”, affecting thousands of passengers.

“Without air traffic control, no flights can take off or land,” the Brussels-Charleroi airport said, criticising a “last-minute decision” with “disastrous consequences”.

Brussels airport said most departing and arriving flights “will have to be cancelled”.

Belgian unions have called for a nationwide day of action on Monday to protest against austerity and reform measures pursued by the country’s governing coalition.

The Board of Airline Representatives in Belgium, which represents about 25 carriers, said the walkout would be the 11th strike affecting Belgian airspace in 11 months.

The unions also plan a large-scale demonstration in Brussels on Monday. Significant disruption is expected to public transport, while schools, government offices and refuse collection services may also be affected.

Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever has been in protracted talks with his coalition partners on a cost-cutting budget that will save 10 billion euros ($11bn) over the next few years by Monday, in a bid to reduce the country’s high deficit.

Earlier in November, De Wever offered his resignation after his coalition failed to reach a deal. However, Belgium’s King Philippe rejected the resignation and gave the prime minister more time to find a solution.

articles.title: Tories welcome Louise Haigh’s hint government could adopt their plan to scrap Natural England – UK politics live
articles.excerpt:
First secretary of state has declined to say whether Natural England will be abolished as part of plans to cut the number of quangos

Natural England could be abolished as part of quango cull, says Lo...
articles.body_text:
First secretary of state has declined to say whether Natural England will be abolished as part of plans to cut the number of quangos

Natural England could be abolished as part of quango cull, says Louise Haigh

Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, has declined to say whether Natural England will be abolished as part of plans to cut the number of quangos.

In a story in the Times today, Patrick Maguire says:

double quotation markThe Times has been told that proposals for greater public control, due to be announced next month in Burnham’s ten-year plan for government, will include cuts to the arms-length bodies Haigh blames for planning delays, pollution and high energy costs.

Natural England, the environment regulator, could be among the casualties. Senior ministers believe it is obstructing government plans to build hundreds of thousands of homes, piling unnecessary costs onto developers and preventing the construction of infrastructure.

Asked about this report, Haigh told Sky News this morning that the government did want to reduce the number of quangos – and she declined to say whether or not this would include Natural England. She said:

double quotation markWe’re considering all arms-length bodies, both devolving, dissolving, and bringing back into departments because we cannot continue with this situation where politicians look round and can’t take responsibility for the actions that people have elected their government for.

At their party conference, the Conservatives proposed abolishing Natural England and the Environment Agency. In a move the party may now regret, Labour issued a response suggesting there was no need for this because the government was making both quangos more effective.

Today Katie Lam, the shadow housing secretary, said:

double quotation markFor far too long, Natural England has been allowed to hold the country to ransom, blocking desperately needed homes and vital infrastructure.

That’s why the Conservatives have pledged to abolish it. Now, it seems Labour are lifting that plan wholesale.

I don’t know who they think they’re kidding: this is a government that has spent two years piling on ever more bureaucracy. Only the Conservatives will take on the anti-growth ideologues and build the homes and infrastructure Britain needs.

Q: Can you confirm that, under the SPS deal announced on Friday, MPs won’t be able to vote down any new regulations on food and drink standards?

Haigh did not challenge that assertion from the FT’s Lucy Fisher. But she said that, under the deal, the UK would get “a seat at the table” when EU laws were being drawn up. “We will be consulted on every stage of the legislation,” she said.

Louise Haigh has finished her speech (more on that soon), and she is now taking questions. The broadcaster John Pienaar is hosting.

Q: Can you negotiate a new relationship with the EU without profound disruption to business?

Haigh starts by defending the deals announced on Friday. She says they will be worth up to £17bn.

That is the extent of where we can go in this parliament, she says.

She confirms “all options are on the table” for the future. But proposals will be set out in Labour’s manifesto.

Pienaar suggests there is not a cigarette paper between Burnham and Haigh on policy issues.

Haigh jokes that Pienaar has not read their WhatsApp messages.

Q: So you are as keen as him on rejoining?

Haigh just says the UK needs the right deal.

(It is understood that she is not as committed to rejoining the EU as Burnham.)

The next question comes from Lucy Fisher from the Financial Times who asks if Haigh, like Burnham, wants to rejoin the EU in her lifetime.

double quotation markThe problem with this lifetime framing is it makes us all wonder when we’re going to die, and compete with each other in the cabinet.

I’m going to abide by collective responsibility in that and say it’s a question for the manifesto.

Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, is speaking to the CBI now.

She started by telling the audience that the government had responded to the concerns of business by getting the EU to discuss a UK exemption from the Made in Europe protectionist legislation it is implementing. She said:

double quotation markWhen Andy Burnham became prime minister, it was obvious that the Made in Europe policy posed serious risks to the UK’s critical industries, including automotive and steel, both fundamental to this government’s industrialisation plans.

Everyone told us that getting Made in Europe on the agenda at the summit would be impossible.

But thanks to the prime minister’s ambition and courage in taking this debate on, we have a far better deal for Britain.

The deal announced on Friday did not explicitly cover Made in Europe. The UK and the EU are still negotiating on that, and concessions for the UK are implicitly linked to the UK offering the EU concessions on the tuition fees paid by EU students attending British universities.

But last week Hamish Falconer, the EU relations minister, told MPs he was he was “pretty optimistic” of a good outcome for Britain in the Made in Europe negotiations.

Rain Newton-Smith, the CBI chief executive, opened the organisation’s conference in London this morning with some relatively positive comments about the PM. Here are extracts from what she said.

Newton-Smith praised Burnham for bringing “hope” back to politics. She said:

double quotation markIn the last few years, we in the UK have been too ready to talk ourselves down. To put on our gloom-tinted glasses. They don’t sit well on me.

The prime minister has brought a dose of hope to our politics. And just as pessimism can be self-fulfilling, confidence can be contagious. It’s time we gave a shot of confidence to our economy. It’s time we got serious about a brighter future for our children.

She said the government needed to reassure business that “public control” of utilities did not mean nationalisation.

double quotation markOn investment … to some, “public control” sounds like code for renationalisation. That is kryptonite to investment. We know that’s not what’s coming – but give us the reassurance we need. Show this is a model built on partnership, not primacy. That government wants private capital at the table – not heading for the exit.

The government has heard this message. See 9.15am.

She said Burnham was right to start a debate about a closer relationship with the EU.

double quotation markThe prime minister is right to have this conversation. Brexit was a wrong turn for our economy. It gave us greater sovereignty. But sovereignty without prosperity is not enough. We didn’t vote to be poorer.

This is no time to re-fight the referendum. But we must come back to the table with bolder ambition.

She said that regional devolution could unlock investment and that the CBI was involved in a scheme to help give mayoral authorities more financial expertise.

double quotation markThere is promise in devolution. Done right, it can give business one front door for decisions that unlock investment. Done wrong, it could fracture confidence… leave regions competing with each other when they should be competing with the world.

The difference is whether authorities have the capacity and skills. Today, I can announce the CBI and our members are partnering with the National Wealth Fund and mayoral authorities across the UK … to parachute in senior financial secondees with the experience to make investment happen.

Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, has declined to say whether Natural England will be abolished as part of plans to cut the number of quangos.

In a story in the Times today, Patrick Maguire says:

double quotation markThe Times has been told that proposals for greater public control, due to be announced next month in Burnham’s ten-year plan for government, will include cuts to the arms-length bodies Haigh blames for planning delays, pollution and high energy costs.

Natural England, the environment regulator, could be among the casualties. Senior ministers believe it is obstructing government plans to build hundreds of thousands of homes, piling unnecessary costs onto developers and preventing the construction of infrastructure.

Asked about this report, Haigh told Sky News this morning that the government did want to reduce the number of quangos – and she declined to say whether or not this would include Natural England. She said:

double quotation markWe’re considering all arms-length bodies, both devolving, dissolving, and bringing back into departments because we cannot continue with this situation where politicians look round and can’t take responsibility for the actions that people have elected their government for.

At their party conference, the Conservatives proposed abolishing Natural England and the Environment Agency. In a move the party may now regret, Labour issued a response suggesting there was no need for this because the government was making both quangos more effective.

Today Katie Lam, the shadow housing secretary, said:

double quotation markFor far too long, Natural England has been allowed to hold the country to ransom, blocking desperately needed homes and vital infrastructure.

That’s why the Conservatives have pledged to abolish it. Now, it seems Labour are lifting that plan wholesale.

I don’t know who they think they’re kidding: this is a government that has spent two years piling on ever more bureaucracy. Only the Conservatives will take on the anti-growth ideologues and build the homes and infrastructure Britain needs.

Good morning. This afternoon Andy Burnham will make a statement to MPs about the UK-EU summit on Friday, where agreements were reached on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme. At one point there were suggestions that he might use this Commons moment to give a speech with further details of his plan for a debate on forming a closer relationship with the EU, including possibly rejoin. Now, that won’t happen today; Burnham has decided to make that announcement part of his 10-year plan, which is being unveiled next month. But dozens of MPs will get the chance to put a question to Burnham, and so we will get a sense of what they feel about the prospect of revisiting the Brexit settlement.

According to the BBC, Burnham will describe the Friday deal as “the single biggest growth measure to be delivered in this parliament”.

He will tell parliament on Monday the “landmark” deal struck with the EU means there is a “very real prospect” the next decade can be “much better” than the last one.

We will hear alternative views at the CBI conference today. All the main UK opposition party leaders are speaking, and Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, and Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, are planning to criticise the agreement with Brussels, according to extracts of their remarks released overnight.

Burnham won’t be there himself. But he is sending his de facto deputy, Louise Haigh, and she is planning to reassure the CBI audience that Burnham’s plan for more public control of utilities does not mean the government is anti-business.

double quotation markThis government will put pragmatism and public interest ahead of failed political ideology. Public control is not anti-business – it’s about getting the foundations right, so that private enterprise can do what it does best.

She will point out that foreign governments already own “significant stakes in our water, electricity and gas networks with returns paid to their taxpayers” and she will say:

double quotation markThe status quo is not the neutral, pragmatic centre ground. It’s the outlier. An exception that no other nation is trying to emulate.

In its overnight briefing on the speech, the Cabinet Office says:

double quotation markChallenging the misconception that public control means wholesale nationalisation, the first secretary will say this approach is not about whether or not markets work, but how effective monopolies have resulted in a lack of genuine competition.

9.30am: Rain Newton-Smith, the CBI chief executive, opens the annual CBI conference with a speech. There are also speeches from Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, at 9.45am and Kemi Badenoch at 12.20pm, and Q&A events with Zack Polanski, the Green party leader, at 2.35pm, Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, at 3.55pm and Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, at 4.40pm.

Morning: Andy Burnham is due to visit a Morrisons in Kent to promote claims his SPS deal with the EU will help keep down food prices.

11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.

2.30pm: Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, takes questions in the Commons.

After 3.30pm: Burnham is expected to make a statement to the Commons about Friday’s UK-EU summit.

articles.excerpt: GLASGOW, Scotland — Ukraine was behind the explosive sinking of the Russian corvette Merkury in the Libyan port of Benghazi over the weekend, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, and the country’s mili...
articles.body_text:
GLASGOW, Scotland — Ukraine was behind the explosive sinking of the Russian corvette Merkury in the Libyan port of Benghazi over the weekend, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, and the country’s military released accompanying videos.

The Merkury, a warship that had been acquired by the Russian navy in 2023, was left mostly submerged after sea drones struck it on Nov. 22. The video released by Ukrainian authorities shows several of the uncrewed, explosive-laden boats slamming into the side of the moored ship.

The Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) says it carried out the operation jointly with Ukraine’s Defense Forces. Zelenskyy said seven Ukrainian-made naval drones were used in the operation and that a Ka-27 helicopter aboard the corvette was also destroyed.

During the same operation, the Russian dry-cargo ship MV Angara was also targeted. The SBU describes Angara as a sanctioned vessel used to move weapons and military equipment on Russian routes to Syria and Libya, and says Merkury had escorted it.

Reuters, citing local medical sources, reported ten injuries in the attack, including Russians and Libyans. Al Jazeera reported one person had been killed.

Satellite imagery taken by U.S. commercial imagery provider Planet and reviewed by Defense News showed a ship ablaze in the port of Benghazi, with a long smoke trail. Additional satellite imagery shared online by open-source investigators appeared to confirm that the ship had been sunk.

The attack is one of the most stark examples of geographic spillover of the war in Ukraine. Libya is particularly fertile ground for a confrontation between Ukraine and Russia, given the country’s unresolved political division: The east, centered on Benghazi, is controlled by the Government of National Stability, backed by Russia, while the western half of the country, centered on Tripoli, is under the control of the internationally recognized Government of National Unity.

The United Nations, which maintains an “advanced mission” for the post-conflict settlement in Libya, put out a statement saying that “Libya can not afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts.”

Reporting has suggested that in addition to spillover of direct confrontation between Russia and Ukraine, the two countries may increasingly be engaged in proxy conflicts across Africa. In Mali, where the Russian Africa Corps – the successor to the paramilitary Wagner Group, now incorporated into the military – backs the government, Ukraine appears to be sharing intelligence and even sending operatives in support of the opposing side.

And in the weeks before Syrian dictator Bashar al-Assad fell in December 2024, Ukrainian military intelligence reportedly sent about 20 drone operators and 150 drones to assist Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), the group that led the offensive against Assad’s Russian-backed government.

Linus Höller is Defense News’ Europe correspondent and OSINT investigator. He reports on the arms deals, sanctions, and geopolitics shaping Europe and the world. He holds master’s degrees in WMD nonproliferation, terrorism studies, and international relations, and works in four languages: English, German, Russian, and Spanish.

articles.title: Natural England could be abolished as part of quango cull, says Louise Haigh
articles.excerpt:
First secretary of state says proliferation of arm’s length government bodies is hampering decision-making

The nature watchdog Natural England could be abolished as part of a cull of arm’s length gov...
articles.body_text:
First secretary of state says proliferation of arm’s length government bodies is hampering decision-making

The nature watchdog Natural England could be abolished as part of a cull of arm’s length government organisations, Louise Haigh has said.

Saying that the proliferation of quangos and other similar bodies had made decision-making by ministers more difficult, the first secretary of state said it could fall within a push to change the landscape of government by scrapping some organisations and bringing others into departments.

Abolishing Natural England could be justified on the basis that it could speed up planning decisions and thus boost housebuilding and growth, but removing or curbing its role would be likely to prompt concern from environmental groups.

Last month, the Conservatives announced that if they won power they would abolish both Natural England and the Environment Agency, saying this would help create more new homes.

Tony Juniper, the chair of Natural England, responded to the reports on Monday morning by saying he was “very proud of all the work we have done during recent years to unite our national ambitions for growth while achieving nature’s recovery, adding: “It’s never been the case that healthy nature is in opposition to economic development, but actually enables it. It’s possible to do both.”

Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, was speaking before a speech to the CBI conference on Monday morning at which she was to make the case for greater government control of public utilities.

After the Times reported Natural England was in line to be abolished, Haigh was asked on Sky News about the proliferation of quangos. She said: “We’ve had successive governments complain about this, but unfortunately, successive governments have created more of these and pushed more decision-making out of their own departments, so that then when they make decisions they don’t agree with, they turn around and look in horror.

“That’s why we’re absolutely committed to devolving responsibilities where they can be devolved.”

Asked if she was considering getting rid of Natural England, she said: “We’re considering all arm’s length bodies, both devolving, dissolving, and bringing back into departments, because we cannot continue with this situation where politicians look round and can’t take responsibility for the actions that people have elected their government for.”

Asked again about the specific fate of Natural England in a later interview on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Haigh again did not push back against the idea it was being targeted for abolition along with other arm’s length bodies.

She said: “So all the ALBs are in my sight for either devolving responsibilities that can be pushed down to mayors and strategic authorities, whether they can be brought back into departments under the direct power of the secretary of state, or whether they can be dissolved entirely.”

In a section of her speech about utilities, according to extracts released in advance, Haigh was to say she would “put pragmatism and public interest ahead of failed political ideology”, adding: “Public control is not anti-business – it’s about getting the foundations right, so that private enterprise can do what it does best.”

Saying almost no other nation had so many essential services run by private companies, and often overseas ones at that, Haigh was to say: “The status quo is not the neutral, pragmatic centre ground. It’s the outlier. An exception that no other nation is trying to emulate.”

articles.title: Capita boss exits and shares crash after civil service pensions failures
articles.excerpt:
Price plunges 67% as Adolfo Hernandez leaves with ‘immediate effect’ amid continued fallout from pension payment problems

The boss of troubled outsourcing group Capita has abruptly departed as he adm...
articles.body_text:
Price plunges 67% as Adolfo Hernandez leaves with ‘immediate effect’ amid continued fallout from pension payment problems

The boss of troubled outsourcing group Capita has abruptly departed as he admitted it has “not delivered” for retired civil servants left waiting for pension payments.

Chief executive Adolfo Hernandez has agreed with the firm’s board to step down with “immediate effect”, it said on Monday. He will be replaced by chief financial officer Pablo Andres for the top job.

Shares in Capita plunged by 67% to as low as 80p, Capita’s lowest share price since October 1991, on Monday morning as it cut profit forecasts and proposed raising £190m in extra capital.

Capita said that adjusted operating profit in 2027 is expected to be £85m to £95m lower than previously expected, due to extra costs in relation to the UK Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) contract, and “short-term contract headwinds”.

Pensioners have reported being forced to borrow money from family to pay for food and heating, with some saying they feared losing their homes because they could not afford their rent or mortgage.

The reshuffle comes after Capita got into hot water for delays in administering the 1.7 million member pension scheme, leaving thousands of civil servants waiting for payments and retirement quotes.

Capita, which has government contracts across education and defence, and collects the TV licence fee, agreed the pension contract with the former Conservative government in 2023. It came into force in December 2025.

The company has taken a hit to its finances as a result of the issues delivering the scheme and the implementation of a recovery plan.

It also faced a grilling by MPs in parliament last month, with one Cabinet Office minister labelling the company’s progress in improving how it runs the scheme as “abysmal”.

Hernandez said he recognised the shortcomings that had affected members of the pension scheme.

He said: “It has been a privilege to lead Capita through this phase of its transformation. Three years ago we set out to turn Capita into a technology led, AI-enabled business services company.

“I am proud of the groundwork we have laid and the progress we have made under my leadership.

“Of course, within that I recognise that we have not delivered the service that members of the civil service pension scheme deserve.”

The Guardian first reported on concerns over the pension scheme last year, and earlier this year the government admitted retired civil servants have been failed by the decision to outsource their pension scheme.

Multiple members of the CSPS scheme then came forward to say they were unable to afford rent and have been forced to use food banks after being left without an income.

In July, the Cabinet Office confirmed it is hoping to take the scheme back in-house after “unacceptable” service levels.

Last week, Capita said: “We know that some members have been experiencing challenges with the [CSPS]. We’re very sorry for any delays and the frustration this is causing.”

MPs have blamed the problems on operational failures including overwhelmed revision teams, poor technology and incorrect pension quotes.

The company plans to raise the £190m in the first half of next year, “to reduce leverage and to allow the business to move forward from a more stable foundation”. The decision was supported by its biggest shareholder, the activist investor Oasis Management Company, it said.

Press Association contributed to this report

articles.title: NOOSHEEN HASHEMI: America's AI leadership needs more than one man
articles.excerpt:
Jensen Huang's Nvidia future faces mounting questions as analysts cast doubt on his return amid concerns over China chip sales and upcoming testimony.

America’s AI industry is about to find out how m...
articles.body_text:
Jensen Huang's Nvidia future faces mounting questions as analysts cast doubt on his return amid concerns over China chip sales and upcoming testimony.

America’s AI industry is about to find out how much of its financing depended on Jensen Huang’s word.Huang has said he would be willing to return to Nvidia. On Tuesday, board chair Harvey Jones said the board does not intend to reinstate him as CEO. For independent companies raising money now, the question is whether Nvidia will still commit early enough to bring other investors into their rounds.According to PitchBook, rounds Nvidia joined accounted for 27.2% of global venture deal value through mid-November. That includes every investor’s contribution, and a handful of very large rounds drove much of the total. Nvidia separately reported $99 billion in equity investments as of July 26. That was the value of its holdings at the time. We don’t know how much Nvidia put into independent open-model developers or how often it led their rounds.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks at Dreamforce 2026 summit in San Francisco, Calif., on Sept. 15, 2026.

Reflection AI shows what Nvidia could do when it chose to lead. Huang reportedly committed Nvidia to half of Reflection’s initial $1 billion target and urged other investors to join. The round grew to $2 billion, and Nvidia put in about $800 million. It was an unusually large deal. The sequence is important: Huang committed Nvidia’s money first, then brought other investors in. Nvidia stood to sell chips to Reflection, and that kind of financing deserves scrutiny. It also shows why a lead investor’s decision canshape a round.

Nvidia still has the means to invest. On Tuesday it reported $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue, up 103% from a year earlier. Its board has said it expects operations, customer commitments and the product roadmap to continue without interruption. Interim CEO Colette Kress said the company is scrutinizing future investments, commitments and guarantees. She also said Nvidia had made no change to the financing conditions on its existing agreements with specialist cloud providers. I expect Nvidia to be more selective about taking new risks. The question for founders and co-investors is which deals it will still lead and how quickly it will decide.

JENSEN HUANG’S NVIDIA DEBACLE REVEALS AMERICA’S REAL PROBLEM: NO SKILLED BUILDERS

As an AI founder and investor, I see how quickly a delay can become a problem for a smaller company. Microsoft, Meta and Google can fund much of their own expansion. An independent lab can have payingcustomers and still need to raise money to train its next model. A specialist cloud provider has to finance the chips before it can sell the computing time. If the lead investor waits, others can wait too. The company still has to decide whether it can afford to reserve the computing capacity or keep the people it hired to do the work.

Racks of GPUs with a closed-loop liquid cooling system are seen inside an operational Microsoft data center in Indonesia on Feb. 4, 2026. (Yasuyoshi Chiba / AFP via Getty Images)

China is already competing for the customers those companies could serve. The Lowy Institute counted nearly 1.8 billion downloads of Chinese models on Hugging Face in the third quarter, compared with 500 million for American models. Huawei shows customers how to run Alibaba’s Qwen on its Ascend chips. As more developers use Qwen, Huawei has a chance to sell them the systems that run it. Beijing’s AI action plan promotes both open-source cooperation and computing infrastructure abroad. That combination could become the next chapter of China’s Digital Silk Road.

BEYOND KILLER ROBOTS: CHINA'S REAL AI THREAT TO AMERICA IS ALREADY HERE, EXPERTS WARN

Governments that want to run AI on their own infrastructure should have a competitive American choice in models and hardware. That means Nvidia and AMD, Broadcom’s custom accelerators and systems from specialists such as Cerebras and d-Matrix. Once a government buys the equipment, adapts its software and trains its engineers, switching suppliers is expensive. Americans can disagree about which chips Nvidia should be allowed to sell to China. Weakening Nvidia or the American companies that build with its technology would give Beijing an advantage while other countries are making those choices.

Nvidia should continue backing independent AI companies. Kress and Jones should tell founders and co-investors who can approve pending deals, when decisions will come and whether Nvidia intends to provide follow-on financing. Institutional investors, sovereign wealth funds and independent venture firms should start putting together rounds of their own. Elon Musk, who has welcomed the idea of hiring Huang, could bring investors together for one such partnership. It would need firm capital commitments and the freedom to make investment decisions independently of xAI and his other companies. If we make a model’s weights public, Beijing can get them too. Our allies also need American models they can run on their own infrastructure, with their own data and under their own rules. If we leave that market to China, we make it easier for Beijing to sell the systems those countries will depend on for years. Before taxpayers guarantee financing for an open-model project, an independent review should establish which U.S. security interest it serves and whether the benefits of releasing the weights justify the risks.

CHINA COULD EXPLOIT US TECHNOLOGY TO THREATEN AMERICAN FORCES, CONGRESSIONAL WATCHDOG LEADERS WARN

I believe private investors should decide which companies deserve their money. I would make a narrow exception when a documented financing gap threatens a viable project vital to national security. The Treasury should convene private investors this week to find out which projects are at risk and how much private capital is ready to move. I would set an initial target of $100 billion in combined public and private commitments. Congress should act urgently to authorize a temporary federal credit guarantee under bipartisan oversight, drawing on the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital. Congress shouldseparately cap taxpayer exposure and set an expiration date. An independent committee should apply published criteria, require recusals for conflicts and approve guarantees only where private investors keep their own capital at risk.

If Nvidia and private investors fill the gaps, the guarantees can go unused. It could take months to learn which deals will proceed. A lab can lose the team it took years to assemble in weeks. Nvidia can give founders answers now, and the Treasury can bring investors together while there are still deals to do.Disclosure: The author has an indirect investment in Reflection AI through her limited-partner interest in a fund managed by 1789 Capital.

Noosheen Hashemi is a Silicon Valley entrepreneur, former Oracle executive and founder and CEO of January AI, using artificial intelligence to transform how people understand and manage their health.

articles.title: Fears for school crossing patrols as councils struggle to recruit lollipop people
articles.excerpt:
Future of familiar school-run figures uncertain as vacancies surge and town halls consider alternatives

They have been a feature of British schooldays for decades, instantly recognisable by their rou...
articles.body_text:
Future of familiar school-run figures uncertain as vacancies surge and town halls consider alternatives

They have been a feature of British schooldays for decades, instantly recognisable by their round signs and yellow hi-vis uniforms. But a struggle to recruit against a backdrop of staff cuts at cash-strapped local authorities is threatening to make lollipop people a thing of the past.

The Recruitment and Employment Confederation (REC) said school crossing patrols were among jobs showing the biggest increase in vacancies in recent weeks, alongside sales roles and exam invigilators.

There is no legal obligation on councils to fill the roles. Last week, East Riding of Yorkshire council said a quarter of school crossing patrol sites were unstaffed, adding that applicant numbers were dwindling. It said it was exploring long-term alternatives at some sites, including infrastructure changes, such as creating zebra crossings.

Parents and carers in Hessle told the BBC that unstaffed crossings were “not really safe for the children”, but the council said some had been vacant for some time “with no applicants”, while others had become vacant after previous lollipop people retired.

A council spokesperson said: “The role of a school crossing patrol may not be as attractive in this day and age, as it requires work for limited hours each school day, offers relatively low pay for the short morning and afternoon shifts they are needed to work, and they are outside in all weathers.

“The short period of time they are needed to work may not suit everyone and limits what people can do during the rest of the day. But we continue to encourage local residents to apply for these jobs and help make a difference to children, parents and the school community.”

Earlier this year, after a council meeting in Redcar and Cleveland where elected representatives expressed concerns about gaps in school crossing patrols, the council leader, Alec Brown, said it was not easy to maintain a full roster.

“It’s difficult, you just can’t have a pool of ready-made lollipop people to step up,” he said after the meeting in March.

A Redcar and Cleveland borough council spokesperson said it advertised vacancies through the council’s recruitment channels and, where appropriate, directly through schools.

“We receive a reasonable number of applications, but one of the main challenges is that these roles are part-time positions with relatively low weekly hours,” the spokesperson added. “We currently have three applicants going through the recruitment process, and once appointed, the service will only have one vacancy remaining.”

The Bournemouth East MP, Tom Hayes, who has been campaigning to save local school crossing patrols, said: “I absolutely think we could be seeing the loss of lollipop people everywhere in the country. It just feels to me like we’re breaking down as a society so many of these touch points, which can hold communities together, the kind of the little things that create the glue.”

The factors of limited hours and low pay have probably been compounded in recent years by an increase in lollipop people facing dangerous and aggressive drivers, leading some councils to provide their crossing patrols with body cameras.

Ally Mitchell took a job as a lollipop person in Edinburgh after being made redundant from a role in the video games industry. It was initially meant to be a stopgap while he looked for a full-time position, but he enjoyed the job so much he stayed on even after securing a role in the charity sector.

“While the additional income is certainly important, what keeps me doing the job is the sense that I’ve become a trusted and respected member of my local community,” he said. “I genuinely enjoy helping people, wishing them a good morning and making a positive contribution to their day.”

Mitchell said school crossing patrols go “beyond road safety”, having a wider impact on communities. “I think we’re living in a world where people can increasingly feel isolated and disconnected from one another,” he said.

“School crossing patrol officers are one of those little everyday points of human contact that help bring communities together.

“You can replace a crossing with road markings or traffic lights, but you can’t necessarily replace the person standing there, remembering the children’s names, greeting their families and becoming part of their lives,” he added. “And I think that would be a real loss.”

Meanwhile, in some areas, those who want to become a lollipop person may struggle to find work, with councils scrapping the positions to save money.

Last year, Durham council – controlled by Reform UK – decided to scrap vacant roles for crossing guards as part of a savings drive, saying: “These posts have been vacant for a prolonged period of time without incident.”

The latest data available, obtained by the GMB trade union under freedom of information laws, found that school crossing patrol officer numbers in England, Scotland and Wales fell by 2,081 in a decade, from 7,128 in 2009-10 to 5,047 in 2017-18.

Earlier this year, Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole council postponed its proposed cuts to patrols after a campaign was launched to save the roles.

The council took the decision to “upgrade” school crossing patrol sites with permanent crossings in 2024.

A council spokesperson said: “While we appreciate there is the loss of a familiar face in the community, permanent crossings provide a safe and reliable facility that is available 24 hours a day, seven days a week, benefiting schoolchildren and the wider community all year round.”

Hayes said the issue was part of a broader pattern. “Whether it’s the librarian behind the counter, who’s going to help you to do your homework, whether it’s the person who works at a Sure Start centre who’s going to help you to raise your kid because they give you the skills that you need, whether it’s the playground that’s broken down, where mums would otherwise have just sat on a bench for ages and got to know each other, there are these just little contact points in the society.

“If you chip away at them, and you do it in the interest of saving money, or you’re doing it in the interest of something more efficient, which are the arguments I have heard, it just undermines who we are as a society, and it makes it harder for people to feel like they can create connection.”

articles.title: War against data centers is costing local communities millions of dollars
articles.excerpt:
Protestors gathered in front of Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y.’s office in Brooklyn, urging the representative to "Stop the Dirty Data Center Deal!" according to the event organizers.

Affordability and...
articles.body_text:
Protestors gathered in front of Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y.’s office in Brooklyn, urging the representative to "Stop the Dirty Data Center Deal!" according to the event organizers.

Affordability and data centers were on the ballot this November. Voters made it clear that they are concerned about both issues: prices are too high and the neighborliness of data centers is in doubt. In a time of economic turbulence, cities and counties are struggling to pay for schools, roads and public safety without the tax revenue data centers generate. Where can part of the solution to affordability and concerns with data centers be found? Vacant lots.

Vacant lots can host data centers that are well maintained, comply with local architectural requirements, have security and bring in much-needed cash for local projects. An eyesore and security problem can become a revenue generator and a secure property. However, some are determined to keep data centers from developing the local economy and unsightly properties at any cost.

In early November, an activist helped block the development of a $5 billion data center that was set to break ground in the next year or so. The data center was supposed to be built on the site of Landover Mall, which closed in 2002. The vacant lot is now overgrown with grass and weeds, stretching across nearly 90 acres in Landover, Md.

AMERICA'S REDDEST STATE CHASES BILLION-DOLLAR BOOM AS OTHERS SOUR ON MASSIVE EMERGING INDUSTRY

Prince George's County, home to the former mall, is facing a $130 million budget deficit. It has lost a Six Flags amusement park, is losing the Washington Commanders to Washington, D.C., and has suffered thousands of federal job losses. Developers projected about $53.5 million a year in local tax revenue if the data center were to be built.

A data center protest outside the Austin Marriott Downtown, Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026. (Jay Janner/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images)

The activist, Taylor Frazier McCollum, isn't moved by those numbers or how they help her neighbors. "Money is, you know, a made-up concept," she said. "We buy into it every day, and we choose that this has value and this doesn't have value and to me the environment has the highest and utmost value and I need to honor that in any way."

INSIDE THE FAR-LEFT'S ANTI-DATA CENTER PUSH AND WHAT EXPERTS SAY IS DRIVING IT: 'PLAYBOOK WE'VE SEEN BEFORE'

The rejection of a project to help revitalize a site that sorely needs it and fill the county's coffers perfectly encapsulates the political debate around data centers. Too often, proposed data centers receive automatic opposition from activists and politicians. As a result, some of America's most vulnerable and desperate communities are losing millions of dollars in tax revenue that could fund schools, fix roads, pay emergency responders and more.

Landover Mall is sadly not the only example. Local opposition blocked or delayed at least 75 data center projects across the country worth approximately $130 billion in the first quarter of 2026, which Data Center Watch describes as the largest single-quarter total on record. That's roughly as much as all of 2025, in just three months.

HOW AMERICA CAN WIN THE AI RACE WITHOUT BURNING VOTERS

In Virginia, Prince William County stands to miss out on as much as $400 million in projected annual tax revenue following the collapse of Digital Gateway, once billed as one of the largest data center complexes in the world. The county had approved the project, but courts invalidated its rezoning approvals. The remaining developer withdrew its legal challenge in July 2026, effectively ending the plans.

On the other hand, communities that are looking to the future and allowing data centers are reaping the benefits. Virginia’s Loudoun County has embraced data centers, which have generated 38% of general fund revenue in the county’s FY2026 budget. That revenue has helped the county lower its real property tax rate every year for a decade, from $1.145 per $100 of assessed value in 2016 to $0.805 in 2026. That's real money back in homeowners' pockets. That is revenue its neighbor, Prince William County, is missing out on.

HOMEOWNERS IN THE HEART OF AMERICA’S AI BOOM ARE GETTING AN UNEXPECTED PAYOFF

In Henrico County, Virginia, data center tax revenue pays for an Affordable Housing Trust Fund that helps first-time homebuyers with down payments. A single mother working toward a nursing degree said her new mortgage costs less than her old rent. In Richland Parish, Louisiana, Meta's data center expansion helped the parish pay for $50,000 teacher bonuses.

THE POWERFUL WAY AMERICAN COMMUNITIES CAN BENEFIT FROM THE NEW TECH BOOM REVEALED BY DATA CENTER CEO

Data center developers have a responsibility to communities: listen to their concerns, be transparent and collaborative about their plans, design in ways their neighbors approve and work to mitigate or eliminate undesirable local impacts. They must also pay their own electric and water costs, establish noise limits and continually work with local community groups and elected officials to address concerns as they arise.

Data center development can be and often is a win-win for developers and the community. But even these efforts are not enough for some. Money may be a "made-up concept" to some, but the lower tax rates in Loudoun County, the down payment in Henrico and the teacher bonuses in Richland Parish are real.

Data centers can turn a decades-long vacant parking lot overgrown with weeds into an economic engine, helping to close a $130 million hole in the budget. Immovable opponents are ignoring the economic benefits data centers can bring and leaving funding for community projects on the table. History shows other counties will take advantage of this lack of foresight and benefit.

Neil Siefring is a senior fellow at Alliance for the Future (@aftfuture). Follow him on X at @NeilSiefring.

articles.title: Zelenskyy says Ukraine responsible for sinking Russian warship in Libya – Europe live
articles.excerpt:
President says Kyiv responsible for sinking Merkury warship in Benghazi on Sunday and also drone attack on cargo vessel MV Angara

Russian warship sinks in Benghazi after suspected Ukrainian drone att...
articles.body_text:
President says Kyiv responsible for sinking Merkury warship in Benghazi on Sunday and also drone attack on cargo vessel MV Angara

Russian warship sinks in Benghazi after suspected Ukrainian drone attack

Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has claimed responsibility for sinking a Russian warship at a Libyan naval base on Sunday, saying it was part of Kyiv’s response to Russia’s continuing aggression.

“An exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia’s war,” he said in a post on X, with a video showing the moment the corvette was hit by Ukrainian drones.

“Our warriors deployed seven Ukrainian-made naval drones. Despite all the enemy’s efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk. It’s one of their newest ships, commissioned in 2023, during the full-scale war,” he said.

Zelenskyy added that a Russian dry cargo vessel MV Angara, which he said was used for transporting weapons, was also sunk.

Elsewhere, Nato and the UN will meet today to discuss the security situation in the region.

Nato’s North Atlantic Council (NAC) will meet to discuss the events of last Friday, when three Russian missiles crashed in Poland amid a broader assault on Ukraine. Poland is expected to ask for further military support from allies.

And the UN security council will meet to discuss Russian attacks on civilian targets, including the consulates of Austria and the Netherlands in Kyiv.

It’s Monday, 23 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

For what it’s worth, the Kremlin, ⁠asked about ​reports ⁠that Ukraine struck ⁠a ​Russian ‌warship ‌in the Libyan ‌port of Benghazi on Sunday, ‌said that information ​would be provided ⁠by Russia’s ​Defence Ministry.

And Ukraine’s SBU has also offered more photos showing the attack…

Meanwhile, Ukraine’s SBU security service also commented on the sinking of the Russian warship in Libya.

It said the corvette “regularly escorted enemy maritime convoys” and was part of Russia’s Black Sea Fleet.

“A Ka-27 multipurpose helicopter was on board the corvette and also sank,” the SBU said.

There was no immediate comment from Russia about the strikes.

Zelenskyy also said that “partners” – presumably the US – want the fourway talks between Ukraine, Russia, the US and Europe to take place before Christmas.

“We are ready to do this literally tomorrow. We have heard from our partners that they want to try to make it happen before Christmas. We hope it happens sooner, and we must come to this meeting with a clear agenda, prepared and agreed by all of us.”

“When the main question comes up, ‘what happens after this war?’, our common answer must be security. Real security. Security for Ukraine, security for all of Russia’s neighbours, security for Europe and the entire Euro-Atlantic area. This is only possible if we work together as closely as possible. I believe this is only possible when Russia has no temptation to test whether security guarantees really work with Nato.”

In the last half hour, Volodymyr Zelenskyy addressed the Nato parliamentary Assembly meeting in Berlin.

He warned that “Russian aggression has shown that when Ukraine is left out, and when there is no clear understanding of how Europe should be protected, anything can happen.”

He also celebrated overnight strikes against Russia, saying Ukraine “keep finding ways to get back on our feet after every Russian attack.”

“Today, Russia can feel our response all the way from western Siberia, where its oil refiners are burning, to the coast of Libya, where its warships are sinking.”

Zelenskyy stressed that Ukraine has repeatedly offered “steps to reduce the fighting,” and “never been the ones to raise the stakes,” but Russia “still gives us no peaceful response.”

He urged Nato leaders to “invest in stronger security and greater resilience,” saying “does anyone here still believe that one day Russia will simply become peaceful and safe again?”

“Just look at the last, last 100 years of Russian history. … There is no reason to believe that Russia will become a different country in one year or five years. So we must act in a way that makes sure that no matter what kind of Russia we face and no matter what threats our countries face, we will always have enough to defend ourselves.”

He urged partners to support Ukraine ahead of winter, particularly helping with air defence systems.

“The stronger our defences are, the less chance Russia has to break through them and the more chance diplomacy has to work.”

The Ukrainian president also slightly pushed back against the suggested Article Five-like security guarantees for Ukraine in case of a peace deal with Russia, arguing that it should simply be allowed to join Nato instead.

“When we talk about Article Five-like guarantees, we need answers. We need answers to some very clear questions. Which countries will support Ukraine if Ukraine is attacked again, what exactly will our partners do in response? Which troops will be stationed on our territory in advance? How much will all these cost and will it really work? All of this is not easy and so far we have no clear, specific answers with respect to such ideas.”

And here’s Zelenskyy’s video from the attack:

Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has claimed responsibility for sinking a Russian warship at a Libyan naval base on Sunday, saying it was part of Kyiv’s response to Russia’s continuing aggression.

“An exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia’s war,” he said in a post on X, with a video showing the moment the corvette was hit by Ukrainian drones.

“Our warriors deployed seven Ukrainian-made naval drones. Despite all the enemy’s efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk. It’s one of their newest ships, commissioned in 2023, during the full-scale war,” he said.

Zelenskyy added that a Russian dry cargo vessel MV Angara, which he said was used for transporting weapons, was also sunk.

Elsewhere, Nato and the UN will meet today to discuss the security situation in the region.

Nato’s North Atlantic Council (NAC) will meet to discuss the events of last Friday, when three Russian missiles crashed in Poland amid a broader assault on Ukraine. Poland is expected to ask for further military support from allies.

And the UN security council will meet to discuss Russian attacks on civilian targets, including the consulates of Austria and the Netherlands in Kyiv.

It’s Monday, 23 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

articles.title: Nine million jobs are in limbo, and Congress can fix it before Christmas
articles.excerpt: Billy Downs, president of Ford's Garage, tells Fox News Digital the challenges of balancing employee compensation with affordability for diners as select Florida franchise locations experiment with a ...
articles.body_text:
Billy Downs, president of Ford's Garage, tells Fox News Digital the challenges of balancing employee compensation with affordability for diners as select Florida franchise locations experiment with a different approach to covering labor expenses.

Ask most Americans who owns the McDonald's on the corner, the Holiday Inn off the interstate, or the gym down the street, and they'll tell you it's a big corporation. They're wrong. Most of those businesses are owned by local entrepreneurs who put their own savings on the line, sign the lease, make the payroll, and live in the town they serve. There are roughly 832,000 of these franchise small businesses in America, and together they support about nine million jobs.

Yet for more than a decade, Washington hasn't been able to answer a simple question for them: Who is the employer?

The answer has flipped with every change in administration. In 2015, the Obama labor board's Browning-Ferris decision blew up decades of precedent and said a parent brand could be on the hook for a franchisee's workers based on "indirect" or even unused control. A 2020 rule restored common sense. In 2023, the Biden board went further than Browning-Ferris, declaring that merely reserving the right to control was enough, before a federal court struck that rule down. The standard has now changed four times since 2015, and another court case could change it again in the next few months. No small-business owner can plan a five-year expansion around a rule that changes every four.

CHICK-FIL-A IS ONE OF AMERICA'S TOUGHEST FRANCHISES, AND THE STARTUP COST MAY SHOCK YOU

This isn't an abstract legal fight. When the International Franchise Association and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce studied the damage from the expanded standard, they found it cost the economy $33.3 billion a year, led to as many as 376,000 fewer job opportunities, and drove a 93% increase in lawsuits against franchise businesses. Ninety-two percent of the brands and owners surveyed said the rule meant less support from their brand.

That last number is the one that should bother Congress most. Under a sprawling joint-employer test, every bit of help a franchisor gives — a training program, an HR template, a workplace-safety manual — becomes evidence that it is really the boss. So the brands pull back. The national company with the lawyers and the compliance staff protects itself. The owner of three sandwich shops is left on her own. A rule sold as protecting workers ends up kneecapping the small employers who hire them.

The fix is sitting in front of Congress right now. The American Franchise Act (H.R. 5267 / S. 3525) writes one permanent, franchise-specific standard into federal law under both the National Labor Relations Act and the Fair Labor Standards Act. A franchisor would be a joint employer only if it both possesses and exercises substantial, direct, and immediate control over essential terms of employment like wages, hiring, and scheduling. Setting brand standards, offering training, or requiring safety qualifications would not, by themselves, make a franchisor the employer. That is how franchising worked for most of its history, and it is how it should work.

Most important, it would be the law — not a board decision that the next administration can toss out on a party-line vote.

This is that rarest of things in Washington: a genuinely bipartisan bill. It was introduced by seven Republicans and seven Democrats. It has 158 cosponsors in the House, cleared the House Education and Workforce Committee in July, and has the backing of the White House. Members like Rep. Kevin Hern of Oklahoma, who owned and operated McDonald's restaurants before he came to Congress, understand from the inside what it means to meet a payroll under rules that won't sit still.

REP ROGER WILLIAMS: 250 YEARS OF HARD WORK PAYS OFF FOR MAIN STREET BUSINESSES

At Unleash Prosperity Now, our new paper, "Nine Million Jobs at Stake: Why Franchising Needs Regulatory Certainty," lays out what's on the line. One in eight American businesses with at least one employee is a franchise, and nearly two-thirds of local franchise owners are first-time business owners. This year alone, franchising is projected to create more than 150,000 new jobs. The conclusion is plain: Clarity is the cheapest pro-growth policy Congress can pass. It would also lift a compliance headache off small-business owners and free them to keep prices down at a moment when Americans have made clear that affordability is what they care about most. It doesn't cost the Treasury a dime, and it lets hundreds of thousands of small employers get back to hiring.

The clock matters. If the American Franchise Act doesn't pass before this Congress adjourns, it dies, and the whole process starts over, with a future labor board free to swing the pendulum back again. (iStock)

The clock matters. If the American Franchise Act doesn't pass before this Congress adjourns, it dies, and the whole process starts over, with a future labor board free to swing the pendulum back again. Franchise owners have already spent 10 years in limbo. They shouldn't be made to wait for another election cycle.

The lame-duck session is usually remembered for what Congress fails to do. Here's a chance to do something useful for Main Street before Christmas. Pass the American Franchise Act.

Stephen Moore is an economist and co-founder of the Committee to Unleash Prosperity.

articles.title: At least 15 killed in Ukraine’s Kyiv region as Russia intensifies attacks
articles.excerpt:
Rescuers in Ukraine have raced to find residents trapped under the rubble of a block of flats that partially collapsed in a Russian strike after attacks on the Kyiv region killed at least 15 people.

...
articles.body_text:
Rescuers in Ukraine have raced to find residents trapped under the rubble of a block of flats that partially collapsed in a Russian strike after attacks on the Kyiv region killed at least 15 people.

Moscow has been pummelling Ukraine with nightly drone and missile barrages as the war-torn country braces for another winter while the full-scale invasion grinds through its fifth year.

An overnight strike on Dymer, about 45km (30 miles) north of the Ukrainian capital, hit a five-storey building, killing at least 11 people, Kyiv regional official Tymur Tkachenko said on Monday.

“Rescuers recovered the body of another person from beneath the rubble,” Tkachenko wrote on Telegram, confirming the death toll had risen to 11.

Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said earlier on Telegram that the dead included a teenager.

It said rescuers were searching for 11 people, including two children, who were “not responding or cannot be reached”.

Rescuers had managed to pull out survivors from the rubble, including a 79-year-old woman and a child, Tkachenko said.

Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine, reporting from Kyiv, said people were believed to still be under the rubble.

“Rescuers are still at the site, working to try to pull people out from under the rubble dead or alive,” she said.

A Russian strike on a supermarket killed three other people and wounded 15, including three children, in Vyshneve, a city just south of Kyiv, Mayor Illya Dikov wrote on Facebook.

“People had simply gone to the store to buy groceries. An ordinary shopping trip turned into a tragedy due to a Russian attack,” Tkachenko said.

A strike on a private home in nearby Bila Tserkva killed one more person and set the building ablaze, he added.

Russia also struck a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said on social media.

Moscow has ramped up attacks on Ukraine and its energy network in particular as temperatures drop to around freezing.

Putin promised on Thursday that Russia would respond to Ukrainian attacks on the Kerch Bridge, a symbol of Putin’s rule over Ukraine’s Russian-annexed Crimean Peninsula, with “much more painful” attacks.

Ukraine hit the bridge three times in a week, severing the part of it used by vehicles and halting train services.

Meanwhile, drones attacked oil storage facilities in Russia’s Tatarstan region, damaging several, but there were no immediate reports of deaths or injuries, according to the Interfax news agency, which quoted local authorities.

“A fire broke out there,” Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova reported from Moscow, adding that the attack targeted the facility in Tatarstan’s Almetyevsk area.

Shapovalova said drone attacks were also reported in the Novoshakhtinsk area in Rostov, hitting a petroleum products plant and causing a fire in a storage tank.

She added that an attack was also reported in the city of Perm in the Volga region, where a large oil refinery is located.

Our correspondents said the attacks in Tatarstan, which is about 1,000km (620 miles) away from the Ukrainian border, demonstrate Kyiv’s ability to penetrate deep inside Russia.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday that Ukraine’s forces sank the Russian corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest ships, commissioned in 2023, near the coast of Libya using seven Ukrainian-made naval drones.

Zelenskyy said they hit a second target, the Russian dry cargo ship MV Angara. The Ukrainian president said it was used by Russia to transport weapons.

“We continue operations in designated waters,” he said on Telegram.

Zelenskyy added that a Russian Ka-27 combat helicopter was destroyed along with the corvette.

articles.title: ‘Environmental crimes’: Israel blamed for toxic pollution in 99% of Gaza
articles.excerpt: More than three years of Israel’s genocidal war has turned Gaza into “a toxic wasteland”, with poisoned water and contaminated soil threatening the survival of Palestinians in the enclave of 2.3 milli...
articles.body_text:
More than three years of Israel’s genocidal war has turned Gaza into “a toxic wasteland”, with poisoned water and contaminated soil threatening the survival of Palestinians in the enclave of 2.3 million people.

Israel’s use of explosives and incendiary weapons has caused environmental contamination across more than 99 percent of Gaza, according to a new report by Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS).

“Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza includes military assaults on its environment, which are environmental war crimes threatening life now and for generations to come,” said Amitabh Behar, Oxfam’s international executive director.

“The destruction and contamination of Gaza will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival. This would breach Israel’s legal obligations under international humanitarian and human rights law,” he said in a statement.

“Palestinians living in Gaza are being exposed to toxins in multiple ways through air, food, water and via direct contact with contaminated soils and debris.”

The report shows how Israel’s destruction of buildings and the environment has contaminated the air, soil, food and water in the enclave.

It also emphasises the urgent need for a full independent investigation to identify and reduce the risks to Palestinian lives.

Pollutants from bombardment, fires, rubble and untreated sewage can reach Palestinians through the air they breathe, the water they drink and the food they eat.

Oxfam’s report, which uses satellite imagery, remote sensing, scientific analysis and other open-source data, gives a comprehensive picture to date of the impact of the Israeli assault on Gaza, which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians. More than 1,500 Palestinians have been killed since the so-called “ceasefire” was signed in October 2025.

In September 2025, a UN international commission of inquiry said Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. And the International Court of Justice is hearing a case of genocide against Israel. In January, the ICJ said it was plausible that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.

The report came a day after world leaders failed to reach a consensus on climate change at the 31st Climate Change Conference (COP31) of the United Nations.

Explosions, fires and the destruction of buildings and infrastructure release pollutants that settle on rubble and soil.

Wind, traffic and debris clearance send them back into the air. Oxfam’s analysis points to the highest concentrations in Gaza City, Jabalia and the North Gaza governorate.

Israel’s continuous bombardment has also generated substantial greenhouse gas emissions, with further emissions expected from clearing debris and rebuilding.

A study cited in the report estimated direct conflict emissions at more than 1.3 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) by January 2025.

By October 11, 2025, Israeli ground operations directly affected about 283sq km (109sq miles) of Gaza’s 365sq km (141sq miles), or 78 percent of the area, Oxfam estimates.

The UN Environment Programme estimates that the assault since October 7, 2023, generated 61 million tonnes of debris, which is about 29 tonnes of rubble per person living in Gaza now. More than 90 percent of Palestinians have been forcibly displaced, most of them multiple times.

Oxfam estimates that the mountains of rubble would require 2.1 million dump truckloads to clear them, equivalent to 736 trips around the circumference of the entire planet.

The amount of rubble that needs to be cleared is about eight times the 7.65 million tonnes estimated in Iraq’s Mosul during the 2017 conflict.

The report identifies at least one potential contamination source across more than 99 percent of Gaza. Gaza City, Khan Younis, Rafah, Jabalia and the Salah al-Din Street corridor showed the greatest overlap of potential hazards.

Unexploded munitions can leach contaminants into soil and groundwater as their casings corrode. Damaged vehicles, batteries and fuel stores add to the risks along military routes and former positions.

A study cited by Oxfam estimated emissions across the wider conflict cycle at 33.2 million tonnes of CO2e, including an estimate of 31.4 million tonnes of carbon emissions that will occur from reconstruction.

According to a report by Palestinian Water Authority cited by Oxfam, Gaza’s daily water supply fell from 334,107 cubic metres before October 2023 to 54,747 cubic metres in June 2024, a drop of about 84 percent. By April 2026, emergency repairs had brought it back to 130,315 cubic metres a day, still 61 percent below pre-assault levels.

Nine of 61 reservoirs were operational, with combined storage sufficient to provide 18 litres per person for one day.

Gaza’s Coastal Aquifer historically supplied 81 percent of the territory’s water. Oxfam says 97 percent of the aquifer was already chemically polluted before October 2023.

Decades of overpumping amid Israel’s air, land and sea blockade of Gaza allowed seawater to seep in. Untreated sewage, farm runoff and waste disposal added to the pollution.

In July 2026, Gaza’s Ministry of Health detected faecal coliforms in 15 of 79 groundwater wells (19 percent) tested. Oxfam identified North Gaza, Gaza City and Deir el-Balah as the areas most at risk from contaminated drinking water. An assessment in 2021 reported faecal coliforms in 2 percent of wells.

July tests found that 61 of 79 wells (77.2 percent) had total dissolved solids above 1,000 milligrams per litre, 400mg above the level at which the World Health Organization says water becomes increasingly unpleasant to drink.

By April 2024, Israel’s assault had destroyed all six of Gaza’s wastewater treatment plants. An estimated 40,000 cubic metres of raw sewage enter the Mediterranean daily, enough to fill 16 Olympic-size pools.

By April 2026, 19 percent of pumping stations and about 30 percent of the sewer network still functioned at least partly.

Gaza’s waste collection fleet fell from 261 vehicles to 48.

Both main landfills remained inaccessible. Of at least 56 temporary dumps, only 11 were accessible and operating.

These sites generally lack barriers to protect soil and groundwater. By April 2026, an estimated 1.45 million people lived in areas affected by rodents and other pests.

Before October 2023, Gaza’s farms supplied about 95 percent of the fresh vegetables people ate. By late 2025, more than 87 percent of cropland was damaged.

Oxfam says only 3 percent was accessible and undamaged.

By October 2024, the UN had reported that more than one million olive trees had been uprooted.

Oxfam identified more than 7,200 damaged greenhouses and documented the destruction of facilities that preserved and distributed Palestinian seeds.

Before the assault, Gaza’s fisheries produced about 4,660 tonnes of fish a year, with fish farms adding 750 tonnes.

In July 2026, an estimated 1.2 million people (59 percent) faced crisis levels of acute food shortages or worse, according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, cited by the report.

The report also records the loss of roughly 95 percent of cattle and a collapse in fishing.

The average daily catch from October 2023 to April 2024 was 7.3 percent of its 2022 level. Oxfam warns that contaminants could enter crops and seafood as production resumes.

Gaza’s gross domestic product fell by 83 percent in 2024 to $362m, the report says.

Damage to farms, workshops and factories has stripped people of income and the means to resume work. Debris removal, repairs and farming could expose workers to asbestos, silica and other hazards for years.

Among the commerce and industry establishments assessed, 92 percent sustained damage, including 72 percent that were destroyed.

A joint World Bank, European Union and UN assessment, cited by Oxfam, put direct physical damage at $35.2bn and economic losses at $22.7bn by October 2025.

It estimated recovery and reconstruction needs at $71.4bn over a decade, including $26.3bn in the first 18 months.

Disease prevalence in Gaza recorded more than 1.9 million cases of acute respiratory infection and about 81,000 cases of acute watery diarrhoea in January and February 2026. More than 36,000 of the diarrhoea cases were among children aged below five years. Gaza recorded more than 496,000 cases of acute watery diarrhoea in 2025.

In 2024, vaccine-derived poliovirus type 2 was detected in Gaza’s wastewater. A child was later diagnosed with paralytic polio, Gaza’s first reported case in 25 years. The report also cites the detection of multidrug-resistant pseudomonas in water at primary healthcare centres.

Oxfam says the destruction of Gaza’s water, food and sanitation systems may be relevant to alleged crimes under the Rome Statute and to assessing whether Israel violated the Genocide Convention.

A genocide finding requires proof of intent to destroy a protected group, in whole or in part. Oxfam calls for full reparations where violations are established.

Its five-stage plan calls for securing access and reducing exposure, testing for contamination, screening sites and making essential repairs, treating contaminated sites and managing hazardous waste, then rebuilding with safeguards and long-term monitoring.

articles.title: Georgia officer shoots 13-year-old after traffic stop linked to earlier shooting, police say
