articles.title: Victorian Greens seek urgent injunction over how-to-vote cards mimicking party’s branding but preferencing it last
articles.excerpt:
Exclusive: Independent candidate Tosh-Jake Finnigan’s cards instruct people to vote in a way that would benefit Liberal party

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

The Victor...
articles.body_text:
Exclusive: Independent candidate Tosh-Jake Finnigan’s cards instruct people to vote in a way that would benefit Liberal party

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

The Victorian Greens are seeking an urgent injunction from the supreme court to stop an independent candidate distributing how-to-vote cards that allegedly mimic the party’s branding and urge people to preference it last.

As prepoll opened on Wednesday morning, Tosh-Jake Finnigan’s campaign team handed out how-to-vote cards that used the minor party’s colour scheme, font and triangle logo with the banner “Vote 1 Green Values”.

The card instructed people to vote in a way that would ultimately benefit the Liberal party. It asked voters to give their first preference to Finnigan followed by an Animal Justice party candidate, another independent candidate and then the Liberals in fourth place.

The Greens are determined to win back the ultra-marginal seat it lost to the Liberals at a February 2025 byelection with a 1.3% margin. Labor is running an open ticket in Prahran, which the Greens fear could deprive it of the preference votes it needs.

On Wednesday afternoon, the Greens state director, Martin Shield, requested Finnigan immediately stop distributing the material and threatened to take legal action if an undertaking was not given to do so in less than two hours.

Finnigan agreed to the request and produced an amended how-to-vote card within hours that included different colours with a revised banner that said “Vote 1 Trans Greens Values”.

“Due to legal threats from the Greens party, I confirm that I am not an endorsed Greens party candidate,” a disclaimer on Finnigan’s revised how-to-vote card said.

But the changes did not satisfy the Greens. On Friday afternoon, the party’s lawyers lodged papers in the supreme court.

At an initial hearing on Friday night, the Greens’ lawyer, Adam McBeth, alleged people handing out Finnigan’s material at prepoll wore shirts with the exact shade of green as worn by genuine Greens party volunteers.

McBeth alleged Finnigan’s team stood next to Greens party volunteers and Greens placards. The party argues voters at prepoll were deliberately misled.

“There is no other reason for an independent candidate who has an infinite range of colours and styles to choose from to so closely mimic the Greens, including the way people paid to hand out were dressed and where they were directed to stand,” McBeth said.

Finnigan, who was self-represented, said they had gone above and beyond to quickly make changes to their initial how-to-vote card and accused the Greens of using “legal manoeuvres” to stop them campaigning.

“It is my belief that they don’t want me to hand out on Saturday, which will be one of the busiest days of prepoll,” Finnigan said.

Finnigan told the court that they did not have enough money to print new cards. They said their campaign team had not been instructed to stand next to the Greens at prepoll.

“I am someone who holds Greens values, of course I am going to have some kind of green shirt,” Finnigan said.

“The honest reason I went for that colour of green is because the colour is called Irish green and I am of Irish background. That’s why I went for it. I just like the sound of Irish green.”

On Friday evening, after the supreme court action was lodged, the Victorian Election Commission (VEC) accepted Finnigan’s subsequent how-to-vote card and published it online.

Justice John Watson said the first how-to-vote card “looked like a pretty deliberate attempt to pass yourself off as a Greens candidate”, but he adjourned the matter until 3pm on Saturday to hear testimony from the VEC.

Finnigan became Victoria’s first openly transgender councillor in 2023 when they were elected to the Colac Otway shire council after a countback. They resigned from the council in October 2024.

The former Labor field campaigner founded the Restore Democracy Sack Dan Andrews party in 2022. They unsuccessfully contested an upper house seat for the party, securing 1% of first preference votes.

After working in the offices of Labor ministers during the 2014 state campaign, Finnigan became a whistleblower in the so-called Red Shirts scandal, which saw taxpayer funds used to pay electorate officers campaigning for Labor.

Finnigan’s campaign Facebook page carrying an authorisation message describes them as a “Green Independent” and contains attack ads against the minor party.

articles.title: Trump turns White House press conference into a 2028 succession audition
articles.excerpt:
The president appeared to put Vance and Rubio through their paces as potential successors, though Stephen Miller unexpectedly stole the spotlight

“Which of you shall we say doth love us most?”

The a...
articles.body_text:
The president appeared to put Vance and Rubio through their paces as potential successors, though Stephen Miller unexpectedly stole the spotlight

“Which of you shall we say doth love us most?”

The ageing King Lear’s question to his daughters, expecting them to compete for his favour and carve up his kingdom, hovered in the White House press briefing room on Friday.

There at the lectern stood Donald “Lear” Trump. Behind him stood his potential heirs, JD “Goneril” Vance and Marco “Regan” Rubio, and to the side sat Trump’s favourite offspring, Stephen “Cordelia” Miller (more of him later). As for Lear’s Fool, the choices were endless.

Ostensibly this was a press conference to trumpet the president’s trip in Asia, but in practice everyone knew it was the first audition for the 2028 presidential election (and boy, is Trump going to enjoy turning the race into a contest for his approval). Vance is widely expected to seek the crown, though it was Rubio who came out on top in the latest Emerson College national poll.

In a jam-packed room, Trump stood centre stage as if hosting The Apprentice all over again. Behind him were the two contenders expressing their aspirations through matching suits, matching Maga red ties, matching US flag pins and matching leather shoes.

The first trial: could Vance and Rubio stand still for 90 minutes without rolling their eyes, yawning or silently mouthing “Kill me!” to the press? Could they force Trump’s word salad down their throats and look as if they were enjoying it? Even when the boss was rambling at length about potholes?

“When you fix a pothole”, began one detour by the octogenarian president. “I don’t want to bore you – they’ll say, oh, he rambled, he rambled terribly. I don’t ramble. I don’t ramble at all, but when you fix a pothole, you have brand new asphalt against old white asphalt that doesn’t look good, but at least you don’t ruin your car, but these roads were flawless …”

But first, the whole thing got off to a strange start. Trump appeared at the podium and remarked: “That’s a big, big a crowd. I’ve never seen this before,” but reporters crammed in the room could barely hear him above the whoosh of an air conditioning unit. An engineer tweaked the sound, but it only gave Trump’s voice an eerie echo.

Had the gremlins that grounded flights and frozen banking sites finally reached the White House? So much for America the hi-tech superpower. Eventually order was restored, though not necessarily in Trump’s brain.

He was evidently flattered by the media comparing his trilateral summit with the leaders of China and Russia to the Yalta meeting between Winston Churchill, Franklin Roosevelt and Joseph Stalin (he did not say which of the three he identified with, though critics could take a guess). Like a gushing teenager, Trump was so thrilled that Chinese president Xi Jinping had come to the airport to greet him, that he mentioned it twice (“He didn’t meet Sleepy Joe with the plane, that I can tell you.”)

The US, Russia and China hold 92% of global nuclear power, he noted, which gave him an excuse to bring up his uncle John Trump, an electrical engineer and former Massachusetts Institute of Technology professor. “A member of my family spent his life at MIT who they say is now the greatest professor in the history of MIT, so I have great understanding of- I guess maybe genetically I’m blessed,” Trump riffed.

At that remark Rubio could resist no longer. A smile spread across his lips and he shot a look at Vance, who felt obliged to smile back. We’re not laughing at you, we’re laughing with you, Mr President.

Indeed, Rubio had been the more fidgety of the pair. As Trump chuntered on, the secretary of state had shifted from foot to foot, fiddled with his tie, played with his lower lip, touched up his hair and given the odd wry smile. Vance, meanwhile, hid behind his beard and miasma of smugness.

But then, at last, came the moment for Lear’s daughters to make their public declarations of love. Vance went up the lectern and pointed out that he had stayed in Washington rather than joining the trip, comparing himself to Macaulay Culkin’s character in Home Alone – a child who is accidentally left behind at Christmas as his family rushes to catch a flight to Paris. “I missed you, sir,” he said to Trump, before praising the president for “securing historic trade deals” and reorganising the global economy to benefit the American worker and economy.

Not bad, but a little wonky. Marco, you’re up next. The secretary of state took aim at the critics who accused Trump of cosying up to dictators at the expense of Democrats, raising his eyebrows and shaking his fist: “These three countries possess the overwhelming majority of nuclear weapons on this planet. The idea that these three leaders should not engage on a regular basis is not just absurd, it’s dangerous.”

Trump began taking reporters’ questions. One young whippersnapper posed a question that will be asked many times over the next two years. “Because you have the vice-president, the secretary of state right behind you, I’m curious which of them do you think would make a better president after you?”

Trump swatted it aside without answering. Vance remained stony faced. Rubio smiled knowingly.

The same reporter put Vance in an uncomfortable spot by asking about his post-midterm tweet. “Would you argue that the war in Iran was worth it to lose the Senate?” The vice-president agreed with the goal of Iran not getting a nuclear weapon but added carefully: “I think the president is the one who makes the decision and the president has said he would do it again. And my view is that my goal is and my job is to support the president of the United States.”

In other words, I hate this war and would never have started it but I have to back the boss. Expect a lot more of this needle-threading in the upcoming campaign.

Later, when Trump asked “Do you want to keep this going or not” amid a cacophony of shouted questions, he turned around to look at Rubio, who laughed, then at Vance, who did likewise with folded arms. The two rivals patted each other playfully. But neither was prepared for the man who would steal their thunder.

“We have the most powerful man in the world in the room right now,” said Trump, referring to Miller, the recently appointed White House chief of ideological zealotry, who stepped up to the lectern with bald pate gleaming under the bright lights.

“I just wanted to say that what President Trump has achieved over the last two years is more than any president has achieved by far in American history!” Miller roared, before offering the kind of vainglorious soliloquy that would make even a Kremlin or Chinese Communist party spokesperson blush. “What you’re going to see over the next two years, as astonishing as that has been under his leadership, the next two years are going to be the greatest two years in American history!”

Trump, who loves nothing more than flattery with exclamation marks, returned to the lectern and announced: “We have breaking news. We have breaking news.” Waving his hands, then with thumbs pointed at Vance and Rubio, he said of Miller: “He was better than these two guys. Do you want to run for president?”

That was a joke, right? Trump was stirring the succession pot again, making his potential heirs uncomfortable. It was fitting that he ended the press conference reminiscing about the night he hosted Ultimate Fighting Championship bouts on the White House South Lawn. He is going to relish every moment of presiding over a Republican cage match for the next two years.

articles.title: Charlie Sheen stunned to learn fellow actor Rob Lowe had been praying for him for years
articles.excerpt:
Actor Rob Lowe revealed to actor Charlie Sheen that he had prayed for him for years to recover from addiction.

Actors Charlie Sheen and Rob Lowe, both of whom struggled with addiction in the past, sh...
articles.body_text:
Actor Rob Lowe revealed to actor Charlie Sheen that he had prayed for him for years to recover from addiction.

Actors Charlie Sheen and Rob Lowe, both of whom struggled with addiction in the past, shared a moment on Sheen’s podcast when Lowe revealed he had been praying for Sheen for years.

Sheen spoke with Lowe on his "Mostly Sheenius" podcast. Lowe has had his own addiction struggles in the past and stars in the new film "Confession," a historical drama set in the Soviet Union in 1938.

"I’d like to clear the air," Sheen said. "I’d like to, you know, not pretend like something didn't happen or whatever. I think it's juvenile, and I don't think — I think it's how we grow for sure, you know, is to just be honest.

"And I've sent a few tweets, back when they were tweets, just some stuff about you that was really unkind and unfair."

CHARLIE SHEEN HAS BLUNT RESPONSE TO QUESTIONS ABOUT HIS HEALTH AND FINANCES

Charlie Sheen was taken aback that fellow actor and friend Rob Lowe had been praying for his recovery for decades. (Dominik Bindl/Getty Images)

When Lowe signaled that he didn't care about the past social media posts, Sheen replied, "OK, but I do."

"They were mean and stupid, and it was all before Dec. 12, 2017," Sheen added. "That's when I got off the dope and quit the booze and all that s---, you know. So, anyway, I just wanted to offer that."

"Well, thank you, thank you," Lowe said, saying that even if the tweets made it to his newsfeed, "I forgot about them. And if they did, I probably just went, ‘Well, that's, you know, Charlie's — one day he's going to he's going to get it.’ Which you did."

Sheen is a major public figure not only for his acting career, but for his controversies and his rocky road to sobriety after years of addiction.

Sheen’s 2025 Netflix documentary series featured him after seven years of sobriety, candidly discussing "his rise to fame and public downfall, joined by family and friends who share untold stories of his journey."

TOM HANKS' SON CHET HANKS SHARES THE LIFE-CHANGING DECISION THAT FOLLOWED REHAB AND ADDICTION

Actor Rob Lowe appears during an episode of Bravo's "Watch What Happens Live with Andy Cohen" in Season 23 of the late-night talk show. (Ralph Bavaro/Bravo via Getty Images)

After Sheen recalled Lowe being at his first intervention years ago, Lowe revealed he had been praying for him for years.

"I know you're not a huge, like, program guy. It saved my life, but that's neither here nor there," Lowe said. "But in the program, as you know, they always say, ‘Take a moment of prayer for the alcoholic who still suffers.’ And you were always my guy," Lowe revealed. "Every time, years and years and years."

"So, you were kind of giving that prayer for a couple decades?" Sheen said in surprise.

"Every time. Every time. Every f---ing meeting I went to, bro!, Lowe said.

"That's amazing. Thank you. That’s so sweet," Sheen replied.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Alexander Hall is an associate editor for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to Alexander.hall@fox.com.

articles.title: Israeli drone attacks kill seven Palestinians in central Gaza
articles.excerpt:
Israeli attacks have killed at least seven Palestinians and wounded others in the central part of the Gaza Strip, as attacks continue despite a “ceasefire” agreement.

Four Palestinians were killed on...
articles.body_text:
Israeli attacks have killed at least seven Palestinians and wounded others in the central part of the Gaza Strip, as attacks continue despite a “ceasefire” agreement.

Four Palestinians were killed on Friday when an Israeli drone struck the Bureij refugee camp in Deir el-Balah, medical sources told Al Jazeera.

Witnesses said the drone targeted a group of civilians within the camp.

Separately, a medical source at al-Awda Hospital reported the arrival of the body of a Palestinian killed by an Israeli drone strike in the Nuseirat refugee camp.

Two Palestinians were also killed when an Israeli drone struck civilians near the entrance to the city of Deir el-Balah.

Al Jazeera’s Hani Mahmoud, reporting from Deir el-Balah, said the injured were brought to hospitals in central Gaza that operate at reduced capacity due to a lack of medical supplies and staff.

Mahmoud added that drones were “causing fear and panic” among Palestinians in Gaza.

“People cannot run simple errands because of the ongoing fear of being attacked and killed on the road,” he said.

The buzzing of drones adds to the sound of explosions from home demolitions and to that of fighter jets, our correspondent added.

The Israeli army on Friday carried out demolition operations near areas under its control in the al-Shuja’iya neighbourhood in the eastern part of Gaza City using explosive-laden drones.

It also carried out three large-scale demolitions near the “Yellow Line”, east of Khan Younis in southern Gaza.

By June 16, 2026, an estimated 201,290 structures in Gaza had been damaged or destroyed, about 82 percent of all structures in the Strip, according to the United Nations Satellite Centre (UNOSAT).

Israeli forces have continued demolishing buildings and homes in the Gaza Strip amid ongoing military operations and disputes over the “ceasefire” line.

Israel has repeatedly violated the so-called “ceasefire” agreement that entered into force on October 10, 2025.

Since then, Israeli attacks have killed more than 1,600 Palestinians in Gaza. Since the genocidal war began in October 2023, Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured 176,000 others.

Separately on Friday, which marks World Children’s Day, Palestinian prisoner groups said that around 350 Palestinian children were being held in Israeli prisons, where they face torture, starvation and deprivation of medical care, education, and family visits.

The Palestinian Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs and the Palestinian Prisoner Society said dozens of children from Gaza were detained during the war, but enforced disappearance and restrictions on visits have made it impossible to determine their numbers.

articles.title: Ukraine strikes Kerch Bridge as Putin ally declares ‘no one needs Europe’
articles.excerpt: Ukraine’s fourth and most complex operation on the Kerch Bridge brought down its road section and may have crippled its rail section over three days of strikes, taking a crucial Russian supply route i...
articles.body_text:
Ukraine’s fourth and most complex operation on the Kerch Bridge brought down its road section and may have crippled its rail section over three days of strikes, taking a crucial Russian supply route into Crimea off the map.

“The short supply route from Russian territory has been destroyed,” declared Ukraine’s General Staff.

“Once again, the myth of Russia’s greatness has been shaken,” said Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU), which took part in the operation.

It was part of a wider set of strikes against oil facilities and supply routes in the Rostov and Krasnodar Krai regions abutting Ukraine – an apparent strategy to asphyxiate Russian forces in southern Ukraine.

“The alternative route is overland, along the front line, where our drones are waiting for the cargo,” said the Ukrainian Ministry of Defence.

For a month, Ukraine’s military said it “systematically destroyed enemy air defence systems, radars, and electronic warfare equipment along the way to the target.”

On November 16, Ukrainian drones damaged the bridge’s road surface and compromised its steel arched span that allows shipping between the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea.

On November 17, the SBU said it used “Palyanytsia kamikaze drones to target the roadway section of the Crimean Bridge, causing it to collapse.”

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Neptune and Flamingo missiles and Ruta drones struck the separate railway span.

During this 48-hour period, Russia’s Ministry of Defence said it intercepted 4,305 Ukrainian drones compared with a daily average of 882 during the previous week.

On November 18-19, Ukraine again used Neptune missiles to strike the railway span, saying rail service had been suspended. It was unclear whether those strikes had permanently disabled the rail bridge.

Russian President Vladimir Putin dismissed the operation as a strike against “a purely civilian facility … We haven’t even transported oil or petroleum products across the bridge.”

Ukraine’s General Staff disagreed, saying it had targeted the Kerch Bridge because it “was a vital artery, supplying fuel, ammunition, equipment, and personnel”.

The Ukrainian Defence Ministry called the bridge “a war machine”.

On the same day as the main strike on the Kerch Bridge, Ukraine also struck Russia’s main overland route to its southern forces, the M-14 Rostov-Crimea highway.

In addition, Kyiv also struck a series of refineries and oil depots in southwestern Russia that are nearest to the front, including in Azov, Ilsky and Afipsky.

“Fuel from such depots has a short route to the front,” it said.

Ukraine has already put Russia’s Black Sea and Azov Sea fleet of oil and fuel carriers out of action, striking at least 300 ships between July and September, leaving fuel supply dependent on road and rail transport.

Southern Ukraine is where Russian offensive efforts are now most active.

Robert Brovdi, the head of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces, has said Russian casualties are heaviest near Dobropillya and Huliaipole in Zaporizhia. Ukraine’s General Staff has also confirmed this is where the highest number of assaults takes place.

Ukraine made a point of saying its Kerch operation was entirely autonomous.

“The strike was carried out exclusively with Ukrainian weapons – our technology, our solutions,” said Ukrainian Defence Minister Yevhen Khmara.

This also meant that Ukraine did not rely on the US-controlled Starlink and Starshield satellite systems, on which it depends for short-range drone navigation. On October 14, those services began to cut out when drones exceed 160km/h (100mph). They were later restored, but Zelenskyy said they were again compromised beginning on November 13.

For the Kerch Bridge operation, Ukraine instead designed a system of drones that acted as signal repeaters. Video released by Ukraine showed an FP-5 missile relaying video up to the moment of impact, indicating that operators had control of it.

During the past week, Ukraine also targeted Russian refineries as far-flung as Volgograd and Samara, Salavat and Tatarstan, in an ongoing strategy to deprive Russia’s war machine of export revenue and diesel.

Almost half of the output of the Volgograd refinery is diesel, Ukraine said – a blow not only to Russia’s military, which consumes the fuel, but also to its promise to export 1.7 million tonnes of diesel this year as part of a deal struck with US President Donald Trump to lower fuel prices.

US negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have reportedly threatened Ukraine with an intelligence cutoff if it continues to strike Russian refineries.

As Ukraine defied them, Putin and Trump took to the global stage as the guests of Chinese leader Xi Jinping in the city of Shenzhen on November 19.

It was the first time Putin and Trump had met since their summit in Alaska in August 2025, and the first time all three men had met.

Kremlin-aligned media made much of the event, picking up Putin’s comparison with the Big Three conference in Yalta at the end of the second world war.

“The world’s three most consequential powers – have met. As the Big Three, they have emerged as the principal force in shaping a new architecture for international and European security,” wrote Putin’s deputy on the National Security Council, Dmitry Medvedev. “Today … no-one needs Europe.”

Asked whether peace in Ukraine was any closer as a result of the summit, Putin said he and Trump were still aligned on the proposals they discussed in Alaska. Those involved Ukraine handing over to Russia the one-fifth of the eastern Donbas region it cannot take by force, and to agree not to join NATO.

In the recent negotiations at Abu Dhabi on November 10-11, Ukraine was reportedly offered a green light to join NATO in return for the Donbas.

At those talks, Russia also turned its emphasis on Europe’s future security architecture.

Putin developed this further in Shenzhen, reported The New York Times and Bild magazine. He apparently offered Kremlin approval of Ukraine’s EU membership as long as Ukraine did not become part of EU defence policy, and as long as the United Kingdom and France refrained from offering a pan-European nuclear deterrent.

It would be “strange to discuss Europe’s security without Europe itself,” Putin said. On Ukraine’s however, he appeared to demand Europe sign onto whatever the US and Russia agreed.

Despite US and Russian attempts to appear to rearrange the world order, Europe did not appear to be listening.

During the past week, it provided Ukraine with a tranche of 1.7 billion euros ($1.97bn) from a 90 billion euros ($104.4bn) Ukraine Support Loan agreed in 2025, and another 8 billion euros ($9.28bn) from the Ukraine Facility, a 50 billion euros ($58bn) fund focused on Ukrainian economic recovery and financial support.

In addition to these two facilities, the EU agreed this week to raise 45 billion euros ($52.2bn), covering most of a 70-billion-euro ($81.2bn) shortfall that Ukraine says it will face next year. Of that amount, 25 billion euros ($29bn) will be for additional military assistance.

In addition to being a staunch supporter of Ukraine, however, Europe continued to be a divided supporter, deciding that its top diplomat should not represent it in talks with Russia and Ukraine, but representatives from its five biggest economies instead.

Kaja Kallas has argued that “all the member states actually agreed that I am the one who is representing Europe in foreign and security policy” when they appointed her to the job of chief of the External Action Service.

“We have institutions in place so we can’t just send any person that has no institutional role like the Americans are sending,” she said this week, in a clear reference to Witkoff and Kushner. “Clearly, we should not copy the same patterns.”

articles.title: FOX News Media kicks off holiday season with seventh annual 'All-American Christmas Tree Lighting'
articles.excerpt: First lady Melania Trump expresses wish for renewed ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine and helps a group of helpers usher in the holiday sprit as they decorate a Christmas tree as part of Fox News' ...
articles.body_text:
First lady Melania Trump expresses wish for renewed ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine and helps a group of helpers usher in the holiday sprit as they decorate a Christmas tree as part of Fox News' All-American Christmas Tree Lighting.

It’s beginning to look a lot like Christmas in Midtown Manhattan after FOX News Media kicked off the holiday season with the All-American Christmas Tree Lighting Friday.

Fox News hosts Emily Compagno, Harold Ford Jr., Greg Gutfeld, Dana Perino and Jesse Watters were joined by first lady Melania Trump for the seventh annual All-American Christmas Tree Lighting during a special edition of "The Five."

The first lady helped decorate the tree before enjoying cookies and hot chocolate with the children in attendance during the festive Christmas celebration. "The Five" co-hosts reminisced on their favorite holiday memories and traditions, and the gathered children shared their Christmas wish lists.

Trump said "world peace" is at the top of her Christmas wish list this year after she successfully secured a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the city of Oleshky in late October.

FOX NEWS MEDIA CEO SUZANNE SCOTT RINGS NASDAQ CLOSING BELL AS NETWORK CELEBRATES 30TH ANNIVERSARY

First lady Melania Trump made a special appearance at Fox News Media's All-American Christmas Tree Lighting Friday. (Fox News)

"I really would like to have more ceasefire. We could do it very fast if both Ukraine and Russia are willing," the first lady told Fox News. "Maybe we will have another ceasefire before Christmas."

Trump called the Oleshky ceasefire a "big success" that rescued hundreds of civilians from violence while expressing hope that those affected will have a great Christmas.

The first lady also spoke about her "Be Best" Fostering the Future initiative, which aims to empower and support children in foster care. She shared a message about the support she hopes Americans will extend to foster children during the holiday season.

"They need support. They need warmth," Trump said. "They need, of course, also financial support because once they are 18-years-old, they are on their own. And that's where my focus is, Fostering the Future."

"We are doing a fantastic job, and we just keep going," she continued. "So, let's hope everybody has a great Christmas and actually a warm home for everybody. That's very important."

MELANIA TRUMP DETAILS HANDS-ON ROLE IN UKRAINE CEASEFIRE THAT EVACUATED NEARLY 800 CIVILIANS

Trump, who oversees the White House’s Christmas decorations, also discussed this year’s theme, "America in Bloom," revealing that the Christmas tree arrives at Pennsylvania Avenue on Monday.

The first lady, alongside Watters, Compagno and Ford Jr., handed out ornaments for children to place them on the tree while asking the kids what was on their Christmas list.

FOX News Media’s All-American Christmas Tree stands at 50 feet tall and is decorated with 18,000 ornaments and 340,000 warm white, true white and red lights. The tree features a six-foot-tall dove topper with 4,800 embedded lights, created by American Christmas, a holiday lighting and display company based in Mount Vernon, New York.

The All-American Christmas Tree Lighting, sponsored by Ace Hardware, include a live performance by Phil Wickham and a blessing by Rev. Franklin Graham and "The Chosen" actor Jonathan Roumie.

FOX News Channel's chief religion correspondent Lauren Green introduced Graham, president and CEO of Samaritan's Purse, and Roumie, who portrays Jesus in "The Chosen." The pair offered a touching blessing to the audience as part of the evening's celebration.

FOX NEWS DIGITAL WALLOPS ALL NEWS BRANDS INCLUDING BROADCAST NETWORKS IN KEY PERFORMANCE METRICS THROUGHOUT Q3

"Fox & Friends" co-host Steve Doocy served as the network’s "Christmas correspondent" for the night, while "Fox & Friends First" co-host Carley Shimkus led the network's social media coverage.

Doocy and Shimkus took viewers behind the scenes for a look inside the network's studios and exclusive interviews with special guests, along with appearances by FOX News Media talent throughout the program.

Fox News personalities Karoline Leavitt, Bill Hemmer, Jimmy Failla and Eric Shawn, among others, were also in attendance. Leavitt shared that one of the first words her six-month-old daughter ever said was "Jesus."

FOX News Media is partnering with Armed Services YMCA this holiday season to support junior enlisted service members and their families as they navigate deployments, relocations and the everyday sacrifices of military life.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

As part of the partnership, FOX employees packed stockings with holiday treats and essentials for deployed service members and wrote personalized welcome-home cards for troops returning for the holidays, sharing a message of gratitude with those who serve.

A heartwarming reunion unfolded when Army Specialist Carlos Garcia, who had been deployed for more than a year, surprised his family with an unexpected homecoming.

"I’m so happy to see him, especially for the Thanksgiving holidays. It’s really, really, really touching for me," his aunt said.

Fox News Digital’s Hanna Panreck contributed to this report.

Nora Moriarty is a Writer at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: These dead pets were meant to be cremated - then their bodies appeared on a livestream
articles.excerpt:
Revecca Calling is devastated after hearing about the bodies that were found and wants to know if her dog, Olaf, really was cremated

A man – bald, goateed, wearing red-tinted sunglasses – walks down ...
articles.body_text:
Revecca Calling is devastated after hearing about the bodies that were found and wants to know if her dog, Olaf, really was cremated

A man – bald, goateed, wearing red-tinted sunglasses – walks down a cracked back road, guiding the camera towards a cluster of plastic-wrapped objects that spill out of the tall grass.

Names are written on the packages – Brandon; Ira; Lucky; Sweet – and numbers. One says 29kg (4.5 stone). Another says 2.5kg. Through the plastic you can make out what appears to be fur, claws and a flattened ear.

It's a mass dumping, the man explains. "We have about 25 animals here that have been dumped in bags. A couple of cats, some dogs."

Warning: This story contains images some might find upsetting

In the weeks since that video was streamed on Facebook, Chris and Geraldine Taylor, who run animal rescue NGO Luna and Furry Siblings (LAFS), say they have uncovered 15 dumping sites in the suburbs of Bulacan, near the Philippines' capital of Manila.

In total they've unearthed the remains of some 170 dead pets. Belgian Malinois, golden retrievers, pugs, puppies and cats have been found dumped off service roads, sealed in septic tanks, floating in rivers and buried in vacant lots.

Many of these animals are thought to have been sent to cremation businesses in the expectation they would be turned to ash.

Now, many grieving owners are having to confront a distressing reality: their beloved pets may not have received the send-off they paid for. The urn in their home may not contain their pet at all. And they may in fact see their so-called fur child again, jettisoned like common waste on the side of a highway.

One saw the livestream and wrote on Facebook: "I think one of those pets is mine." Below, they attached a photo of a beaming Alsatian.

A string of grisly discoveries in the suburbs near Manila has put thousands of grieving pet owners on edge

When Chris arrived on that back road three weeks ago, he couldn't have known he was uncorking a scandal that would see at least one business reportedly shut, four people placed under investigation, and a personal invite to sit down with a senator to discuss animal-cruelty laws.

Chris, a former police officer, and his wife are retired, but only formally. For the past three years, they've been running an animal rescue shelter out of their home in San Jose del Monte, 30km (18.6 miles) north-east of central Manila.

On 30 October, he'd driven into town to report a case of animal neglect at the local district office. When he arrived, he was told the official in charge had just left to respond to another complaint: a report of dumped animals on a nearby roadside.

Chris had seen this once before: 14 dogs that were found and soon reburied. This time, he followed the official to the scene and started documenting – taking photos, scanning the bodies for microchips and uploading footage to his Facebook page.

"I figured there's got to be more to this," he explains. "So we put out word: if anybody knows anything, any other dump locations... just report it. Let us know."

In the days that followed, tip-offs started trickling in. More dumpsites emerged.

"The long vacant lot on the left side... that's where the smell comes from," read one message.

"When we ran to this place it smelled of rotting animals," read another, accompanied by a photo of a map with a location circled in red.

Chris Taylor, pictured here with a dog unrelated to the scandal, has uncovered the remains of some 170 dead pets in recent weeks

By crowdsourcing intel in this way, and collaborating with authorities, LAFS has so far uncovered a total of 15 dumpsites, containing an estimated 170 animals.  "Some of them were just bags of bones," Chris says. "Others were liquefied."

LAFS has meticulously documented the crime scenes. Often wearing little more for protection than an N95 mask and rubber gloves, Chris crouches in the underbrush and slices open discarded plastic bags, picking through the contents while Geraldine holds the camera.

Their Facebook videos have racked up more than 30 million views. Commenters ask Chris if he has seen their pet among the bodies, or if he can turn a carcass over so they can check for identifying marks.

Some are successful. On that first night in October, all 25 bodies were returned to their owners.

There's a question which hangs uncomfortably over every dumpsite: who would do something like this?

As more owners came forward, a common denominator emerged. Many said they'd taken the animals to be incinerated at the same place: a crematorium called Ahjay Paws in the city of Bacoor, not far from Manila.

"So I posted: anybody that's had Ahjay's services... these might be your animals," says Chris. "And man, it just flooded in."

Ahjay Paws, the company that was supposed to cremate Olaf, is under investigation

The Philippines has long been a dog-loving nation, but since the Covid-19 pandemic the "fur parenting" community has exploded.

A 2021 study found the country had the highest rate of dog ownership in the Asia-Pacific. Since then, the pet dog population has increased 4.7% year on year, according to another study, exceeding 21 million in 2025.

As the numbers soar, businesses have stepped up to address an inevitable implication: more deaths.

"Cremation here in the Philippines has become quite a big thing with the boom of the pet industry," says Anna Cabrera, director at the Philippine Animal Welfare Society (Paws). "There's even a ceremony where they hold wakes for the pets."

These events offer grieving owners a last chance to see their beloved pets before they're taken to a crematorium and transmuted into an urnful of ashes.

Pet care - including for those that have died - has become a booming industry in the Philippines

Revecca Calling, who lives south of Bulacan in the city of Cavite, says she paid Ahjay Paws 8,500 Philippine pesos (£100; $133) to cremate her dog Olaf in January. The price was calculated according to weight, and included a 30-minute viewing where she could say her final goodbye.

Calling says Ahjay Paws told her they couldn't record the cremation, as it might endanger the staff. They took away Olaf's body, and a few days later handed back a small urn that purportedly contained her cremated remains.

When nine months later Calling heard that dozens of animals' bodies had been found dumped on an empty plot of land, potentially at the behest of a pet cremation business, she was devastated.

"Pet owners entrust these services with something very important: the remains of a beloved family member," she says. "We need to know what happened."

Pets have been found dumped in bags like this - with labels giving their names and weights

Earlier this month, the Philippines' National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) filed criminal complaints against four individuals in connection with dumped pets. Among them is the owner of Ahjay Paws and two people who ran Bulacan's Pet HPHT Crematory.

According to the NBI, Ahjay Paws had initially arranged to acquire a cremation machine from Pet HPHT – but when it didn't arrive, they opted to send the pet remains to Pet HPHT instead. When the volume of those remains became more than Pet HPHT could handle, that firm paid a third party to bury them.

One interpretation is that the dumping incidents are a result of logistical failures: two businesses that bit off more than they could chew and took desperate measures to make the problem go away.

But there's another theory: that the dead pets could be evidence of a lucrative racket, with people's money taken to incinerate their pets but the animals then being dumped instead.

There is a word for this kind of deception in Philippine law – estafa; where a perpetrator knowingly misleads a victim to financially defraud them – and the NBI say they are investigating it as a possibility in this case.

Two weeks ago, Ahjay Paws' owner denied responsibility for the dumping in San Jose del Monte, according to local media. The company is apparently no longer operating, and the BBC has been unable to contact it.

The BBC has also reached out to Pet HPHT and invited it to respond. On Facebook, the firm said the dumping allegations were "completely false and have no basis".

The pet-dumping scandal, in which Olaf may have been a victim, has blown up into a national controversy

Another grieving pet owner, Emelia Legada, says she paid Ahjay Paws 10,000 Philippine pesos (£120; $160) to cremate her dog Harvey six months ago.

"I just can't accept the pain of not knowing what might have happened to him," she says. "I really want to confirm whether Harvey was properly cremated, and whether the ashes I received were truly his."

Many are wrestling with the same uncertainty. As Cabrera puts it: "God knows what that was inside those urns."

In response to those anxieties, a veterinarian in nearby Quezon City has started offering complimentary forensic ash testing. For those whose pets have been found among the bodies, other crematoriums have offered to do the job properly, and for free.

The animal welfare society, Paws, is volunteering legal services to help people file complaints with the authorities, and has received more than 150 requests so far. It is also calling for a nationwide audit of all pet cremation businesses.

On 2 November, Percival Vilar Cendaña of the Philippines' progressive Akbayan Party appeared on national television. He was there to speak about the pet-dumping scandal, which, in the span of a few days, had flared into a national disgrace.

"Our worst fears have been confirmed," he told the Bilyonaryo news channel. "Now we see that these are not isolated incidents. It is true that this is a syndicate that is conducting widespread operations."

Neither the police nor the NBI have confirmed that the dumpings were carried out by a "syndicate", nor that they were "widespread". Many details surrounding the case remain murky. But the hysteria is real – and Cendaña was giving voice to a common sentiment.

"Those who deceived these poor fur parents should be jailed," he said.

At least three individuals have surrendered to the NBI and been charged with violating the city's Code of Sanitation, the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act, and the Sanitation Code of the Philippines.

But many feel this doesn't go far enough, and say it fails to hold anyone liable for the way the animals' remains were treated.

Cabrera says the country's animal-cruelty law doesn't cover the treatment of animals after death. And "there's no crime if there's no law".

The scandal has prompted a groundswell to change that. Lawmakers like Cendaña are pushing for a national commission on animal welfare to ensure their dignity in life and death.

Meanwhile, Cabrera says Paws will seek "moral and exemplary" damages on behalf of aggrieved pet owners.

Chris Taylor dealing with items resembling clothing found at a dumpsite (blurred at source)

One woman whose dog was suspected to have been found among the dumped bodies told the BBC she couldn't speak about it because she was "feeling weak".

"I haven't slept for three days from all the crying," she said.

Chris has also been losing sleep, taking calls from grieving pet owners who have watched his videos. "Hundreds of people call me in tears, just sobbing," he says.

"They're in so much pain. And half the time you're telling them: 'you're not going to find your pet. It's been too long; we're not going to be able to identify it.' And it just crushes them."

As well as new laws, Chris wants stricter enforcement of existing rules. He wants to know how he managed to unearth so much in the space of a fortnight, and why people keep coming to him saying they don't trust the police to take their concerns seriously, he says.

The BBC contacted Philippine National Police (PNP) for comment, but didn't hear back. Earlier this month, PNP chief Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr said authorities were determined to hold accountable those who allegedly took advantage of grieving pet owners, saying such exploitation "must be addressed with the full force of the law", according to ABS-CBN.

"Fraud is not measured solely by the amount of money taken, but also by the damage inflicted on the people whose trust has been betrayed," Nartatez said.

"To the affected pet owners, we recognise the pain and distress this incident has caused your families."

Yet the police themselves have come under official scrutiny.

On Monday, the National Police Commission announced an investigation into officers in Cavite and Bulacan after they suggested LAFS might be involved in the pet dumping because they were often first on the scene. The officers did not present evidence for their claims. The investigation also covers reports that officers visited the Taylors' home and took photographs.

Meanwhile, countless grieving pet owners are suspended in purgatory: desperate for closure on what happened to their dogs and cats, and calling on authorities to do more.

"We want the case to be properly investigated and those responsible to be held accountable," says Calling.  "I believe that no secret remains hidden forever."

Legada, for her part, says: "I just want to find out what really happened to Harvey and where his remains are. I want to know whether he was properly cremated."

She also wants people to know: "You can't trust anyone these days."

articles.title: Man accused of sparking deadly Los Angeles wildfire found guilty
articles.excerpt:
Verdict in case against former Uber driver Jonathan Rinderknecht comes after first trial ended with hung jury

The 30-year-old accused of sparking the deadly Palisades fire in Los Angeles was found gu...
articles.body_text:
Verdict in case against former Uber driver Jonathan Rinderknecht comes after first trial ended with hung jury

The 30-year-old accused of sparking the deadly Palisades fire in Los Angeles was found guilty of two federal arson charges in a Friday verdict that came months after his first trial concluded with a hung jury.

For two weeks, a fresh batch of jurors listened to prosecutors mount their case against Jonathan Rinderknecht.

They argued the former Uber driver was responsible for the January 2025 wildfire, which claimed 12 lives and devastated the Pacific Palisades, an affluent enclave on the California coast.

Rinderknecht, in prosecutors’ account, used a lighter to set a brush fire in the hillside area. The state cast him as a disgruntled young man who sought retribution against the world for personal gripes, including failed romances, and perceived societal injustices like wealth inequality.

Firefighters suppressed the so-called Lachman brush fire last January, but its embers simmered underground, before being swept by powerful winds and erupting above ground into the Palisades inferno that destroyed thousands of homes and businesses.

Rinderknecht had maintained his innocence, pleading not guilty to the revised charges of destruction of property by means of fire and arson affecting property used in interstate commerce.

For the retrial, jurors were instructed explicitly to not consider the adequacy of the fire department’s response to the Lachman and Palisades blaze. The department has faced criticism for failing to fully extinguish the Lachman fire that eventually reignited.

The note came after some of the first trial’s jurors were wary of pinning the blame squarely on Rinderknecht, citing the fire department’s past actions. Of that deadlocked panel, two voted for guilty, while 10 others were not convinced.

Rinderknecht’s defense team also doubled down during the retrial on an alternative explanation for the Palisades fire, suggesting the initial brush blaze was ignited by fireworks.

Prosecutors dismissed the theory as “baseless” in a court filing where they raised concern over the reliability and late introduction of a defense witness, whose testimony would reference stains at a private residence that supposedly indicated fireworks had been discharged.

Rinderknecht will be sentenced on 17 March.

articles.title: Fiona the hippo honored by US Senate in unanimous resolution praising Cincinnati Zoo staff
articles.excerpt:
Fiona, the beloved hippo at Cincinnati Zoo, has died after swallowing a visitor's knit hat.

Fiona the hippo received a formal tribute from the U. S. Senate on Friday, one day after the beloved Cincin...
articles.body_text:
Fiona, the beloved hippo at Cincinnati Zoo, has died after swallowing a visitor's knit hat.

Fiona the hippo received a formal tribute from the U. S. Senate on Friday, one day after the beloved Cincinnati Zoo resident died following a medical emergency.

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, introduced the resolution honoring Fiona's life and legacy while expressing the chamber's gratitude to the zoo's staff for their care and dedication. The measure passed by unanimous consent.

Speaking from the Senate floor next to a photo of the hippopotamus, Moreno described Fiona's death as a "devastating loss" and a tragic accident.

BELOVED HIPPO FIONA DIES AT CINCINNATI ZOO AFTER SWALLOWING VISITOR'S HAT

Fiona, a Nile Hippopotamus, eats her specialty birthday cake to celebrate turning three-years old this Friday, in her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden, Thursday, Jan. 23, 2020, in Cincinnati. (AP Photo/John Minchillo)

"The people who come to our city, our state, that now don’t have Fiona there," Moreno said. "It’s going to leave a hole in the zoo and a hole in their heart."

The tribute came one day after the Cincinnati Zoo announced that Fiona died after ingesting a knit hat that accidentally landed in her enclosure last week. According to the zoo, a visitor tossed the hat into the air outside the exhibit, where it caught on a ceiling fan and was launched over the viewing windows into her habitat.

"The vet staff tried everything they could to help her after she ingested a hat that ended up in her habitat by accident last week," the zoo said in a Thursday statement. "Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome."

'WORST AQUARIUM EVER' REVIEW SENDS WHALING MUSEUM'S SALES SOARING 250%

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, walks into the Senate Reception Room in the U.S. Capitol on Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026. (CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Fiona, a Nile hippopotamus, rose to international fame in January 2017 after she was born six weeks premature, weighing just 29 pounds. Her survival drew millions of followers online and inspired books, clothing, beer and an ice cream flavor.

Tributes poured in across Ohio and Capitol Hill following her death, with Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., praising Fiona on X as a "beloved presence" and the Cincinnati Bengals remembering her as "The queen of the Queen City."

A representative for Moreno's office and the Cincinnati Zoo did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

Fiona, a 9-year-old Nile hippo at the Cincinnati Zoo, died Thursday after ingesting a knitted hat that accidentally landed in her habitat. (Cincinnati Zoo)

Fox News Digitals' Louis Casiano contributed to this report.

Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

The US government released an eighth tranche of records regarding Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAPs), marking the latest step in an effort to declassify government files on UFOs.

After US President Donald Trump called for UFO files to be released in an executive order earlier this year, the Pentagon has declassified hundreds of files. The first tranche was released 8 May 2026.

The footage in this video makes up three of the 43 files released in this tranche. All three clips were filmed from aboard US military platforms in the Middle East in 2020, 2023 and 2026.

articles.title: Verdict reached in Los Angeles retrial over 2025 Pacific Palisades wildfire that killed 12 people
articles.excerpt:
The ‘Outnumbered’ panel discusses new details about an alleged arsonist in the Palisades fire, including a search history tied to UnitedHealthcare CEO murder suspect Luigi Mangione.

A man accused of ...
articles.body_text:
The ‘Outnumbered’ panel discusses new details about an alleged arsonist in the Palisades fire, including a search history tied to UnitedHealthcare CEO murder suspect Luigi Mangione.

A man accused of sparking the deadly 2025 Pacific Palisades wildfire that killed 12 people and destroyed nearly 7,000 homes was found guilty on all counts Friday after a federal retrial in Los Angeles, months after his first trial ended in a mistrial.

Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, a former Uber driver with dual U.S.-French citizenship, had been charged with two federal arson counts — including destruction of property by means of fire — in U.S. District Court. He was retried on a scaled-down grand jury indictment after his initial three-week trial ended in a hung jury in June.

Ahead of the second trial, federal prosecutors dropped one of the original three charges against Rinderknecht and modified the two remaining federal arson counts, reducing his maximum possible prison sentence from 45 years to 40 years.

PALISADES FIRE SUSPECT ALLEGEDLY DRIVEN BY 'SOCIETAL REVENGE,' BEHAVIORAL ANALYST TESTIFIES IN COURT

Jonathan Rinderknecht, 29, was charged with igniting the blaze that eventually became the Palisades Fire in Los Angeles. (USAttyEssayli/X)

Prosecutors accused Rinderknecht of "maliciously" sparking a brush fire on Jan. 1, 2025 — initially dubbed the Lachman Fire — that was quickly extinguished, only to smolder underground in brush roots before strong winds fanned it into a massive inferno days later.

The blaze tore through the seaside enclave of Pacific Palisades, leveling entire neighborhoods and causing property damage estimated between $35 billion and $150 billion.

SPENCER PRATT UNITES WITH KAREN BASS' BROTHER TO SUE THE LA MAYOR OVER PALISADES FIRE DESTRUCTION

Federal prosecutors also alleged in court filings that Rinderknecht was partly inspired by Luigi Mangione, who pleaded guilty to federal charges in the December 2024 murder of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson in New York City.

According to prosecutors, Rinderknecht searched online for phrases including "free LuigiMangione," "lets take down all the billionaires" and "reddit lets kill all the billionaires" in mid-December 2024. When investigators asked Rinderknecht why someone might set a fire in the affluent Pacific Palisades, he allegedly said it would stem from resentment of the rich, adding that "we’re basically being enslaved by them" and comparing the act to the killing Mangione committed.

PALISADES FIRE SUSPECT WAS ALLEGEDLY 'FIXATED' ON LUIGI MANGIONE AND HELD 'RESENTMENT OF THE RICH': COURT DOCS

An aerial view of the fire damage caused by the Palisades Fire is shown in the Pacific Palisades, Calif., Jan. 22, 2025. (Mike Blake/Reuters)

Mangione’s attorney, Karen Friedman Agnifilo, previously told Fox News Digital in a statement that her client "does not support violent actions and does not condone past or future political violence," calling attempts to link him to unrelated crimes "irresponsible, dangerous and prejudicial."

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

An aerial view shows homes destroyed in the Palisades Fire with the Pacific Ocean in the distance on January 27, 2025 in Pacific Palisades, California. (Mario Tama)

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB

Rinderknecht pleaded not guilty and maintained his innocence, contending in a court filing earlier this year that he merely witnessed the Jan. 1 fire after hiking up a hill to watch New Year's fireworks and immediately called 911. His defense attorney, Steve Haney, argued that prosecutors lacked physical evidence tying his client to arson and contended the massive Jan. 7 blaze was set separately by someone else.

The first trial collapsed in late June after jurors deadlocked 10-2 in favor of acquittal. Following that mistrial, a woman identifying herself as Juror No. 4 told reporters there was "no proof" and said the prosecution's "holdover fire" theory didn't work for her, calling a retrial a "waste of our American dollars."

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Burned homes are reduced to skeletal outlines days after the Palisades Fire swept through the Pacific Palisades neighborhood of Los Angeles. (FOX News)

U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli vowed at the time to press forward, writing on X that the evidence was strong and prosecutors fully intended to "retry this case before a new jury and obtain guilty verdicts on all charged counts."

The Palisades blaze erupted around the same time as the deadly Eaton Canyon fire roughly 30 miles east in Altadena, which killed 19 people and was later blamed on sparks from an electrical transmission tower. Together, the two blazes rank as the deadliest wildfire disaster in Los Angeles County history.

Fox News' Adam Sabes and Reuters contributed to this report.

Greg Wehner is a reporter for Fox News Digital covering U.S. news and crime, with a focus on breaking developments, law enforcement, public safety and major stories shaping communities across the country.

articles.title: NSW passes Mount Pleasant coalmine law as Greens claim change an attempt to head off One Nation
articles.excerpt:
Labor says allowing mine to increase production reflects ‘gravity of situation facing hundreds of workers’ – but critics call it ‘unprecedented and dangerous’

Get our breaking news email, free app or...
articles.body_text:
Labor says allowing mine to increase production reflects ‘gravity of situation facing hundreds of workers’ – but critics call it ‘unprecedented and dangerous’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The New South Wales government has passed special legislation to allow a coalmine in the Hunter Valley to increase production by 32% in its final act of parliament before the March state election, in which the region will be a key battleground for One Nation.

After a marathon session in the legislative council on Friday, the Minns government and the Coalition voted at 1.36am on Saturday morning to allow the Mount Pleasant mine to increase its annual extraction rate from 12.5MT to 16.5MT until 2032.

At the start of debate, the resources minister, Courtney Houssos, told the upper house “this is a unique bill applying to unique circumstances”.

“Taking the decision to intervene in the way we have is not an easy one, but it is an important one,” she said. “And it does reflect the gravity of the situation facing hundreds of workers and their families in the Hunter.”

The legislation has drawn outcry from legal and anti-corruption experts, climate groups, crossbenchers and civil liberties organisations, after the high court ruled last month that an approval for an expansion that would increase the mine’s annual output to 21MT by 2048 was invalid.

In a 3-2 split ruling, the high court found the state’s Independent Planning Commission (IPC) failed to properly consider imposing conditions to minimise greenhouse gas emissions that would be generated by the mine when the coal is sold and burned overseas.

Despite saying he would not bypass the court’s decision, the NSW premier, Chris Minns, subsequently announced the legislation, claiming it would save 400 jobs ahead of Christmas.

On Friday, the government and Coalition used their numbers to block almost 200 amendments to the bill sought by the Greens, who called the legislation “exceptional and unprecedented and dangerous”. Animal Justice party MLC Emma Hurst also opposed the bill.

“Labor describes the circumstances as exceptional, says this case is unique, and assures the public that other companies shouldn’t expect the same treatment,” the Greens climate spokesperson, Sue Higginson, told the parliament.

“But a political assurance offers no protection against the precedent being set.”

She accused the premier of being motivated by a desire to withstand a threat from One Nation to Labor seats in the Hunter.

“It’s very clear to us why Chris Minns has gone here, and that is because we’re really on the eve of an election, and One Nation is right now his threat,” she said at a press conference on Thursday.

The Hunter region, the centre of NSW’s coalmining industry, is emerging as a key battleground at the March 2027 state election. The One Nation NSW upper house candidate and former coalminer Stuart Bonds contested the Labor-held federal seat of Hunter in 2025, winning 41% of the two-candidate preferred vote. The party’s NSW leader, Mike Newman, is running in the Labor-held lower house seat of Cessnock.

Higginson told the upper house that in bringing the bill, the government had turned its back on the advice of the state’s Net Zero Commission, which has said further coalmine expansions are incompatible with meeting legislated emissions reduction targets.

“But who seems to care any more? What does the rule of law matter when [the premier] visits the Hunter and decides he needs to do something for someone so that he can remain somewhat popular in his own mind?” she said.

The Coalition, which supported the bill, said it was “about people”.

“It’s about the hundreds of workers at MACH Energy’s Mount Pleasant mine who, since the high court handed down its decision in October, have been left wondering whether they will still have a job in the new year,” Nationals MLC Sarah Mitchell said.

She said “losing hundreds of jobs in one go would completely devastate the Hunter region”.

The legislation ties consent for the mine expansion to a jobs guarantee protecting workers at the mine. Data provided to the government by the mine for the jobs guarantee, which covers more than 720 workers, is subject to an independent audit.

At a press conference on Wednesday, Minns said the legal proceedings would return to the land and environment court for consideration, but it would be “a tragedy if, in the meantime, that community effectively shut down as a result of this decision”.

“Most of the workers from Mount Pleasant live in Muswellbrook, and if the mine closed, the unemployment rate would jump by 5% just in that small town,” he said, speaking alongside workers at the mine and the Mining and Energy Union, which has welcomed the legislation.

In a report published on Tuesday, the parliament’s legislation review committee found the Mount Pleasant bill would “effectively undermine” proceedings that were still before the land and environment court and “would undermine procedural fairness” by removing avenues for legal challenge.

That report also highlighted concerns with a so-called Henry VIII clause that the barrister and anti-corruption campaigner Geoffrey Watson warned this week posed a “serious corruption risk” to the state.

The clause, allowing the resources minister of the day to override state laws as they apply to the Mount Pleasant development, was amended by the government in the lower house. Following the amendments, it cannot be used to prevent changes from being subject to Icac investigations or to change the permitted coal production limit.

The Nature Conservation Council of NSW said the government had been “embarrassed into amending its own coalmining bill”, while the Greens said the amendments did not go far enough to constrain the power any resources minister might hold under the clause.

The Law Society of NSW said on Thursday it was concerned that without further amendments, the Henry VIII clause risked “undermining the rule of law”.

Houssos told the upper house on Friday the government had carefully considered concerns and moved amendments to the clause because it “recognises the importance of appropriate safeguards and accountability”.

articles.title: In a year of AI solving maths problems, Anthropic may have just solved the biggest
articles.excerpt:
Anthropic just went public with a major IPO this week

An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothe...
articles.body_text:
Anthropic just went public with a major IPO this week

An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.

Levent Alpöge said, external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut, that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.

If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. Alpöge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".

The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.

As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.

It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.

Named for the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.

Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.

Alpöge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.

"The precise timing is horrible," Alpöge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier."

"I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.

The complete proof that Alpöge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 lines long.

Terrance Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday, external that verification of the proof is still some way off.

"I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.

No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.

OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.

More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.

The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.

Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths, external and physics, external.

A group of maths scholars said, external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".

"We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.

A month later, OpenAI released, external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.

It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

articles.title: Fossil fuel talks deadlock pushes COP31 climate summit into overtime
articles.excerpt:
The COP31 climate summit has gone into overtime as nearly 200 countries remain deadlocked over a draft deal that no longer mentions fossil fuels.

The two-week talks in Antalya, Turkiye, were due to e...
articles.body_text:
The COP31 climate summit has gone into overtime as nearly 200 countries remain deadlocked over a draft deal that no longer mentions fossil fuels.

The two-week talks in Antalya, Turkiye, were due to end on Friday, when a late closing session approved some technical matters, but not the wider political deal.

“We are close to the finish line, but we are not there yet,” COP31 President and Turkiye’s Environment Minister Murat Kurum told delegates.

Environmental groups tracking the two-week conference said the meeting lacked ambition to address the ‌worsening climate crisis and was on track to be the “worst COP ever”.

A third draft is expected on Saturday, the AFP news agency reported.

An opening draft from cohost and lead negotiator Australia on Monday called for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels. A slimmer version on Thursday removed every mention of them after Saudi Arabia and other major oil and gas producers objected.

Oil producers have also resisted similar language at past talks, including at COP28 in 2023. The revised text also dropped a $120bn target for money to help poorer countries adapt to climate change.

The European Union said the draft “risks turning this climate COP into a fossil summit”. Panama, which signed a letter with a dozen other countries demanding “a clear transition away from fossil fuels”, threatened to walk away from the talks.

“It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover document that does not even mention fossil fuels, and we simply will not put up with it,” Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, told a news conference.

The draft proposes raising the share of the world’s final energy consumption that comes from electricity to 35 percent by 2035. It does not say the power must come from renewables, and some countries want the target to say “clean”.

Some countries also reject a push to expand carbon capture, a technology that traps emissions from power plants and factories. They say it is costly and unproven, and could let polluters keep burning oil and gas.

“We want to see the references to false solutions removed,” said Vanuatu’s climate minister, Ralph Regenvanu.

Developing countries are angry that rich nations are falling short on climate finance. “We didn’t come here to beg,” said Ghana’s environment minister, Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings.

A UN report last month found the world is set to pass the 1.5-degree-Celsius (2.7F) warming limit set under the 2015 Paris Agreement.

The United States, the largest historical emitter, is absent for a second year after President Donald Trump ended climate cooperation.

The US-Israel war on Iran and higher living costs have also drawn attention away from the talks.

Environmental groups say the summit lacks ambition.

“This has been the worst COP ever,” said Mohamed Adow, director of the think tank Power Shift Africa.

They then dive into whether the San Francisco 49ers are the best team in the NFL after defeating the Dallas Cowboys.

The New England Patriots' playoff hopes took a massive blow on Friday.

Drake Maye fractured his right fibula in the Patriots' 35-10 loss to the Detroit Lions in Germany, according to ESPN. The 24-year-old will not need surgery on the injured leg, but the injury will sideline him deep into the season and may even end it, according to the report.

The two-time Pro Bowler did not suffer any ligament damage. The bad news didn't stop there for the Patriots, as star wide receiver A.J. Brown is expected to be sidelined for multiple weeks with a hamstring injury he suffered in the team's loss in Germany, according to ESPN's report.
