articles.title: US police departments warn GTA VI users to ‘keep it in the game’
articles.excerpt:
Although there is no definitive link between violent video games and behavior, departments take to social media

While critics have been raving after the recent and long-awaited arrival of Grand Theft...
articles.body_text:
Although there is no definitive link between violent video games and behavior, departments take to social media

While critics have been raving after the recent and long-awaited arrival of Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest entry in the famously violent video game series has also prompted real-world warnings from authorities.

Police departments across the US met the game’s release on Thursday with reminders that the car thefts, reckless driving, violence and other criminal mayhem depicted in the blockbuster title should not be re-enacted on the country’s streets.

There is insufficient evidence supporting a scientific causal link between violent video games and violent behavior, according to the American Psycyhological Association. Nonetheless, several departments have taken to the internet with warnings – and even jokes – aimed at keeping GTA VI’s lawlessness firmly in the virtual world.

The Atlanta police department delivered one of the clearest messages in a social media post.

“GTA is not a real place, but Atlanta is!” the department warned. “Don’t confuse virtual entertainment with real-life decisions.”

“Drunk[en] driving, reckless driving, auto theft and violence have real consequences,” the department continued, before delivering a final warning: “Keep it in the game. Don’t bring it to our streets.”

In Texas, the Prosper police department also seized on the game’s release to remind drivers to follow traffic laws, avoid using their phones behind the wheel and respect speed limits.

“Save the reckless driving for the game,” the department wrote.

Police in San Juan, Puerto Rico, joined the growing number of departments weighing in on the GTA VI excitement, posting a warning on Instagram. “Vice City might be calling,” the agency wrote, referring to the game’s fictional setting. “But we just wanted to remind you that what happens in GTA 6, stays in GTA 6!”

Meanwhile, a frightening real-life traffic incident prompted the Hays county sheriff’s office in Texas to draw its own comparison to the video game. In an October Facebook post, the department released dashcam footage from a late-night traffic stop.

The recording showed a patrol vehicle and another car parked along the shoulder of a highway when a speeding vehicle struck the side of the police cruiser. The sheriff’s office responded with a sharply worded message referencing GTA.

“I-35 IS A HIGHWAY, NOT A GTA LOBBY,” the department said, using a term referring to a digital space where gamers playing Grand Theft Auto gather. “One of you speed demons managed to hit our patrol vehicle during a traffic stop, nearly striking the stopped vehicle and our deputy. THEN YOU FLED THE SCENE?!”

Not every police department, however, viewed the gaming frenzy as a potential source of trouble. In North Carolina, the Greensboro police department suggested that the release could actually give officers some welcome relief by keeping many members of the public occupied at home.

“GTA 6 needs to hurry up and get here so y’all can stay at home and let us catch a break,” the department joked on X. The post went viral, racking up over a million views.

California’s Newark police department took a more straightforward approach, posting what it described as “friendly reminders” for staying out of trouble in the real world. Its message encouraged fans to enjoy the game without attempting to recreate its criminal activities.

Meanwhile, the Hebron, Ohio, police department turned its attention away from real-world officers and toward the fictional police force tasked with maintaining order in Vice City. In a tongue-in-cheek social media post, the department expressed sympathy for the virtual officers facing what could be a chaotic few days.

“To whichever officer at the Vice City police department looked around this morning and said, ‘Seems pretty quiet so far’ … your co-workers would like a word,” the post read. “Thinking of you all at VCPD over the next few days.”

articles.title: French police officers sentenced for beating of music producer Michel Zecler
articles.excerpt:
The three officers were seen on video beating up music producer Michel Zecler in his studio

Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Pari...
articles.body_text:
The three officers were seen on video beating up music producer Michel Zecler in his studio

Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.

The three were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report stating that the producer - Michel Zecler, 47 - had violently resisted their attempt to arrest him.

Their lies were exposed because the whole scene at Zecler's recording studio was caught on CCTV, revealing the producer had suffered some 30 punches, kicks and baton strikes while offering little resistance at all.

Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Philippe Tondeux, 50, and Pierre Plantier, 37, all received five year sentences, with different amounts suspended.

Lapersonne had three years of his sentence suspended and Tondeux three and a half years suspended. Plantier had four years suspended, and will serve his one year with an ankle monitor.

All were told they could never serve in the police again.

The case became a cause célèbre for critics of the police, who say it exposed systematic racism among officers. With police again facing criticism for alleged use of excessive force in stopping recent protests, the verdict was hotly awaited by Zecler's supporters.

Much depended in the two-week trial on Zecler's own testimony that the officers called him a racial slur during the beating.

This was denied by the three policemen, who in court admitted the beating and the faked report but denied there was a racial motivation. But the court preferred the evidence of the producer, because - unlike the police - everything else he said was verifiably true.

Because the racist element was accepted by the court, the sentences were toughened.

The case was heard by a panel of five judges.

The incident took place during the Covid lockdown in 2020. Zecler was accused by the officers for not wearing a mask when doing so was obligatory as he approached his studio on foot.

They later claimed his behaviour aroused their suspicions, and they thought he might be carrying drugs. No evidence of this emerged.

After Zecler entered the lobby, the police followed - without a warrant - and tried to bring him outside. Zecler refused to go out, and the beating ensued. Zecler cried for help and some people appeared from the basement and pushed the police outside.

The officers then smashed a glass pane and sent a tear-gas grenade into the building, forcing those inside to come out - after which Zecler was again hit. He was then arrested.

During the trial Zecler said had it not been for the CCTV video, he would have been in court not as a victim but as a potential criminal.

In their last words before the court, all three police officers apologised for what they had done. Tondeux said he was sorry "for the image of the police that I have given".

articles.title: French police officers found guilty of racist assault on black music producer
articles.excerpt:
Beating of Michel Zecler in 2020 sparked outrage over police brutality after it was caught on security cameras

Three French police officers who beat a black music producer they said was not wearing a...
articles.body_text:
Beating of Michel Zecler in 2020 sparked outrage over police brutality after it was caught on security cameras

Three French police officers who beat a black music producer they said was not wearing a face mask during the Covid pandemic have been found guilty of intentional, racist violence.

The brutal assault on Michel Zecler, now 47, was caught on security cameras in his building in 2020 and triggered outrage in France over police brutality. The trial this month was considered a turning point for the recognition of racist violence.

The officers were sentenced to between one and two years in prison, with additional years suspended. They were banned for life from serving in the police.

The officers had stopped Zecler outside his Paris music studio on 21 November 2020, accusing him of failing to wear a mandatory face mask. They pushed him into the entrance of his office and violently beat him in an assault recorded by his studio’s security cameras.

Zecler sustained about 30 punches and truncheon blows to the face and body over a five-minute period, according to the investigation. He was left with craniofacial trauma, a wound to the lip and scalp, and a complete rupture of his biceps tendon, leaving him unable to work for 45 days.

Zecler told the court the officers used a racist slur against him on several occasions during the beating. He said the attack had “completely devastated him” and had left a lasting physical and psychological impact.

The three officers, Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Pierre Plantier, 37, and Philippe Tondeux, 50, were found guilty of breaking into Zecler’s studio and committing intentional violence in a group. The judges decided racism was an aggravating factor in the attack.

The officers were also found guilty of forgery after they tried to cover up their actions by falsifying an official police report saying Zecler had been violent towards them. The police used that report to accuse Zecler of attacking them and trying to grab one of their weapons, but the video footage did not back up the claims, showing he was not violent.

The state prosecutor said that without the CCTV footage, the false police report on Zecler could have resulted in him being convicted of attacking a police officer in what would have been a serious miscarriage of justice.

The state prosecutor, who asked not to be named in the media, told the court the case had caused “immense harm to Michel Zecler but also to society as a whole”.

She said the officers had “betrayed” their uniform. She told the judges: “I ask you to believe Michel Zecler, to recognise him as a victim of these racist insults.”

The three police officers, who had not realised their attack was being recorded on security cameras, had apologised in court for beating Zecler, but denied racism.

Zecler’s lawyers and supporters said the trial had shone a spotlight on police violence in France, which victims and researchers say is systemic but authorities and law enforcement unions say is limited to isolated cases. Many members of the public who had come to support Zecler and watch the trial said it was an important moment in confronting institutionalised racism.

One of Zecler’s lawyers, Serge Money, said while summing up the case: “A verdict can force a society to really look at an injustice that up until now had been tolerated, minimised, and I dare to use the word: institutionalised.”

He said: “The Zecler trial is the trial of impunity, for all those who before him and after him will experience the same thing.”

Money told the court: “I want you to give voice to all those who didn’t have security cameras, and to all those who were not believed.”

Nine young performers who had been rehearsing in the basement at Zecler’s studio had been violently arrested when they came to assist Zecler.

Their lawyer, Seydi Ba, told the court that France needed to know how “police violence, lies and racism” would be considered by a court.

articles.title: US lawmakers push for tougher AI chip rules amid China export crackdown
articles.excerpt:
United States lawmakers say more regulations are needed to protect advanced AI chips once they leave the country, even as they support the recently imposed chip export controls.

This week, the US Dep...
articles.body_text:
United States lawmakers say more regulations are needed to protect advanced AI chips once they leave the country, even as they support the recently imposed chip export controls.

This week, the US Department of Commerce announced a new rule to restrict how advanced US AI chips can be accessed remotely in the wake of the previous Nvidia CEO’s affair with a suspected spy for Beijing. The move would close what officials described as a loophole that allows Chinese companies to tap into computing power through data centres in third countries, bypassing US restrictions.

The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), which sits under the Commerce Department, said the rule would require data centre customers in Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Brazil to apply for a special licence to buy advanced chips from US companies, including Nvidia, because they “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion”.

“The export controls should have been in place, certainly,” Democratic Representative Pramila Jayapal told Al Jazeera. “I also think it’s a bigger conversation about who dominates the AI market. We should not have this consolidation of all the AI knowledge in a couple of companies because that poses an enormous threat on multiple levels, including national security.”

In October, Jayapal introduced a policy framework that would require every AI company operating in the US to obtain a federal charter in an effort to protect the public interest.

The AI charter, the framework says, is modelled after existing regulatory frameworks, combining the round-the-clock federal oversight, strict safety mandates, and structural separation built into national bank charters with the rigorous pre-release federal testing required for nuclear materials and dangerous weapons.

The framework also bans AI companies from building empires, releasing risky models, stealing through surveillance, exploiting workers, or causing harm.

Jayapal is a member of the House of Representatives Judiciary Committee, whose ranking members announced a probe to determine whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had blocked efforts to stop the suspected smuggling of advanced Nvidia chips to China.

Lutnick is facing criticism, including from members of US President Donald Trump’s cabinet, for allegedly refusing to impose restrictions on companies accused of diverting advanced chips to China, including Megaspeed, which is at the centre of the Nvidia probe.

The House Foreign Affairs Committee also announced that the Trump administration had approved exports of 879,000 chips manufactured by Nvidia and AMD to Chinese companies between December 2025 and May 2026.

Democrats, who will control both chambers of Congress in January, expressed a desire to better limit chip exports amid growing scrutiny over the extent to which US computing power may have reached China.

“I’m excited to get these gavels and go through the investigatory work that’s necessary, but also to rein in and regulate artificial intelligence. The very industry is asking to be regulated by Congress,” Democratic Representative Everton Blair told Al Jazeera.

The US accounts for nearly 75 percent of the world’s AI spending and computing power, followed by China.

US tech giants, including Amazon, Microsoft and Google, operate nearly 90 major AI computing hubs globally, according to an Oxford University study. The same research found that US companies were building 63 AI computing hubs outside the country as of 2025.

Stephen Ezell, vice president for global innovation policy at the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation (ITIF), said Washington would find it difficult to enforce the BIS rule.

China has rejected the restriction, calling it “economic coercion” by the US.

On Friday, after his return to the White House from his historic trilateral meeting with the Chinese and Russian presidents in Shenzhen, China, Trump promised to prohibit US companies from developing data centres in other countries.

“We’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it,” Trump said.

It was unclear what Trump had envisioned, or how he would enforce it.

At the same time, he urged Americans to embrace data centres in their neighbourhoods, despite communities’ increasing concern about the centres’ impact on quality of life, environment and energy demands.

Analysts say the recent export regulation has likely not had much effect on China’s efforts to become the global leader in AI semiconductor chips.

“China does not want to depend upon American or other foreign semiconductors. They want to develop them themselves, and one can argue that we’ve slowed them down a little bit with our export controls, but in no way has it changed China’s aspirations to become the global AI semiconductor chip leader,” Ezell said on Al Jazeera’s This Is America.

articles.title: Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to assassinate US-Ukrainian rapper
articles.excerpt:
Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "initiated" the attempt.

Denmark's security and intell...
articles.body_text:
Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "initiated" the attempt.

Denmark's security and intelligence agency said it had stopped individuals who were intending to kill the person, named by Danish media as rapper Kyivstoner, at a concert in September. Two people were charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service, and pleaded not guilty.

Denmark's foreign minister said Russia's defence attaché will now be expelled.

Russia's Embassy in Denmark called the allegations "unsubstantiated" and said Copenhagen failed to provide evidence of Moscow's involvement.

In a statement posted on social media, the embassy claimed a "Danish model" had emerged, which it described as a "Russian trace" allegedly being discovered and "exploited for a propaganda spectacle". It accused Denmark of "provocations" intending to "frighten the Danish population in order to justify... a prolonged confrontation with Russia".

Russian state media cites the foreign ministry in Moscow as saying it will respond to the expulsion of its official "accordingly".

Danish media named the target of the assassination attempt as the rapper known as Kyivstoner, whose real name is Albert Vasiliev.

Denmark's security and intelligence agency (PET) said the individuals who allegedly tried to assassinate him were associated with a banned Danish gang named Loyal to Familia. The group is "known for extensive, serious and violent criminal activity", according to the agency.

PET, which worked with police on the case, said three individuals were stopped while travelling by car near the music venue where Kyivstoner was set to perform on 25 September.

Firearms and knives were found in the vehicle, PET said.

Since then, two people linked to the case have been charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service.

Both individuals pleaded not guilty to the charges, local media reported.

In July, Russia's FSB security service accused Vasiliev and the Ukrainian authorities of organising a "terrorist attack" on military facilities and personnel in Russia. The rapper denied this allegation on social media.

In a statement on Friday, Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said the alleged assassination attempt was Russian "intimidation" and an attempt to make Denmark "waver" in its support for Ukraine.

Russia's defence attaché must leave the country within seven days, Rasmussen said.

He also said Denmark wants the EU to restrict the ability of Russians to travel throughout Europe, saying even though Denmark is already very reluctant to issue visas, Russians can still get a Schenegen visa in another country and travel to Denmark. Denmark wants these visas to apply only in the country that has issued them, he added.

articles.title: Knicks star Jalen Brunson reveals how he really feels about 'King of New York' nickname
articles.excerpt: If you want to know where Jalen Brunson's mindset is after leading the New York Knicks to its first NBA title in 53 years last season, just listen to what he has to say about being called "King of New...
articles.body_text:
If you want to know where Jalen Brunson's mindset is after leading the New York Knicks to its first NBA title in 53 years last season, just listen to what he has to say about being called "King of New York" after the Finals.

When you help lead the New York Knicks to its first NBA title in 53 years, in a city that hasn’t seen a "Big Four" team win their championship since the New York Giants in 2011, you get called the "King of New York."

After all, ask anyone around the five boroughs and they’ll tell you: New York City is a basketball town when the Knicks are on top.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Jalen Brunson, the NBA Finals MVP and Knicks superstar point guard, has been hearing "King of New York" thrown around from friends and fans alike since the victory over the San Antonio Spurs this past summer. It’s a moniker synonymous with greatness in a city that begs for it with all its teams and superstar athletes.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Jalen Brunson is seen at the New York Knicks ticker-tape parade along the Canyon of Heroes in New York City on June 18, 2026. (NDZ/Star Max/GC Images)

To hear it means you’ve accomplished greatness in a city that demands it each season, or else the year is a failure. There’s pressure enough to play in the "World’s Greatest Arena" in Madison Square Garden as the face of the Knicks, but how does Brunson handle being called "King of New York?"

His answer tells you exactly where his mindset is this season, and the many to come.

"To be honest with you, I don’t want to say it’s annoying. It’s more of like when people say that, it’s cool to hear," he told OutKick in a recent interview, while highlighting his partnership with Lowe’s ahead of their big Black Friday activation. "A lot of people who I know, know I don’t like it. So, they’ll just say it to annoy me."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Brunson doesn’t have to explain why he doesn’t like it. The Villanova product has always gone about his business, staying humble and never being boisterous, though he has every reason to be considering what he’s accomplished alongside his Knicks teammates.

Yes, he’s won a championship, perhaps the one title that meant more than the rest in this great city. But his answer says many things, including one isn’t enough.

However, to be called "King of New York" — the same nickname Babe Ruth, Mickey Mantle, Lawrence Taylor, Mark Messier, Eli Manning, Derek Jeter and many others have worn over the years — is something Brunson appreciates.

Even if he doesn’t feel that way himself.

"The one thing that I’ll always think about is when you’re working to achieve something, like a goal to win a championship, you’d be surprised of all the little things that come with it," he explained. "The things that are cool, the things that are not. The pros and cons to it.'

"So, just to be thrown in that conversation with a lot of New York athlete greats, I mean, it’s a real honor. It’s something I don’t take lightly. I would never proclaim myself that."

KNICKS STAR JALEN BRUNSON IS A MAN OF THE PEOPLE, REVEALS THE ONE THING HE CAN'T LIVE WITHOUT

He may not call himself "King of New York," but that’s not going to stop the scores of Knicks fans who can’t help themselves if they see him outside The Garden.

He’s earned it, but in Brunson’s mind, there’s more to be accomplished, including defending that title this season.

Jalen Brunson celebrates with the Larry O'Brien Championship Trophy during the New York Knicks championship ticker-tape parade and victory rally in New York City. (Angelina Katsanis/Getty Images)

Brunson will be in the midst of his back-to-back title pursuit with the Knicks on Black Friday, but as Lowe’s "Bucket Expert," he’s also spreading the word about the company’s exciting deals including a customer-favorite "Black Friday Mystery Bucket."

On Nov. 27, the first 150 MyLowe’s Rewards members at participating Lowe’s stores will receive exclusive giveaways, and additionally, more than $15 million in prizes will be available for four lucky MyLowe’s Rewards members at every store.

The first 50 members at each store will receive a free Lowe’s Black Friday Mystery Bucket packed with 10-plus products and offers, and four members of the first 50 will win one of the day’s top prizes: A free appliance under $2,000, an EGO Outdoor power tool, a Blackstone grilling package or a CRAFTSMANtools package.

With deals abundant, Brunson is excited to be involved.

"It’s a really cool thing to be a part of. I’m just honored to be associated with Lowe’s and this deal. Happy to be a part of it," he said.

Jalen Brunson of the New York Knicks looks on during a game against the Toronto Raptors on Nov. 17, 2026, at Scotiabank Arena in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. (NBAE via Getty Images)

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Brunson added, "You’re doing yourself a disservice," if you intend on hitting Lowe’s on Black Friday and not signing up for MyLowe’s Rewards, as those who are not members can sign up for free ahead of Nov. 27.

After those first 50, the next 100 members will receive an exclusive Lowe’s Golden Mini Bucket, plus $5 in MyLowe’s Money, 20% off a purchase the following weekend, a free paint sample and a HomeCare+ offer.

Scott Thompson is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Trump threatens ‘tremendous penalties’ on US tech firms that build datacenters abroad
articles.excerpt:
President gives wide-ranging White House press conference and says he has ‘fantastic relationships’ with Putin and Xi

Donald Trump threatened on Friday to impose “tremendous penalties” on American te...
articles.body_text:
President gives wide-ranging White House press conference and says he has ‘fantastic relationships’ with Putin and Xi

Donald Trump threatened on Friday to impose “tremendous penalties” on American tech companies that build datacenters outside the US, though he gave no details and told reporters he had not yet informed his own officials about the plan.

In a discursive press conference from the White House briefing room, Trump also said he would “look into” the report that Iran had been planning to possibly detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington DC, and backed JD Vance over comments the vice-president made blaming Republican midterm losses on the Iran war.

Trump also expounded on his friendship with the Russian president Vladimir Putin, whom he met alongside China’s Xi Jinping at the Apec summit on Thursday, adding he had “fantastic relationships” with both autocratic leaders.

At the White House, Trump told reporters he wanted datacenters built by US companies to stay on US soil.

“We’re not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try to do it,” he said.

He said Americans should welcome datacenters, and urged communities to extract concessions from developers, repeating a point he made before the midterms.

“You ought to take advantage of the datacenters. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off,” he said.

With many Americans turning against the datacenters being built near their homes, the US tech industry is making a show of conciliation by promising to take fewer government handouts, to be more transparent, and to give more money to towns and cities willing to allow server warehouses to be built.

The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced US computing chips and servers, in a move it said was designed to limit China’s ability to use US chips to train its artificial intelligence models – though a House committee said on Wednesday the US had signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months.

China’s ability to obtain advanced AI chips made by the US firm Nvidia, in which Trump is an investor, has been spotlighted in recent weeks after its CEO, Jensen Huang, was fired over his affair with a woman alleged to be spying for China.

In the same press conference, Trump was asked about reports Iran was planning to potentially detonate an explosive laced with nuclear material – a so-called “dirty bomb” – in Washington DC. The president called it a “rumour” and said: “If they do, we’re going to fight.”

He added: “We know a lot about what’s happening in Iran. We know everything they say. We know who they are, where they are. We’ll find out about it.”

Responding to a question about reports of a rift with Vance, Trump said the vice-president’s remark blaming the Republican collapse on the Iran war was “a very accurate statement”.

“I didn’t say I was unhappy with it,” the president said. “I would have added one other thing if it were asked … would you do it again? And absolutely, the answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”

Trump was asked whether Vladimir Putin could really be considered a friend to America since Russia is a close ally of Iran.

“I can’t speak to America,” he said, adding: “I consider [that] I have fantastic relationships with Putin. That’s a very good thing. I have fantastic relationships with President Xi. That’s a good thing, and our country is safe because of that.”

He praised Putin as he repeated his grievances over the Department of Justice’s investigation into the Russian attempts to influence US voters ahead of the 2016 presidential election.

“I’ve been dealing with Putin … [since] the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax,” he said.

Trump also spoke about two prominent Democrats. He said Gina Hinojosa, who won the race for Texas governor over Trump’s Republican ally Greg Abbott, called him. “She was really nice,” Trump said. “It was a very productive call. And she wants to have a strong border, and I think we’ll be able to work something out.”

And he said Hakeem Jeffries – who Trump previously called a “thug” but is now in line to be the next speaker of the House, and the first Black speaker – is “a smart guy. He’s a streetwise guy.”

articles.title: Russian missiles and drone hit Poland during attacks on Ukraine
articles.excerpt:
Polish PM calls strikes, which took place amid western military exercises, ‘an intentional provocation’ by Moscow

Two Russian cruise missiles and a jet-powered drone crashed in Poland, according to o...
articles.body_text:
Polish PM calls strikes, which took place amid western military exercises, ‘an intentional provocation’ by Moscow

Two Russian cruise missiles and a jet-powered drone crashed in Poland, according to officials, during Russian air attacks on Ukraine that took place amid major western military exercises by allied countries.

Poland accused Moscow of “provocation” after the strikes in the south-east area of the Nato country.

Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said it was “one of the largest attacks” since the full-scale Russian invasion in 2022, with at least eight people killed and nearly 30 injured in Ukraine.

“The Russians spread this attack across many cities and regions of Ukraine. Absolutely all the targets were ordinary civilian infrastructure – things that literally sustain people’s lives,” he said.

Zelenskyy said Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, went ahead with the strike after “weak meetings” with the US president, Donald Trump, and China’s Xi Jinping, and his “failure to attempt to somehow redraw the world”.

The Ukrainian president added: “Russia is trying to compensate for its military and diplomatic impotence with precisely this kind of terror.”

Poland’s defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, confirmed three violations of Polish airspace, with no injuries reported.

He said he believed it was “not accidental” that the incident took place on the same day as major western military exercises involving troops from 11 countries in the “coalition of the willing”, including the UK.

The incidents were reported in Nowy Lipowiec, Mołodycz and Rudnik nad Sanem in south-eastern Poland, between 30 miles (50km) and 60 miles from Nowa Dęba, where the exercises are taking place.

Poland’s prime minister called the incident “an intentional provocation” by Russia.

Donald Tusk said he had spoken with Nato’s secretary general, Mark Rutte – who will visit Warsaw on Saturday – who agreed with him that “it does not seem to be a coincidence” that the attack took place on the night before the drills.

“It clearly shows … that coming months … will certainly pose great challenges for all of us,” he said.

“Today’s incident shows clearer than ever before why Poland must participate in decisions on Ukraine’s future,” he added, arguing that Warsaw has a “better understanding” of the threat posed by Russia.

Rutte said on X: “Spoke with @donaldtusk about the grave violations of Polish airspace overnight. NATO jets were scrambled in response. We stand in solidarity with Poland and will continue to strengthen our ability to deter and defend.

“This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine. I condemn Russia’s attacks as well as its ongoing war. We continue to stand united as Allies and will continue to support Ukraine.”

​The UK defence secretary, Wes Streeting, who is in Poland for the exercises, described the incursion as “very serious” in a post on X, adding: “The impact of Russia’s illegal war is being felt across Ukraine and increasingly in neighbouring countries. The UK stands in solidarity with our allies.”

Maj Gen Ireneusz Nowak, commander of the operational command of the Polish armed forces, said as many as 11 objects had been identified as posing a danger to Polish airspace.

He also highlighted the unprecedented scale of the overnight attack on Ukraine, saying Russia used seven bombers and fired 26 Kalibr cruise missiles, 72 Kh-101 cruise missiles and more than 500 drones.

Air traffic control at Rzeszów-Jasionka airport – an international passenger hub and major transit point for military aid to Ukraine – was briefly evacuated overnight, for the first time since the start of the full-scale war in Ukraine.

After the incidents, Tusk summoned army and security service chiefs to an emergency meeting to discuss the situation.

Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, said the latest violations “demonstrate the threats posed by Russian aggression to the whole of Europe and the transatlantic community”.

He added: “While Moscow tries to initiate discussions about the ‘new security architecture of Europe’, Russian missiles and drones directly undermine the existing security order in Europe. The first step toward strengthening it would probably be to cease such attacks.”

Polish authorities repeatedly warned in recent months against potential security incidents as they feared an escalation in Russia’s war against Ukraine.

In July, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile fell in Poland’s Lublin region after veering off course during a nightly Russian attack on Ukraine.

In September last year, more than 20 Russian drones crossed into Polish airspace, with Tusk warning that the country was “closer to military conflict than at any time since the second world war”.

In November 2022, a Russian missile Kh-55 crashed near Bydgoszcz, more than 300 miles from Ukraine’s territory, but was only discovered in early 2023.

articles.title: What we know about the latest Russian missile strikes on Ukraine
articles.excerpt:
Russia targeted bridges in Kyiv and railway stations overnight in a major attack launched days after Ukraine badly damaged the strategically important Crimean Bridge.

Ballistic missiles hit key cross...
articles.body_text:
Russia targeted bridges in Kyiv and railway stations overnight in a major attack launched days after Ukraine badly damaged the strategically important Crimean Bridge.

Ballistic missiles hit key crossings in the capital during a nationwide assault which Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said was "one of the most massive strikes" of the war so far and left at least nine dead.

Russian President Vladimir Putin had threatened to retaliate for the attack on the Crimean Bridge, which the Kremlin built to link Russia and the occupied peninsula.

The latest Russian strikes coincided with a flurry of talks around the war, and came as the Kremlin pushed back against a US claim that Russia could be open to Western-backed security guarantees for Ukraine.

The BBC's Sarah Rainsford is in Kyiv after the night of strikes.

articles.title: Putin launches Ukraine barrage hours after Trump meeting amid alleged Russian missile breach of NATO airspace
articles.excerpt:
Video from Lviv, Ukraine, captures the aftermath of Russian strikes hours after Putin met with Trump and Xi in China. (Video: East2West.)

Just hours after Russian President Vladimir Putin stood along...
articles.body_text:
Video from Lviv, Ukraine, captures the aftermath of Russian strikes hours after Putin met with Trump and Xi in China. (Video: East2West.)

Just hours after Russian President Vladimir Putin stood alongside President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at a historic summit in China, Moscow unleashed one of its largest attacks on Ukraine, killing at least eight people, striking three major bridges in Kyiv and sending suspected Russian missiles and a drone into NATO-member Poland.

The massive overnight assault Friday came as the Trump administration announced progress toward expanding peace negotiations with Russia, exposing the stark contrast between the diplomatic optimism emerging from Thursday's meetings and the escalating war on the ground.

A European intelligence source told Fox News Digital that Putin is preparing an intensified winter military campaign and believes that a combination of sustained battlefield pressure and U.S.-led diplomatic negotiations could eventually force Ukraine to surrender additional territory.

TRUMP'S HISTORIC SUMMIT WITH XI, PUTIN MARKS DIPLOMATIC MILESTONE, BUT BREAKTHROUGHS REMAIN ELUSIVE

Smoke rises in the city during a Russian missile strike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Kyiv, Ukraine, Nov. 20, 2026. (Gleb Garanich/Reuters)

The source described the photograph of Putin standing alongside Trump and Xi as a long-sought diplomatic achievement for the Russian leader, even as Moscow prepares to increase pressure on Kyiv.

According to the source, Russia's calculation is that Ukraine could be compelled to accept territorial concessions by spring, particularly in the country's east.

"They are very convinced that by spring Ukrainians will give up," the source told Fox News Digital, describing what the source assessed to be Moscow's strategy.

The source also warned that Russian military pressure is increasing despite Ukraine's recent successful strikes against critical Russian infrastructure. "It's going to be a very difficult winter for Ukrainians," the source said.

Retired Gen. Philip Breedlove, former NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe, told Fox News Digital that the timing of Russia's latest assault should leave little doubt about Putin's intentions, arguing that the Russian leader has repeatedly responded to President Donald Trump's diplomatic overtures with renewed attacks on Ukraine.

"Putin never has been a partner for peace in Ukraine," he said. "And Putin will never be a partner for peace in the future for Ukraine." Breedlove said that Putin's objective is to subjugate Ukraine, install a leadership loyal to Moscow and exploit the country's resources.

RUSSIA PLOTTING 'MASSIVE STRIKE' DURING MIDTERMS, ZELENSKYY WARNS, URGES US TO STOP PUTIN

Chinese President Xi Jinping, U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin greet each other before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting at the Shenzhen International Communication Center on November 18, 2026, in Shenzhen, China. (Photo by Iori Sagisawa-China Pool/Getty Images)

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia fired more than 400 drones and over 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic missiles, targeting the country's energy, transportation and logistical infrastructure.

The barrage killed six people in Kyiv and two in the western city of Lviv, while more than two dozen others were wounded, according to a Reuters' Nov. 20 report.

Three major bridges spanning the Dnipro River in Kyiv — the Podilsko-Voskresenskyi, Darnytskyi and Pivdennyi bridges — were struck, disrupting transportation between the eastern and western sections of the capital.

Russian attacks also damaged railway infrastructure and energy facilities, triggering emergency power outages as temperatures drop ahead of winter.

In Lviv, two people were killed in a strike on the Sknyliv railway station, while additional injuries were reported following attacks on residential buildings and a hospital in other Ukrainian regions.

UKRAINE'S ZELENSKYY ON DEFYING US IN ATTACKING RUSSIAN OIL: 'OUR RESPONSE MUST BE PAINFUL'

Overnight, Russia launched its largest aerial assault on Ukraine since the war started as fires burned in Kyiv on May 25, 2025. (Reuters/Gleb Garanich)

Zelenskyy accused Moscow of using the attacks to compensate for what he described as military and diplomatic setbacks.

"This was one of the largest attacks," Zelenskyy said in a statement published on Telegram Friday.

Russia's Defense Ministry confirmed carrying out a massive operation, saying it targeted facilities connected to Ukraine's military-industrial complex, including missile and drone production sites and transportation infrastructure.

The competing claims about the targets and the extent of the damage could not be independently verified.

People are seen on top of the Kerch Bridge surveying damage following an explosion on June 3, 2025. (APTN/Ukrainian Security Service)

The strikes followed Putin's warning Thursday that Russia would retaliate against Ukraine for repeated attacks on the Kerch Bridge, which connects Russia with the occupied Crimean Peninsula.

Ukrainian forces launched three attacks on the strategic crossing in four days, damaging its road section and disrupting rail traffic.

The bridge, inaugurated by Putin in 2018, serves as both a transportation route and a powerful symbol of Moscow's control over Crimea, which Russia annexed in 2014.

UKRAINE STRIKES 'ONE OF THE LARGEST OIL REFINERIES' IN SOUTHERN RUSSIA AHEAD OF PUTIN-TRUMP MEETING IN CHINA

A Polish army soldier carries an AS3 Surveyor interceptor drone, part of the U.S. "MEROPS" counter-drone system, during a live-fire demonstration at the Deba training grounds in Poland on Nov. 18, 2025. (tur Widak/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

The overnight assault also raised concerns beyond Ukraine's borders after Polish officials reported three separate incursions into the country's airspace.

Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said one of the objects was identified as a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile, while another was believed to be a missile and the third likely a jet-powered drone.

Authorities were investigating debris near Nowy Lipowiec, Mołodycz and Rudnik nad Sanem in southeastern Poland.

"There has been a violation of Polish airspace and an incursion by objects from the Russian Federation," Kosiniak-Kamysz said, according to Reuters.

Poland said it would seek additional NATO assistance to secure the alliance's eastern flank.

Breedlove warned that the reported incursions into Polish airspace were part of a broader pattern of Russia testing NATO's resolve. "Mr. Putin will push further and further when there is no cost to him, when NATO doesn't respond, when the United States doesn't respond, in his mind, there is no reason to stop. He will continue," Breedlove told Fox News Digital.

UKRAINE RELEASES VIDEO SHOWING DAMAGE TO PUTIN'S PRIZED BRIDGE FOLLOWING 'UNPRECEDENTED OPERATION' IN CRIMEA

An explosion is seen on June 3, 2025, along the Kerch Bridge linking Russia and Crimea. (APTN/Ukrainian Security Service)

The attacks came less than a day after the Trump administration announced what it described as progress toward a broader diplomatic framework involving Russia, Ukraine and European governments.

During talks in Berlin Thursday, U.S. envoy Jared Kushner said Moscow had agreed to engage in an expanded negotiating format that would include European representatives.

"Russia has agreed to engage in the multilateral format with the Europeans," Kushner said, according to Fox News Digital's Nov. 19 report.

Zelenskyy urged Washington to organize the next round of discussions quickly, insisting that European governments must play a full role in negotiations affecting the continent's security.

In this pool photograph distributed by Russian state-owned Sputnik agency, President Vladimir Putin chairs a meeting with Russian government members at the Novo-Ogaryovo residence on August 7, 2024. (SERGEI BOBYLYOV/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

But Moscow's position remained less clear Friday, with Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov saying an invitation for European officials to visit Moscow did not mean they had been accepted into the existing U.S.-brokered negotiating format, according to The Associated Press.

The European intelligence source suggested Russia believes the diplomatic process itself could strengthen its negotiating position by allowing Moscow to broaden discussions beyond Ukrainian territory to the future security arrangements of Europe.

According to the source, Moscow is seeking to gain time, maintain military pressure and increasingly focus negotiations on wider European security questions.

The source also described Russian efforts to maintain troop numbers without announcing another large-scale nationwide mobilization.

"They have been able to avoid open mobilization, but they have hidden mobilization," the source said.

According to the source, Russian recruitment efforts include targeting people facing financial difficulties, debt or other social vulnerabilities, alongside continued recruitment from prisons.

RUSSIA'S PUTIN VOWS A RESPONSE 'FAR MORE PAINFUL' AFTER UKRAINE ATTACKS PRIZED BRIDGE IN CRIMEA

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Ukrainian Prime Minister Yulia Svyrydenko visit the Dormition Cathedral of the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra, which was hit during Russian missile and drone strikes, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Kyiv, Ukraine June 15, 2026. (Ukrainian Presidential Press Service/Handout via REUTERS)

The source argued that Moscow is prioritizing manpower over the quality and training of new recruits.

"More quantity, less quality," the source said, warning that inadequately prepared recruits face a greater risk of being killed on the battlefield.

Those recruitment claims have not been independently verified by Fox News Digital.

The source's broader assessment was that Russia believes it can sustain military operations long enough to increase pressure on Ukraine's leadership to accept territorial concessions.

For Kyiv, the latest barrage demonstrated the immediate challenge facing U.S.-led peace efforts: negotiations are advancing while Moscow continues large-scale military operations and Ukraine strikes strategic targets deep inside Russian-held territory.

President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin attend a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa on November 19, 2026, in Shenzhen, China. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

The events also highlighted the growing risks for NATO as the consequences of Russia's war extend beyond Ukraine's borders.

Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this report.

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict, global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

articles.title: German attack drones pass live-fire tests, with first deliveries planned this year
articles.excerpt: GLASGOW, Scotland — Two German one-way attack drone variants passed live-fire trials this month, clearing a step toward initial deliveries and troop training before the end of the year, Germany’s mili...
articles.body_text:
GLASGOW, Scotland — Two German one-way attack drone variants passed live-fire trials this month, clearing a step toward initial deliveries and troop training before the end of the year, Germany’s military procurement office said.

Though the systems have yet to complete qualification, the German Army plans to begin equipping its armored brigade in Lithuania in 2027.

The trials, held the week of Nov. 9, tested whether Stark’s Virtus and Helsing’s HX-2 could reliably hit designated targets and whether their warheads worked as intended on impact. The Bundeswehr conducted key parts of the testing at its weapons and ammunition test center in Meppen. The procurement office announced that both systems passed but did not disclose how many shots it fired or the weapons’ success rates.

Photos attached to the statement showed both an OWE-V Virtus and an HX-2 loitering munition moments before impact into a tank.

Both systems are loitering munitions, weapons that can remain airborne over an area while searching for targets before a human operator decides whether to authorize a strike. The live-fire campaign focused on the final part of that process, from the approach to the target through the effect of the warhead, rather than certifying the systems for service.

The military noted that before loitering munitions can be used within the German Armed Forces, they must be thoroughly tested on the “interaction of the various system components.”

German lawmakers were previously skeptical of approving armed drones for the country’s military, and some arms control researchers have raised concerns about autonomous targeting in loitering munitions.

The tests follow a Feb. 25 vote by Germany’s parliamentary budget committee approving contracts worth €268 million ($294.4 million) apiece for Stark and Helsing. Options could add €1 billion to each deal, but further purchases depend on the systems proving technologically mature and lawmakers approving the spending, Defense News reported in February. The vote marked a shift that’s part of a larger rethinking of Germany’s military posture in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Germany is trying to shorten the time between signing a contract and getting the weapons to troops by allowing concurrent development, testing, qualification and preparations for use. The procurement office said it brought soldiers into testing early so their feedback could inform changes to the systems. Lawmakers attached reporting requirements to the spending plan, and cancellation clauses allow the government to walk away if a system fails qualification.

The procurement office said it expects initial deliveries this year so troops can begin training. It did not say how many weapons would arrive in that first batch. The army intends eventually to link the munitions with its reconnaissance and strike systems, with the 45th Armored Brigade in Lithuania slated to become the first major formation to receive them starting in 2027.

Linus Höller is Defense News’ Europe correspondent and OSINT investigator. He reports on the arms deals, sanctions, and geopolitics shaping Europe and the world. He holds master’s degrees in WMD nonproliferation, terrorism studies, and international relations, and works in four languages: English, German, Russian, and Spanish.

articles.title: Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk
articles.excerpt:
Watch: CCTV shows explosion after Poland says airspace violated by Russian missile

Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime ...
articles.body_text:
Watch: CCTV shows explosion after Poland says airspace violated by Russian missile

Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.

Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.

Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.

Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.

The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".

The moment of impact was caught by a camera on a farm, and officials later made clear there was no risk to residents.

Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near Mołodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.

He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.

Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," said Rutte, who was due to visit Warsaw on Saturday.

A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine.

"It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa Dęba," Tusk told reporters on Friday.

Hours later, five coalition defence ministers - from the UK, France, Poland, Estonia and Lithuania - visited the military training ground where the drill was taking place.

UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told reporters that what had happened earlier was "yet another example of Russian provocation that is designed to divide Europe and to deter Ukraine's allies from supporting their fight for freedom and democracy".

In Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the missile incident was "utterly unacceptable".

The UK defence secretary toured the site of the Koalicja operation with four other European colleagues

European Council President António Costa expressed his "strong solidarity" with the Polish people and said Russia had to come to the negotiating table to bring the war to the end.

The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory.

At least eight people were killed on Friday as Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea.

This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland. In July a cruise missile also landed in Poland, leaving a 10m-wide (33ft) crater. That incident also took place during an attack on the western Ukrainian city of Lviv.

Casualties in Poland have been rare, while Ukraine suffers deadly attacks on a daily basis. However, two Polish farmers were killed by a missile in November 2022, which was believed to have been a Ukrainian air-defence missile responding to a Russian attack.

Moldovan officials said on Friday that their airspace had also been violated on Friday, when a drone crossed briefly into its territory during Russia's attacks on Ukraine.

The Moldovan defence ministry has recorded 118 such violations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say

Thousands of European troops to rehearse Ukraine deployment in event of peace

articles.title: Cheese aged in military fortress founded by Napoleon just named best in the world
articles.excerpt:
Daredevils take part in one of Britain's wackiest contests by throwing themselves down a steep hill for the annual cheese rolling competition. The winner receives a 7-pound circle of cheese.

A cheese...
articles.body_text:
Daredevils take part in one of Britain's wackiest contests by throwing themselves down a steep hill for the annual cheese rolling competition. The winner receives a 7-pound circle of cheese.

A cheese made from raw cow’s milk and aged for two years in a historic military fortress in France just took home the top prize in the 2026 World Cheese Awards, a global competition that judged more than 5,000 cheeses from over 40 countries.

Held in Córdoba, Spain, on Nov. 12, the annual showcase aims to highlight local cheesemaking and food and drink culture, according to the Guild of Fine Food, which organizes the World Cheese Awards.

This year, the judges’ overall winning pick was Fromageries Arnaud's Comté Fort des Rousses 24 Months, which gets its name from the former military fortress Fort des Rousses in eastern France, near the Swiss border.

AMERICA'S BEST PIZZERIAS CROWNED IN NEW RANKINGS AS PIZZA EXPERT GIVES SLICE OF SKEPTICISM

Founded in the early 1800s by Napoleon Bonaparte, who viewed the location as "a strategic military position," according to the historic fort’s website, Fort des Rousses served as a military base and training camp before eventually being turned into aging cellars in 1998.

With 50,000 square meters of vaulted stone cellars, the fortress is one of France’s largest cheese caves, housing nearly 140,000 wheels of Comté, the fort’s website says.

A panel of judges and a Super Jury of global experts crowned a French cheese, shown above, as the world’s best in the 2026 World Cheese Awards. (Jean-Marc Zaorski/Getty Images)

Comté is a cooked and pressed cheese made from unpasteurized cow’s milk traditionally made in the Jura Massif mountain region of France, according to Comté USA.

A young Comté typically smells of butter, dried apricots and caramel.

Meanwhile, a Comté that’s aged for a long time will be more fruity, spicy and nutty, the organization’s website states.

The Comté Fort des Rousses 24 Months was aged by cheese maturer, or affineur, JuraFlore, which has been aging cheeses since 1907.

Judges at the recent World Cheese Awards are shown above. This year's competition drew over 5,000 entries. (Guild of Fine Food (KARGO Kommunication))

Their Charles Arnaud cellar in Fort des Rousses, which produced this year’s world champion, is dedicated solely to Comté cheeses, according to the website.

"What I liked about this cheese was the complexity," said finalist judge Rafa Dominguez Gonzalez.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"Those beautiful, nutty, savory flavors really left a mark on me," he added.

"Some people argue that time is the fifth ingredient in cheese," said Patrick McGuigan, a cheese author and educator who co-hosted the judging of the finalists.

Judges blindly assessed the cheeses’ appearance, aroma, texture, flavor and mouthfeel, awarding points based on their evaluations, according to the World Cheese Awards website.

The winning cheese is aged for two years in the cellars of a former military fortress founded in the early 1800s by Napoleon Bonaparte. (Jean-Marc Zaorski/Getty Images)

The number of points awarded in the initial round of judging determined whether a cheese won a bronze, silver or gold medal.

Once all the cheeses were scored, the judges chose 108 "Super Gold" winners among the gold medal recipients, which then advanced to be judged by a 14-member super jury.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Each judge selected a favorite cheese for the final round of evaluations, which yielded a three-way tie between the winning Comté, Ossau-Iraty from France and Le Gruyère AOP from Switzerland, with each cheese earning 81 points.

Competition organizers broke the tie by subtracting each cheese’s highest and lowest scores, which led the Comté to win the title of World Champion.

French emperor Napoleon Bonaparte founded Fort des Rousses in the early 1800s. It was used as a military base and training camp before being used to age cheese beginning in 1998. (VCG Wilson/Corbis via Getty Images)

The 14 finalists hailed from Spain, Portugal, Italy, France and Switzerland, with cheeses including a pecorino variety from Italy and an aged goat’s milk cheese from Spain, which featured a coating of edible flowers.

Fox News Digital reached out to JuraFlore and the Guild of Fine Food, the organizers of the World Cheese Awards, for comment.

Sadie Chafe is a writer on the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Poland condemns Russian ‘provocation’ after airspace violations
articles.excerpt:
Poland has said Russia violated its airspace three times overnight, in what Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said was a “provocation” by Moscow.

Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz told a new...
articles.body_text:
Poland has said Russia violated its airspace three times overnight, in what Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said was a “provocation” by Moscow.

Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz told a news conference on Friday that investigations were under way at three locations – Nowy Lipowiec, roughly 60km (37 miles) from the Poland-Ukraine border, Molodycz, about 50km (31 miles) to the south, and Rudnik nad Sanem, about 50km to the west.

Kosiniak-Kamysz added that the three objects were probably two missiles and a drone.

The incursions were reported as Poland held military exercises involving the “Coalition of the Willing“, a group of European countries coordinating help and support for Ukraine.

The potential crash site near Nowy Lipowiec is about 76km (47 miles) from where European troops were taking part in military exercises to prepare for a potential post-war mission in Ukraine, aimed at helping to stabilise the country and rebuild its military once the war ends.

“These exercises, combined with the presence of defence ministers from France, the United Kingdom, and the Baltic states – along with eight chiefs of staff, including those from our key allies – suggest that the convergence of these events is no accident,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said.

The defence minister said Poland would ask NATO for more support securing the alliance’s eastern flank.

NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said in a post on X that the incident was “clearly dangerous” and that NATO stood in solidarity with Poland.

Tusk said Rutte would visit Warsaw on Saturday. The Polish prime minister added that there was no doubt the objects that landed in Poland were Russian.

“It seems we are dealing with an intentional provocation,” he said. “Today, it is clearer than ever before that ⁠Poland must participate in decisions and discussions regarding the future of Ukraine and security in Europe.”

British ⁠Prime Minister Andy Burnham condemned Russia’s violation of Polish airspace, calling it “utterly ⁠unacceptable”.

“Europe will not be ⁠deterred from our support for Ukraine,” he said at an EU-UK summit news conference in ‌Brussels. “We will not allow [Russian President Vladimir] Putin to divide our continent, and ‌we recognise that the front line in Ukraine is the front line for freedom and democracy everywhere.”

Drones have repeatedly strayed into the airspace of countries on NATO’s eastern flank during Russia’s war in Ukraine, fuelling tension with the Western military alliance and stoking fears that the conflict ⁠could spread.

The incident in Poland came against the backdrop of Russian attacks in Ukraine that killed eight people, injured dozens more and damaged bridges and transport infrastructure.

articles.title: Blood Gold: The Munduruku’s fight for survival in the Brazilian Amazon
articles.excerpt:
Fault Lines investigates how illegal gold mining poisons and threatens Indigenous communities in the Brazilian Amazon.

For the Munduruku people of the Brazilian Amazon, the fish they depend on for su...
articles.body_text:
Fault Lines investigates how illegal gold mining poisons and threatens Indigenous communities in the Brazilian Amazon.

For the Munduruku people of the Brazilian Amazon, the fish they depend on for survival have become poisoned with mercury. As soaring gold prices drive illegal miners deeper into the rainforest, mercury used to extract the gold contaminates rivers and enters the food chain, putting entire communities at risk.

In Blood Gold, Fault Lines meets Indigenous families confronting the health consequences of illegal mining and fighting to protect their land. With rare access to an illegal mine, senior correspondent Josh Rushing witnesses how mercury is used to extract gold. He meets a researcher documenting the contamination of Indigenous communities and a federal prosecutor working to stop the mercury trade. The film examines why illegal mining persists despite government crackdowns and who pays the price for the world’s appetite for gold.
