articles.title: Islam set to be the largest religion by 2035: Where will most Muslims live?
articles.excerpt:
Muslims are projected to outnumber Christians worldwide by 2035, according to projections released by the Pew Research Center.

Both religions will keep growing. Between 2020 and 2070, the number of M...
articles.body_text:
Muslims are projected to outnumber Christians worldwide by 2035, according to projections released by the Pew Research Center.

Both religions will keep growing. Between 2020 and 2070, the number of Muslims is expected to rise by 80 percent, from 2.02 billion to 3.64 billion. Christians are projected to grow by 30 percent to 2.96 billion, roughly in step with the world population.

Muslims are projected to grow faster than any other major religious group. Hindus and Jews are expected to grow more slowly than the world population, while the number of Buddhists and people with no religion is projected to shrink.

The main reason is birth rates. Between 2020 and 2025, Muslim women had an average of 3.1 children, compared with 2.5 for Christian women and 1.6 for all other women. A population needs about 2.1 children per woman to replace itself.

Births minus deaths are projected to add 1.6 billion Muslims and 792 million Christians by 2070.

Most of the growth will happen where Muslims are already the majority. The 53 Muslim-majority countries are expected to gain 1.2 billion Muslims by 2070, 74 percent of the global increase.

Indonesia had the world’s largest Muslim population in 2020, at 239 million. Pakistan, just 12 million behind, is projected to take the top spot. Pew’s figures compare 2020 with 2070, so they do not say exactly when, but with Pakistan’s Muslim population set to double to 461 million while Indonesia’s grows 15 percent, the switch is likely to come well before 2070.

By 2070, India’s Muslim population is projected to rise from third to second, growing from 213 million to 334 million. Nigeria jumps from fifth to third, more than doubling to 282 million and pushing Indonesia to fourth.

Four of the top 10 in 2070 are in Africa: Nigeria, Egypt, Ethiopia and Sudan. Ethiopia and Afghanistan join the list, replacing Iran and Algeria, while Sudan’s Muslim population more than doubles to 116 million and climbs above Turkiye.

Pew’s projections cover 201 countries and territories, home to 99.98 percent of the world’s population. They assume current trends in fertility, mortality and religious switching continue, and could change with wars, disasters or economic shifts.

articles.title: Former Secret Service investigator sounds alarm over AI scams as Americans grow increasingly anxious
articles.excerpt: Jason Brown, a former U.S. Secret Service cyberfraud investigator, warns that AI-powered voice cloning and impersonation scams are making it increasingly difficult for Americans to distinguish real co...
articles.body_text:
Jason Brown, a former U.S. Secret Service cyberfraud investigator, warns that AI-powered voice cloning and impersonation scams are making it increasingly difficult for Americans to distinguish real communications from fake ones.

A former Secret Service cyberfraud investigator warned that Americans are increasingly on edge following a wave of major technology disruptions, while artificial intelligence is making scams targeting families and consumers more sophisticated.

Jason Brown, a former U.S. Secret Service cyberfraud investigator and iCounter's director of customer advisory and counter fraud lead, told Fox News Digital on Thursday that Americans have reason to be increasingly cautious about technology.

"There's been a lot of stuff that has happened in the past week in particular that people are concerned about," he continued, citing recent technology outages involving Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and several financial institutions.

TIMELINE: AMERICA HITS A TECH WALL AS OUTAGES CRIPPLE EMAIL, GROUND FLIGHTS AND DISRUPT MAJOR BANKS

The more details a scam includes, the more likely it is built from your publicly available data. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

Brown acknowledged that some incidents involved infrastructure problems while others remained under investigation.

With the holiday season approaching, Brown warned that AI has made it easier for criminals to create convincing fraudulent messages, eliminating many of the warning signs consumers previously relied on.

"AI has just made the criminal a lot more efficient and a little bit more effective," Brown said.

Spelling mistakes, poor grammar and awkward phrasing — once common indicators of fraudulent messages — are becoming less reliable as criminals use AI to generate more convincing communications, he explained.

AI VOICE SCAM TRAPS MOM IN 5-HOUR KIDNAPPING NIGHTMARE

Former U.S. Secret Service cyberfraud investigator Jason Brown warned that artificial intelligence is making scams more sophisticated and increasingly difficult for Americans to recognize. (Fox News Digital)

AI also allows criminals to impersonate familiar voices, potentially tricking victims into believing they are speaking with a family member in distress.

Brown described a scenario in which a scammer uses a short voice recording to impersonate someone's relative and demand thousands of dollars in gift cards.

"AI just makes them a lot more efficient and a lot less prone to errors," he said, warning that Americans must become more skeptical of suspicious messages.

"Unfortunately, we're at a point where everybody needs to have that level of distrust," he said.

As holiday shopping ramps up, Brown said scammers are likely to impersonate major delivery companies, including UPS, FedEx and the U.S. Postal Service.

FAKE E-ZPASS EMAIL THREATENS $100 FINE OVER UNPAID TOLL

Scammers may impersonate major delivery companies during the holiday shopping season, sending fraudulent messages claiming packages cannot be delivered without additional payment. (Ute Grabowsky/Photothek via Getty Images)

He warned that fraudulent messages may claim packages cannot be delivered until additional postage is paid, with scammers demanding payment through cryptocurrency or gift cards.

"If it comes from crypto, especially if it comes from gift cards, that's a red flag for sure," Brown said.

Beyond the emotional toll, Brown warned that increasingly sophisticated scams can result in significant financial losses. He cited FBI reporting that he said identified more than 22,000 AI-related fraud cases in 2025, with losses exceeding $890 million.

Brown noted that businesses are also vulnerable to schemes in which criminals impersonate trusted vendors and redirect legitimate payments into fraudulent accounts.

AGING MEANS LEARNING HOW TO PREVENT COSTLY SCAMS TARGETING OLDER AMERICANS

Former Secret Service investigator Jason Brown warned holiday shoppers to be cautious of suspicious delivery notifications appearing to come from UPS, FedEx or the U.S. Postal Service. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

The holiday season can create additional vulnerabilities as executives travel, employees take time off and temporary workers join company operations, he said.

Brown urged Americans to independently verify suspicious messages and take additional precautions when communicating with family members, including establishing a "safe word" to help confirm someone's identity during an unexpected call.

"Another thing that we always talk about with family members, set up a safe word ahead of time. Have that conversation now," he said, adding that even if a caller provides the correct word, people should still end the call and contact the person independently using a trusted number.

"The biggest safety valve for anybody in a scam when it comes over the internet via your cell phone over the computer is stop, think, and then independently verify," he added.

Michael Sinkewicz is a writer for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to michael.sinkewicz@fox.com

articles.title: Lionel Messi of Inter Miami tops Major League Soccer salaries
articles.excerpt: Lionel Messi remains the highest-paid player in Major League Soccer, with $28.3m in guaranteed compensation, according to a salary release on Thursday by the players’ union, with Chicago’s Robert Lewa...
articles.body_text:
Lionel Messi remains the highest-paid player in Major League Soccer, with $28.3m in guaranteed compensation, according to a salary release on Thursday by the players’ union, with Chicago’s Robert Lewandowski second.

Argentinian legend Messi topped the league list revealed by the MLS Players Association with compensation almost $8m higher than last year, although his figures include only playing compensation, not income from other sources.

Messi signed a contract extension through 2028 last year.

Poland’s Lewandowski, who joined the Chicago Fire earlier this year, was second overall with $19.51m, followed by Orlando’s Antoine Griezmann of France at $13.94m, South Korean star Son Heung-min of Los Angeles FC at $11.15m and Swiss international Breel Embolo of Atlanta United at $10.81m.

Among MLS clubs, Miami topped all teams in total guaranteed compensation at $59.37m, with Chicago second at $41.29m, Atlanta third at $38.35m, the Los Angeles Galaxy fourth at $34.91m and LAFC fifth at $32.91m.

The league’s lowest total team compensation was Philadelphia Union at $12.64m, with Sporting Kansas City second-lowest at $13.30m and DC United third-lowest at $14.55m.

The figures are through October 9 and are annualised for players who arrived in the summer transfer period.

articles.title: UK government borrowing rises less than forecast in surprise boost for chancellor John Healey
articles.excerpt:
UK economy defies City predictions and Iran war fallout, with gap between spending and income about £1bn lower than expected in October, at £17bn

The UK government borrowed less than expected in Octo...
articles.body_text:
UK economy defies City predictions and Iran war fallout, with gap between spending and income about £1bn lower than expected in October, at £17bn

The UK government borrowed less than expected in October despite a rise in debt interest costs, in a boost for chancellor John Healey amid the pressure on Britain’s economy from the Middle East war.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said public sector net borrowing – the difference between government spending and income – was £17bn in October, about £800m higher than the same month a year ago. City economists had forecast borrowing would increase by more, to £18bn.

In the financial year so far, public sector net borrowing was £111.3bn, the ONS said – £7.3bn less than in the same period last year, helped by stronger tax receipts.

Grant Fitzner, the ONS chief economist, said: “Borrowing so far this financial year remained lower than in the same period last year with receipts growing faster than spending. Income-related taxes’ receipts grew particularly strongly.

“However, monthly borrowing was up on last October, partly down to higher debt interest.”

The latest figures showed rising borrowing costs on financial markets drove the UK’s debt interest payments to £11.2bn in October - £2.8bn more than in the same month last year, and the highest figure for any October since monthly records began in 1997.

Some government bonds are directly linked to the retail prices index measure of inflation, with payments rising in line with it. RPI has increased in recent months as the Iran war has pushed up energy costs.

Public sector net debt rose to £3.1tn, equivalent to 95.8% of GDP – 1.9 percentage points higher than last year and at levels last seen in the early 1960s.

Chief secretary to the Treasury, Emma Reynolds, said Britain was showing “standout resilience despite the global impact of the conflict in Iran.

“This year we’ve cut borrowing faster than any other G20 country. Now we’re going to cut waste and bureaucracy by reprioritising spending and making public services more efficient with AI,” Reynolds added.

Britain’s economy has continued to grow at the second-fastest rate in the G7 despite the fallout from the war in the Middle East, bolstered by AI investment and households continuing to spend.

In his budget last month, Healey raised taxes on banks to fund relief for households being squeezed by the energy shock from the Middle East war.

Against a highly uncertain global backdrop, Healey stuck to the government’s fiscal rules with £15bn of headroom – less than the £23.6bn buffer left by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, as the conflict drove up the UK government’s borrowing costs.

After a low-key budget statement designed with febrile bond markets in mind, economists warned the chancellor had set himself up for a “brutal” spending review next year.

Avoiding a return to austerity for unprotected government departments could require a £17bn top-up to the spending plans for 2030-31, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies. That is before taking into account an additional £11bn needed to fund a commitment to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP.

Official figures on Wednesday showed inflation in the UK rose in October to 3.6% amid the global surge in energy prices triggered by the Iran war. Economic forecasters predict a further rise in inflation, with the Bank of England anticipating a peak of close to 5% next year.

Threadneedle Street raised interest rates from 3.75% to 4% earlier this month and warned further increases might be required to combat inflationary pressures unleashed by the Iran war. Financial markets predict three quarter-point rate increases before the end of next year.

Rob Wood, the chief UK economist at the consultancy Pantheon Macroeconomics, said: “The October budget did little to address the more serious challenges facing the public finances, so we continue to have doubts about the government’s ability to follow through on its fiscal plans, suggesting upside risks to borrowing in the coming years.”

articles.title: The Gambia stood up for the Rohingya, now the world must act
articles.excerpt:
Member of the National Assembly of The Gambia and a Member of Parliamentarians for Global Action. Member of the National Assembly of The Gambia and a Member of Parliamentarians for Global Action.

The...
articles.body_text:
Member of the National Assembly of The Gambia and a Member of Parliamentarians for Global Action. Member of the National Assembly of The Gambia and a Member of Parliamentarians for Global Action.

There are moments in history when a nation is defined not by its size, wealth, military strength or political influence, but by the courage of its conscience.

On Thursday, the International Court of Justice found that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in northern Rakhine State, in breach of its obligations under the Genocide Convention. For the Rohingya, it is a long-overdue recognition. For The Gambia, it concludes a case our country brought to the Court seven years ago.

The Rohingya have lived in Myanmar’s Rakhine State for generations. Their basic human rights have been systematically denied over time, leaving them stateless and subject to dehumanising rhetoric, hate speech and legal persecution. Following the Myanmar military’s “clearance operations” in 2016 and 2017, over 700,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh. The military killed an estimated 10,000 civilians, raped and sexually assaulted women and girls, and burned villages to the ground. There are currently 1.2 million Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh, the majority in the camps of Cox’s Bazar, and 520,000 remain in Myanmar.

When confronted with reports of unimaginable suffering, persecution, displacement and the destruction of communities, The Gambia chose to act. In 2018, our then Minister of Justice, Abubacarr Tambadou, visited the camps in Bangladesh as part of an Organisation of Islamic Cooperation delegation. As a former prosecutor at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, he recognised the signs of genocide in the accounts of the survivors.

With the support of the OIC’s 57 member States, The Gambia brought the case to the International Court of Justice in November 2019. It was the first time in the court’s history that a state with no direct connection to the alleged crimes had filed a case under the 1948 Genocide Convention, which obliges all state parties to prevent and punish genocide wherever it may occur.

Yet, The Gambia’s action before the Court was never only about legal obligations or diplomatic considerations. We asked ourselves one fundamental question: if we remain silent in the face of such suffering, what does our silence make us?

As Gambians, we know the value of dignity. We understand what it means to yearn for justice. We know the pain that comes when our rights are denied, and voices are silenced. Our own history of political struggle taught us that freedom, accountability and human rights are lived realities that shape the lives of us all.

Perhaps that is why this case has resonated deeply with many Gambians: it speaks to our common humanity. In January, Rohingya survivors of the violence testified before the court about what they had lived through. We recognise that the fear of being driven from one’s home knows no nationality, and compassion does not stop at national boundaries.

The years since the case was filed have required patience and perseverance. International justice can often move frustratingly slowly. However, the court’s order in January 2020, the rejection of Myanmar’s objections in 2022, and the interventions from 11 states (Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, the Netherlands, the UK, the Maldives, Slovenia, the DRC, Belgium, and Ireland) on how the Convention should be interpreted have reaffirmed our shared commitment.

The judgement by the world’s highest court today is a reminder that the obligation to prevent genocide applies to every state, large or small, near or far. This is the first time in the history of the court that a state has been found responsible for committing genocide. The court concluded that the widespread rape and sexual violence committed by Myanmar’s security forces were part of the genocide, and that Myanmar failed to prevent genocide and to punish those responsible.

Myanmar is now under a clear obligation to comply fully with the judgement. It is required to investigate and prosecute those responsible, to facilitate the safe, voluntary and dignified return of displaced Rohingya and to protect them from discrimination and persecution. Justice for the Rohingya will also require the restoration of their citizenship and the recognition of their right to be called Rohingya.

Parliamentarians also have a role to play. As the court made clear today, punishing genocide requires laws that explicitly criminalise it. The court has held Myanmar to that standard, and we must hold ourselves to it, too. We must ensure that genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes are fully incorporated into our domestic laws, and that our courts can try them wherever they are committed.

In our National Assembly, we will ask our government about the next steps, monitor Myanmar’s compliance, and ensure that The Gambia continues to press for that compliance at the United Nations and within the OIC. Other states must now step in by ensuring that Myanmar complies, supporting Rohingya refugees and ensuring they will not be sent back into danger.

As Gambians, we have chosen empathy over indifference, principle over convenience, and action over silence. The Rohingya have shown extraordinary courage and determination in their search for justice, and today international law has finally answered them. Our collective responsibility now is to call for compliance and prevent any future acts of genocide.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Vape users hospitalised after losing consciousness, prompting public health warning in New South Wales
articles.excerpt:
Testing confirms presence of etomidate, a strong and fast-acting sedative used as a general anaesthetic overseas but not registered for medical use in Australia

Get our breaking news email, free app ...
articles.body_text:
Testing confirms presence of etomidate, a strong and fast-acting sedative used as a general anaesthetic overseas but not registered for medical use in Australia

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Three people who lost consciousness and were hospitalised in New South Wales after using certain vapes have tested positive for the unregulated anaesthetic agent etomidate, health officials said.

NSW health on Friday issued a public warning about vape liquids containing etomidate, a strong and fast-acting sedative used as a general anaesthetic overseas but not registered for medical use in Australia.

The three people who were hospitalised had used non-nicotine refillable vapes, the state health department said. Testing of their blood and urine confirmed the presence of etomidate.

The department would not confirm how old the three patients were, where they were hospitalised, or their condition on Friday.

The discovery of etomidate in vapes in NSW comes about four months after Victorian health officials announced they had found the powerful anaesthetic agent in an illicit vape sold in Melbourne.

On Friday, NSW health warned vapes sold as space pods, space oil, kpods, piu piu vapes, or zombie vapes may contain etomidate, or other substances, including ketamine, THC and potent opioids.

The medical director of the NSW poisons information centre, Dr Darren Roberts, said etomidate’s effects were unpredictable when used in a vape.

Roberts said etomidate could cause confusion, drowsiness, slow breathing, vomiting, muscle spasms or movements that were hard to control, and people who took it could become unresponsive.

These effects could be life threatening, especially if used with other drugs that could cause sedation, such as alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines, and GHB, Roberts said.

He said etomidate could also cause long-term harm when used regularly, including the disruption of hormones produced by the adrenal gland.

These hormones are important in regulating stress responses and need to be replaced if they aren’t produced naturally, he said.

“The contents found in non-nicotine vapes vary,” Roberts said. “You can’t assume what’s inside.”

He urged anyone considering using a vape to ask themselves what could be in it.

“You won’t get into trouble for seeking medical care,” he said. If you feel unwell, or if your friend feels unwell, after using a vape, do something about it.”

NSW health officials said it recommended people administer Naloxone to anyone who became responsive after using any drug, in case they had ingested opioids.

Naloxone is an opioid overdose treatment, which is free at pharmacies and does not require a prescription.

Naloxone won’t reverse the effects of etomidate, as the sedative does not belong to the opioid class of drugs, but it is still safe to give, health officials said.

The officials said anyone who witnessed someone experiencing unexpected symptoms after using drugs should call triple zero immediately or seek urgent medical attention.

articles.title: UK and EU to agree youth mobility scheme, BBC understands
articles.excerpt:
Watch: Burnham says he wants 'best deal for Britain' at UK-EU summit

Up to 100,000 young people from the EU would be allowed to travel, work and study in the UK per year under a new youth mobility sc...
articles.body_text:
Watch: Burnham says he wants 'best deal for Britain' at UK-EU summit

Up to 100,000 young people from the EU would be allowed to travel, work and study in the UK per year under a new youth mobility scheme set to be agreed on Friday, the BBC understands.

The same number of young Britons would be allowed into Europe under the scheme, expected to be approved at the UK-EU summit in Brussels. Downing Street has not commented on the details, but said talks were "down to the wire" on Thursday.

The prime minister has said a "Channel action plan" on immigration could also be struck, while negotiators are seeking agreements on food trade rules and carbon emissions pricing.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has accused Andy Burnham of "reopening the divisions" of the Brexit referendum.

A new youth mobility scheme would aim to make it easier for young people to work and travel both in the EU and UK.

The UK already has schemes in place with 13 non-EU countries including Australia, Canada and India.

In 2024, the EU proposed allowing 18 to 30 year-olds to work or study in the EU and UK for up to four years.

Labour, which was then in opposition, rejected the deal - arguing it amounted to reinstating freedom of movement.

Since coming to government, the party has suggested it would consider a more restricted scheme with a time limit, a cap on the numbers coming to the UK and a ban on participants from claiming benefits.

The UK's request to limit numbers has proved to be a sticking point in negotiation ahead of the summit, along with the EU's request that EU students should pay the same tuition fees at UK universities as domestic students.

Speaking to broadcasters on Thursday evening, Burnham was asked if there were any circumstances in which the UK would walk away from a deal on Friday.

"There would always be those circumstances because I'm in this to get the best deal for Britain, always," he said.

"But what's in it for us is the possibility of lower food prices and I can't turn my back on that, lower costs for business, cutting red tape, and a really big win potentially of more collaboration on immigration - a Channel action plan - which is a really big deal if we can land that tomorrow.

"So I hope people can understand why I have pushed this because it could be a really good deal for Britain."

Burnham previously said the UK and EU could link up their law enforcement efforts, including sharing more data and criminal records of foreign nationals.

The prime minister's spokesman has said if a deal were secured, the government would introduce legislation to Parliament next week to implement changes.

The Brexit debate is back – and there are nerves about what happens next

Faisal Islam: What's in the Brexit reset food deal and are there trade-offs?

The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left

An agreement on trade could remove checks and paperwork faced by food companies exporting to the EU.

The government argues this could add £5bn to the economy and cut food prices.

However, it could mean the UK will have to follow certain EU rules on products, for example on gene-edited crops or labelling.

Burnham has also said the summit would allow the UK to raise concerns about the Made in Europe scheme, which is designed to protect industries from unfair Chinese competition.

Burnham has previously suggested he could commit Labour to building a closer long-term future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member - however, he has ruled out major changes before the next election.

The party's 2024 manifesto promised not to return to the EU, the single market, customs union or freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa.

Earlier this week, former deputy prime minister David Lammy urged the prime minister to go into the next general election promising to rejoin the EU.

However, the subject has divided his cabinet with one minister warning of the costs that would come with reversing Brexit.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, speaking to The Sun, external, said he does "not believe for a minute" the country would "ever vote to rejoin" the EU.

He added: "I think what Burnham is doing is playing a very cynical political game. He's trying to pick up votes from the Lib Dems, pick up votes from the Greens, and using it as a massive distraction from all the problems that he can't deal with."

Speaking to the BBC's Today programme on Thursday, Badenoch said she wanted to see easier trading with the EU, but "not trade at any cost".

She also said the new deals could see UK companies having to follow EU rules, even those that do not trade with the bloc.

Appearing on BBC Breakfast on Friday, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage described the agreement as a "very, very expensive and costly error" and said Burnham has no "democratic mandate to do any of this".

He added that the Labour party manifesto was clear that the UK would not go back towards the single market and asked: "Where is our democracy?".

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey told BBC Newsnight that while he agreed with Burnham on "the harms of Brexit", he did not think the prime minister was "going to go anywhere near far enough".

"We need to go further and faster," he said, including returning to freedom of movement - which Sir Ed said would help tackle immigration and boost the UK economy.

Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletter to keep up with the inner workings of Westminster and beyond.

articles.title: EU and Britain to agree steps towards relations reset
articles.excerpt:
British and European Union leaders are set to meet at a summit billed as a chance to reset relations a decade after the Brexit vote.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham will meet with European Commission ...
articles.body_text:
British and European Union leaders are set to meet at a summit billed as a chance to reset relations a decade after the Brexit vote.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham will meet with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa, who heads the European Council, on Friday in Brussels. In the second such meeting since Britain formally left the bloc in 2020, deals on food, emissions and youth mobility are expected to be sealed.

The previous summit in 2025 was billed as a “stable foundation” upon which to rebuild the relationship between London and Brussels. Friday’s meeting is being sold as a chance to start on a reset of relations.

Burnham said earlier in the week that it was an “obvious truth” that Britain had lost more than it had gained from Brexit, which followed a non-binding referendum in 2016 in which 52 percent of the British public voted to leave the EU. He has signalled that a reformed relationship with Brussels is on his agenda.

The most valuable agreement on the table concerns the cross-border exchange of animals, plants and related products. Britain has estimated that the removal of the current controls could be worth 5.1 billion pounds ($6.7bn) annually.

A potential deal on emissions trading systems could see London and Brussels mutually exempt each other from carbon border levies on goods like steel.

An agreement on youth mobility, which would allow 100,000 people from the EU to live and work for up to three years in the UK, and vice versa, is also reportedly set to be signed. The UK had originally wanted half that number.

The EU is also pushing for students to qualify for “home fees” at British universities – often one third of the international price. London, however, has only agreed to apply “significantly reduced” fees.

The UK also wants to be part of the EU’s “Made in Europe” rules. Brussels has said it may be open to this, but it would require the UK to accept its policies. That could prove tricky for Burnham, given that the UK still hosts a significant Eurosceptic population.

articles.title: Sandpapergate: Australian gov’t demands CA to ensure transparency in forum
articles.excerpt: Cricket Australia (CA) should ensure its forum into Sandpapergate is handled as independently and openly as possible, a government spokesperson said on Friday, as former players slammed the governing ...
articles.body_text:
Cricket Australia (CA) should ensure its forum into Sandpapergate is handled as independently and openly as possible, a government spokesperson said on Friday, as former players slammed the governing body’s attempts to defuse an escalating controversy surrounding ⁠the 2018 ball-tampering scandal.

CA bosses said on Wednesday that an independent forum would be set up to allow players to give their accounts of the incident, but the results would not necessarily be made public and no sanctions would follow.

The move has been ridiculed by past players and pundits, ⁠including former captain Michael Clarke, who said the Australian public had been lied to about who was party to the cheating during the 2018 South Africa Test series.

A spokesperson for Sport Minister Anika Wells said integrity mattered to “every kid with a bat or a ball”.

“This is Cricket Australia’s process to run and it is a matter for them to work through. Australians will expect this to be run independently and as openly as possible,” the spokesperson ‌said in a statement.

“We have a summer of cricket to look forward to and I’m sure all of Australia will get behind our team.”

CA did not provide immediate comment when asked by the Reuters news agency on Friday for more details about its forum.

The eight-year-old Sandpapergate scandal has reignited this month following allegations by former Australia batter Usman Khawaja that other players and staff knew of the ball-tampering – not just the three who were found culpable and sanctioned after a rapid investigation by CA’s integrity unit during the South Africa tour.

CA banned then-captain Steve Smith and David Warner for 12 months, and Cameron Bancroft for nine.

Test captain Pat Cummins and fellow ⁠pace bowler Mitchell Starc have since rejected Khawaja’s allegations, saying they had no prior knowledge of ball tampering.

But three ⁠other players involved in the 2018 tour came forward to back up Khawaja’s account, including Warner and Bancroft, who said “the whole team” knew, including coaching staff and a media manager.

Bancroft claimed the idea to rough up the ball with sandpaper to make it swing was Warner’s, but that the conversation had taken place “within a wider team environment”. He added that he had lied about the extent of the plot to protect CA’s investigation into the incident.

Clarke, who captained Australia from 2011 to 2015, said Bancroft’s explosive 4,000-word statement shared with the media on Wednesday had made CA’s forum redundant.

“The public don’t want any more bullshit,” ⁠he said on his podcast, Beyond23.

“The public want the complete truth to allow us to move on.”

The scandal has heaped pressure on Cummins, one of the game’s most devastating pace bowlers, who boasts a strong portfolio of ⁠corporate sponsors.

Cummins called Khawaja’s allegations “complete and utter nonsense” in an hour-long news conference last ⁠week, and criticised his former teammate for being “casual” with others’ lives and reputations.

He declined to comment to a large media scrum camped outside his Sydney home on Thursday and at training, but his manager said Cummins’s position remained steadfast and he had no need to respond to Bancroft’s statement.

A poll of 13,000 readers of Melbourne’s Herald Sun newspaper had 82 percent saying ‌they believed Khawaja’s, Warner’s and Bancroft’s accounts of Sandpapergate, versus 18 percent for Cummins and Australia’s bowlers who denied prior knowledge.

A majority of 6,000 readers in a poll in the Sydney Morning Herald said they did not expect Cummins to remain as captain for the first Test of the ‌home ‌summer against New Zealand, which starts December 9.

Former Australia bowler Mitchell Johnson said the public pressure on Cummins to stand down as captain would be too much.

“I just can’t see how his captaincy and personal brand survives this,” Johnson wrote in a column for The West Australian newspaper.

articles.title: Baby born with heart abnormalities ‘didn’t have a chance’ after non-medical free birth, NSW inquest hears
articles.excerpt:
Inquest into the deaths of four babies after free and home births hears routine checks and follow-up may have saved their lives

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Four babie...
articles.body_text:
Inquest into the deaths of four babies after free and home births hears routine checks and follow-up may have saved their lives

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Four babies who died in New South Wales – three after free births and one after a home birth – might have survived if they had had routine checks and follow-up , a coronial inquest has heard.

Baby DH, Baby D, Baby R, and Baby B died in the state’s northern rivers region between 2022 and 2024.

The inquest in Lismore has heard women chose free or home births for reasons including traumatic experiences, a lack of trust in clinicians, and a lack of services.

Baby DH died about eight hours after he was born in a free birth – with a doula but no medical professionals present. The court earlier heard he turned purple, was struggling to breathe and had became floppy.

His parents gave evidence they were worried but the doula kept reassuring them their baby was OK, then left.

The doula denied many of their claims, and denied that she gave them any clinical advice.

Expert neonatologist and associate professor Nicholas Evans said on Friday that Baby DH’s complex heart abnormalities “would have been readily detectable” in a routine pregnancy scan after which he would have been referred to a paediatric cardiologist.

It was a “missed opportunity”, he told the court.

Paediatric cardiologist Dr Paul Brooks said it was “highly likely” all the abnormalities would have been identified in a routine scan before birth.

Even if the extent of the abnormalities wasn’t clear, he told the court, the scan would have shown the baby needed to be born at a major hospital with cardiac surgery capabilities.

“The site of [Baby DH’s] birth meant that he didn’t have a chance.”

Baby D’s mother did not know she was having twins, and at first thought she’d delivered Baby D’s placenta, only to realise it was a stillborn second twin.

Experts at the inquest agreed it was impossible to know exactly why Baby D died. They discussed the possibility it was because self-described birth keeper Sita Tara Kali did not clamp the umbilical cord before cutting it, but Evans told the court that it was ultimately most likely from respiratory distress because of his compromised heart function.

Baby D might have survived if someone who could do advanced resuscitation had arrived in under 10 minutes, he said, but the “root cause” was that it was not known the mother was carrying twins before the births.

“If [twins] had been diagnosed, at 18 weeks, as it would usually in pregnancy, there would have been very close monitoring.”

Baby R likely died of “severe post-maturity” after being born at 43 weeks and one day in a free birth. The standard is to induce birth or perform a caesarean section at 42 weeks, as the ageing placenta puts the baby at risk.

The mother had been for an ultrasound at 12 weeks, which had put the date of birth at 28 July, 2020.

But the mother distrusted hospitals and trusted Kali, her birth keeper, the court previously heard.

Kali told her to calculate her due date from the date of conception, an unreliable measure that put the date of birth in mid-August.

That recalculation, Evans wrote in his report to the court, was the “root cause” of the issue.

“The standard practice now is that you don’t allow a pregnancy to go beyond 42 completed weeks,” Evans said on Friday.

Expert midwives earlier told the court they didn’t have statistics for babies born beyond 43 weeks because it was so rare.

A 19 August ultrasound showed the pregnancy had become a medical emergency – but Kali advised her to “go home and rest”. It is “more likely than not” that the baby would have survived had she gone to hospital after the ultrasound, Evans said.

Baby B’s mother was warned multiple times she needed to go to hospital to give birth to her twins, but she was determined to have a home birth. Rather than let her have a free birth, four midwives assisted her and the head midwife repeatedly counselled her about the risks.

The mother declined ultrasounds as well as a test for early onset group B streptococcus (GBS) – an organism present in 15 to 20% of women that infects the babies of about 2% of carriers.

Baby B likely died of GBS, pneumonia and sepsis, Evans told the court on Friday, while his twin fell ill but survived. Many infected babies survive in hospital thanks to antibiotics, he added.

articles.title: ‘We don’t want our future decided by the military’: Young Germans protest
articles.excerpt:
Berlin, Germany – Last month, high school student Phil Werring received a letter from the German Armed Forces, known as the Bundeswehr.

In an official document, a military registration form, Werring ...
articles.body_text:
Berlin, Germany – Last month, high school student Phil Werring received a letter from the German Armed Forces, known as the Bundeswehr.

In an official document, a military registration form, Werring was asked to answer compulsory questions – and optional ones if he was interested in joining the army.

After initially ignoring the first letter, two weeks later he received another, warning him of a 250 euro ($275) fine if he did not answer.

Logging in via a QR code, he started working his way through the questionnaire.

“The mandatory questions included ones on whether you have any diseases, your weight, height and whether you played sports, while other questions asked about whether you had a driving licence and what languages you spoke,” the 18-year-old, who lives with his three younger siblings and parents in Muenster, western Germany, told Al Jazeera.

“I only answered the mandatory questions, so it took me around 15 minutes to complete, but if I had filled it all out, it would have taken me a lot longer. I know that not answering all the questions can increase my chances of being called in by the military for a check-up, but I still didn’t want to answer them all.”

Official figures show that by the end of October, nearly 600,000 letters had been sent out this year to young Germans, of which about 286,800 were sent to young men and 271,700 to women and people of other genders. The form is only mandatory for men to complete.

Military conscription, meanwhile, has been a headline-grabbing issue in Germany since the start of the year, after the Military Service Modernisation Act came into effect on January 1 . It set out new targets to grow the army by the mid-2030s, increasing its full-time force to about 260,000, plus 200,000 reservists.

The recruitment drive is one element of Germany’s broader military expansion plans, initiated in 2022 after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Berlin is also increasing defence budgets and surveillance powers for intelligence services.

According to the Ministry of Defence, its efforts are yielding positive results. Official figures indicate that the Bundeswehr has already exceeded the statutory force build-up range for 2026, with personnel numbers in October about 6,400 higher than the same month last year.

Yet as recent protests have shown – including a series of school strikes and a large-scale demonstration organised by a loose alliance called “Gen Z Regelt” (Gen Z Sorts It) – many young people are pushing back against the plans.

Gen Z Regelt is rallying again on Friday, with nearly 20,000 people across 40 cities, including Berlin, Cologne, Frankfurt and Munich, signed up so far.

“The military questionnaire had many personal questions, and I found the experience quite scary, and it made me angry,” Werring said. “As I filled out the form, I realised how serious the government is about taking these steps to reintroduce compulsory military service, and that I may have no choice but to serve and risk my life for companies making millions selling arms. It made me realise that I must be active against these steps towards militarisation and support resistance efforts against these war preparations.”

Linus Schneider, 16, fears that as more money goes towards rearming Germany, the less there is for schools like those in his home city of Munich, which are not in good shape.

“The roofs have been leaking at my school for three years now,” he told Al Jazeera. “Something wasn’t installed properly when the building was built a few years ago, and the city has been saying that they don’t have as much money as they did a few years ago, so they can’t fix the issue. This has led to a lot of problems at school; for example, sometimes we can’t have gym class at all because there are buckets of water in the sports hall.”

Munich is the largest city in one of Germany’s wealthiest states, Bavaria.

Schneider added, “I also hear from friends in other schools that their roofs are in such a bad condition that they are worried about the roof falling on them. We literally don’t have good roofs over our heads. There are big cuts to education and healthcare, while at the same time, military spending has increased drastically.”

According to the current draft budget for 2027, to be agreed on later this month, defence spending is expected to rise to 109.7 billion euros ($120.5bn) from 82.7 billion euros ($90.8bn) the year before. The Ministry for Education and Family, meanwhile, projects a budget of 15.9 billion euros ($17.5bn) compared to 16.6 billion euros ($18.3bn) this year.

Sebastian Koos, a sociologist at the University of Konstanz who researches youth and protest movements, said the wave in Europe was an “important spark” for the German movement.

“There are some similarities and overlaps with the problems, such as the cost of living and cuts to education. But I think the issue of military conscription makes the situation for young people here unique,” he told Al Jazeera.

Koos said that while several different organisations participate in the Gen Z Regelt protests, a common thread is a sense of hopelessness.

“There are also many issues and demands that are being put together. They are also worried about economic and social inequality, right-wing extremism, the cost of living, as well as climate change. This is a lot to digest, and it is very difficult to get a sense of hope if you are confronted with so many different conflicts.”

Friday’s protest will include thousands of students protesting against compulsory military service, organised by the youth-led alliance, School Strike Against Conscription.

Werring will be among those taking to the streets in his local area.

“I’m still figuring out what I want to study, but I am interested in the medical sector. I want to help people, not shoot or harm anyone. I don’t want my future to be interrupted by the military,” he said.

Schneider is in trouble with the school head teacher for getting involved in the protests, but he still plans to join Friday’s rallies.

“We want to make our own decisions about our future,” he said. “We don’t want our future to be decided by the military or the state. And I think that’s quite an important reason why we’re protesting. We also didn’t want war. I think it’s crucial that we stand together in the face of these increasing state repression that [Chancellor] Friedrich Merz is overseeing.”

articles.title: Tashima says Balogun red card row at World Cup prompted FIFA presidency bid
articles.excerpt: Japanese football official Kozo Tashima said on Friday that ⁠the handling of Folarin Balogun’s red ⁠card at the 2026 World Cup was what prompted him to run for FIFA president against Gianni Infantino....
articles.body_text:
Japanese football official Kozo Tashima said on Friday that ⁠the handling of Folarin Balogun’s red ⁠card at the 2026 World Cup was what prompted him to run for FIFA president against Gianni Infantino.

FIFA suspended forward Balogun’s automatic one-match ban for a red card in July, allowing the American striker to play against Belgium after United States ⁠President Donald Trump said he had personally asked President Infantino to review the sanction.

The decision triggered a swift and fiery backlash and, along with an aborted attempt to sell a stake in FIFA tournaments, led to opposition to Infantino’s re-election as president.

Tashima said he wanted to restore trust in FIFA, drawing parallels with ⁠2016, when Infantino took charge after a corruption scandal.

“Ten years ago something similar happened, and Mr Infantino became president to reform and improve things,” the Japan Football Association (JFA) honorary president told a news conference.

“He has certainly done wonderful things. But in this year, 2026, 10 years later, events have occurred that ignored governance.

“I have worked in football, especially as a player and coach. As such, I cannot accept Balogun’s red card in any way. On top of that, no explanation has been ‌given even now. I felt very indignant about this, and that is why I decided to stand here.”

Following the Balogun incident, FIFA’s disciplinary committee said it had the authority to suspend the one-match ban, and that it operated independently.

FIFA last month said it would amend the rule in its disciplinary code, which had allowed for the reversal of the ban.

The election, set to be held in March next year, will be the first time since he won the post in 2016 that Infantino will face a challenge after being re-elected unopposed in 2019 and 2023.

French Football Federation President Philippe Diallo also announced a challenge on Monday with the backing of European governing body UEFA. Infantino has the support of Asia and Africa’s ⁠confederations.

“I have not actually received a nomination from any continental confederation. So I’m well aware that I’m at a considerable ⁠disadvantage in this race,” Tashima said.

“It’s a fact that Gianni’s support has been gradually declining. I will keep appealing to voters.”

Diallo said at a news conference on Tuesday that he would reach out to Tashima to “unite forces”. Tashima said he was open to the idea of coordinating with the Frenchman’s team to avoid splitting the anti-Infantino vote.

“I don’t think the French candidate’s ⁠entry puts me at a disadvantage. In fact, France has ties to Africa and other regions, so Mr Diallo’s entry may bring those votes,” he added.

“Watching his press conference, I saw that he pointed out FIFA’s accounting and other ⁠figures in great detail. I find it reassuring that such a professional has joined.”

Tashima is a former Japan international and youth coach and the first Japanese candidate to stand for FIFA president. He has served on the FIFA Council since 2015.

The 68-year-old said that if elected, he would shun the spotlight.

“A foreign media person described me very accurately. They said that if I’m elected, I might become the least conspicuous president ever,” he said.

“That may have been ‌a bit of irony, but I’m fine with it. It’s not the president who should stand out, but the players.”

He added that he would need to be modest in his campaigning, much of which would be funded by his own money.

“The JFA’s budget for this year is already set, so of ‌course, ‌I would like support from the JFA, but we’ll also have to gather funds, for example by creating a fund or running crowdfunding,” he said.

“I won’t spend wastefully. I also have no intention of flying by private jet or anything like that.”

articles.title: US maritime agency warned Iran blockade was adding to rising Gulf premiums
articles.excerpt:
The United States government’s maritime agency flagged the disruptive impact of Washington’s blockade of Iran on commercial shipping in an internal memo, documents obtained by Al Jazeera reveal.

In a...
articles.body_text:
The United States government’s maritime agency flagged the disruptive impact of Washington’s blockade of Iran on commercial shipping in an internal memo, documents obtained by Al Jazeera reveal.

In an alert, the US Maritime Administration (MARAD) acknowledged the Iran war’s negative impact on insurance premiums and cargo capacity after US Central Command (CENTCOM) announced that it had disabled a Panama-flagged bulk carrier for attempting to breach the blockade.

MARAD administrator Stephen M Carmel shared the alert with a subordinate on October 12, following CENTCOM’s attack on the vessel Ocean Molica and unattributed attacks on three other tankers in and around the Strait of Hormuz.

“Why it matters: This materially escalates the previous alert: merchant ships now face kinetic action from both sides, and the threat has spread to Gulf anchorages and the Gulf of Oman,” said the memo, titled “Alert – Hormuz risk expands beyond the strait”.

“That increases the likelihood of further war-risk premium spikes, crew refusals and effective tanker capacity contraction.”

Carmel shared the alert with MARAD colleague Michael Yarrington in an email requesting information about the impact of the attacks on insurance premiums and an update on the agency’s efforts to “rebuild” war risk insurance.

It is unclear whether the alert originated within MARAD or another agency.

“How is the insurance market responding to all this?” Carmel wrote to Yarrington, an official at MARAD’s Office of Marine Insurance.

Yarrington replied that a colleague had reached out to contacts in London for information and forwarded a summary of rising insurance premiums compiled from news reports.

Yarrington also shared a description of “core deliverables” considered crucial to MARAD’s work on war risk insurance, the details of which were redacted from the emails before their release.

Al Jazeera obtained the documents through a Freedom of Information Act request to MARAD, which is responsible for promoting the US maritime industry.

MARAD, which sits under the US Department of Transportation, the White House, the Department of Defence and CENTCOM, did not respond to requests for comment.

The emergence of the memo acknowledging the negative fallout of the blockade comes as a definitive end to the Iran war remains elusive after months of on-again, off-again negotiations between Washington and Tehran.

US President Donald Trump last week dismissed the need for a peace deal with Iran, days after suggesting that the conflict could end “fairly soon” and that renewed US strikes were “highly unlikely”.

“Those days have long since passed,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Thursday. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”

Todd Huntley, a retired US Navy captain who leads the National Security Law Program at Georgetown University Law Center, said MARAD’s monitoring of the blockade was likely aimed at informing its advice to other branches of the US government.

“As far as I know, MARAD will issue general alerts on incidents or threats, but will not then discuss the consequences, eg, increases in insurance rates,” Huntley told Al Jazeera.

“I do think that some US officials either didn’t consider this risk or ignored it when ordering and implementing the blockade.

“To me, it was pretty obvious this was a likely development given past Iranian actions and threats.”

Ian Ralby, the CEO and founder of maritime security consultancy I.R. Consilium, said the Trump administration appeared to be less concerned about the “strategic considerations” of the blockade than preventing ships from contributing to Iran’s economic survival.

“The President has made it clear that he is unperturbed by the global economic fallout from the War – including the blockade – so it may also be the case that the potential consequences of the blockade were considered but dismissed as unimportant,” Ralby told Al Jazeera.

Global shipping has been roiled by attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waters since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28.

Some 130 attacks on vessels have been recorded in the region since the start of the conflict, resulting in the deaths of at least 25 seafarers, according to the International Maritime Organization (IMO).

October was the worst month for shipping since the war began, with 35 vessels targeted, according to the IMO.

While most attacks during the war have been blamed on Iran or Iranian-aligned forces, CENTCOM has claimed responsibility for destroying or disabling at least two dozen vessels, some of which it has identified as belonging to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) shadow fleet.

The turmoil in the strait has sharply driven up costs for shipping lines.

The cost of insurance for an oil tanker carrying crude from the Middle East to East Asia surged about 200-fold from January to the end of October, reaching $12.29 per barrel, according to the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC).

As of July, insurers charged 3.5 percent–7.5 percent of a vessel’s market value for war risk cover, up from 0.10-0.25 percent before the war, according to industry estimates cited in the Parliament of Singapore, a major logistics and shipping hub.

Amid rising shipping costs, prices of crude oil and fertiliser have surged as much 60 percent and 112 percent, respectively, at various points during the war.

Boon Chuan Lim, an independent researcher in Singapore whose research on the turmoil in the Strait of Hormuz has been published in the Borsa Istanbul Review, said it was noteworthy that the Trump administration had placed enforcement of the blockade alongside other attacks when assessing disruption risk.

“A disabling strike adds a potential source of loss for vessels exposed to that enforcement, though the implications depend on each vessel’s circumstances,” Lim told Al Jazeera.

He added that danger was not limited to the narrow corridor in the strait.

“Geography matters, too,” Lim said. “Risk is not confined to the strait: Ships at anchor, bunkering or approaching ports can also be exposed.

“Insurance terms depend on the vessel, route, area and duration of exposure, so a wider threat can raise costs and complicate operations beyond the transit itself, but it does not mean every vessel faces the same additional premium.”

The Republicans’ crushing defeat in the US midterm elections on November 3 has been widely attributed to the fallout of the war, particularly higher fuel prices.

US Democrats achieved their best electoral performance in decades in a stinging rebuke of Trump ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Democrats have so far secured 56 seats in the 100-member US Senate and at least 257 seats in the 435-member House of Representatives.

articles.title: Academy trust pays out after Prevent threat over children’s Palestine badges
articles.excerpt:
Lion Academy Trust apologises after threatening four pupils in east London with referral to counter-extremism scheme

An academy trust will pay out tens of thousands in compensation to four children w...
articles.body_text:
Lion Academy Trust apologises after threatening four pupils in east London with referral to counter-extremism scheme

An academy trust will pay out tens of thousands in compensation to four children who were told they could be referred to Prevent for wearing Palestine flag badges to school.

The school, part of Lion Academy Trust, has issued a formal apology after it sent letters to the children’s parents saying they might be referred to the counter-extremism programme or to local hate crime teams.

The issue dates back to November 2023 when the children’s school, Barclay primary school in Leyton, east London, held a non-uniform fundraising day for Children in Need.

The four children, all British Muslims aged between six and 10 at the time, attended wearing items displaying Palestinian colours or the Palestinian flag, in memory of children who had been killed in Gaza and those who continued to suffer during the conflict, which was ongoing at the time.

One child wore a Children in Need Pudsey sticker featuring a bow tie in Palestinian colours. Another wore a homemade badge bearing the Palestinian flag and colours.

Parents of the four children said they had repeatedly asked the school to apologise for their treatment of the children and had launched a legal challenge when none was forthcoming.

At a hearing at Central London county court on Thursday, the court heard that the academy trust had now made a formal apology to the children and their families and would pay them substantial compensation.

Lawyers for the children alleged direct discrimination, indirect discrimination and harassment on grounds including race, ethnicity, religion and belief, together with breaches of their rights to freedom of expression and freedom of thought, conscience and belief.

Shahid Achhala, the father of one of the children, said: “What happened to our son was deeply disturbing and should never have happened to any child. He was just eight years old, expressing compassion and solidarity with children suffering in Gaza, including members of his own extended family. Instead of being supported and protected by the school entrusted with his care, he was deliberately subjected to mistreatment that caused him considerable emotional distress.

“For almost three years, we have had to fight legally for accountability and an acknowledgment of the wrongs we believe were committed. While we welcome Lion Academy Trust’s apology, we cannot overlook the distress caused to our son and our family, or the fact that this matter could have been resolved long time ago.”

The families were represented by law firm Leigh Day and supported in their legal claim by Prevent Watch, which provides casework support to individuals and families affected by the Prevent duty.

Layla Aitlhadj, a director at Prevent Watch, said: “In this case, parents who were protecting their children’s rights were told that their concerns were ‘false and malicious’. They held firm through three years of pressure. Today the families, and the wider community who stood with them, have been vindicated.”

The academy trust has been approached for comment.

articles.title: Texas inmate's execution takes over an hour as prison staff struggle to find suitable veins
articles.excerpt: Texas inmate Reinaldo Dennes repeatedly complained of severe pain during a lengthy lethal injection as prison staff struggled to establish IV access, while officials maintained that all execution proc...
articles.body_text:
Texas inmate Reinaldo Dennes repeatedly complained of severe pain during a lengthy lethal injection as prison staff struggled to establish IV access, while officials maintained that all execution procedures were followed.

A Texas inmate's execution lasted more than an hour Thursday as prison staff struggled to find suitable veins for a lethal injection, with the condemned man repeatedly complaining of severe pain before being pronounced dead.

Reinaldo Dennes, who was convicted of capital murder in the 1996 killing of Houston diamond dealer Janos Szucs, repeatedly cried out during the procedure at the state penitentiary in Huntsville, according to The Associated Press.

Dennes was pronounced dead at 7:08 p.m., one minute after the procedure was completed.

The procedure lasted 63 minutes from the time Dennes was strapped to the gurney until its completion, as prison staff struggled to find suitable veins for the intravenous needles used to administer pentobarbital.

CHRISTA PIKE'S EXECUTION DOCTOR SAYS MISPLACED IV SENT LETHAL DRUGS INTO HER ARMS INSTEAD OF VEINS

Texas death row inmate Reinaldo Dennes was executed Thursday after a lengthy lethal injection procedure during which he repeatedly complained of pain. (Texas Department of Criminal Justice via AP)

The execution comes amid renewed scrutiny of lethal injection procedures following a failed execution attempt in Tennessee in September involving death row inmate Christa Pike, who survived two doses of pentobarbital that her attorneys said did not properly enter her bloodstream, causing serious injuries.

Dennes repeatedly complained of pain after Thursday's procedure began, groaning and calling out to God, according to witnesses cited by The AP.

"My right leg is killing me!" he later shouted, describing the sensation as a cramp.

"I don't think this is normal. Take me, father. Don't let me suffer like this. C'mon," he added.

CHRISTA PIKE'S ATTORNEYS SAY SHE'S IN CRITICAL CONDITION AFTER BOTCHED LETHAL INJECTIONS

The state of Texas execution chamber in Huntsville, Texas, is seen on May 27, 2008. (Texas Department of Criminal Justice via AP; AP Photo/Pat Sullivan)

Texas Department of Criminal Justice spokesperson Amanda Hernandez said all procedures were followed appropriately but acknowledged that staff made multiple unsuccessful attempts to establish IV access before placing needles in Dennes' left foot and the left side of his neck.

Hernandez said she did not know how many attempts were unsuccessful but maintained that the locations ultimately used complied with the state's execution procedures.

She also suggested that Dennes may have exaggerated his discomfort, noting that he complained of pain before the drugs began flowing and in areas where no IV had been placed.

According to The AP, when asked whether Dennes was faking his pain, she replied, "I think, yeah, there were allegations. ... There was nothing abnormal on our part."

INDIANA, FLORIDA AND ALABAMA CARRY OUT RARE US TRIPLE EXECUTION DAY

Texas Department of Criminal Justice officials defended the execution of Reinaldo Dennes, saying all procedures were followed appropriately despite his repeated complaints of pain. (Texas Department of Corrections/AFP via Getty Images)

"This isn't the first time we had to insert IVs into other locations. It's also not the first time we've had an inmate make allegations of pain immediately," Hernandez said.

Dennes was the second person executed in the United States on Thursday, following Florida's execution of Thomas Mitchell Overton, 71, who was convicted of killing a pregnant woman and her husband during a home invasion.

Overton's execution marked Florida's 20th of the year, a state record, according to the AP.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Texas Department of Criminal Justice for additional comment.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Michael Sinkewicz is a writer for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to michael.sinkewicz@fox.com
