articles.title: Tears of joy, prayers for return home: Rohingya react to genocide ruling
articles.excerpt: Dhaka, Bangladesh — Umme Ruman was watching the news on her mobile phone from her shelter in Camp 1E of the Rohingya refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. She had been waiting for the Internationa...
articles.body_text:
Dhaka, Bangladesh — Umme Ruman was watching the news on her mobile phone from her shelter in Camp 1E of the Rohingya refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. She had been waiting for the International Court of Justice (ICJ) verdict since the afternoon. But poor internet connectivity kept interrupting the live broadcast.

Then she opened Facebook and saw a headline: “ICJ confirms Myanmar committed genocide.”

Overwhelmed, she jumped. Her sister-in-law was cooking. Ruman rushed to hug her. Before she could explain what had happened, she broke down in tears.

“I celebrated with tears of joy because, for the first time, the world acknowledged what happened to us,” she said.

On Thursday, the ICJ found Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya during brutal military operations in 2017, in which the court found more than 10,000 people had been killed.

The landmark judgement in the case, brought before the court by The Gambia, recognised the atrocities committed against the community after years of denial. For refugees who have spent nearly a decade waiting for justice, the ruling brought a wave of relief, emotion and renewed hope.

“For me, this is not simply a legal verdict. It is proof of our suffering,” Ruman said.

Across the camps, people followed the announcement on mobile phones, laptops and large screens. Some watched with friends. Others gathered with their families. Many turned to Facebook and YouTube to follow the proceedings.

Eighteen-year-old Mohammad Rehan watched with his community teacher and friends on a laptop. “Some women were crying, while others were praying to Allah,” he said. “I did not do anything special. I just sat there and listened, hoping to hear some good news that would give us a peaceful life in the future.”

For Rehan, the first thought was that the verdict could potentially open the door for the Rohingya to return home. “Just imagining that made me so happy,” he said.

The news soon spread through the blocks. Rehan said people were celebrating, while elderly refugees discussed the case and The Gambia’s role in bringing it before the court. The small West African nation was not directly affected by the violence against the Rohingya. Still, it acted as a party to the 1948 Genocide Convention, under which all member states have an obligation to prevent and address genocide. In 2022, the court ruled that The Gambia had standing to bring the case.

Rehan’s mother was also delighted when he told her about the ruling. “She was saying that we had won and that we would be able to return to our homeland,” he said.

The celebrations came against a backdrop of difficult living conditions. Rain fell over the camps on Thursday as Cyclone Akvan bore down on the Bay of Bengal, adding to the discomfort of families living in cramped shelters.

It was a reminder that while the verdict had brought recognition to their suffering, it had not changed the daily realities of refugee life. Nurul Amin, a Rohingya youth, said he was happy when the court recognised the genocide, but the announcement also brought back painful memories.

“I was happy, but I was also remembering what happened to us in 2017. I was remembering the horrific military operation, the violence I experienced and the home I had to leave behind,” he said.

Rohingya activist Rohimullah said the announcement was difficult to put into words. It reminded him of those the community had lost and the darkest days of their displacement. He described the judgement as a moment of relief and renewed hope, but said it could not bring back loved ones or erase painful memories.

Nasir Uddin, a professor of anthropology at the University of Chittagong who researches the Rohingya crisis, said the ICJ ruling was important to ensure justice and accountability from the victims’ perspective.

“In the 21st century, we talk about liberal democracy, globalisation and global justice. Yet such a massive genocide happened before our eyes. The judgement was essential to establish the concept of global justice,” he said.

Michael Kugelman, a resident senior fellow for South Asia at the Atlantic Council, said the ruling meant that Dhaka would need stronger assurances from Myanmar about the safe return of Rohingya refugees under any repatriation arrangement.

“I think that this will also have some impact on the dynamics around negotiations between Bangladesh and Myanmar on the return of Rohingya refugees, now that an international court has said that they experienced genocide,” Kugelman told Al Jazeera.

For the Rohingya, however, the hope of going home remains central. They want accountability for those responsible for the atrocities, the restoration of their rights and citizenship, and a safe and dignified return to Myanmar.

Nurul Amin said he hoped the international community would look beyond the humanitarian crisis and address the political causes of their displacement. He said he wanted freedom in Myanmar, democracy and an end to discrimination and military dictatorship.

“We are hoping this judgement will lead to something more – that we will finally be able to return home with our rights and dignity,” he said.

Maung Solaiman Shah contributed to this story.

articles.title: Pro-life group says Trump admin didn't give key abortion drug commitments before Overton FDA nomination pulled
articles.excerpt: Erik Baptist, senior vice president of legal strategy at Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, explains why the group opposed Heidi Overton’s FDA confirmation without commitments from the Trump administr...
articles.body_text:
Erik Baptist, senior vice president of legal strategy at Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, explains why the group opposed Heidi Overton’s FDA confirmation without commitments from the Trump administration to restore in-person dispensing requirements for abortion drugs and address concerns about the agency’s mifepristone safety study.

A leading pro-life group said it opposed advancing Heidi Overton's nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration without commitments from the Trump administration on abortion drug policy. The White House withdrew her nomination this week amid questions about her support in the Senate.

In an interview with Fox News Digital, Erik Baptist, senior vice president of legal strategy at Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, said his group asked the Senate to hold up Overton’s confirmation until it received "firm commitments" from the administration on two fronts regarding abortion drug policy.

Baptist said the group wants the next FDA nominee to commit to ending mail-order access to abortion drugs authorized under the Biden administration and changing how the agency studies the safety of those pills.

"Right now, we’re seeing more abortions in this country than before the Supreme Court’s decision overturning Roe v. Wade," Baptist said. "That’s precisely because of what the Biden FDA did to authorize mail-order abortion drugs. We’re seeing upwards of 15,000 abortion drugs and abortions occurring in pro-life states. Those states can’t meaningfully enforce their laws while this nationwide policy is in place."

WHITE HOUSE PULLS TRUMP'S FDA PICK HEIDI OVERTON ON EVE OF SENATE PANEL VOTE

The White House said Heidi Overton lacked the votes on Capitol Hill and pulled her nomination. (Bonnie Cash/UPI/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"Under the Biden-era policy, anybody can obtain these drugs online and receive them through the mail," he continued. "When I say anybody, we’ve seen news story after news story every week about men and other predators obtaining these drugs to coerce or poison women into taking them against their will. Until that policy changes, no pregnant woman is safe from these drugs. My question to this administration is: How many more women have to be poisoned or coerced with abortion drugs before you take action on this drug?"

Under the Biden administration, the FDA eliminated the in-person dispensing requirement for mifepristone, allowing it to be prescribed without an in-person visit by certified prescribers and dispensed by certified pharmacies through the mail.

On the group's second point of concern, Baptist said the FDA needs to conduct a new study to show the safety — or lack thereof — of mifepristone.

"The problem is that the study is significantly flawed," he said. "It’s almost designed to fail and not lead to future changes to the drug regimen. We have asked for more robust data because significant information is currently lacking, including transparency into the agency’s methodology and an invitation for outside experts who have studied this drug over the last few decades."

"This is something that should be bipartisan. Everybody should support better data, more transparency and outside experts who can inform an agency that has never conducted such a study before," he added.

Several pro-life groups and Republican lawmakers have urged the Trump administration to complete the FDA’s safety review of mifepristone and consider reinstating safeguards, while some have called for removing the drug from the market.

The FDA said the review is ongoing, with study results expected in December 2026 and a final report expected by March 2027.

The White House pulled Overton’s nomination to lead the FDA earlier this week, one day before a Senate committee vote. President Donald Trump picked Overton, a physician and White House advisor, in August to succeed Marty Makary, who resigned from the position in May.

Kyle Diamantas has led the agency in an acting capacity since Makary’s departure.

WOMAN WHO SAYS ABORTION PILLS NEARLY KILLED HER URGES RFK JR TO ACT AS GROUP DEMANDS MAIL-ORDER CRACKDOWN

Heidi Overton had appeared alongside President Donald Trump in the Oval Office as he signed an executive order calling for changes to childhood vaccine recommendations. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Overton also previously served as vice chair and chief policy officer at the America First Policy Institute, a conservative think tank, where she criticized expanded access to abortion pills in a 2023 policy brief.

The White House said Overton lacked the votes on Capitol Hill and pulled her nomination, although Sen. Bill Cassidy, chair of the Senate health committee, contended that he believed she could have been confirmed.

"The White House abandoned a viable confirmation path for Dr. Overton. The WH said that this was because she did not have the votes to pass. This was odd as I was having productive conversations with members," Cassidy, R-La., wrote on X. "I believe she would have had the votes to pass out of committee and pass the full Senate."

Baptist said he did not know whether the White House was concerned about pro-life votes or other constituencies but thinks Cassidy "was making progress with the administration to secure the commitments we were seeking and asking the Senate to hold the administration accountable for."

Cassidy had criticized Overton for supporting Trump’s decision to recommend changes to the childhood vaccine schedule, but the senator said he had been convinced she was right for the job after she committed to "follow the science." She had appeared alongside Trump in the Oval Office as the president signed an executive order calling for changes to childhood vaccine recommendations, including a recommendation to administer measles, mumps and rubella vaccines separately once individual shots become available domestically.

Cassidy said at a September hearing that there was no scientific evidence for Trump’s suggestion that the combined shot could be "quite lethal" and warned the remark could discourage vaccination.

"Yes, senator, the MMR vaccine is safe and effective," Overton told Cassidy.

Pressed on what she would do if Trump asked her to disregard the FDA’s safety standards, Overton said she would give the president her best advice and follow the legal requirements for reviewing individual products.

Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., asked Overton directly whether Trump was wrong. Overton reiterated that the vaccine was safe and effective and called it the best tool available during the measles outbreak. Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., questioned why she had not corrected Trump in the Oval Office.

"Why should we expect you to stand up to the president as FDA commissioner?" Markey asked.

Sen. Bill Cassidy, chair of the Senate health committee, said he believed Heidi Overton could have been confirmed to lead the FDA. (Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images)

Baptist said he wants the next FDA commissioner to be somebody who "understands science" and has experience managing an agency.

"The FDA is a very large bureaucracy with multiple constituencies, so understanding how science is conducted and how drugs are approved will be essential to any successful candidate or nominee for the position," he said.

But, Baptist said, the administration does not have to wait for an FDA nominee to take the position before it can take the action on abortion pill policy that his group desires.

"The good news is that it doesn’t have to be the nominee who makes these commitments. The administration can do it because it has admitted that it can take these actions immediately using its own authority," he argued. "That power is within the administration’s possession. It’s a matter of political will, not legal ability."

"With regard to fixing the study, I think they can make those changes now," Baptist continued. "They don’t need to wait for a confirmation, especially when they’re saying they’re going to finish the study in December of this year. We might not have an FDA commissioner at that point, or even a nominee. So they need to fix it immediately and course-correct the study before it’s fatally flawed and completed next year."

Fox News' Stepheny Price contributed to this report.

articles.title: US warned supplying nuclear-powered submarines to Australia would diminish its own fleet for ‘many years’
articles.excerpt:
Congressional Budget Office also questions whether Australian-flagged vessels could be compelled into a conflict with China under Aukus deal

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcas...
articles.body_text:
Congressional Budget Office also questions whether Australian-flagged vessels could be compelled into a conflict with China under Aukus deal

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Providing nuclear-powered submarines to Australia would diminish the US navy’s own fleet for “many years”, a new report for the US Congress has cautioned, questioning whether Australian-flagged vessels could be compelled into service in a conflict with China.

The US navy’s latest shipbuilding plan does not countenance the Aukus agreement in its forecasts at all, noting only in a footnote that the transfer of any Virginia-class submarine to Australia “has not been factored into the plan”, the report says.

But the Congressional Budget Office has evaluated the impact of Aukus, releasing detailed analysis on Friday morning, finding “the US submarine industrial base is currently struggling to meet the Navy’s demand for submarines”.

“Increasing production further to replace SSNs [attack submarines] sold to Australia would increase the challenges that the Navy and the shipyards are facing,” the report found.

“The sale of SSNs to Australia would reduce the number of attack submarines available to the Navy for many years.”

Under the so-called “Pillar One” of Aukus, the US has agreed to sell between three and five in-service Virginia-class submarines to Australia, beginning in 2032.

The CBO analysis questioned whether any submarines transferred to Australia could be utilised in the event of a US conflict with China.

“Would China be less deterred if the United States reduced the number of its attack submarines to help Australia develop its own submarine force?”

The report argued that because of the longstanding, and robust, alliance between the US and Australia, boosting the Australian navy’s submarine fleet could help offset the US Navy’s “potential loss of capability”.

“That loss might even be more than offset because the Australian submarines would be based in the Western Pacific region and therefore could respond more quickly to any conflict with China over Taiwan or other issues in the South China Sea.

“However, Australia would control its own submarines, and their participation in any particular conflict would not be guaranteed.”

In 2023, Australia’s defence minister, Richard Marles, said Australia would make no promises it would deploy its submarines in support of any US conflict with China, and that any future Australian submarines would be “under the complete control of the Australian government of the day”.

Submarine-building rates in the US have been tenaciously laggard. The country’s shipyards are currently producing Virginia-class submarines at a rate of 1.13 a year: that rate needs to lift that to two submarines a year to service America’s own needs, and 2.33 a year to have additional boats to transfer to Australia.

The CBO report said submarine-building rates had slowed over the past two decades, and Virginia-class submarines were delayed between 24 and 36 months.

“Building … submarines took five to six years in the 2000s but now takes an average of 10 to 11 years, according to current schedules.”

The US legislation governing Aukus states that the president of the US can only transfer a submarine to Australia if losing that submarine from US service “will not degrade the United States undersea capabilities”.

The US can refuse to transfer any submarines to Australia without penalty, under the terms of the Aukus agreement.

Critics of Aukus have said there is vanishingly little chance the US will have the capacity to sell any of its in-service submarines to Australia.

The former foreign affairs minister Bob Carr told Guardian Australia both countries were “living a lie” in upholding the fiction that the submarine deal would happen. “It’s now conventional wisdom in Washington as well as in Canberra that we’re not going to get the subs.”

But the deal has avowed, bipartisan broad political support across both the US and Australia. Marles said earlier this month: “Aukus is happening, our alliance is happening, and all of that continues unimpeded.”

Pete Hegseth, the US secretary of defense, affirmed his support for the Aukus agreement, and the two countries’ commitment “to advance the alliance and strengthen deterrence in the Pacific” at a meeting with Marles in September.

The US Congressional Research Service has openly countenanced an “alternative division of labour” under which no Virginia-class submarines are ever transferred to Australian control.

The research service’s latest report on Aukus, issued in January, considered a revision of the Aukus deal under which the submarines earmarked for sale to Australia were instead retained under US command to be sailed out of Australian bases.

The report argued both for and against the US selling three Virginia-class submarines to Australia, beginning in 2032. But it makes the case that, in the event of a “conflict or crisis” with China over Taiwan, submarines under Australian command could not be ordered into operation, whereas US-commanded vessels, operated out of Australian bases, could be immediately deployed.

articles.title: House China panel calls for cutting defense contracts over aerospace ties to Beijing's military
articles.excerpt:
Congressional watchdog leaders Randall Schriver and Mike Kuiken warn China could exploit American chips and AI to strengthen its military.

A new congressional report is urging the U.S. to restrict in...
articles.body_text:
Congressional watchdog leaders Randall Schriver and Mike Kuiken warn China could exploit American chips and AI to strengthen its military.

A new congressional report is urging the U.S. to restrict investments in China’s aerospace sector and withhold taxpayer funding from companies that build military capabilities for U.S. adversaries, warning that Western commercial partnerships transferred technology and expertise to Chinese firms with military ties.

The 65-page report, titled "China's Wingmen: How Western Government Policy Enabled China's Rise in the Skies," follows a year-long investigation by the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, led by Chairman John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and Ranking Member Ro Khanna, D-Calif. It examined how legal commercial partnerships transferred advanced technology and manufacturing expertise to Chinese military-linked companies.

China's People's Liberation Army (PLA) is the country's military, which the committee says has benefited from civilian aerospace technology transfers.

"American and European companies transferred technology to China that could be used against our brave men and women in uniform. With the CCP’s military-civil fusion there are no private companies in China," Moolenaar said in a statement shared with Fox News Digital.

CHINA COULD EXPLOIT US TECHNOLOGY TO THREATEN AMERICAN FORCES, CONGRESSIONAL WATCHDOG LEADERS WARN

China's domestically produced C919 passenger jet sits on display at the Singapore Airshow on Feb. 4, 2026, in Singapore. (VCG/VCG via Getty Images)

"The PLA will exploit civilian technology and use it to advance its military ambitions and that is what happened here."

The report singled out European aerospace giant Airbus, which receives U.S. defense contracts while maintaining manufacturing partnerships in China. Although Airbus sold its stake in an AVIC affiliate in 2025, its commercial partnerships with the Chinese aerospace conglomerate continue, according to the committee.

The bipartisan panel examined at least six U.S.-China joint ventures involving American defense suppliers GE Aerospace, Honeywell Aerospace and RTX subsidiary Collins Aerospace.

Investigators found that GE transferred foundational avionics technology to a joint venture with a subsidiary of AVIC, the Chinese state-owned conglomerate that develops military aircraft, including the J-20 stealth fighter. The committee said GE withheld its original joint venture agreement despite repeated requests.

RUSSIA IS HELPING CHINA CLOSE GAP WITH US FORCES AMID TAIWAN TENSIONS, WARNS LONGTIME MILITARY LEADER

An Airbus aircraft assembly facility in Tianjin, China, on Oct. 25, 2025. The European aerospace manufacturer opened its second A320-family final assembly line in the city that month. (VCG/VCG via Getty Images)

The American companies maintained that their Chinese partnerships supported civilian aircraft and complied with U.S. export controls. The report also cited previous export-control settlements involving all three companies but did not establish that the partnerships under investigation violated U.S. law.

"We appreciate the Committee’s work ensuring the U.S. retains its position as the world’s commercial aviation leader while protecting our most sensitive technologies. We have and will continue to follow relevant U.S. laws and regulations, as the report acknowledges,"a Collins Aerospace spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

The committee urged the Federal Aviation Administration not to certify Chinese-manufactured aircraft, citing state subsidies and Beijing's refusal to release a final report on the 2022 China Eastern Airlines crash.

"The report’s only recommendation directed at the FAA is that they do not certify Chinese-made aircraft, which the agency has not done," an FAA spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

A J-20 stealth fighter jet of the Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) Air Force performs at the China International Aviation and Aerospace Exhibition, or Airshow China, in Zhuhai, Guangdong province, China Nov. 9, 2022. (China Daily via Reuters)

A representative for Airbus did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

articles.title: US missile shortages create a range problem, report shows
articles.excerpt: The U.S. has burned through stockpiles of critical long-range missiles, which may force military forces to fall back on munitions with ranges of under 300 miles, according to an analysis this month by...
articles.body_text:
The U.S. has burned through stockpiles of critical long-range missiles, which may force military forces to fall back on munitions with ranges of under 300 miles, according to an analysis this month by the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

The report analyzed data on munitions expenditures that were current as of November 3 to provide estimates of how missile usage against Iran is affecting U.S. defense posture globally.

“In the 39-day campaign until the April 8 ceasefire and subsequent operations, the United States expended between a third and two-thirds of key munition inventories,” according to the report.

It points out that, while the Pentagon has made agreements with manufacturers to boost production rates and Congress may provide funding, time is of the essence to rebuild the U.S. arsenal, as the current strain on stockpiles has created vulnerabilities.

“Does the United States have enough munitions to renew the fight? The short answer is yes—against Iran. Against China, there is great concern. Rebuilding inventories will require a multiyear commitment extending beyond the current crisis,” the analysis notes.

CSIS produced a list of missile types sorted into nine categories. Seven of the nine categories were classed as having “detrimental effects” in terms of resupply capacity.

According to this analysis, Patriot missiles, Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) missiles, and Standard Missiles, which are vertically launched surface-to-air missiles, are listed as “heavily used, no substitutes,” indicating that stockpiles are in dire condition.

Long-range ground-attack missiles including Tomahawks, AGM-158 JASSM cruise missiles, and Precision Strike Missiles (PrSMs) are described as being “heavily used” with “some substitutes.”

The only missile types listed as having “no significant constraints in most scenarios” are short-range munitions – including air-to-air missiles and short- and medium-range missiles, including GBU-39B small-diameter bombs and the AIM-120 AMRAAM, which is primed to strike low-altitude targets.

CSIS observes that, while the U.S. is still capable of leveraging existing missiles against targets in the short term, shortages of long-range munitions create operational challenges.

“The United States has large numbers of munitions with the same explosive yield and accuracy as the long-range systems described above but with ranges under 300 miles,” according to the report.

The U.S. is at risk of losing its ability to project power through ballistics across long distances.

At the same time, munitions with shorter ranges increase the importance of establishing air superiority. This could create complexities if the U.S. faces a powerful adversary that has sufficient air power and defenses to fend off shorter-range weapons and prevent them from being effective.

“Although production rates are increasing, demand exceeds supply—from both the United States and allies—so timelines have lengthened,” the report warns. “The problem is not money, assuming Congress continues its support, but time.”

Zita Ballinger Fletcher previously served as editor of Military History Quarterly and Vietnam magazines and as the historian of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration. She holds an M.A. with distinction in military history.

articles.title: Pentagon lacks ‘overarching plan’ for munitions production, watchdog warns
articles.excerpt:
Facing depleted stockpiles, the Pentagon is briskly trying to ramp up manufacturing of munitions.

The problem is that it is ordering missiles, artillery shells and other munitions without regard to w...
articles.body_text:
Facing depleted stockpiles, the Pentagon is briskly trying to ramp up manufacturing of munitions.

The problem is that it is ordering missiles, artillery shells and other munitions without regard to what the military actually needs, according to a new report.

“DoD does not have an overarching plan that links munitions production and funding to requirements,” warned the Government Accountability Office study.

Pentagon officials told investigators that “in lieu of a plan, DoD and the services can be reactive to global events rather than driven by total requirements.”

The GAO report is the public version of a classified study completed in September 2026.  Thus, it doesn’t include “information that DOD deemed classified or sensitive, such as trends in DoD munitions inventories, persistent shortfalls and how these shortfalls have affected DOD’s support to war plans.”

Nonetheless, the report does hint at a mismatch — real and potential — between what the Pentagon is buying and what the military needs.

The Army is desperately trying to boost production of 155mm howitzer shells after shortages were exacerbated in support of allies and partners. That effort is already plagued by manufacturing woes such as a new Texas plant that cost nearly $500 million, but failed to produce any shell components.

Now the question is exactly how many shells the Army needs.

The “Army’s ramp-up in production of 155-millimeter artillery shells to address shortages exacerbated by U.S. support to allies and partners was not driven by a need to address DoD’s total munitions requirement,” GAO said.

“DOD is taking steps to increase production in response to real shortages,” Diana Moldafsky, a director of GAO’s Defense Capabilities and Management team, told Defense News. “That said, we found some cases where DOD increased production in response to immediate shortages without basing the increase on its total requirement for that munition.”

Nor does the Pentagon have a good grasp on how much ammunition it actually has.

Each military service has its data system to track munitions inventories, which is then aggregated by DoD’s Munitions Readiness Initiative to provide, in theory, a near real-time glimpse of stockpiles as well as supply chain links.

“In total, MRI pulls from 37 DOD data sources through a mix of automated connections and some manually updated data,” GAO noted.

However, the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition and Sustainment “does not consistently reconcile MRI munitions inventory data against the services’ own data systems.” Nor does it have “a data management plan detailing how data is aggregated in the MRI tool from across the services.”

“MRI does aggregate from the individual services’ data systems, but we found instances where the numbers in the tool differed from the services’ databases,” said Moldafsky.

Authority over munitions inventories is also fragmented among multiple offices within the DoD and the program executive offices in individual services. Working groups that are supposed to bring them together lack authority and accountability.

All of which points to the root of the problem: no one is really in charge. “DoD has not identified an office or entity and delegated to it authority that empowers the leadership to make decisions that improve munitions inventories departmentwide and hold them accountable for the outcomes achieved, such as improving munitions inventory levels,” the GAO report notes.

GAO recommended that DoD create an overarching plan to match munitions requirements, production and funding, as well as metrics to track progress. Without it, the report warns, the “DoD and the services are not well-positioned to address persistently low munitions inventories or risk, for example, investing in munitions that are projected to exceed the total munition requirement.”

Michael Peck is a correspondent for Defense News and a columnist for the Center for European Policy Analysis. He holds an M.A. in political science from Rutgers University. Find him at theuncommondefense.com. His email is mikedefense1@gmail.com.

articles.title: More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged
articles.excerpt:
Northern Uganda is suffering from a severe drought

In Uganda's northern Karamoja region, Elijah Lobur and his family now eat just one meal a day.

A severe drought that began in April has destroyed c...
articles.body_text:
Northern Uganda is suffering from a severe drought

In Uganda's northern Karamoja region, Elijah Lobur and his family now eat just one meal a day.

A severe drought that began in April has destroyed crops, while food brought in from elsewhere has become increasingly unaffordable.

"Seven months without rain has brought us to this point where we now live in hunger," the 44-year-old farmer, who lives with his grandmother, wife and five children, told the BBC.

"Even some of the wild plants that we used to eat have withered and dried up."

Local officials say more than 90% of crops have failed in the region, where agriculture is largely rain-fed.

Further south, in Malawi, Mathews Nkhambala has experienced the devastating effects of flooding.

In April 2024, barely a year after Tropical Cyclone Freddy devastated the country's southern region, floods displaced people in Chikwawa district.

Nkhambala fled to higher ground with his wife and four children as floodwaters swept through his village.

"As we reached a safe height, we saw our house swept away right in front of our eyes. Everything I had was gone," he told the BBC.

He lost a harvest of 15 bags of sorghum and part of his farmland. His children were so traumatised that they stopped going to school.

"They refused to go to school for many months. They were so disturbed," he recalled.

After relocating and trying to rebuild his life, Nkhambala is now facing another climate challenge - this time a lack of rain.

"This time we fear there may be no harvest. I have no clue what I will do."

A government assessment after Cyclone Freddy found that Malawi had experienced more than 50 disasters linked to storms, floods, landslides and droughts since 1980, affecting millions of people.

While Uganda and Malawi are suffering the effects of climate change and their governments are asking for assistance adapting to the new global weather patterns, they are among 23 African countries yet to submit National Adaptation Plans (NAPs) to the UN climate convention secretariat.

These are the plans that detail how climate change has affected them and the risks they face, and so help make a case for what assistance they need. Without them, experts say, it becomes difficult to secure funding.

"Our region has experienced cyclical droughts for decades, but there has been no action plan to tackle these climate impacts," said Milton Lorpia, who works for Warrior Squad Foundation in Karamoja region of Uganda.

"If only such a plan were in place and implemented, it would certainly have helped us."

Mathews Nkhambala and his wife fear their harvest may fail this year

The African Group of Negotiators at the ongoing UN climate summit (COP31) in Turkey is pushing for adaptation finance to be tripled by 2035, from an annual $40bn (£30bn) baseline that it says developed countries committed to providing by 2025. The interpretation of that commitment remains contested.

The proposal was not accepted for formal negotiations at the summit, although African negotiators have continued to push for it.

The funding is intended to help vulnerable countries prepare for and withstand climate change-induced extreme weather, such as droughts, floods and wildfires.

But the European Union, one of the largest providers of climate finance, says the priority should be ensuring existing commitments reach vulnerable countries rather than setting new funding targets.

"We haven't come to the table with additional monies or additional capital. It's about what we have committed already and ensuring it's deployed," Darragh O'Brien, who leads the EU delegation at COP31 on behalf of the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, told a press conference.

He acknowledged that developing countries faced difficulties accessing available funding, saying the process needed to be improved.

Wopke Hoekstra, the European Commission's climate commissioner, also argued that the summit should focus on delivering existing pledges rather than making new ones.

"If you are a vulnerable nation in the Pacific or one of the LDCs (Least Developed Countries) and the money is in the bank but does not land on the ground then it is effectively meaningless," he said.

'It can kill us': Kenyans fear impact of El Niño with floods predicted

Hoekstra said the EU had provided $30bn of the $100bn in climate finance committed by developed countries in recent years, adding that other wealthy nations should contribute more.

The scale of the need is substantial. According to the UN's Adaptation Gap Report published last year, sub-Saharan Africa requires about $51bn annually in adaptation finance, while the Middle East and North Africa needs $112bn.

Globally, developing countries will need about $300bn annually by 2035, according to the UN's latest report. Yet they received only about 10% of that amount from developed countries in 2024.

Climate-related loss and damage in Africa is projected to cost $440bn between 2020 and 2030, according to Nairobi-based think tank Power Shift Africa.

Under the 2015 Paris climate agreement, developed countries are required to provide financial support to developing nations, including for climate adaptation.

But why have so many African countries failed to prepare plans that could help them identify their needs and build resilience?

"If you look closely, the countries that are yet to submit their NAPs are already dealing with multiple crises, including debt distress, economic pressures and other issues," said David Abudho, climate justice lead at the aid agency, Oxfam.

"Their governments' ability to invest in climate adaptation is limited."

Sheila Apiny, regional climate justice adviser at ActionAid, said the lack of plans reflected a wider shortage of financial and technical support.

"The absence of NAPs in so many countries is, in itself, evidence of an adaptation finance and capacity gap," she argued.

She said this created a vicious cycle - countries lack support to prepare their plans, while not having the plans makes it harder to secure funding for climate resilience.

"When countries lack adequate adaptation planning and, more importantly, the resources to implement those plans, governments are forced into a cycle of responding to disasters instead of preventing or reducing their impacts," said Amos Wemanya, senior climate adviser at Power Shift Africa.

"Instead of investing in early warning systems, climate-resilient agriculture, water security and flood protection, scarce public resources are repeatedly diverted towards emergency relief and reconstruction. This costs more over time and leaves communities increasingly vulnerable."

Under the 2015 Paris climate agreement, developed countries are required to provide financial support to developing nations, including for climate adaptation

African negotiators acknowledge that adaptation plans help countries prioritise investments and attract funding, but argue that their absence should not be used to deny them financial support.

"Of course, having a comprehensive NAP helps countries prioritise investments and prepare proposals for climate finance," said Mahlet Eyassu Melkie, a senior strategic adviser to Ethiopia's COP32 presidency.

"But Africa's adaptation financing needs are based on scientific assessments, climate vulnerability, national priorities and regional estimates – not simply on whether every country has submitted a particular planning document."

The UN Development Programme, which has helped more than 45 countries prepare their plans, said NAPs can help governments mobilise international support and coordinate climate action.

Fred Njehu, a Pan-African political strategist at Greenpeace Africa, said their absence could nevertheless create significant obstacles.

"It is fair to acknowledge that missing adaptation plans act as a major functional barrier that severely bottlenecks the speed, volume and quality of international funding a country can access," he said.

But having a plan does not guarantee the money needed to implement it.

"Even countries that have completed their NAPs have not received money anywhere near what they require for implementation of their adaptation plans," Apiny said.

Kenya offers an example of how adaptation measures can help communities cope with climate pressures.

The walls of the sand dams store water underground when the rivers dry up

In the country's arid and semi-arid south-east, concrete sand dams slow the flow of seasonal rivers, allowing sand to accumulate and store water underground. Communities can access it during dry periods using hand pumps or by scooping it out.

UK charity Sand Dams Worldwide and its local partner, the Africa Sand Dam Foundation, said they had built about 1,300 such dams, improving access to water as droughts become more frequent and intense.

But many vulnerable communities elsewhere on the continent are still waiting for similar interventions.

Back in drought-hit Karamoja, Lobur wonders how different things might have been if farmers had access to small-scale irrigation schemes.

"We do have some underground water sources in some places. If there were proper plans and programmes, we could have tapped them to grow food, but we are having to live in hunger instead," Lobur said.

"My grandmother keeps reminding us how she lost eight children during a famine-like situation in 1982, and we all fear we might perish like that too."

Survivors of Uganda's deadly landslide seek justice at the UN

What is the Paris Agreement and why does 1.5C matter?

Global nature talks reach deal but money remains an issue

articles.title: Al Gore says climate change supporters 'keep quiet' about their beliefs for fear of retaliation
articles.excerpt:
Former Vice President Al Gore suggested that climate change supporters ‘keep quiet’ about their real beliefs to avoid retaliation amid dwindling polling.

Former Vice President Al Gore suggested on CN...
articles.body_text:
Former Vice President Al Gore suggested that climate change supporters ‘keep quiet’ about their real beliefs to avoid retaliation amid dwindling polling.

Former Vice President Al Gore suggested on CNN Thursday that people "keep quiet" about their support for action to address climate change for fear of backlash despite the issue's dwindling support ahead of the midterm elections.

"Inside Politics" host Dana Bash spoke to Gore about the 20th anniversary of his climate change documentary, "An Inconvenient Truth." She noted that while climate change was a major factor during the Obama and Biden administrations, the issue was hardly a factor in Democratic campaigns for the 2026 midterm elections.

"What is your message to 2028 candidates and how much they should talk about it?" Bash asked.

"And I guess, quite frankly, are you worried that Americans and leaders just don't care as much as they did 20 years ago?"

20 YEARS LATER, AL GORE AND HIS DIRECTOR DEFEND THEIR CONTROVERSIAL CLIMATE MOVIE 'AN INCONVENIENT TRUTH'

Former Vice President Al Gore discussed the 20th anniversary of his documentary "An Inconvenient Truth" on CNN Thursday. (Paul Marotta/Getty Images)

"Oh, I think they do," Gore responded. "There‘s a political version of what they call the business world 'greenhushing.' It’s different from 'greenwashing.' Greenhushing is when people continue to do the right thing, but they keep quiet about it, lest the evil Eye of Sauron focus on them. And I think that’s going to change in the wake of this election."

Gore made the comments after several polls showed that climate change ranked near or at the bottom of voters' concerns leading up to the November election. Last month, a Gallup poll ranked climate change last among eleven issues leading up to the midterms, with only 29% of voters considering it "extremely important" and 17% considering it "very important."

A Fox News Poll in September found only 1% of voters viewed climate change as the top issue facing the country.

Still, Gore maintained that the scientists interviewed in his film were "dead on" in their predictions and told CNN that he believes humanity can still respond to the climate crisis.

BILL MAHER CALLS OUT AL GORE FOR COMPARING TRUMP ADMINISTRATION TO NAZIS

Climate change ranked the lowest among voters' concerns in a Gallup poll ahead of the midterm elections. (Adobe Stock)

"When the underbrush of argumentation is cleared away and the central choice is revealed as a choice between what's right and what's wrong, then because of how we were created, I believe the outcome becomes foreordained. And I think we're very close to that point now," Gore said.

During the interview, Gore also said he's seen "tremendous momentum" in the right direction regarding climate change since 2006, with only a few instances in the wrong direction.

In a comment to Fox News Digital, Democratic strategist and pollster Doug Schoen agreed with Gore that climate change is still a major issue within the party and will continue to be one in 2028.

"Climate change will be a defining issue in the 2028 Democratic primary for president," Schoen said. "And the 20th anniversary of the film 'An Inconvenient Truth' simply underscores the continuing resonance of the climate issue with Democratic activists."

AL GORE WARNS ABOUT TRUMP'S 'JIHAD' OF CLEAN ENERGY TRANSITION

Democratic strategist Doug Schoen agreed with former Vice President Al Gore that climate change was still a major political issue. (Matthias Nareyek/Getty Images for Paramount Pictures)

Longtime Democratic consultant Julian Epstein disagreed, telling Fox News Digital, "If Democrats try to moralize, shame, virtue signal, they will again lose the public on this. If Democrats propose an austerity plan that goes after carbon, raises prices and does little to develop meaningful alternatives, they will also lose the public.

"Polls have consistently shown that 95% of working-class voters are not for the green agenda if it means higher energy prices," he continued. "What we need is an ‘all of the above’ strategy on energy that keeps prices down while developing as many alternative sources as possible."

Lindsay Kornick is an associate editor for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to lindsay.kornick@fox.com and on Twitter: @lmkornick.

articles.title: Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
articles.excerpt:
European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv.

"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating po...
articles.body_text:
European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv.

"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".

They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing.

Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks.

Trump had earlier held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, south-eastern China, with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One.

In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part.

Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".

"That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine."

But Putin also said that "every day" Russia heard that European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. "But we are not planning to attack anyone... Is that normal? I do not think so," he said. Still, Putin added, Russia understood that "discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans".

Jared Kushner told reporters that the US president had come away from Shenzhen believing that "peace is achievable".

Striking an upbeat note, Kushner said that the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of the US envoys "on our behalf" that the Europeans should be at the table and that Moscow was now "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on the idea enshrined in Nato's Article Five that requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who also was at the summit in Germany's capital, has long sought a guarantee equivalent to Nato's collective defence clause, and there has been little indication that Putin would accept that kind of condition.

Russia rejects outright the idea of Ukrainian membership of Nato, but reports say US negotiators have mulled the idea of giving Kyiv Article Five-style guarantees without being part of the Western defensive alliance if it agrees to painful territorial concessions.

Zelensky and the three European leaders – Merz, Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron – were not as upbeat as Kushner, and the Ukrainian president made clear that the Russian president had spurned every proposal so far: "Putin has always said no."

The German chancellor was equally sceptical, although he said with US involvement the chance of peace was increasing. Europe was willing to enter "serious discussions on European security" with Russia, he explained, "as long as it's matched with a serious discussion and only first a peace agreement with Ukraine".

"These talks have to begin, and we will accept if conditions are acceptable for Europe and Ukraine," said Merz.

He also said any attempts to divide Europe into spheres of influence run by major powers was unacceptable, amid concerns on the continent that this issue may have been on the agenda at the trilateral talks in Shenzhen.

Analysis: Trilateral summit high on spectacle, short on substance

"A 'Yalta format' will not bring peace," Merz said, referring to the post-World War Two agreement between the US, the USSR and Britain in 1945.

He also sought to downplay the Shenzhen summit as above all "a photo opportunity."

"The US understands that there can be no peace without us. We, in turn, know that with the United States by our side, the prospects for peace increase," Merz added.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk also took exception to Trump's description of Putin as a "friend" at the Shenzhen summit, saying:  "Mr Putin is not our friend and will never be."

Meanwhile, Macron urged Ukraine's allies to do the "maximum" to deliver the much-needed air defence systems Kyiv needed to repel deadly Russian attacks.

The French leader also urged the allies to "reopen the question" of Ukraine's membership in Nato.

There have been mixed messages from Moscow on European participation to the talks. Last week, following a visit to Moscow, the US envoys, Steve Witkoff and Kushner, appeared certain that Europe would soon have a seat at the negotiating table.

But the Russians were more circumspect and this week Putin's aide Yury Ushakov said a "great deal" would have to be done before the format could be expanded, suggesting that several more rounds of discussions would have to be held before any four-sided talks could take place.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Several buildings were damaged in the latest Russian attack on Ukraine's capital Kyiv

While Russia has engaged with several rounds of talks over the last year, little in Moscow's rhetoric or actions suggests that the Kremlin is considering scaling down its war on Ukraine.

It continues to pound Kyiv's energy infrastructure to cripple it as winter takes hold, increasing numbers of civilian casualties are being recorded across the country, and Kremlin officials have not budged from Russia's demands for Ukrainian sovereign territory.

As delegations were meeting in China and Germany on Thursday, several buildings in Kyiv's historic centre came under attack from drones. One person was killed in a strike on a residential building in the Podilskyi neighbourhood, while the Dutch and Austrian embassies as well as Saint Volodymyr's Cathedral reported damage.

And Putin also vowed that Moscow's response to a Ukrainian strike on the Crimean Bridge linking Russia with occupied Crimea would be "considerably more painful" than what Kyiv had achieved.

He also said he had discussed a "possible ceasefire in a number of areas" but had decided against it after the attack on the bridge.

Still, Putin claimed to be "interested" in ending the war and was ready to make compromises, while Ukraine and Europe were not.

"I assure you, we have no desire at all to continue this armed conflict," Putin said, despite the fact that Russia has in recent months intensified its attacks on Ukraine's critical infrastructure as cold winter approaches.

Kyiv and its European allies say that – in the absence of any major success on the vast front line – the Kremlin leader is seeking to break Ukrainian resistance by leaving millions of civilians without electricity and water supply.

UK to provide Ukraine with 1,000 long-range strike drones

articles.title: Legendary Las Vegas buffet to close for renovations after rumors swirled of its demise
articles.excerpt:
'The Five' panel discusses Las Vegas casinos getting rid of their buffets because of profit losses.

Visitors planning a trip to Las Vegas in the near future will miss out on one of the Strip's best-k...
articles.body_text:
'The Five' panel discusses Las Vegas casinos getting rid of their buffets because of profit losses.

Visitors planning a trip to Las Vegas in the near future will miss out on one of the Strip's best-known all-you-can-eat destinations, at least temporarily.

Caesars Palace announced Nov. 18 that its Bacchanal Buffet will temporarily close Monday, Jan. 4, 2027, for a major renovation, according to a news release shared with Fox News Digital.

The closure is expected to last until summer 2027, the hotel said.

BARGAIN BUFFET REFUSES TO DIE WHILE LUXURY DINING TAKES OVER VEGAS

Diners hoping to visit before construction starts have until Sunday, Jan. 3, to dine at the venue.

The upcoming project marks the second restoration for the 25,000-square-foot dining hall since it opened in September 2012, the resort said.

Caesars Palace, pictured, announced Nov. 18 that its Bacchanal Buffet will temporarily close Jan. 4, 2027, for a major renovation. (Denise Truscello/WireImage)

While a 2021 remodel updated several sections, the 2027 renovation will focus on the dessert area and five specialty kitchens serving Italian, Mediterranean, Asian grill and barbecue, sushi and sashimi and regional Asian dishes, the press release said.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Caesars Palace said the updates will bring new menu options and dining experiences to the Strip venue.

"We’re doubling down on Bacchanal Buffet with this renovation," Terrence O’Donnell, senior vice president and general manager of Caesars Palace, said in the release.

A preview of the planned renovation of Caesars Palace's 25,000-square-foot Bacchanal Buffet. (Caesars Entertainment)

"This next chapter brings fresh flavors and new experiences to the buffet, giving guests even more to look forward to when we welcome them back next summer."

The redesign will incorporate wood counters and shelving, brushed-metal finishes and illuminated onyx panels at the dessert station, the company said.

News of the months-long shutdown quickly drew mixed reactions among frequent Las Vegas visitors.

"Bacchanal is the first name out of everyone's mouth when someone asks about a Vegas buffet, so a renovation closure is going to surprise a lot of people booking winter trips," one Reddit user wrote.

"I think this is horrible news," another user wrote.

Caesars Palace's Bacchanal Buffet previously underwent a remodel in 2021 that updated several sections of the Las Vegas Strip dining hall. (iStock)

Others wondered why a partial remodel would take six months or so.

Some even questioned if the buffet would ever reopen.

"I have that fear myself. Six months seems like too long of a time for some minor renovations," another person replied.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Some Vegas fans pointed out, however, that extended construction timelines are standard on the Strip.

"Lengthy renovations are nothing new in Vegas. The question is how much of an improvement it will be," the commenter wrote.

As Fox News Digital reported in the summer, many of the famous buffets of Las Vegas fell victim in recent years to the COVID-19 pandemic, its social-distancing requirements and the trend of wealthier visitors seeking higher-end restaurants.

"Lengthy renovations are nothing new in Vegas," an online commenter wrote about the buffet's upcoming temporary closure. "The question is how much of an improvement it will be." (iStock)

There were over a dozen traditional Vegas buffets on the Strip in 2020, The Wall Street Journal reported.

Unlike many Strip resorts, budget casinos rely heavily on repeat local customers and value-conscious gamblers, making inexpensive buffets an effective way to drive casino traffic.

Fox News Digital reached out to Caesars Palace for additional information.

Kelly McGreal is a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. She and the team cover travel, food and drink, health, relationships and more. She also produces the weekly American Culture Quiz and handles other special projects.

articles.title: Cowboys great Michael Irvin outlines franchise's timeline to retain 'America’s Team' status
articles.excerpt:

More than three decades ...
articles.body_text:
Nick Wright, Chris Broussard, and Kevin Wildes ask if the Dallas Cowboys missing the playoffs would be a failure, and who will be atop Broussard’s MVP Ballot entering week 9.

More than three decades have passed since the Dallas Cowboys last advanced to a Super Bowl. In the years since, the franchise has experienced limited postseason success and has not returned to the NFC Championship Game.

Even so, the Cowboys remain one of the NFL’s most popular teams, frequently appearing in nationally televised windows and routinely drawing prime time interest. Their history, including five Super Bowl titles, which rank second among NFL teams, has helped the franchise retain its widely recognized "America’s Team" moniker.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

However, Cowboys Ring of Honor member Michael Irvin says the popular nickname should be retired unless Dallas starts winning.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Former Miami Hurricanes player and NFL Hall of Famer Michael Irvin looks on prior to the CFP Semifinal Vrbo Fiesta Bowl against the Ole Miss Rebels at State Farm Stadium on Jan. 08, 2026 in Glendale, Arizona. (CFP/Getty Images)

Irvin was a key part of the Cowboys’ three Super Bowl-winning teams in the 1990s, a run that built on the "America's Team" status. The retired wide receiver is giving his former team a decade-long runway to prove it should keep the label.

COWBOYS LEGEND DIGS DEEP INTO THE TEAM'S MISSING 'FIBER' THAT'S RESULTED IN SUPER BOWL DROUGHT

"A whole generation goes by and never experiences the glory of a championship story from the Dallas Cowboys," Irvin told CNBC on Thursday. "A generation is considered 40 years in the bible. So the Cowboys got about 10 years [to win a Super Bowl and keep the 'America’s Team' title]."

A general view of AT&T Stadium during the NFC Wild Card game between the San Francisco 49ers and the Dallas Cowboys on Jan. 16, 2022, in Arlington, Texas. (Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

Irvin wore the famed "star" on the side of his helmet for his entire NFL career and was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2007. He finished his career with more than 11,000 regular season receiving yards.

The Cowboys have missed the postseason in each of the past two seasons and could face another early offseason this year. Dallas is competing in an uneven NFC East, with the Philadelphia Eagles dealing with notable injuries and the Washington Commanders struggling.

COWBOYS STAR QUINNEN WILLIAMS REPEATS SIX WORD ANSWER 12 TIMES IN PRESSER AFTER MAJOR COACHING CHANGE

After the Cowboys' defense faltered again in a 46-40 loss to the San Francisco 49ers last Sunday, defensive coordinator Christian Parker was relieved of his play-calling duties. The Cowboys enter Sunday’s game against the 1-8 Tennessee Titans at 4-6, needing a win to keep their playoff hopes alive.

Dallas Cowboys receiver Michael Irvin (88) in action against Philadelphia Eagles defensive back Troy Vincent (23) at Veterans Stadium. (Lou Capozzola/USA TODAY NETWORK)

Parker, 34, spent the previous two seasons as the Eagles passing game coordinator & defensive backs coach.

In the the 10 games he's handled defensive playcalling for Dallas, the team ranks 32 in the NFL in total yards allowed and rushing yards given up. The 49ers put up 584 yards against Dallas in Week 10, the most the Cowboys’ defense has allowed in a home game in franchise history.

Chantz Martin is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Religious messages agriculture secretary emailed to staff deemed unconstitutional
articles.excerpt:
A federal judge ruled that messages sent by Brooke Rollins to USDA workers suggest Christianity is a shared faith and violate the first amendment

Religious messages that US agriculture secretary Broo...
articles.body_text:
A federal judge ruled that messages sent by Brooke Rollins to USDA workers suggest Christianity is a shared faith and violate the first amendment

Religious messages that US agriculture secretary Brooke Rollins emailed to the agency’s 100,000 employees were unconstitutional, and she must be careful to avoid proselytizing when communicating with workers, a federal judge ruled Thursday.

Rollins sent the messages, which included Christian messages and images, from her official email account on holidays such as Independence Day, Thanksgiving, Christmas and Easter. She did not send messages commemorating holidays from other religions.

“And so, like the very first disciples to encounter our risen Lord in the Upper Room almost two thousand years ago, this Easter let us too be alive with hope, full of Paschal joy, and confident in the mission each of us has been called for,” Rollins wrote in a 5 April email, marking Easter.

US district judge Trina Thompson in San Francisco said the emails violated the first amendment’s establishment clause, pointing to her position of authority, her use of an official email account and the messages suggesting that Christianity is the shared faith of Department of Agriculture (USDA) workers.

The USDA did not respond to a request for comment.

Employees cannot realistically opt out of reading emails from their agency director, and the messages could coerce them to hide their own faith or feel pressure to adopt Rollins’ Christian faith, Thompson ruled.

When disseminating religious messages, Rollins must stop if a colleague asks her to. “Cannot create a hostile work environment through persistent unwelcome advances” and “cannot use official authority to pressure subordinates” are commands that were quoted directly from a USDA policy on workplace religious expression that Rollins herself adopted.

Rollins may discuss her faith with interested colleagues, share why her faith is meaningful to her, politely invite co-workers to religious events and express her views in appropriate conversations, Thompson ruled, again quoting directly from Rollins’ policy.

Six USDA employees and the National Federation of Federal Employees, a labor union representing 19,000 USDA workers, brought the suit in May.

articles.title: Hasan Piker complains the far left has less leverage with Democratic Party because the Dems won too many seats
articles.excerpt:
Progressive streamer Hasan Piker complained that the Democrats won so big in the midterms that they will be less dependent on the far left for support.

Far-left streamer Hasan Piker lamented that Dem...
articles.body_text:
Progressive streamer Hasan Piker complained that the Democrats won so big in the midterms that they will be less dependent on the far left for support.

Far-left streamer Hasan Piker lamented that Democrats were so successful in the midterms they aren’t as dependent on their far-left flank.

The Democrats won a resounding victory in the midterms, which surprised not only the Republican Party, but the far left. Just a month before the midterms, Piker had talked about using the far left to pressure candidate James Talarico to push progressive policy, saying, "We are the force that allowed him to win this seat of power, and if he wants to maintain it, he’s got to play ball."

On Wednesday night, however, Piker played a different tune, noting that the Democratic Party was so successful it is no longer as dependent on support from its most left-wing members.

HASAN PIKER DECLARES 'WOKE IS BACK,' FANTASIZES ABOUT PUTTING DONALD TRUMP IN PRISON

"I think that there was a way that we could possibly get out of this fight with clear concessions on our agenda. We didn't. Part of that was because nobody expected the margin to be so vast," he said.

"If the margin was 10, then we could have made an impact. If the Democratic Party's margin of victory was 10 and not like f---ing 40, OK, then yeah, we could have had a big caucus, a socialist caucus, a fighter caucus, whatever you want to call it, that could potentially bully the party to be more responsive to the needs of the masses."

Livestreamer Hasan Piker lamented that the Democratic Party was so successful in the midterms that it is no longer as dependent on the far left's votes. (Noushad Thekkayil/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Piker also hit back at some critical comments from his fans.

"’This is you at your worst,'" he read aloud one comment before responding. "Why? Because I have to explain to you as an adult who is a political pundit how, you know, how change never really happens in Washington, D.C.?

"It hurts your feelings to hear someone explain to you why these things happen while simultaneously telling you how much I oppose it? Does it hurt your feelings to hear how this goes?" he asked. "It's just reality.

"I'm going to continue to explain how the sausage gets made, even if that hurts your f---ing feelings, because you're too dumb to understand."

Republican consultant Mary Marslender reacted to Piker's commentary.

"Hasan Piker is furious that Democrats won too many seats because it weakened the (Democratic Socialists of America's) ability to hold the Democratic Party hostage. Piker’s complaint reveals that the far left prefers narrow majorities so it can force its destructive socialist experiments on our country and European-style street chaos," she told Fox News Digital.

FAR-LEFT STREAMER HASAN PIKER GLOATS AFTER DEM BLOWOUT, PROMISES ‘JAIL’ FOR CONSERVATIVE ENEMIES

Livestreamer Hasan Piker had previously talked about potentially using the far left's leverage to push Texas Democrat James Talarico to govern with a left-wing agenda. (Piker via Sam Barnes/Web Summit via Sportsfile via Getty Images | Talarico via Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

Democratic strategist and co-host of "The Huddle" podcast Dan Turrentine told Fox News Digital, "There is the world as Hasan Piker wished it would be, and the real world. Socialists are utterly irrelevant in the next Congress. They are not the majority of America, nor are they the majority of the Democratic Party. In fact, in the next Congress, socialists will be a tiny 2.7% of the House Democratic caucus and there will be only one in the Senate, Bernie Sanders."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Far-left pundit Hasan Piker berated his listeners, saying that this latest bad news can be understood with a basic grasp of politics. (Phillip Faraone/Getty Images for Politicon)

Alexander Hall is an associate editor for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to Alexander.hall@fox.com.

articles.title: El Salvador’s Bukele expected to formalise bid for third presidential term
articles.excerpt:
Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele is set to formally register his candidacy for his country’s upcoming presidential race, as he seeks a third consecutive term.

Thursday was the registration deadline ...
articles.body_text:
Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele is set to formally register his candidacy for his country’s upcoming presidential race, as he seeks a third consecutive term.

Thursday was the registration deadline for the election, which is slated for February 28, 2027.

The 45-year-old president has been widely expected to seek re-election, a move that would further consolidate his party’s leadership in the Central American country.

Bukele is the founder and leader of the Nuevas Ideas party, which controls El Salvador’s Legislative Assembly by a wide margin.

While El Salvador’s constitution previously prohibited presidents from seeking immediate re-election, the Supreme Court overturned that rule in 2021, paving the way for Bukele to run for a second term in 2024.

Then, in 2025, the Legislative Assembly passed a constitutional amendment allowing Bukele to seek a third term. The amendment also extended the length of a presidential term from five to six years.

Bukele secured his party’s nomination for the 2027 race in July. He is expected to return to the ballot alongside his current vice president, Felix Ulloa.

Bukele’s time in office has been defined by a crackdown on criminal gangs that has won him massive popularity at home and turned him into an icon for the political right across Latin America.

In 2022, his government announced a so-called state of emergency to address high levels of crime in the country.

It empowered the police to make sweeping arrests, but it also heralded the suspension of key civil liberties. Some people were detained without charge. Mass trials have been carried out, with hundreds of defendants being sentenced at a time.

More than 1 percent of the country’s population is estimated to have been arrested as a result, with little due process for those seeking to contest their guilt, according to human rights groups.

Advocates also warn that rights abuses, torture and poor conditions are systematic in Salvadoran prisons.

The state of emergency has been extended for years, although it was initially intended as a temporary measure and the government claims El Salvador’s gangs have been all but dismantled.

The United States Treasury has also accused Bukele’s government of negotiating with the gangs in secret, offering incentives to help lower crime.

But experts say human rights activists and members of the news media have seen their ability to monitor abuses and corruption in the country hampered under Bukele.

Some, like human rights lawyer Ruth Lopez, have allegedly been detained for their work without access to legal support. She has spent more than a year in “incommunicado detention”, according to the group Amnesty International.

Under Bukele, El Salvador has also passed a Foreign Agents Law that allows the government to restrict civil society groups that receive funding from abroad.

Those efforts have prompted allegations that Bukele has weaponised the state against his critics.

But those concerns have done little to dent his popularity, and Bukele is considered the clear favourite to win the election.

A handful of candidates, including Maytee Iraheta of the right-wing Nationalist Republican Alliance and Rafael Aguirre of the left-wing Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front, are also set to contest the presidency.

articles.title: Religion should be removed from terrorism definition under Australian law as it gives ‘false credibility’, watchdog says
articles.excerpt:
Independent National Security Legislation Monitor says reference to religion has ‘contributed to discrimination and violence against religious minorities’

Get our breaking news email, free app or dai...
articles.body_text:
Independent National Security Legislation Monitor says reference to religion has ‘contributed to discrimination and violence against religious minorities’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Religion should be removed from Australia’s terrorism definition and making bomb threats should not result in life imprisonment, the country’s national security laws watchdog has said.

The highly anticipated report from the Independent National Security Legislation Monitor (INSLM), released Thursday, reviewed how terrorism has been defined in Australia over the past 25 years after a suite of laws were introduced following the September 11 attacks in the United States.

It comes as the Australian Federal Police (AFP) and the Australian Security and Intelligence Organisation (Asio) warn the rise of extremist, violent nationalism has changed the threat landscape and the motivations behind some terrorist attacks cannot be categorised into single ideologies.

Among the recommendations are suggested changes to the definition of terrorism to remove religion, which the INSLM head, Jake Blight, said gives accused terrorists “false credibility” and has a detrimental impact on religious minorities.

“Having a law that requires proof that terrorists were advancing a ‘religious’ cause gives these terrorists false credibility and reinforces their narrative that they are doing holy work,” the report said. “The same individuals will still be able to be prosecuted, but should be described as violent ideologues.

“Reference to religion in the definition of terrorism has also, in practice, contributed to discrimination and violence against religious minorities, especially Muslim Australians. This has a negative impact on social cohesion.”

The current definition of terrorism under the federal criminal code requires agencies to prove an act intends to cause serious harm to people or property in order to advance a political, religious or ideological cause.

A change in terrorism laws to remove religion as a primary motivation and place it as an example of a broader “ideology” category is in line with international best practice, Blight’s report said.

The INSLM noted the UN special rapporteur’s report earlier this year recommended defining terrorism acts by political and ideological causes and omitting religious motives, as references to religion have “discriminatory and stigmatizing effects that outweigh the benefits of criminally denouncing them”.

In his submission to the INSLM, Australia’s special envoy to combat Islamophobia, Aftab Malik, said keeping religion in as a terrorism motivation created a “climate of suspicion” around Muslims and “provided ammunition for far-right extremist narratives”.

Eleven Muslim advocacy and community groups, including the Australian Muslim Advocacy Network, welcomed the report’s recommendations and urged the Australian government to amend the laws.

“Every time someone in authority says that a motivation is ‘religious’, it uplifts ISIS, far-right and harmful media narratives all at once, by officially perpetuating the false premise that Islam encourages terrorism,” their joint statement said.

“This makes all Muslims feel under siege.”

The Executive Council of Australian Jewry, Australia’s peak Jewish body, described the report as “high-quality” but said removing religion as a motivating factor made “little sense when so many notorious terrorist acts have featured motifs, words and images that unmistakably refer to religious doctrines and beliefs”.

“The inclusion of ‘faith’ as a type of ideology does not solve the problem. Faith is not the same as religion and religion is more than an ideology,” the organisation’s co-chief executive, Peter Wertheim, said.

“It is clearly not appropriate for Australian law to decide which beliefs are an authentic expression of a religion and which are not. Even the adherents of a religion may have divergent views about such matters.”

The INSLM’s report made six other recommendations, including separating credible threats of terrorism from actual acts.

Under existing laws, a person found guilty of making a credible terrorist threat can be sentenced to life imprisonment with a mandatory minimum sentence of six years.

The report said the punishment was “disproportionate, unnecessarily complex and out of step with international standards” and recommended terrorism threats be treated as a separate charge with a maximum sentence of no more than five years.

The legislation monitor also recommended raising the bar on designating damage to property and electronic system as acts of terrorism while excluding advocacy, protest, dissent and industrial action.

Asio’s director-general, Mike Burgess, has warned of the rise in violent nationalist extremism in recent years. In an October submission to a parliamentary inquiry into radicalisation, Asio said around 65% of its counter-terrorism caseload related to religiously-motivated violent extremism while 35% related to ideologically-motivated extremism.

Baltimore Ravens defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver backed the franchise Thursday after head coach Jesse Minter sent veteran cornerback Marlon Humphrey home and benched him for Sunday's game against Carolina.

Humphrey is a healthy scratch for claiming on his podcast that Baltimore is "best at making criminals." Even after Humphrey apologized Wednesday, Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott dismissed the remarks as "not enough" before Minter stepped in.
