Speaking to the media following a Berlin meeting of the Coalition of the Willing (a group of about 35 countries formed to offer financial and diplomatic support for Ukraine), Jared Kushner – Donald Trump’s special envoy and son-in-law – said that the US president dialed into the meeting with European allies.

This comes after Trump’s meeting with Vladimir Putin in Shenzen, China earlier today. Kushner did not reveal any details about the president’s summit, but said that Trump came away from the trilateral China meeting thinking “peace is achievable”.

My colleagues are covering the latest here:

Democrats are celebrating after, with Mary Peltola’s victory in Alaska, they have officially secured 56 Senate seats after the midterm elections. But Jamie Davis, who lost an incredibly close election for a Senate seat in Louisiana and could have made it 57, told the Guardian it “stings to come close”.

In Louisiana, which has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 2008, Davis lost to the Republican congresswoman Julia Letlow 49.1% to 50.9%. He was about 25,000 votes short in a state that cast about 1.5m votes.

“Truthfully, I mean, it kind of stings to come close, but what hurts more than anything else is the fact that, still today, people don’t realize and know what we did,” Davis said. “There are still some people out there right now today who do not realize that I only came within a point – I think it’s one point, 1.1 or 1.2 points of winning this election.”

Across the south, Democrats are now wondering what might have been, as other Senate seats were also close. Barry Moore beat Everett Wess in Alabama by nine points, which is a landslide in many states and a catastrophe compared with Donald Trump’s 30-point margin in 2024. Angie Nixon, whose progressive politics and opposition to the Israeli government looked like a mismatch with Florida’s conservative electorate, came within three points of unseating the Republican incumbent, Ashley Moody, in a special election.

In the weeks since, Democrats have questioned which of those states might have been winnable had the national party cast its light in the south. And many have zeroed in on Louisiana.

Unlike Florida, Louisiana is not an expensive media market. And Louisiana does not have the depth of partisan political identification to be overcome in a place like Alabama.

Turnout nationwide ran about three points higher in November than four years ago. In Louisiana, it ran eight points higher, in line with states facing competitive US Senate elections like Michigan and Maine.

Senator Bill Cassidy and Trump have long been at odds. Cassidy voted for his impeachment and asked him not to run in 2024. Trump targeted the Louisiana Republican in the primary, endorsing Letlow.

The Callais decision from the US supreme court originated in Louisiana and prompted the state to postpone primary elections and set off redistricting battles this year. Combined with Cassidy’s third-place finish in the primary, the motivating effect of these events on Black voters should have also set off alarm bells among Democratic fundraisers and operatives, Davis said.

“When it became open, that’s the time when Republicans and Democrats and independents all should have been on notice that there’s an open seat in the Senate,” Davis said. “And not just automatically think that the seat is going to turn to be Republican.”

Donald Trump said that he will hold a press conference at the White House on Friday at 12pm ET following a “great and highly consequential trip” to the Philippines and China, which included a trilateral summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

The president announced the briefing on Truth Social, and also said he would discuss the trade deals he signed on his trip.

Republican Senate majority leader John Thune said Thursday that he’ll wait to see “what was discussed, and maybe what was agreed to” following Trump’s meeting in China with president Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin.

But Thune told reporters that “as far as I’m concerned, I’m with Ukraine” amid its war with Russia. Thune added he thinks most senators would agree with him.

“I think that’s going to be where most of my colleagues find themselves,” he said.

Donald Trump told NBC News he ⁠had discussed ⁠artificial ​intelligence (AI) with Chinese president Xi Jinping during ⁠his visit to China and the leaders ⁠both agreed that having guardrails ​was ‌good.

“We spoke ‌about SI, and we ‌both agreed that we want, we’re you know very much into SI, but we do ‌think that having guardrails, you know, at ​least on a minimal basis is a positive thing,” Trump said, ⁠using his preferred term for ​artificial intelligence, ​Super Intelligence, ​or SI.

Asked what “minimal ​basis” ‌meant, Trump ​said, “Well, ​we didn’t get into definitions.”

The Trump administration’s plans to build a “smart border wall” through a 500-mile stretch of Texas that includes the Big Bend national park recently got the green light from the supreme court. But those efforts are likely to slam into a big, blue wall.

Last week’s decision – the result of a continuing challenge to the administration’s decision to waive dozens of federal laws to speed wall construction in the Big Bend region – dealt a major blow to environmentalists and park enthusiasts, as well as locals who value the region’s remoteness, landowners who could see their properties devalued and businesses that rely on outdoor tourism.

But the ruling also came less than a week after Republicans suffered staggering losses in the midterms – including the once-in-a-generation flipping of Texas from red to blue. The state elected a Democratic governor after more than 30 years, and its first Democratic senator since the 1980s. The blue tsunami that handed both chambers of the US Congress to the Democrats with sizable majorities also flipped the Texas state house and weakened Republican control over the state senate.

That could all throw a wrench in the Trump administration’s plans.

The border wall is a federal project, so the White House will still have a great deal of power to push it forward. But for the first time, US Customs and Border Protection (CBP), the agency overseeing construction, will now face open hostility from the Lone Star state’s government as it contemplates resuming building efforts.

“Texas sovereignty and land should be protected,” Gina Hinojosa, the governor-elect, said in response to the ruling. “By letting the federal government bulldoze our land, the supreme court is continuing to put corporate profits before the people of Texas.”

Former president Barack Obama told newly elected House Democrats to not “get complacent” at a private reception hosted by Hakeem Jeffries, the current minority leader and likely House speaker in the new Congress. According to several reports, Obama was the special guest at an event that incoming members were ferried to in buses away from Capitol Hill on Wednesday, where he told the soon-to-be lawmakers, several of whom flipped Republican-held seats and won gerrymandered seats, to “hang on to your values, your commitments, your convictions”.

“Push for what you believe in, but understand the job you’ve taken is in a democracy. You’ve got to figure out how to actually get shit done with your colleagues,” Obama added. “And they’re not all representing the same constituencies that you are, and you want them to keep winning because that’s how you stay in a majority, and actually, over the long term, get stuff done.”

As the US catches up on Donald Trump’ shistoric trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping of China and Russia’s Vladimir Putin, the likely House speaker Hakeem Jeffries has weighed in on the summit.

“The President treats Russia like a friend and Canada like a foe,” Jeffries wrote on social media. “America just elected a Congress that knows it’s the exact opposite.”

The National Security Agency is seeing a third day of disruptions to its internal network, NSA Net, which allows staff to share highly classified information with each other, according to the New York Times.

The Times reports that employees at the NSA’s Maryland headquarters are under “code orange” for Thursday day shift, which requires non-essential workers are to stay home unless contacted by their supervisors.

Earlier this week the NSA said that it experienced a “temporary degradation” during scheduled routine maintenance, after reports that NSA Net had gone down.

In a statement, the agency said some internal systems were affected but that “mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational” and its ability to defend national security continues.

However, the NSA did not say what caused the outage, and whether the system was back to normal.

Over the coming weeks, Chuck Schumer and Chris Van Hollen, along with any late challengers, will vie for the party’s top Senate leadership post before lawmakers cast their votes. Here are four things to know about how the election works.

A secret, closed-door election: Unlike the public speaker of the House vote, where lawmakers cast ballots on the chamber floor, the Senate leadership contest takes place behind closed doors. Senators vote by secret ballot, and individual votes are not disclosed.

The winner only needs a caucus majority: The Democratic leadership race is decided solely by members of the party’s Senate caucus. Now that Democrats are set to have 56 seats in the new year, the winner will need secure 29 votes for the top role.

The vote is scheduled for next month: As things stand, the election is set for 1 December. Both incumbent senators and incoming Democratic members will participate, while retiring and outgoing senators will not vote, despite many having publicly weighed in on the race.

Republicans choose their leaders separately: Republicans hold their own closed-door leadership elections in both chambers. Earlier this month, House Republicans selected hardliner Jim Jordan as their leader after Mike Johnson opted not to run for minority leader. In the Senate, Republicans unanimously backed John Thune to continue leading the conference.

Following the news that Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be the next House speaker, leading to a full chamber vote which he is likely to win in the new year, it’s worth turning our attention to the ongoing battle in the upper chamber.

Here, top Democrats Chuck Schumer is vying to become Senate majority leader but is facing a challenge from progressive Chris Van Hollen. Despite the fact that Schumer is confident he has the votes to succeed, a number of lawmakers have pledged support for Van Hollen and say there needs to be change from leadership when Democrats take control of the Senate in the new year.

On Wednesday, Van Hollen said in a video on social media that he is continuing to meet with members one-on-one, and any discussion about expediting the closed-door vote to select the leader on 1 December has been quashed.

“We need to use this opportunity to change the way the Senate Democratic caucus does business,” Van Hollen said.

A reminder that my colleagues are covering the latest from the Apec summit. Donald Trump is now on his way back to Washington, following the first-of-its kind trilateral summit between Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

Trump said the leaders were “making history”, and “no peace is ever forged by declining opportunities”. The US president also noted that the three countries are “uniquely positioned” to discuss nuclear weapons.

Attorney general Todd Blanche’s wife, Kristine Blanche, who was appointed earlier this year to a US government advisory board on alternative medicine, has a website on which she marketed dietary supplements and treatments with unproven medical and health claims.

Blanche is a licensed physician assistant who says she has a PhD in breast thermography from the University of Science, Arts and Technology in Montserrat, a British territory in the Caribbean. She is also an advocate for alternative medical cures and holistic health.

Her site also links to a page called “Dr Blanche’s Dispensary”, where patients can buy supplement pills she recommends. She suggested that one product, a liquid herbal compound, could be used to treat the Epstein-Barr virus, although she misspelled “Epstein”.

There is no medication approved by the FDA to treat or cure Epstein-Barr, and the product itself does not claim to treat the virus.

Blanche also listed five supplements in her store, priced up to $63 a bottle, which she said can help treat human papillomavirus (HPV).

Another treatment Blanche offers, priced online at $595, claims to help men “boost” their testosterone levels and lose weight.

An anti-vaccine group led for years by Robert F Kennedy Jr said Meta has “taken down” posts on its accounts, after a Guardian report found the group was sharing false and misleading information about vaccines.

The Guardian reported on Wednesday that Children’s Health Defense (CHD) had earlier this year been allowed back on Facebook and Instagram, four years after Meta removed it from Facebook and Instagram for repeatedly violating its misinformation policies.

CHD said in posts on X that within hours of the Guardian’s article running, “ALL of our accounts have been targeted”. It accused Meta of censorship.

“Our posts are being taken down AGAIN simply for sharing the truth about vaccines and the experiences of families whose children were injured by vaccines,” CHD posted on Wednesday night, adding: “People have every right to discuss vaccine injuries and share their experiences without being silenced by big tech.”

Meta and CHD did not immediately return emails seeking comment.

Among the content that was no longer up as of Wednesday evening was a video that the group had posted on Facebook that said the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is “not so safe and effective”.

Another video no longer available had been titled “Vaccines: Your child could die”, and made the misleading claim that vaccines are deadly.

A third video that was no longer up said the HPV vaccines are “very dangerous”, have “caused hundreds, thousands of deaths”, and do not prevent cervical cancer.

All three posts had been visible on CHD accounts at the time the Guardian story was published on Wednesday.

Chinese state media has issued a four-point “peace declaration by the Chinese, Russian and US leaders” following their meeting.

The same statement was later issued by Russia.

Chinese president Xi Jinping, Russian president Putin and US president Trump held a meeting in Shenzhen on 19 November 2026. The Russian and US leaders expressed their gratitude to China for hosting this historic meeting. The three heads of state exchanged in-depth views on the current international situation and committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security.

1. As permanent members of the UN security council, China, Russia and the US are committed to promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges and fulfil its fundamental mission of maintaining international peace and security.

2. The three countries plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations. They reaffirmed the importance of stable energy flows.

3. The three heads of state recognised that the principle of state consent and respect for the immunity of state officials are of paramount importance, and agreed that the international criminal court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction.

4. The three heads of state reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought. The three countries will engage in dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing nuclear proliferation.

Elon Musk denied being Maga on Wednesday, despite aligning himself intensely with Donald Trump’s Make America Great Again movement since 2024.

“I’m not Maga,” the world’s richest person told the New York Times Dealbook summit, which he attended via video call from China, where he is one of several US business leaders who have accompanied Trump on his trip to Asia.

“I’m not sure what Maga means, but if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican party, then I certainly don’t have that,” the chief executive of SpaceX and Tesla added.

Musk famously declared at a 2024 campaign rally in Madison Square Garden: “I’m not just Maga. I’m dark, gothic Maga.”

In a 45-minute interview with Andrew Ross Sorkin, a New York Times columnist, Musk also said it would be good for Washington to have split control between the two parties, and that he thinks “there are positives and negatives in both”.

He also accused Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, of “lying” about restrictions on access to his firm’s Starshield satellite system; praised Jensen Huang, the ousted Nvidia chief executive; and said that “no one I met at Anthropic set off my evil detector”.

Asked about his previous negative comments about Anthropic, Musk said that before he agreed to rent computing power to the AI firm: “I went to met with a lot of people at Anthropic. I didn’t just move forward with the deal.”

“My interaction so far with the Anthropic team is that they seem like good people and they seem principled,” Musk added. “They seem diligent and they seem seem to care about the future.”

Musk donated at least $250m of his own money to help Trump win the election in 2024, and recently spent nearly $500m in the US midterms to support Republicans, many of whom lost.

Denmark’s parliament on Thursday approved a hard-wrought agreement with Greenland and the United States to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.

The vote follows months of pressure by president Donald Trump seeking to control Greenland, a semiautonomous territory of Denmark, a Nato ally.

The trilateral deal - between Trump and the Danish and Greenlandic leaders – paves the way for more US bases in Greenland and eases tensions over Trump’s repeated calls for the vast island to become part of the US.

The 109-0 vote in the Folketing amounts to a final step, with the deal expected to enter into force once Denmark and Greenland has signed on. Greenland’s parliament approved the deal earlier this month, also with no opposition.

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Hakeem Jeffries said it is the job of Democratic lawmakers to “fight Maga extremism” as he stood on the brink of becoming the first ever Black house speaker.

Democrats on Wednesday resoundingly nominated Jeffries to serve as speaker of the House when the new Congress is sworn in next year.

A New York congressman who has served as the Democratic minority leader since 2023, Jeffries is set to become one of Donald Trump’s most prominent opponents for the final two years of his presidency, when Democrats will control both the Senate and House of Representatives and are expected to undertake aggressive efforts to check his powers.

After his nomination was secured during closed-door voting, 251-11, ahead of a full House vote, Jeffries promised to take on the Trump administration’s Maga approach to governing the US. “Our job is to fight Maga extremism, not each other,” he said, “and to get big things done for the American people.”

Democrats nominated Jeffries despite concerns from some progressives that he represents a politically risky status quo for a party that is looking to capitalize on a surprisingly good performance in the midterms, where voters swept them back into power in the House and Senate with significant majorities.

He would become the first Democratic House speaker since Nancy Pelosi, who will retire from Congress at the end of this year.

Meanwhile today, president Trump has left China after hailing his trilateral meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, saying the three leaders were “really making history”. Trump said the US, Russia and China, the world’s largest nuclear powers, were “uniquely positioned” to discuss reducing their nuclear stockpiles.

articles.title: Saudi-led coalition intercepts Houthi missiles targeting Riyadh and south
articles.excerpt:
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis says it has intercepted missiles fired towards Riyadh and Saudi Arabia’s southern region after a loud boom was heard in ⁠the capital.

The attacks on T...
articles.body_text:
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis says it has intercepted missiles fired towards Riyadh and Saudi Arabia’s southern region after a loud boom was heard in ⁠the capital.

The attacks on Thursday are the latest in weeks of strikes by the Yemeni armed group targeting Saudi military, civilian and oil infrastructure.

Saudi-led coalition spokesman Major-General Turki al-Maliki said on X that its forces “dealt with” a Houthi missile threat launched towards Riyadh.

An initial assessment showed debris had fallen and that material damage had been reported, he added, saying the extent ⁠⁠of the damage was still being determined.

Hours later, in a separate post, the spokesman said air defences intercepted and destroyed four ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), towards the southern region, bordering Yemen.

The coalition said it had earlier also destroyed a ballistic missile launchpad used in the attempted attacks on Riyadh.

The Houthis claimed responsibility for targeting vital sites in the Saudi capital on Thursday, including the international airport and the financial centre, as well as Khamis Mushait and Abha city in the south, where alerts were sounded.

A Saudi aircraft, meanwhile, carried out air raids on the Houthi-controlled Yemeni capital, Sanaa, earlier on Thursday, the group-run Saba news agency reported, without providing further details.

The latest attacks in Saudi Arabia coincided with an announcement by Yemeni government forces that they carried out about 750 air strikes and operations against the Houthis on several fronts, including in Taiz and Lahij, where the humanitarian situation is worsening day by day.

Earlier on Thursday, the United Nations children’s agency, UNICEF, said in a statement that “more than 330,000 people, including an estimated 174,000 children, have been displaced since the beginning of the renewed military escalations”.

“The number of casualties is likely to increase as renewed fighting continues around densely populated areas, particularly in Taiz” and Lahij, UNICEF said.

Meanwhile, Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council issued a decision designating the Houthi group a “terrorist” organisation on Thursday. It said anyone who cooperates with the group will face prosecution and punishment, with penalties that could include execution or prison terms of 30 years or more, Al Jazeera’s Yasser Hassan reported from Taiz.

Humanitarian organisations have released new figures on the casualties in the war, as fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has intensified since the group captured strategic areas along Yemen’s Red Sea coast last month.

The World Health Organization said this week that the death toll from the latest escalation that began in August has reached 2,260, with 10,519 wounded.

The renewed conflict between the two sides ⁠has shattered a 2022 UN-brokered truce that largely halted the exchange of attacks ⁠between the Saudi-led coalition, which backs Yemen’s internationally recognised government, and the Houthis, who control the most populous parts of the country.

articles.title: Netanyahu’s last stand and the dangerous politics of survival
articles.excerpt: Israel’s caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has used the weeks since Israel’s October 27 election to launch a series of attacks on his opponents, and has called into question the legitimacy o...
articles.body_text:
Israel’s caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has used the weeks since Israel’s October 27 election to launch a series of attacks on his opponents, and has called into question the legitimacy of the vote’s result.

The longtime Israeli leader is likely on his way out of power – as long as the country’s opposition, led by Gadi Eisenkot, can form a viable government.

That may involve leaning on parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, and Netanyahu has taken the opportunity to use that to tarnish the reputations of the Arab parties, and baselessly accuse them of cheating in the elections.

The environment that Netanyahu has helped generate has led to right-wing protesters threatening civil war, and critics have also accused him of deliberately fomenting war with Iran to retain office.

Separately, the Shin Bet domestic intelligence agency, led by Netanyahu’s ally David Zini, reportedly sought permission to tap the phones of five Arab lawmakers over suspected foreign interference, and to have politicians who are Palestinian citizens of Israel arrested on election day, requests the attorney general rejected.

Opposition leaders including Yair Lapid and Joint List chief Yousef Jabareen said the measures were evidence of an “attempted coup”. Meanwhile, law enforcement officials are said to be investigating whether the prime minister’s office itself fabricated the allegations of vote-buying.

For analysts and a number of Israel’s politicians, Netanyahu’s actions reflect an overriding determination to stay in power, or, failing that, engineer a government that is reliant on the support of him and his allies.

Netanyahu faces numerous threats to both his legacy and even his freedom that, without the kind of influence he has wielded as prime minister, could prove far-reaching.

Calls for a state inquiry into Netanyahu and his government’s failings in the run-up to the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack on Israel have persisted for almost as long as the genocidal war Israel launched on Gaza in response. Those calls have grown more urgent following a series of reports suggesting that Netanyahu had been personally warned by senior Egyptian and Emirati officials about a potential attack. Establishing a state inquiry also featured prominently on the legislative slate of the parliament’s new session last week.

Similarly, both the war in Gaza and the constitutional crisis triggered by Netanyahu’s attempts to weaken judicial oversight over the government have provided useful cover against the corruption charges he has faced since 2019. Accused of bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three separate cases, Netanyahu has seen his trial, running since May 2020, repeatedly delayed by his duties as prime minister. If found guilty, Netanyahu could face a prison sentence of up to a decade.

“Netanyahu is behaving like a wounded animal,” said Israeli analyst Ahron Bregman, of King’s College London. “For him, losing the elections is not just a political but also a personal matter, not least because of his corruption trial, which could result in him being sent to jail. Losing the premiership is losing his shield. Hence, for Netanyahu, nothing is off the table.”

The chance of political violence in Israel has increased. In the days after the election, right-wing protesters gathered outside Eisenkot’s home, warning him not to form a government with the Arab-led parties, and calling him a “traitor”.

And in a letter shared publicly, Rabbi Gedalia Axelrod, a former head of Haifa’s rabbinical court, evoked the religious edict of din rodef, the “law of the pursuer”, the same principle invoked by Yigal Amir to justify his killing of former Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin in 1995 over the Oslo Accords agreement with the Palestinians.

“The longer it takes for Eisenkot to form a government, the higher the risk of political violence becomes,” said Ofer Cassif, a member of parliament representing the left-wing Hadash party. “Netanyahu is willing to do anything, and I mean anything, to stay in power. He’s a psychopath. People on the right talk about civil war, and I’m not ready to discount that … Netanyahu built a cult around him, and it may easily raise arms against his rivals.”

It remains unclear what, if any, immediate legal consequences Netanyahu may face for his alleged efforts to undermine the legitimacy of the election.

Aides accused of passing false information to the police on the eve of the election could face criminal scrutiny, while Shin Bet chief Zini could see both his agency’s independence and his own position fundamentally undermined by allegedly participating in efforts to subvert the democratic process.

“Netanyahu battles for his survival and doesn’t care if those around him disappear into oblivion, but he might not succeed this time,” said Yossi Mekelberg, a senior consulting fellow at Chatham House. “He doesn’t care about them, or even his political legacy. All he cares about is survival, about fighting for the next day and trying to cling on, no matter what the cost.”

articles.title: Could Trump, Putin and Xi end the nuclear age?
articles.excerpt: Excitement abounds around the possible tripartite meeting in Shenzhen, China, between Presidents Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin, and Donald Trump during the November 18-19 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperatio...
articles.body_text:
Excitement abounds around the possible tripartite meeting in Shenzhen, China, between Presidents Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin, and Donald Trump during the November 18-19 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

Some are calling it Yalta 2.0. We’d rather think of it as Reykjavik 2.0, while also welcoming some of the broader diplomatic breakthroughs and global reordering achieved at Yalta almost 82 years ago.

Dmitri Trenin, who directed the Carnegie Moscow Center for many years and is now president of the Russian International Affairs Council, wrote encouragingly: “The US president has mentioned that an unprecedented trilateral meeting… would make sense if it were focused on denuclearisation.” Trenin wrote this in Al Jazeera while explaining why Russia could play a helpful role in negotiating a new nuclear agreement between its Iranian ally and the United States.

While anything that might help end the dangerous, destructive, and potentially apocalyptic conflagration in Southwest Asia would be more than welcome, we think the leaders can and should aim even higher: Why not rekindle the spirit of the 1986 meeting between US President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, at which they came within a hair’s breadth, arguably one word, of agreeing to eliminate not only all ballistic missiles, as Reagan originally proposed, but all nuclear weapons, as Gorbachev countered. Reagan replied, “Yes, all”, and Secretary of State George Shultz agreed. “Let’s do it,” he said.

The chance to achieve the most extraordinary diplomatic breakthrough in history slipped through Reagan’s grasp when he insisted on unlimited testing of his Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI) fantasy rather than limiting SDI to the laboratory for 10 years. The world’s hopes were dashed, and we have not come close since.

Sure, we’re up against obstacles, and the odds are long. Trump has responded to the midterm shellacking by appointing Stephen Miller as chief of staff, in effect giving the middle finger to those who didn’t support the Republicans, which is not a hopeful sign. Putin knows that much of Russia’s power comes not from its economic prowess or its conventional military but from possessing the largest nuclear arsenal in the world. And Xi has made it clear that China won’t engage in arms control talks until the largest nuclear arsenals are reduced – meanwhile, China has been rapidly increasing the size of its arsenal.

That said, there are good reasons why all three could support this proposal. After his party’s midterm defeat, Trump, probably the most recalcitrant of the three, may be desperate for an achievement that could cement at least a piece of a positive legacy – and in this case a very big piece, a resounding piece. And he has been all over the map on the nuclear issue. In February 2025, he said, “There’s no reason for us to be building brand-new nuclear weapons. We already have so many. You could destroy the world 50 times over, 100 times over. And here we are building new nuclear weapons, and they’re building nuclear weapons.” He also said, “We’re all spending a lot of money that we could be spending on other things that are actually, hopefully, much more productive.”

This is apparently something he’s been contemplating for many years. In 2016, he told Maggie Haberman and David Sanger of The New York Times: “I personally think it’s the biggest problem the world has, nuclear capability. I think it’s the single biggest problem… Power of weaponry today is beyond anything ever thought of, or even, you know, it’s unthinkable, the power… And to me, it’s the single biggest, it’s the single biggest problem.” He credits his “very brilliant” MIT physicist uncle, John Trump, with making him aware of this danger.

In 1986, he sought the advice of Bernard Lown, cofounder of International Physicians for the Prevention of Nuclear War (IPPNW), which won the Nobel Peace Prize, on negotiating nuclear disarmament with Gorbachev. He told Lown he would get Reagan to send him to Moscow and that he would secure disarmament and end the Cold War in one hour. Lown commented, “I sat there dumbfounded. ‘Who is this self-inflated individual? Is he sane or what?’”

On January 23, 2025, Trump told the World Economic Forum in Davos: “And I will tell you that President Putin really liked the idea of – of cutting way back on nuclear. And I think the rest of the world, we would have gotten them to follow. And China would have come along too. China also liked it. Tremendous amounts of money are being spent on nuclear, and the destructive capability is something that we don’t even want to talk about today, because you don’t want to hear it. It’s too depressing. So, we want to see if we can denuclearise, and I think that’s very possible. And I can tell you that President Putin wanted to do it. He and I wanted to do it. We had a good conversation with China. They would have been involved, and that would have been an unbelievable thing for the planet.”

Whether Trump is sane is even more heatedly debated today than it was 40 years ago, but the possibility that he is iconoclastic enough to take a dramatic step that reverses the course of history should not be in doubt. The question is whether he’s capable of taking such a step in favour of humanity rather than against it.

The same is true of Putin. Putin told a meeting of the Valdai International Discussion Club in Sochi in 2017, “Should you ask me if nuclear disarmament is possible, I will tell you: Yes, it is possible. Does Russia wish to achieve universal nuclear disarmament or not? The answer is in the affirmative, too. Yes, it does, and it will be working for it.”

Shortly before the invasion of Ukraine, the leaders of the US, Russia, China, France, and the United Kingdom jointly declared: “We affirm that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought… We remain committed to our Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) obligations, including our Article VI obligation to pursue negotiations in good faith on effective measures relating to cessation of the nuclear arms race at an early date and to nuclear disarmament.”

Sceptics will rightly point out that this was before the invasion of Ukraine and a series of slightly veiled nuclear threats that Putin issued. But it at least offers a glimmer of hope, especially in the context of a security agreement that promises peaceful coexistence for all participants.

In 2017, in a speech at the United Nations Office in Geneva, Xi said clearly, “Nuclear weapons, the Sword of Damocles that hangs over humankind, should be completely prohibited and ultimately destroyed over time to make the world free of nuclear weapons.”

While not disavowing this sentiment, Xi has more recently indicated that China would not participate in arms control discussions until the gap between its arsenal and those of the largest nuclear powers – the United States and Russia – had narrowed. Fine. To most people, that means China increasing the size of its arsenal to the 5,000-plus weapons that both Russia and the United States possess.

We have a different proposal: How about if the US and Russia reduce their arsenals to the 600 or so that China now possesses?

We see this being done in three four-year stages, much as Reagan and Gorbachev envisioned 40 years ago. In the first stage, the US and Russia pare down their arsenals, while China forgoes its expansion. During this trust-building stage, the wars in Iran and Ukraine would need to end quickly, alongside a recommitment to the UN Charter and peaceful development by not just China, Russia, and the US, but all nuclear-armed states.

The second four-year stage would be more complex, as it would involve bilateral, trilateral, and multilateral negotiations among all nine nuclear-armed states to address the specific reasons why each of the states possesses nuclear weapons and find ways to reduce or eliminate those incentives. Intense diplomacy would be required during this period, resulting in all nine nuclear powers joining the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (TPNW). The TPNW would give all nine states a 10-year timeline to eliminate their arsenals.

However, they could accomplish this in four years, given that the starting point would be arsenals of no more than 600 nuclear warheads. This last four-year stage would involve reductions, verification, and eventual elimination of arsenals. It could be done in plenty of time for the centennial celebration of the United Nations and the centennial commemoration of the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

The nuclear age should end well before it turns 100.

If Reagan and Gorbachev could come so close 40 years ago, we should not rule out the possibility that Putin, Xi, and Trump could do so today. As John Kennedy said in his great American University commencement address in 1963: “Our problems are man-made – therefore, they can be solved by man. And man can be as big as he wants. No problem of human destiny is beyond human beings. Man’s reason and spirit have often solved the seemingly unsolvable – and we believe they can do it again.”

A version of this article first appeared on Al Jazeera Arabic.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Iran warns Bahrain monarchy its survival is at risk amid push to 'evict' US Fifth Fleet
articles.excerpt:
Iran’s attacks on Bahrain threaten key US naval hub, raise stakes for American forces, says Iran expert.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) warned Wednesday that Bahrain's monarchy faces...
articles.body_text:
Iran’s attacks on Bahrain threaten key US naval hub, raise stakes for American forces, says Iran expert.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) warned Wednesday that Bahrain's monarchy faces an existential threat as Iranian drones and missiles targeted U.S. military installations in the Gulf kingdom.

Tehran's warning came amid renewed attacks on Bahrain, home to the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet, and a regional expert warned of Iran's decades-long efforts to destabilize the island nation and assert territorial claims.

"This is a regime that has tried to inflame tensions there for quite literally several decades and has claims to the island nation as well," Behnam Ben Taleblu, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD), told Fox News Digital.

BAHRAIN INTERCEPTS IRANIAN DRONES TARGETING US RADAR AFTER 2-MONTH LULL IN GULF STRIKES

Bahrain's King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa (Benoit Tessier/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)

"The Islamic Republic is also trying to use military force to evict the United States from the region," he added.

In a warning directed at Bahrain's ruling Al Khalifa family, IRGC Brig. Gen. Hossein Mohebbi accused the monarchy of cooperating with military action against Iran, relying on U.S. protection and challenging Shiite religious authority.

"Colluding in the aggression against Islamic Iran, living inside the American security bubble, and encroaching on the authority of the Shiite religious leadership are three fundamental mistakes being made by the Al Khalifa regime," Mohebbi wrote on X.

IRAN VOWS ‘ASTONISHING’ STRIKES AND LIFTS MISSILE-RANGE LIMIT AS US TARGETS LAND ROUTES

Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi, left, and President Donald Trump. (Majid Asgaripour/WANA/Reuters; Bonnie Cash/Pool/Sipa USA/Reuters)

"If it persists in them, its survival under the new regional security order will be in doubt," he warned.

Mohebbi's threat also followed a Bahraini crackdown on Shiite religious leaders.

On Monday, a criminal court sentenced dozens of Shiite clerics to life in prison on terrorism-related charges after prosecutors accused them of collaborating with Iran and plotting to undermine the government.

Bahrain's Public Prosecution agency said investigators uncovered communications between some defendants and Iranian authorities, including the IRGC, and accused the clerics of supporting terrorism and sabotage aimed at overthrowing the monarchy.

"The Islamic Republic has a panoply of gripes against Bahrain as well as against the ruling royal family of that country," Taleblu said.

"Some are sectarian, some are political, some are strategic, and some, again, have to do with the U.S. force presence in the region," the expert explained.

IRAN HAS 'SUBSTANTIALLY INCREASED' EFFORTS TO TARGET AMERICANS ABROAD, US INTELLIGENCE MEMO WARNS

Fox News' Jennifer Griffin reported that Iran appeared to hit the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet, but no casualties were reported. (Fox News)

Bahrain hosts the headquarters of the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet, a critical hub for American naval operations across the Persian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waters.

The latest regional escalation follows repeated Iranian drone attacks targeting American military equipment in Bahrain, including a U.S. radar installation Tehran claimed to have targeted for the third time in less than a week. U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) said the attacks were intercepted.

Bahrain also reported intercepting Iranian attacks early Wednesday, a day after the IRGC claimed to have struck a base used by American forces.

"The regime is also looking for places close to its territory where it can land blows against the U.S.—as well as against the order that has allowed the U.S. to be in the region for quite some time—and to be able to do so on the cheap," Taleblu said.

IRAN ESCALATES IN HORMUZ, CLAIMS STRIKE ON OMANI ISLAND IT SAYS 'ENEMY' USES FOR US MILITARY OPS

Smoke rises after an Iranian drone was intercepted over the Bahrain Financial Harbour towers, which houses the Israeli embassy, amid the U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran, in Manama, Bahrain, March 6, 2026. Picture taken on a mobile phone. (Stringer/Reuters)

"They want to be able to generate pain against the U.S. more broadly in the region and do so in places that have already been hit."

Taleblu also said Iran's strategy is designed not only to damage American military assets but to increase pressure on Bahrain's monarchy to reconsider hosting U.S. forces.

"They've done this to limit the space for the U.S. to actually operate from the region and try to create tougher political conditions for the ruling family in that country to keep that U.S. force presence there."

He warned that the growing missile and drone threat could force Washington to reassess its long-term military presence in the Persian Gulf.

"Now that the war is out of the shadows and the weapons being used are missiles and drones, the future of the U.S. footprint in the region will be based on whether America can afford to build and defend bases so close to an adversary's territory under fire," Taleblu said.

"The test case as to what the U.S. does with the Fifth Fleet in Bahrain, and with the radars in that country, could actually be a harbinger of what the future of the U.S. footprint in the CENTCOM AOR — and in particular, the Persian Gulf region — looks like post-war with Iran," he added.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title: Badenoch says using amputee athletes to justify cutting disability benefits was ‘message of hope’ – UK politics live
articles.excerpt:
PM has asked Badenoch to withdraw her suggestion that benefits should be cut because ‘double amputees run marathons’

Alexandra Topping is a Guardian political correspondent.

Kemi Badenoch was in a s...
articles.body_text:
PM has asked Badenoch to withdraw her suggestion that benefits should be cut because ‘double amputees run marathons’

Alexandra Topping is a Guardian political correspondent.

Kemi Badenoch was in a straight-talking mode on the media round this morning, calling the historic meeting between Trump, Xi and Putin “disturbing”, saying it looked like they were trying to “carve” up the world” between them.

Speaking on the Today programme, the leader of the opposition said the meeting was “absolutely not reassuring”.

double quotation markThere are three world leaders who look like they’re trying to carve up the world between them, a tri-polar world where Xi gets Asia, America gets the western hemisphere and Russia gets Europe, and that is very concerning, especially seeing Donald Trump call President Putin his friend.

Russia is not America’s friend, it certainly hasn’t been during my lifetime. But also at a time when we’re all worried about where the Ukraine war is going, the message that is sending to President Zelensky and of course the other summit that is taking place … is very concerning indeed.

And what I want to know is where we fit in in all of this. I don’t want to be in a polarised world run by Russia. I’ll do everything I can to make sure that doesn’t happen.

Badenoch went further than the prime minister, who was asked about the meeting by Ed Davey at prime minister’s questions yesterday. The Liberal Democrat leader said “the security implications of Trump, Putin and Xi cosying up” should highlight the need for a fresh deal with the European Union.

Burnham replied that he would be in Berlin for a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing to support Ukraine in China, but stopped short of expressing concern about the meeting of the three world leaders.

double quotation markThe thing that we need to do is continue to stand squarely by Ukraine and that is what this government will do.

And on this issue, I do pay tribute to all sides of the house because that is what we’ve managed to do in the years since the conflict began and that is the right thing to do … Let that clear message go out as that meeting takes place in [China] – this country is squarely with Ukraine.

Good morning. At PMQs yesterday Andy Burnham said that Kemi Badenoch should withdraw the “double amputees run marathons” comment that she used to justify the Tory plan to cut sickness and disability benefits by £14bn. It was “crass and insensitive”, he said.

This morning Badenoch defended what she was saying claimed that, in fact, she was delivering a “message of hope”.

In an interview on the Today programme, asked if she accepted that her remark was insensitive, Badenoch said she didn’t. She went on:

double quotation markI will speak the truth and I will say what I believe is common sense. And what I know is that, if people can work, then we should encourage them to work.

And what I’m saying is actually a message of hope, that if people even with significant, problems can work, then those who have ADHD and mild anxiety should go to work.

When the presenter, Nick Robinson, put it to her that it was unreasonable to use an exceptional case as a guide to what most disabled people should be doing, Badenoch did not agree. “We do use extreme examples to illustrate things,” she said.

Robinson tried again, saying she was taking “one extreme case [to] imply that anybody on disability benefits should just get on with it”. Badenoch accused him of “faux outrage” and “tone policing”. She added:

double quotation markPeople are free to disagree, but they know where I’m coming from.

I will post more from the interview shortly.

Today the news will be dominated by two summits. This afternoon Burnham is in Berlin for a meeting of the pro-Ukraine coalition of the willing. We have coverage of this on our Europe live blog.

And in China, Vladimir Putin, who invaded Ukraine, Xi Jinping, his leading ally, and Donald Trump, who is seen by many as a closet Putin ally, are meeting now. You can read about that here.

We will have comments open in about an hour. That is because I will be doing a Q&A this afternoon, probably from about 3pm, and I will try to answer as many questions as possible. Do post them below the line.

9.30am: Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state and Cabinet Office minister, takes questions in the Commons.

10am: The Conservative party announces the results of the first round of voting in the election of its candidate for London mayor for 2028. James Cleverly, the former home secretary and former foreign secretary, is expected to get more than 50% of the vote, meaning a second round of voting should not be necessary.

11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.

Noon: Heather Hallett, the Covid inquiry chair, publishes her report on the test, trace and isolate system.

Around 12.15pm (UK time): Andy Burnham arrives in Berlin for a meeting of the pro-Ukraine coalition of the willing. He is expected to speak to the media later in the afternoon after the plenary has finished.

1pm: Chris Bryant, the Northern Ireland secretary, attends a meeting of the British-Irish Intergovernmental Conference in Dublin.

articles.title: BAE to slash 1,000 jobs across head office and air business to streamline orders
articles.excerpt:
Job cuts to exclude shop floor, aircraft maintenance and trainees but move prompts calls for more orders to support British defence giant

BAE Systems has announced plans to cut more than 1,000 jobs f...
articles.body_text:
Job cuts to exclude shop floor, aircraft maintenance and trainees but move prompts calls for more orders to support British defence giant

BAE Systems has announced plans to cut more than 1,000 jobs from its workforce, triggering calls for ministers to place extra orders with Britain’s biggest defence contractor.

The company said it is aiming to cut 1,070 jobs at its head office and air business in the UK, as it tries to meet customer demands for “greater speed and efficiency in getting critical capabilities into the hands of those who need them”.

The cuts represent about 2% of its 50,000 strong workforce in the UK, which includes about 18,500 in its air business and about 1,000 in its head office in London. They will be made through voluntary redundancies and will exclude people working on the shop floor, aircraft maintenance at RAF bases and early career trainees.

A spokesperson for BAE said the cuts represented the “next stage of our ongoing focus on enhancing our agility and competitiveness, so we can help to maximise the value of every pound our customers spend on defence.

“We recognise that this news may be unsettling for our people and we’re focused on achieving potential workforce reductions through a voluntary process,” they said.

BAE last year received an order for 20 Typhoon fighter jets from Turkey, in a deal announced at the factory by Keir Starmer. However, that order is thought to provide only two years of work at the Lancashire factories – not enough to sustain jobs until production starts on the next generation of fighters. BAE will lead production of the sixth-generation Tempest fighter in an alliance with Italy and Japan.

A source with knowledge of the matter said that the job cuts were linked to uncertainty over the Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jet programme, more than cost-cutting.

The move comes even as BAE has benefited from a boom in defence spending since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Last month, the company told its investors it had secured £33bn in orders so far this year and that it expected further contracts before the end of 2026. It also raised its free cashflow guidance for its financial year by 10%, from about £2bn to £3bn.

Sharon Graham, the general secretary of the union Unite, warned that there would not be a manufacturing industry left in the UK “if the government doesn’t start making critical decisions”.

“To stop the erosion of defence jobs and get the growth we need, the government needs to announce contracts for British-built Typhoons and Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) immediately,” she said.

BAE unveiled the uncrewed CCA – which is named Brontanax – at the Farnborough International airshow in July.

Andrew Snowden, a Conservative MP in Lancashire where BAE has two air manufacturing hubs, echoed Graham’s call for more government support.

He told the Lancashire Post: “The government should act now to support BAE by placing orders for British-built Typhoons and Collaborative Combat Aircraft, giving skilled workers and the supply chain here in Lancashire a clear pipeline of work.”

It comes with the government also under pressure to reach a decision on its Skynet military satellite replacement. American weapons maker Lockheed Martin was thought to be the Ministry of Defence’s preferred choice, but ministers have delayed the choice after Unite argued it would lead to UK job cuts at rival Airbus’s existing factories.

An MoD spokesperson said: “We know that any potential voluntary redundancies can cause concerns and our thoughts are with those potentially affected.

“This government is delivering the biggest boost in defence spending since the cold ar, having already agreed £4bn worth of investments since July.

“This includes awarding BAE a £708m contract extension to lead the Global Combat Air Programme developments and supporting the £8bn contract to supply Turkey with 20 Typhoon jets last year, which sustains 6,000 jobs at two BAE sites.”

articles.title: Trump's China trip: Historic Xi-Putin talks, 'superintelligence' boast and other top moments
articles.excerpt:
President Donald Trump meets with Russian President Vladimir Putin ahead of trilateral talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

President Donald Trump's visit to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic C...
articles.body_text:
President Donald Trump meets with Russian President Vladimir Putin ahead of trilateral talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

President Donald Trump's visit to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit featured an elaborate welcome, warm exchanges with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, and a declaration of American technological dominance on Chinese soil.

The gathering in Shenzhen culminated in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, China and Russia, with nuclear arms reductions and the war in Ukraine among the issues on the table.

Here are some of the standout moments from Trump's visit.

XI BREAKS PROTOCOL TO PERSONALLY WELCOME TRUMP AHEAD OF HISTORIC TRILATERAL SUMMIT AND MORE TOP HEADLINES

Trump declared the United States the world leader in "superintelligence" during remarks at the summit Thursday, making the assertion in one of China's major technology hubs.

"The United States is also proud to be the world leader in superintelligence, the greatest technological transformation since the Industrial Revolution," Trump told APEC leaders.

The remarks came as Washington and Beijing compete for leadership in artificial intelligence and advanced semiconductors.

Trump joined Xi and Putin for the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, China and Russia just after 3 a.m. ET, calling the gathering an opportunity to reduce nuclear weapons and address global conflicts.

"As the world's three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth," Trump said.

The president also said he had held extensive discussions with Putin about ending the war in Ukraine.

Russian President Vladimir Putin shakes hands with Chinese President Xi Jinping during a meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders' Summit in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, China November 18, 2026. (Sputnik/Sergei Bobylyov/Pool via Reuters)

"I think things are happening," Trump said. "I think that he and I hope the other side would like to see an end to that war."

Trump also raised preventing Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons and said he would propose ways for the three countries to protect their sovereignty from the International Criminal Court, which he accused of exceeding its jurisdiction.

A Bloomberg reporter was barred from the trilateral meeting after asking Trump during his bilateral with Xi whether Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had been "disloyal to the United States," according to White House pool reports. Chinese officials warned that shouting questions was considered extremely rude and that reporters could be removed for doing so, despite White House efforts to secure the Bloomberg reporter's access.

Xi personally greeted Trump upon his arrival in Shenzhen Wednesday, meeting the president at the foot of the aircraft stairs in an elaborate welcome.

The two exchanged greetings before standing together for the American and Chinese national anthems. A military flyover followed, with five jets leaving trails of colored smoke overhead.

TRUMP ARRIVES IN PHILIPPINES AHEAD OF XI JINPING SUMMIT IN CHINA AFTER GOP MIDTERM LOSSES

Trump later praised the reception as a display of "great respect."

SHENZHEN, CHINA - NOVEMBER 18: U.S. President Donald Trump (L) is greeted by President of the People's Republic of China Xi Jinping at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport on November 18, 2026 in Shenzhen, China. Trump is visiting China to attend the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping on November 18-19. (Photo by Win McNamee/Getty Images) ( )

Chinese President Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump, and Russian President Vladimir Putin greet each other before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting at the Shenzhen International Communication Center on November 18, 2026 in Shenzhen, China. (Photo by Iori Sagisawa-China Pool/Getty Images)

Trump offered warm words for both Xi and Putin during the summit, praising his personal relationship with the Chinese leader and referring to the Russian president as a "friend."

"President Xi and I have formed an outstanding personal relationship," Trump said during their bilateral meeting. "Some people are unhappy when they hear that, but I'm very happy about it."

US President Donald Trump (R) is greeted by China's President Xi Jinping as he arrives at Shenzhen Baoan International Airport to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, in China's southern Guangdong Province, on November 18, 2026. (Mandel NGAN / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)

Trump also told Xi, "You're my friend, and we have a very special relationship."

"Some people are unhappy when they hear that, but I'm very happy about it," he went on, telling the Chinese leader: "And I think as long as you and I are in charge of things, we'll never have a problem."

During a separate encounter with Putin, Trump was heard saying, "Who is he? It's my friend. Nice to see you," according to video shared by Clash Report.

The friendly exchanges came despite ongoing tensions between Washington and Beijing over trade and technology and Trump's efforts to negotiate an end to Russia's war in Ukraine..

Russian President Vladimir Putin shakes hands with Chinese President Xi Jinping during a meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders' Summit in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, China November 18, 2026. (Sputnik/Sergei Bobylyov/Pool via Reuters)

"I think things are happening," Trump said. "I think that he and I hope the other side would like to see an end to that war."

Trump also raised preventing Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons and said he would propose ways for the three countries to protect their sovereignty from the International Criminal Court, which he accused of exceeding its jurisdiction.

A Bloomberg reporter was barred from the trilateral meeting after asking Trump during his bilateral with Xi whether Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had been "disloyal to the United States," according to White House pool reports. Chinese officials warned that shouting questions was considered extremely rude and that reporters could be removed for doing so, despite White House efforts to secure the Bloomberg reporter's access.

Xi personally greeted Trump upon his arrival in Shenzhen Wednesday, meeting the president at the foot of the aircraft stairs in an elaborate welcome.

The two exchanged greetings before standing together for the American and Chinese national anthems. A military flyover followed, with five jets leaving trails of colored smoke overhead.

TRUMP ARRIVES IN PHILIPPINES AHEAD OF XI JINPING SUMMIT IN CHINA AFTER GOP MIDTERM LOSSES

Trump later praised the reception as a display of "great respect."

SHENZHEN, CHINA - NOVEMBER 18: U.S. President Donald Trump (L) is greeted by President of the People's Republic of China Xi Jinping at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport on November 18, 2026 in Shenzhen, China. Trump is visiting China to attend the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping on November 18-19. (Photo by Win McNamee/Getty Images) ( )

Chinese President Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump, and Russian President Vladimir Putin greet each other before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting at the Shenzhen International Communication Center on November 18, 2026 in Shenzhen, China. (Photo by Iori Sagisawa-China Pool/Getty Images)

Trump offered warm words for both Xi and Putin during the summit, praising his personal relationship with the Chinese leader and referring to the Russian president as a "friend."

"President Xi and I have formed an outstanding personal relationship," Trump said during their bilateral meeting. "Some people are unhappy when they hear that, but I'm very happy about it."

US President Donald Trump (R) is greeted by China's President Xi Jinping as he arrives at Shenzhen Baoan International Airport to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, in China's southern Guangdong Province, on November 18, 2026. (Mandel NGAN / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)

Trump also told Xi, "You're my friend, and we have a very special relationship."

"Some people are unhappy when they hear that, but I'm very happy about it," he went on, telling the Chinese leader: "And I think as long as you and I are in charge of things, we'll never have a problem."

During a separate encounter with Putin, Trump was heard saying, "Who is he? It's my friend. Nice to see you," according to video shared by Clash Report.

The friendly exchanges came despite ongoing tensions between Washington and Beijing over trade and technology and Trump's efforts to negotiate an end to Russia's war in Ukraine..

articles.title: Kenya’s marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir gets three-year ban for doping
articles.excerpt: Kenya’s reigning world and former Olympic marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir has been suspended for three years after testing positive for the banned substance EPO, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU)...
articles.body_text:
Kenya’s reigning world and former Olympic marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir has been suspended for three years after testing positive for the banned substance EPO, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) said.

Jepchirchir admitted to breaching anti-doping rules relating to the presence of a prohibited substance or its metabolites and to the use or attempted use of a prohibited substance or prohibited method, the AIU said in a statement on Thursday.

EPO, a synthetic form of erythropoietin, is a laboratory-made version of a natural hormone produced mainly by the kidneys that signals the bone marrow to make more red blood cells, according to the Mayo Clinic.

Athletes sometimes misuse synthetic EPO as a performance-enhancing drug to boost oxygen delivery to muscles and improve endurance.

Jepchirchir was provisionally suspended last month after the AIU, which investigates doping in track and field athletes on behalf of the sport’s governing body, World Athletics, returned an adverse analytical finding for EPO from an out-of-competition sample collected in Kenya before her Sydney Marathon victory in late August.

Jepchirchir has accepted the disqualification of all of her competitive results since July 17.

The 33-year-old won women’s marathon gold at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021 and the world title last year. She is also a former world record holder in the half marathon.

The Sydney Marathon, which noted that Jepchirchir’s in-competition test had returned negative, said Irine Cheptai is set to be elevated to 2026 women’s champion.

The AIU said it also sanctioned two other high-profile Kenyan runners.

Veronica Loleo, a half-marathon silver medallist at the 2026 world road running championships, was banned for three years after testing positive for EPO in an out-of-competition test.

Meanwhile, Ronald Korir, who placed fourth in the 2023 Berlin Marathon, received a six-year ban after abnormalities were found in his athlete biological passport, which he failed to explain. The AIU analysed 20 blood samples taken from Korir from May 6, 2023, to August 18, 2025, and identified abnormalities.

“The Kenyan authorities have made a lot of progress in the fight against doping in the last five years, but these cases highlight that there is still a long way to go,” AIU chief executive Brett Clothier said in a statement.

“The Kenyan government is aware of the current situation and has committed to further strengthen the Anti-Doping Agency of Kenya and take action to address the criminal networks that facilitate doping within the country.”

These were the latest in a long series of doping cases involving distance runners from Kenya.

Women’s marathon world record holder Ruth Chepng’etich, also from Kenya, was banned for three years in 2025 after admitting a charge related to a positive test for a banned diuretic. Former New York Marathon winner Albert Korir was given a five-year ban in March.

articles.title: Tusk appears to mock Trump’s Putin comment as Ukraine’s allies meet in Berlin – Europe live
articles.excerpt:
After US president called Putin a friend, Poland’s PM said: ‘God, protect us from such friends’

Poland’s prime minister Donald Tusk – one of Europe’s five negotiators – does not seem to be impressed ...
articles.body_text:
After US president called Putin a friend, Poland’s PM said: ‘God, protect us from such friends’

Poland’s prime minister Donald Tusk – one of Europe’s five negotiators – does not seem to be impressed by what he saw in Shenzhen.

“God, protect us from such friends,” he said on X in an apparent reference to Trump’s enthusiastic greeting with Putin.

Poland’s foreign minister Radosław Sikorski was similarly alarmed, telling reporters:

“Indeed, it is difficult to judge, by their fruits we shall know them, but the optics of this hugging Putin, calling him a friend, causes us some concern.

Because the question arises – who is he more of a friend with, Putin or our president? And what will he possibly do if push comes to shove, which friend will he choose?”

Meanwhile, a key bridge connecting annexed Crimea to Russia has been attacked again last night, a Russian-appointed regional governor has said, two days after Ukrainian strikes caused serious damage to it.

“Following a new attack on the Crimean Bridge, traffic has been temporarily halted. All relevant services are on site and at work. An assessment of the damage is under way,” Sergei Aksyonov, the Kremlin-appointed governor of the Russian-occupied Crimea, wrote on Telegram.

The Russian transport ministry said on Thursday that no one was wounded in the attack and that train services across it had been halted.

Wednesday’s ‌attack is third this week on the highly symbolic bridge that links Russia with Crimea, which ​it seized from Ukraine in 2014. A 227-metre section of the road spanning the Kerch strait was destroyed this week, but the rail corridor appears to be operable despite sustaining some damage.

On Ukraine, Trump says at the beginning of the trilateral meeting:

“We are going to be discussing the war between Russia and Ukraine, and we already have. President Putin and I have had a long discussion today for quite a while. That’s what pretty much what the discussion was about.

I think that he and – I hope - the other side would like to see an end to that war.”

God knows what that’s supposed to mean in practice.

The trilateral meeting is now getting under way, with Trump declaring “together we are making history” with the three leaders facing “a special responsibility to maintain open, respectful and productive dialogue on issues impacting not just our people, but the entire planet.”

Our coverage of the Apec summit is here, but I will pick up any lines on Ukraine:

Poland’s prime minister Donald Tusk – one of Europe’s five negotiators – does not seem to be impressed by what he saw in Shenzhen.

“God, protect us from such friends,” he said on X in an apparent reference to Trump’s enthusiastic greeting with Putin.

Poland’s foreign minister Radosław Sikorski was similarly alarmed, telling reporters:

“Indeed, it is difficult to judge, by their fruits we shall know them, but the optics of this hugging Putin, calling him a friend, causes us some concern.

Because the question arises – who is he more of a friend with, Putin or our president? And what will he possibly do if push comes to shove, which friend will he choose?”

Several European leaders from the Coalition of the Willing are meeting in Berlin today, just hours after US president Donald Trump, Russia president Vladimir Putin and China president Xi Jinping are due to meet in Shenhzen.

The trilateral meeting is due to get under way any moment now, though the tone of Trump’s earlier talks with Putin will already be worrying for Europeans.

“Who is he? He’s my friend!” said Trump, absolutely beaming, as soon as he saw Putin.

These images will send a shiver down the spine of Europe’s top leaders as they prepare to leave for Berlin to attend the “coalition of the willing”’s latest coordination meeting.

Europe’s newly appointed negotiating team of Andy Burnham, Emmanuel Macron, Giorgia Meloni, Friedrich Merz and Donald Tusk plus the EU’s Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa will be joined by several other leaders for a meeting with US peace envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, where they are expected to get a read out from the meeting in China.

Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Nato’s secretary general Mark Rutte are expected to attend, as are several other key European leaders, including Finland’s Alexander Stubb, Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen, Sweden’s Ulf Kristersson, Norway’s Jonas Gahr Støre, and Ireland’s Micheál Martin (and many others).

I will bring you all the latest from Berlin and reactions to Trump’s trilateral meeting.

It’s Thursday, 19 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

articles.title: Trump meets Putin and Xi as trilateral US, Russia, China talks begin
articles.excerpt:
United States President Donald Trump is meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts for highly anticipated trilateral talks at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

Trump, Chines...
articles.body_text:
United States President Donald Trump is meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts for highly anticipated trilateral talks at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin began talks on the sidelines of the summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday in an unprecedented gathering of the world’s three superpowers.

The talks between the leaders of the world’s largest nuclear powers are unlikely to produce major agreements, analysts say, given deep differences over Ukraine, Iran, nuclear weapons and trade. But the meeting has unnerved smaller countries that fear their interests might be disregarded.

Ahead of the trilateral gathering, Trump held separate bilateral meetings with both Xi and Putin on Thursday.

The US president described Xi as a “friend” and said Washington and Beijing enjoyed a “special relationship”.

“As long as the two of us are in charge, I don’t think we’ll have a problem,” Trump said in opening remarks at his meeting with the Chinese leader. He also boasted that “no other countries can do what we can”.

Trump said the US has done “amazing” things in the past two years, since he returned to power, while praising China for many of its gains over several years.

Xi, meanwhile, said that he remained committed to working with Trump to steer ties between their countries on the “correct course”.

Relations between Beijing and Washington have been stable and improving, Xi said to Trump at the start of their third meeting this year, which lasted for about an hour.

“We have established a new definition of a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability, giving it new substance based on respect, fairness and reciprocity,” Xi said.

Ahead of the bilateral meeting, Trump said the Board of Trade that he and the Chinese president agreed to form at their Beijing summit in May has brought balance to the two countries’ relationship. He said the US and China had split their tariffs in a “fair way”.

Earlier in the day, during talks with Putin, Trump also called the Russian leader a “friend”.

“We’ve had a great relationship for many years. We know each other for a long time, and I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start. But I think they’ll come out of this,” Trump told Putin.

A video published by the White House showed the two leaders shaking hands and Trump briefly whispering to Putin at the start of their meeting.

In another video posted by the White House Rapid Response X account, Trump was shown pointing at Putin and saying, “He’s my friend.”

Kremlin foreign policy aide Yury Ushakov said the two leaders “discussed the conflict in Ukraine and bilateral relations issues”.

“The meeting between the Russian and US leaders went well,” Ushakov said, according to Russia’s state news agency TASS, adding that Putin left the talks “in an excellent” mood.

“There were no particularly significant statements made at the Putin-Trump talks; everyone is preparing for the trilateral meeting,” he added.

Thursday also features the main event of the APEC summit, as representatives of the 21 Pacific Rim economies gather for discussions that will include high-stakes diplomacy, Al Jazeera’s Katrina Yu said, reporting from Shenzhen.

“Xi Jinping, who spoke at the banquet last night during the opening ceremony, said the discussion will centre on promoting mutual openness, innovation-driven growth and results-oriented cooperation,” said Yu.

On the US-China-Russia talks, James Bays, Al Jazeera’s diplomatic editor, said that when it comes to Trump, “his personal role always matters to him”.

But, he added, “something worth bearing in mind: you have three leaders here, Trump, Xi, and Putin. Putin has been in power; he’s been in the main driving seat in Moscow for 26 years; Xi’s been there for 14 years; and they know President Trump only has 26 more months.”

Speaking to Fox News earlier on Thursday, Trump highlighted the pomp surrounding his arrival. Xi greeted Air Force One on the airport tarmac on Wednesday, which contrasted with the more muted greetings offered to other leaders.

“This is a great president, one of the great presidents of China, and he’s never gone to the airport to meet somebody,” Trump said when asked what he wanted to get out of the trilateral summit.

Trump has insisted that nuclear arms control be a central topic of the meeting, despite Beijing’s repeated objections to talks on the issue with Washington and Moscow, which have far larger nuclear arsenals.
