articles.title: Iowa's Kirk Ferentz threatens to fire coaches if they mention style points with great old-school statement
articles.excerpt:
Kirk Herbstreit shared a video of his dog Peter enjoy a nice medium rare steak at a fancy NYC steakhouse, and Craig Carton goes scorched earth on the football announcer.

Kirk Ferentz cares about one ...
articles.body_text:
Kirk Herbstreit shared a video of his dog Peter enjoy a nice medium rare steak at a fancy NYC steakhouse, and Craig Carton goes scorched earth on the football announcer.

Kirk Ferentz cares about one thing and one thing only, and that is winning football games. Whether his Iowa Hawkeyes win by one point or by six touchdowns, he just wants to look up at the scoreboard after 60 minutes and see that his team scored one more point than the opposition.

The 71-year-old has accomplished that goal more often than not during his 28 seasons in charge of the Hawkeyes, posting a record of 217-130, but in today's day and age, where a committee selects which teams make the field in the College Football Playoff, the fashion in which you win does matter.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Ferentz, however, could not possibly care less about that fact, and made his opinion quite clear with a perfect, old-school statement about it.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF RANKINGS: TEXAS REWARDED FOR THRILLING WIN VS LSU, GEORGIA REMAINS TOP DOG

Iowa Hawkeyes head coach Kirk Ferentz leads his team onto the field before a game against the Minnesota Golden Gophers at Huntington Bank Stadium in Minneapolis, Minn., on Oct. 24, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

"If that comes up back there (Iowa's offices) I'm not big on firing coaches, but that could be grounds for firing," Ferentz told reporters when asked if he's considering chasing style points in the final two games of the season.

"I mean, we're just trying to win the game. For 28 years, that's been our goal is to put our guys in the best position to win a game. I'm not being judgmental towards anybody else, but hopefully we're going to play smart football and just try to do what's best to win each and every game in front of us. If that's not good enough, then that's not good enough."

With Iowa sitting at No. 15 in the latest CFB Playoff Rankings, the Hawkeyes likely need some help from the teams ahead of them over the final two weeks of the season in order to sneak inside the Top 12 and make their first-ever appearance in the field.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Iowa Hawkeyes head coach Kirk Ferentz talks on the sideline during pregame warmups against the Washington Huskies at Husky Stadium in Seattle on Oct. 9, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

The most glaring issue for Iowa to snag a spot is that its final two games come against Illinois and Nebraska, two teams currently sitting at 6-4, where a close win against them wouldn't necessarily influence the Playoff committee to bump up the Hawkeyes.

Ferentz may not want to hear about running up the score, but getting into the endzone an extra time or two against the Fighting Illini and Cornhuskers wouldn't be the worst strategy imaginable.

Iowa Hawkeyes head coach Kirk Ferentz leads his team onto the field before a game against the Minnesota Golden Gophers at Huntington Bank Stadium in Minneapolis, Minn., on Oct. 24, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Iowa ranks 73rd in the country in scoring (24.8 points per game), but has blown out each of its last three opponents by a combined score of 72-17.

The Hawkeyes stunned Michigan on the road in September in dramatic fashion and also blanked Wisconsin 30-0 in October for their two most impressive wins of the year. Their 13-10 loss at Minnesota is keeping them outside of the Top 12 as the season quickly comes to a close.

Mark Harris is a writer for OutKick. Follow him on X @itismarkharris.

articles.title: Markwayne Mullin defends move to take government plane to football game amid flight stoppage – US politics live
articles.excerpt:
The secretary of homeland security flew to attend a college game Saturday, after thousands of flights were cancelled

During today’s hearing Markwayne Mullin defended his decision to take a government...
articles.body_text:
The secretary of homeland security flew to attend a college game Saturday, after thousands of flights were cancelled

During today’s hearing Markwayne Mullin defended his decision to take a government plane to attend a football game between Louisiana State University and the University of Texas on Saturday, while thousands of flights had been cancelled and the airspace closed during the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) nationwide grounding over the weekend.

“You want to bring up the fact that I took my family and my great nieces to an LSU game that was scheduled for weeks prior because I wanted to be a good uncle,” Mullin said, following questions from Congressman Bennie Thompson, the committee’s top Democrat.

Mullin went further, and said that had he not traveled to the game it could have created “confusion” because he was due to meet Louisiana governor Jeff Landry.

Mullin added that his absence might have shown “distrust that we’re not even willing to fly” after the FAA reopened the airspace.

“We had discussions at 10 o’clock Saturday morning. Should we cancel it? We had deep conversations about it,” the homeland security secretary said. “We were saying our skies were completely open. On Saturday alone, 36,000 planes flew and flew safely. Before I took off, the airspace had been open for almost 24 hours.”

Mullin noted that he paid for the trip himself because it was for non-official business, even though he is required to use the government aircraft for security reasons, and scolded Democrats for their line of questioning.

“The hypocrisy from you and from the members that want to make a big deal out of it … you guys would have done the same thing, but you would have called it a campaign event,” he said.

And in other news, from the basement of Capitol Hill …

Thomas Massie, the outgoing Republican congressman, shared pictures of his new office in the final weeks of the 119th Congress.

“It’s half a cubicle, but I have an extra seat for one staffer,” Massie said. “It’s traditional to kick non-returning members out of their offices early and ship them to this cubicle farm. The assumption is lame duck members just quit working … not me!”

A reminder that Massie lost his primary in May, after bucking with Donald Trump on several occasions. Earlier this month, Massie also launched a failed effort to impeach defense secretary Pete Hegseth, but his resolution was effectively killed when Republicans sent it to committee for further review. Democrats, however, have vowed to relaunch the attempt in the new year when they take the majority in both chambers.

One note, tomorrow’s meeting between Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen is set to last fewer than 60 minutes.

“No more than an hour” has been set aside for the historic summit between the three leaders, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told Russian state media on Wednesday.

The US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, faces mounting questions over his handling of the Nvidia affair as Democratic lawmakers demand answers over his family firm’s vast stake in the tech company.

Cantor Fitzgerald, the investment firm Lutnick ran for decades before joining the Trump administration, held shares in Nvidia worth “hundreds of millions of dollars” while Lutnick made key decisions affecting the tech firm’s ability to operate, according to Democrats on three key congressional committees.

“The American people deserve to know: did the secretary of commerce seriously and perhaps irreversibly compromise US national security interests to make money for his adult children and Cantor Fitzgerald?” said Jamie Raskin of Maryland, Gregory Meeks of New York and Sydney Kamlager-Dove of California.

Cantor Fitzgerald insists it had “no role” in the Trump administration’s decisions about Nvidia.

But in a letter on Tuesday to Lutnick’s son Brandon, who now serves as chair of Cantor Fitzgerald, the trio of lawmakers demanded documents and records, including communications concerning Nvidia.

They said that they wanted to “understand whether any actions or decisions by Secretary Lutnick concerning export controls, enforcement measures, or national security policies may have been improperly influenced by Cantor Fitzgerald’s holdings or business interests”.

And responding to the nomination of Hakeem Jeffries to be the next – and first Black – House speaker, Chuck Schumer told reporters:

double quotation markI’m so glad he was elected by such an overwhelming margin. He’s going to be a great speaker. It’s historic. I’ve known him from the very early days when he was even running for Congress, and I look forward to working with him together.

Chuck Schumer, the current Senate minority leader facing a challenge for majority leader from Maryland senator Chris Van Hollen, also expressed confidence he would get the position.

Asked by a reporter if he was concerned about his election, Schumer replied: “No. I will be elected majority leader. I’m confident we have the votes.”

In that case, he was asked, should Van Hollen give up his bid? “That’s going to be up to him,” Schumer said. “I think what we all want to do is roll up our sleeves together, everybody, and deliver for the American people. That’s what we’re focused on. That’s what we’re focused on.”

Celebrating Mary Peltola’s historic win in Alaska, Chuck Schumer described her victory “an exclamation point on what has been a great election year”.

Peltola, a former US House lawmaker, is the first Democrat the state has elected to the Senate since 2008. Her victory comes just two years after Alaska voters unseated her while supporting Trump by a double-digit margin.

“We now have a margin of nine Democratic senators,” Schumer told reporters. “This is the greatest landslide in midterms in over 70 years.”

He said the Democrats had won due to “great candidates like Peltola” but also “because we focused on what the American people cared about: lowering their costs, ending corruption, ending the chaos.”

He went on: “The real work starts today. We’ve won the election. We’ve won the American people’s votes, but now we have to earn their trust.”

More from today’s hearing with DHS secretary Markwayne Mullin, where Democratic representative Seth Magaziner questioned the secretary about the fatal ICE shooting of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Maine.

In July, an ICE agent shot and killed the 25-year-old father during a traffic stop in Biddeford, 15 minutes from Scarborough, just days after an agent killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston, Texas.

The shooting renewed calls for accountability in the agency. In particular, it renewed scrutiny over ICE’s hiring practices after it came to light that the officer that killed Guerrero, David Brouillette, had a troubling history of violent behavior, including past complaints of domestic violence and abuse, as well as mental health issues. Brouillette, who was hired during a federal recruitment surge, also has a record of deep-seated anti-immigrant hostility.

Magaziner asked Mullin how many ICE agents were currently on the streets who had not completed full background checks. Mullin said they had all completed training, to which Magaziner reminded him was not his question. Mullin course-corrected: “Every ICE agent we have in service right now have full background checks.” The ones that don’t are on administrative leave until they do, he added.

Magaziner, of Rhode Island, pointed out to Mullin that Brouillette’s background check had not been completed when he fatally shot Guerrero, nor had he completed standardized training when he was “put on the street with a mask and a gun” by the Trump administration. “He was put on the street after completing just an online course, he didn’t even do any of the in-person training in Georgia,” Magaziner said. “Has everyone who is out there on the street today completed the full 13-week in-person training?”

Mullin said they had, and those who haven’t had been put on administrative leave. He said there had also been additional training introduced.

He couldn’t answer how many people had been put on the street who hadn’t had the full training, and then appeared to defer responsibility to his predecessor.

double quotation markUnfortunately, congressman, there were some decisions that were made before I was secretary that we were having to undo.

You can watch a clip of the exchange here.

Canadian prime minister Mark Carney emphasized Canada’s efforts to strengthen their own sovereignty by moving away from dependence on the US economy, infrastructure and defense.

He spoke to DealBook, a New York Times summit with global leaders, from China, where he has struck a deal with Xi Jinping to reduce tariffs between the two countries – a sign that Carney is breaking with US policy towards China. The two countries have been at odds since Donald Trump returned to the White House two years ago, and has continually threatened to annex Canada and has placed tariffs on Canadian goods.

Canada is also seeking closer ties to Europe by increasing trade, collaborating on defense, research and intelligence. For example, Europe and Canada are trying to launch their own satellite system to reduce dependency on Elon Musk’s Starshield.

More trade deals are being struck with other countries, including the Philippines and India.

Carney emphasized that the US remains a key ally, but said Canada’s diversification could give them the upper hand in talks to better their relationship with the US.

“Our cards are that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us,” Carney said.

The Canadian prime minister did add, however, that Trump is “very different” behind closed doors. “He’s very personable,” Carney said, despite his fraught relationship with the US president. “He listens a lot more in private.”

During today’s hearing Markwayne Mullin defended his decision to take a government plane to attend a football game between Louisiana State University and the University of Texas on Saturday, while thousands of flights had been cancelled and the airspace closed during the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) nationwide grounding over the weekend.

“You want to bring up the fact that I took my family and my great nieces to an LSU game that was scheduled for weeks prior because I wanted to be a good uncle,” Mullin said, following questions from Congressman Bennie Thompson, the committee’s top Democrat.

Mullin went further, and said that had he not traveled to the game it could have created “confusion” because he was due to meet Louisiana governor Jeff Landry.

Mullin added that his absence might have shown “distrust that we’re not even willing to fly” after the FAA reopened the airspace.

“We had discussions at 10 o’clock Saturday morning. Should we cancel it? We had deep conversations about it,” the homeland security secretary said. “We were saying our skies were completely open. On Saturday alone, 36,000 planes flew and flew safely. Before I took off, the airspace had been open for almost 24 hours.”

Mullin noted that he paid for the trip himself because it was for non-official business, even though he is required to use the government aircraft for security reasons, and scolded Democrats for their line of questioning.

“The hypocrisy from you and from the members that want to make a big deal out of it … you guys would have done the same thing, but you would have called it a campaign event,” he said.

All three national security officials testifying to the House homeland security committee unequivocally said the recent cyber outages were not related, nor were they the result of malicious cyber activity.

Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, said: “Based on what we know today, after a great deal of diligence, these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.”

Markwayne Mullin, the Department of Homeland Security secretary, noted that his team has seen, “nothing that would indicate they are related”.

“Our cyber experts have been engaged in day one in all of these incidents, and I want to be very clear on this on this point: there is no indication whatsoever that there is any malicious cyber activity related to any of those incidents,” Christopher Raia, the deputy FBI director, told lawmakers.

Of those who voted against Jeffries’ nomination, seven incoming members of the left-flank explained their decision to not support the current minority leader in his nomination for speaker.

“We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations. While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership. Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no,” Democratic members-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier, Adam Hamawy, Frederick Haynes, Melat Kiros, Donavan McKinney, Chris Rabb and Claire Valdez said in a joint statement.

House Democrats have nominated current minority leader Hakeem Jeffries as their candidate for speaker in the next Congress.

My colleague Chris Stein reports that, according to a person familiar, Jeffries received 251 yes votes of 262 cast, and 11 members voted no on his nomination.

Jeffries faced no opposition in his candidacy to lead the House, and will face a full chamber vote in the new year, when Republicans will be in the minority.

The Associated Press is reporting that Donald Trump plans to hold a separate meeting with Vladimir Putin on Thursday, citing an anonymous US official.

The meeting would be in addition to the blockbuster trilateral talks the two will hold with host Xi Jinping on Thursday.

If confirmed, it would be their first bilateral since they met in Alaska in 2025 for talks that failed to reach a deal on the war in Ukraine.

Trump had already suggested he might meet with Putin, as well as with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, but neither option had been added to his official schedule.

FBI director Kash Patel was called out by Republican Andrew Garbarino, the chair of the House homeland security committee, within minutes of the hearing beginning on Wednesday.

Garbarino began the hearing saying it was “disappointing” that Patel refused to testify to the committee.

“Despite repeated attempts over the span of several months, between then and now, to find any date when he could testify, director made clear that he had no intention of appearing. Director Patel’s refusal to testify marks a significant departure from well-established committee precedent,” Garbarino said.

Bennie Thompson, the top Democrat on the committee, echoed Garbarino’s concerns.

Christopher Raia, the deputy FBI director, is testifying to the committee instead.

As we noted earlier, a House homeland security hearing is under way with the department secretary, Markwayne Mullin, deputy FBI director Christopher Raia and director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, all testifying before lawmakers.

articles.title: The leave campaign has been resurrected, so how should Burnham respond?
articles.excerpt:
No 10 is confident the PM can make the case for closer EU ties, while others worry about leaving the campaign solely in his hands

The launch of a pro-Brexit campaign was one of the few genuine surpri...
articles.body_text:
No 10 is confident the PM can make the case for closer EU ties, while others worry about leaving the campaign solely in his hands

The launch of a pro-Brexit campaign was one of the few genuine surprises this week in Westminster, even if the arguments were straight out of a familiar playbook.

The video launched on X over the weekend, with scenes of riots in France, champagne flowing in Brussels, and European politicians saying how desperate they were for Britain’s cash.

Among Westminster’s anti-Brexit veterans, there was immediate chatter about whether a counteroffensive was needed. “I think the immediate reaction was – are they off to the races while we are still putting our pants on?” one said.

For now, the rebuttal of Stay Out’s claims – including that returning to the EU would cost £750m a week – is mostly being done on social media by interested pro-rejoin freelancers, without any kind of central organisation.

One MP said: “It is hard for us to begin any kind of new pro-rejoin campaign until we know exactly the direction the government is heading.

“There are organisations that exist already, like Best for Britain, but I think making the case to the public would need a fresh movement. I think we want to stay away from the kind of marches that People’s Vote movement did with the blue berets if we can possibly avoid it.”

Inside No 10, there is a confidence that Andy Burnham can make his own case for a closer relationship with Europe, without the need for any external pressure group. Stay Out – which is run by the former deputy chief Brexit negotiator Oliver Lewis – will be dubbed “the status quo campaign”.

There is reason to be confident. Strategists have seen Labour polling that shows almost three-quarters – 71% – of all voters support a closer relationship with Europe if it helps bring down prices and grow the economy.

It will be the prime minister, they say, who can front any campaigning that is needed, who can argue that Brexit has done more harm than good, damaging the economy, making it harder for British people to travel and businesses to trade and fuelling the small boats crisis.

However, there will be some fears that this has been tried before when David Cameron attempted to make the case for remain in 2016. But Labour strategists say this is a fundamentally different political moment. “Cameron could not make this kind of emotional connection with people, it was business leaders, facts and figures, and he was arguing for the status quo,” one said. “We are the change campaign now.”

While some cabinet members urged caution last week over Burnham’s uncertain direction on Europe, most trust the prime minister can set out a viable post-summit plan. “All of us, honestly, are slightly running to catch up with a different way of doing things,” one said. “We all easily lapse into the worries about leave-voting seats.

“But there is obviously an argument to be made that the old rules don’t apply. And Andy’s way of doing things is laying out political argument. And we have to believe in that as the way to affect public sentiment.”

There are some close to Labour who worry about leaving the argument solely to Burnham. “Can they do this from the bowels of Downing Street?” one asked. “You do need rebuttal out there and people ready to go out and fight and say, this is bollocks. And it felt like that infrastructure is not there yet.”

Another veteran of the remain campaign said there was concern about being “left out on a limb” if a rejoin campaign was resurrected. “I think whether they like it or not, there will be an apolitical campaign trying to push the maximalist position on Europe. They have people willing to help but it’s not organised in any way.”

Many of those who worked on the remain campaign and the subsequent People’s Vote are scarred by the experience, particular the final months which descended into bitter infighting. But the same is also true for some of the most high-profile veterans of Vote Leave – who also want to steer clear of Stay Out.

As in the pro-Brexit campaigns, there are often willing funders to push pro-European campaigning. “It will happen because there will be money for it,” one campaign veteran said. “But you could not pay me any money to go back to that issue.”

articles.title: Californians sound off on Newsom’s death penalty move, midterms and failed billionaire tax
articles.excerpt: Fox News Digital hit the streets of Los Angeles to gauge reaction to some of the most contentious issues facing the state and the nation, including California’s failed billionaire tax proposal, the mi...
articles.body_text:
Fox News Digital hit the streets of Los Angeles to gauge reaction to some of the most contentious issues facing the state and the nation, including California’s failed billionaire tax proposal, the midterms and more. (Fox News)

LOS ANGELES — From California Gov. Gavin Newsom's decision to commute hundreds of death sentences to the defeat of a proposed billionaire tax, the state's biggest political controversies have sparked sharply divided reactions.

With Democrats preparing to take control of Congress in January, Californians also have strong opinions about what the party should prioritize, from healthcare and affordability to releasing the Epstein files and investigating the Trump administration.

Fox News Digital hit the streets of Los Angeles to hear directly from locals who offered blunt assessments of the issues shaping California’s political landscape and the country’s next chapter.

GAVIN NEWSOM WIPES OUT CALIFORNIA'S DEATH ROW IN HISTORIC MASS COMMUTATION

Gavin Newsom announced Nov. 5 that he planned to commute all 548 of California's death sentences to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

California has not executed an inmate since 2006, and voters in the state have previously rejected proposals seeking to abolish the death penalty. Newsom maintains, however, that California "cannot morally kill" those on death row. Dozens of California district attorneys have sued to challenge Newsom's clemency.

The decision has drawn mixed reactions, with some victims' families expressing support while others, along with prosecutors, have strongly opposed the move. Critics question how the governor could spare the lives of inmates convicted of carrying out some of the nation’s most brutal homicides.

Fox News Digital asked people in Los Angeles whether they support Newsom's death penalty commutations. Some voiced support for the move, questioning the death penalty's constitutionality.

"I'm OK with that. ... I don't think you need to kill anyone. They can die in prison. That's fine," Los Angeles resident Lawrence said.

"One hundred percent," Milan of Los Angeles said. "I think death row should be abolished entirely.

CALIFORNIA PROSECUTORS SLAM NEWSOM'S DEATH ROW COMMUTATIONS, ACCUSE GOVERNOR OF PUTTING 'POLITICS OVER PEOPLE'

Gov. Gavin Newsom commuted the death penalty for all of California's 548 death row inmates. (Anadolu via Getty Images)

"Anyone on death row should have the chance to continue the rehabilitation because the whole point of our judicial system and jail system in the whole first place was for people who did something wrong to be rehabilitated, to go back into society," she added.

"To be honest, yeah," Los Angeles local Sam said in support of Gov. Newsom’s commutations. "I think it's worse to spend your whole life in jail, so if you really want to punish somebody, then probably life in prison without parole is worse than the death penalty."

"I'm not really sure. It depends on the level of the crime," Los Angeles resident Zoe said. "To me, being in prison forever would be worse than being put to death. So, for me, I'd rather them suffer for the rest of their life."

Others, however, defended capital punishment for those convicted of serious crimes, including murder.

"I'm for capital punishment," Dave of Santa Monica told Fox News Digital.

"I think [Newsom] should stick with the federal guidelines around capital punishment," Los Angeles local David told Fox News Digital. "If you are proven beyond a reasonable doubt to be guilty of murder, there's probably only one way to handle that."

California was among the states that helped fuel a nationwide Democratic wave in the 2026 midterm elections, with Democrats flipping five Republican-held House seats in the state and contributing to the party's takeover of Congress.

The gains followed California voters' approval of Proposition 50 in 2025, which redrew congressional districts to favor Democrats in response to Republican-backed redistricting efforts in Texas.

California voters spoke with Fox News Digital about how they voted and which policies they want the Democratic majority to tackle first when they assume office in January.

One Los Angeles resident said the first thing on his list is the Epstein files, and another said she would like Democrats to halt U.S. involvement with the war in Iran.

"Epstein files," said Sam. "Just the fact that all this is being swept under the rug for so long. We pay taxes. Rich people, billionaires don't pay taxes. The whole system's f---ed up. It's bulls---. The only way to fix it is to burn everything down, like a house with a bad foundation."

"Stopping all of the illegal actions that are taking place, things that were supposed to have congressional approval. They should, those should be stopped," said Zoe, referring to U.S. military action involving Iran. "Wars, dropping bombs on people."

DEMS' CALIFORNIA REDISTRICTING MASTERMIND FLIPS SCRIPT AFTER HELPING PARTY WIN 5 GOP SEATS: 'KILL'

Democrats won a majority in both the House and the Senate in the 2026 midterm elections. (Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Healthcare also emerged as a top priority for California Democrats.

"One thing and one thing only: healthcare," said David, adding he voted for candidates on the "left side."

When asked by Fox News Digital how such a program would be funded, he responded, "Taxing those that have the most amount and are doing incredibly well in this country. Taxing them a little bit more isn't going to hurt them."

Other Californians said they want Republicans and Democrats to work across the aisle and focus on collaboration over partisan clashes.

"I hope that their first, like, publicity goal, in a sense, is to take out that separation of far right and far left, because there should just be like a purple in a sense," Milan said.

"I would like them to work with the Republicans and the president," Dave told Fox News Digital. When asked if he thought they would, he responded, "No, I don't."

One of the most watched measures on California’s 2026 midterm ballot was Proposition 40's billionaire tax, a proposed one-time 5% tax on California billionaires to generate $100 billion for healthcare and education.

California voters rejected the proposal, with roughly 53% voting against it and 47% supporting it, according to The Associated Press. Its defeat marked a blow for progressives that had championed taxing the state's wealthiest residents.

California's wealthy technology executives poured millions of dollars into political action committees to defeat Prop 40, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin, who spent over $100 million. Gov. Newsom notably opposed the measure and implored his constituents to follow suit.

Several Los Angeles residents questioned why the wealth tax failed in heavily Democratic California, with one attributing its defeat to "propaganda."

"I think that's crazy. I think it was like over a few million votes for it. I know there's not a few billion billionaires who voted. So, I think it's due to propaganda," Milan said.

DEMOCRATS SET SIGHTS ON ELON MUSK PROBE AFTER MIDTERM WINS, BUT PRITZKER DRAWS A SURPRISING LINE

Attendees cheer during a speech by U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., during the campaign kickoff for the California Billionaire Tax Act in Los Angeles Feb. 18, 2026. (Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images)

"That was a surprise. I don't know how many billionaires there are in California but ... it's less than 1%, and, so, I'm very surprised it didn't pass," Lawrence said. "I don't know who voted for that."

"That sucks, to be honest," said Sam. "If these billionaires can get away with not paying taxes and me or anybody else has to pay their taxes basically on a middle class or lower income salary, I think it's f---ing disgusting, honestly. And I think these people should be taxed, 100%. I mean, the wealth gap here is insane. Like, the inequalities between the haves and the have nots."

Others welcomed the proposal's defeat, arguing that imposing additional taxes on billionaires could drive wealthy residents out of California and hurt the state's economy.

"I don't want the billionaires to leave California," Zoe countered.

"That's good that that failed for the sake of the economy of California. ... I mean, they’re the ones paying most of the taxes, right?" Dave told Fox News Digital.

Democrats are expected to launch several investigations into President Donald Trump, his Cabinet and business allies once they assume the congressional majority in January.

Top House and Senate Democrats told Fox News Digital they are considering investigations, congressional hearings and potential impeachment proceedings targeting Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and border czar Tom Homan.

Republicans have characterized Democrats’ planned proceedings against Trump officials as politically motivated, and the administration has already shown it is prepared to push back against congressional investigations.

Fox News Digital asked Los Angeles residents whether they would prefer Democrats to prioritize affordability and other issues affecting Americans or focus on investigating the Trump administration.

"They can do both. They can walk and chew gum at the same time," said Lawrence.

President Donald Trump, seated next to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, speaks during a Cabinet meeting at the White House in Washington, D.C., March 26, 2026. (Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters)

"If it's easy stuff that isn't going to take time out of doing what needs to be done to help the people, I would say go for it," Zoe told Fox News Digital.

Several Los Angeles residents argued that Democrats should prioritize issues directly affecting everyday Americans but also acknowledged the importance of holding the Trump administration accountable.

"Both are necessary, but I think most people are much more concerned with healthcare than they are about holding anyone responsible, although I think both are important," David said.

"The daily citizen matters a lot more than this drawn-on fight that is going to happen," said Milan. "This fight matters very much to hold the Trump administration accountable. They need to be held accountable, but that is gonna take a long time and a lot of back and forth."

Fox News Digital reached out to Newsom's office for comment.

Nora Moriarty is a Writer at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: ‘Neighbourhood support teams’ to pave way for national care service, Cooper announces
articles.excerpt:
Health secretary said programme would help about 566,000 vulnerable people in England by April

More than half a million of the most vulnerable people in England will be offered help from joint NHS an...
articles.body_text:
Health secretary said programme would help about 566,000 vulnerable people in England by April

More than half a million of the most vulnerable people in England will be offered help from joint NHS and social care teams that will pave the way for the promised national care service, Yvette Cooper has announced.

Elderly people, care home residents, those with dementia and people near the end of their lives will receive assistance from the new programme.

By next April about 566,000 people – 1% of the population – will benefit from joined-up “neighbourhood support teams” providing personalised care.

In a speech on Wednesday at the King’s Fund health thinktank, Cooper described the measure as a “downpayment” on the national care service promised by Andy Burnham to address the social care crisis.

The service will be expanded and eventually cover about 2 million people with particular health needs, including parents and babies, and under-25s who are not in education, employment or training.

Once fully operational, the major shift in key care services is expected to help relieve the pressure on overcrowded hospitals by cutting 4.3m bed days and reducing the number of people – mainly the frail elderly and those with dementia – who experience “corridor care”.

“The most frail and vulnerable, 4% of the population, account for 70% of emergency bed days in hospital, even though for many of them, an extended hospital stay is not where they want to be,” Cooper said.

The teams will be made up of GPs, district nurses, occupational therapists, geriatric consultants, physiotherapists, clinical pharmacists, mental health workers and social workers.

Age UK welcomed the announcement as “fantastic news for older people, especially those living with frailty and in declining health”.

The pledge to create the new teams is a major milestone in the government’s ambition to transform how the NHS works through “three big shifts”: from an analogue to digital service, from treatment to prevention of illness, and from hospital-based care to much more help being provided in community settings and people’s homes.

The teams will identify the most vulnerable members of their local community and devise a plan for keeping them as well as possible, including providing care in their own home or care home for as long as possible.

They will receive regular checks to assess their health, from teams who know them, to ensure they are receiving the right support. Patients and their families will also have access to a 24/7 helpline that will act as a single point of contact, though it is unclear when that will start.

Everyone being helped by the joint teams of NHS and local council personnel will also have an individual care plan that makes clear what their needs are and who should be helping with them.

The teams will review patients’ medicines, check they are having physiotherapy and that they have a care plan in place, for example.

Cooper said the teams would provide a more proactive and personalised approach that would make care much easier to access while also reducing the strain on the NHS, which has been struggling to meet the growing demand for care from the ageing and increasingly sick population.

Remote monitoring, “virtual ward” rounds and face-to-face visits to patients in their own homes in west Hertfordshire has led to people spending three fewer days in Watford general hospital, saved the local NHS £3.8m, and proved very popular with those cared for in that way.

The health secretary cited the NHS founder Nye Bevan’s belief in local community services, not just hospitals, and the then Labour health secretary Barbara Castle’s ambition in 1976 to reduce dependence on hospitals and promote integration of health and social care, as well as Burnham’s attempt as health secretary in 2009-10 to reform social care.

Sarah Woolnough, the King’s Fund’s chief executive, cautioned that while “bringing care closer to home has been an ambition for successive governments”, it had not happened – and may not happen now – because money had not been provided to enable the switch.

Helen Morgan, the Liberal Democrats’ health spokesperson, said: “To bring hospitals back from the brink we need more care at home, but a phone number isn’t a care package. With no new money and nothing starting until April, this does little for the thousands of frail patients facing a winter stuck in hospital.”

The creation of the new teams builds on Cooper’s announcement last week that GPs in England will receive £40m this winter to help give 300,000 vulnerable patients better care at home, to reduce their risk of ending up in hospital.

articles.title: Ex-Tory defectors barred from shaping Reform’s immigration policy, says Zia Yusuf
articles.excerpt:
Comments by Reform’s home affairs spokesperson raise questions about unity at top of the party

Former Conservative defectors to Reform UK have been barred from shaping the party’s immigration policy,...
articles.body_text:
Comments by Reform’s home affairs spokesperson raise questions about unity at top of the party

Former Conservative defectors to Reform UK have been barred from shaping the party’s immigration policy, its home affairs spokesperson has claimed, excluding in effect the majority of the party’s MPs.

“If you are in the category of being concerned about [former Conservatives being involved in Reform], none of the above are going to be involved in immigration policy or borders policy,” Zia Yusuf told a podcast by the Spectator magazine.

Michael Gove, the Spectator editor and former Conservative minister, challenged Yusuf over how Reform intended to bring down migration numbers, given there were so many former Tory MPs in its ranks – including the former immigration minister Robert Jenrick – who had failed to do so while in government.

Yusuf said: “There’s a reason why Nigel’s given me this brief and not them.”

Yusuf was embroiled in a feud with Jenrick before the former Tory minister made the jump to Reform earlier this year, becoming its economics spokesperson.

In addition to Jenrick, the former home secretary Suella Braverman, the former DWP shadow minister Danny Kruger and the former Foreign Office shadow minister Andrew Rosindell are among the Tory MPs to have defected to Reform.

Yusuf qualified his comments by saying Braverman and Jenrick had either been sacked or resigned “over immigration policy or issues around culture”. The comments raise questions about unity at the top of Reform.

Braverman, Reform’s education spokesperson, and Jenrick have waded into immigration and cultural issues since joining Reform. The claims that former Tories have no role in immigration policy for Reform also appear to be at odds with, for example, Jenrick’s announcement in June of plans for a levy on migrant labour.

Reform’s grassroots members have long appeared suspicious of former Conservatives in their midst. Farage himself has frequently had to push back against claims that his party had become “the Conservative party 2.0” and said in January that Reform would not accept any more defectors after local elections were held on 7 May. Jenrick and others who defected nonetheless maintain a strong influence within Reform.

Tom Milford, a former spokesperson for Jenrick, has become Reform’s head of press, while the MP himself continues to generate slickly produced videos for social media covering a range of topics including law and order.

Jenrick is often mooted alongside Yusuf and Richard Tice as the most likely successor to Farage if he was to stand down.

The Labour party said Yusuf had “admitted that most Reform MPs can’t be trusted on their migration policies”.

Anna Turley, the Labour MP and minister of state for border security and asylum, said: “They don’t trust two-thirds of their MPs to work on their immigration policies, yet they expect the country to trust them to secure Britain’s borders.”

articles.title: Russian national accused of surveilling US tech company
articles.excerpt:
A Russian flag flies above the Russian Embassy in Berlin, Germany. (Kristian Tuxen Ladegaard Berg/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

A grand jury indicted Russian national Igor D’iu on Wednesday on charges o...
articles.body_text:
A Russian flag flies above the Russian Embassy in Berlin, Germany. (Kristian Tuxen Ladegaard Berg/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

A grand jury indicted Russian national Igor D’iu on Wednesday on charges of conspiring to act as an agent of a foreign government, acting as an agent of a foreign government without notice to the Attorney General, interstate stalking, and fraud in connection with identification documents in connection to alleged espionage of a U.S. company in Silicon Valley.

"Igor D’iu was allegedly recruited, directed, and funded by the Russian government to stalk employees of a major U.S. technology company, using physical surveillance, electronic tracking devices, and fraudulent identities to gather intelligence," Roman Rozhavsky, Assistant Director of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division, said in a statement.

D'iu was arrested in October after allegedly being recruited by co-conspirators through the messaging platform Telegram to clandestinely target employees of a Silicon Valley defense and technology company.

FOREIGN SPY ‘HONEYTRAPS’ TARGETING AMERICA’S TECH ELITE SPARK ALARM AMID NVIDIA CEO SCANDAL

D’iu's co-conspirators, who provided him with instructions, equipment, and financial support, told him his espionage was for "the Motherland," explaining that the company he was spying on was supplying weapons used against Russia in Ukraine, according to an arrest affidavit.

A Patriot system received by Ukraine is seen on the Day of Ukrainian Air Force on August 4, 2024 in Unspecified, Ukraine. At the event for the Day of Ukrainian Air Force with the participation of President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyi, the first General Dynamics F-16 Fighting Falcons received by Ukraine were demonstrated. (Vitalii Nosach/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images)

UKRAINE RELEASES VIDEO SHOWING DAMAGE TO PUTIN'S PRIZED BRIDGE FOLLOWING 'UNPRECEDENTED OPERATION' IN CRIMEA

"Russia may rely on covert operatives and criminal intermediaries as it attempts to gain an edge in its war against Ukraine, but those tactics do not place its government or its collaborators beyond the reach of the law. This arrest should serve as a warning to anyone looking to undermine U.S. interests or threaten our national security: No matter where you are or who you’re working for, justice will find you," Rozhavsky added.

D'iu is accused of entering the U.S. illegally, traveling from Istanbul, Turkey to Mexico City, Mexico in June, at which point his co-conspirators connected him with an individual who was able to smuggle him across the border.

The operative was then instructed to surveil employees of the company at a Paolo Alto, California coffee shop, even directing him to attempt to remotely access information from employees' laptop computers at the cafe, according to the affidavit.

The Russian national engaged in sweeping surveillance activities, including searching for employee addresses and even following a female employee for 30 miles.

Aerial photograph looking northeast over downtown Palo Alto, California, with University Avenue running through the heart of the commercial district. (iStock via Getty Images)

"The employee attempted to evade D’iu by making irregular turns, taking back roads, and entering a grocery store parking lot. D’iu allegedly aggressively continued following her, including through U-turns and illegal left turns, and ran a red light to remain behind her vehicle. Fearing for her safety, the employee called 911 and was instructed to drive to the San Francisco Police Department’s Mission Station. D’iu allegedly abandoned his pursuit after the employee contacted a police officer. Investigators also obtained evidence that D’iu had followed other company employees on preceding days," a Department of Justice statement about the indictment read.

"The Americans who build our defense technology help keep this country safe by arming our warfighters with the tools and weapons they need to prevail against our adversaries and enemies," Acting Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General M. Scott Proctor said in a statement.

"As alleged, D’iu entered our country illegally at the direction of foreign handlers to surveil, follow, and gather information about some of those who work in this vital industry. Such conduct, if proven, is a flagrant violation of U.S. sovereignty and an unacceptable attempt at intimidation. We will use every tool at our disposal to find, prosecute, and punish such conduct, wherever and whenever it happens," Proctor concluded.

D'iu faces up to 21 years in federal prison and $850,000 in fines if convicted on all charges. He is next set to appear in federal court on Nov. 21.

China's President Xi Jinping stands as President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin shake hands before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, China, on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press via AP)

The news breaks as President Donald Trump briefly shook hands with and met Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) welcome banquet in Shenzen, China today.

There's a new leader in the clubhouse when it comes to avoiding baby momma drama. He's a 32-year-old man who climbed into a tree last Tuesday night allegedly to avoid the mother of his child or children.

Deputies from the Pierce County Sheriff’s Office in Tacoma, Washington, responded to reports of a man stuck in a tree around 7:30 p.m. on Nov. 10 and found him "perched approximately 30 to 40 feet up in a tree."

INFLUENCER AND HER LAWYER FATHER ARRESTED FOR ALLEGED MURDER-FOR-HIRE PLOT INVOLVING HER BABY DADDY

articles.title: Protesters heckle Trump's ex-Border Patrol chief offstage after Dem governor condemns College Republican event
articles.excerpt:
Video shows protesters heckling former Border Patrol chief Gregory Bovino off the stage at a Rutgers College Republicans event.

Protesters heckled former Trump Border Patrol commander-at-large Gregor...
articles.body_text:
Video shows protesters heckling former Border Patrol chief Gregory Bovino off the stage at a Rutgers College Republicans event.

Protesters heckled former Trump Border Patrol commander-at-large Gregory Bovino off stage during a Monday night speech at Rutgers University, hours after New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill called the Rutgers College Republicans’ decision to host him "wrong" and urged the club to reconsider.

Bovino previously criticized Sherrill online, accusing her of prioritizing illegal immigrants over New Jersey residents. After returning to the stage, he called her "Sugar Pop Sherrill" and "Kim Jong Sherrill." Speaking to reporters afterward, he said she wanted to "trounce this freedom of speech," described the "Kim Jong Sherrill" label as "very fitting" and called the governor a "totalitarian." He also told Blaze News that Sherrill had timed her social media comments to "foment violence" against conservatives.

At Monday night’s Rutgers College Republicans event, protesters began shouting within minutes of Bovino taking the stage. Rutgers police escorted him offstage and ordered the hecklers to leave or face arrest, according to local reports. Bovino returned about ten minutes later to resume his remarks and answer questions. Hundreds of protesters also gathered outside.

30% OF COLLEGE STUDENTS SAY VIOLENCE ACCEPTABLE WAY TO STOP SPEAKERS ON CAMPUSES, SURVEY FINDS

Attendees at Greg Bovino's talk at Rutgers shout him down and heckle the former border patrol commander off stage. (FreedomNews.TV)

"What’s so crazy is that you all allowed a Nazi to be here," a protester yelled as the heckling began. Another shouted, "Your fascist death cult is failing!" Video from inside the event captured chants of "Get out of New Jersey!" and "Immigrants are welcome here!" Outside, hundreds of protesters carried images of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, who were shot and killed by federal agents in Minneapolis.

Before Bovino’s Monday appearance, Rutgers told Fox News Digital it was committed to protecting freedom of expression and maintaining campus security. The university also said hosting a student-organized event did not constitute an endorsement of the speaker or his views. Rutgers had not responded to Fox News Digital's follow-up request for comment about the disruption by publication.

Hours before Bovino’s speech, Sherrill said in a social media post that she was "deeply disappointed" by the Rutgers College Republicans’ invitation, adding, "Giving him a platform is the wrong decision."

Sherrill said that if the club went ahead with the event, she would ensure the state worked with Rutgers to protect "the safety of everyone and the rights enshrined in our Constitution," and she urged attendees to question Bovino about his record.

SHERRILL COMMITS $20.2M TO DEPORTATION DEFENSE WHILE CONDEMNING RUTGERS OVER BORDER PATROL SPEAKER

New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill is seen. (Getty Images)

Fox News Digital contacted Sherrill's team for comment on the disruption at Bovino’s event but received no response before publication.

Bovino served as Trump's commander-at-large of the U.S. Border Patrol and oversaw immigration enforcement and deportation operations, including Operation Metro Surge in Minneapolis. He was removed from command in January following the shootings of Good and Pretti and retired from the Border Patrol in March.

A woman walks at the campus after Rutgers University President Robert Barchi held a town hall meeting to students and people in Newark, New Jersey, April 8, 2013. Rutgers University plans to commission an independent review of how the school handled allegations that its men's basketball coach physically and verbally abused his players, Rutgers officials said on Monday. REUTERS/Eduardo Munoz (UNITED STATES - Tags: SPORT BASKETBALL EDUCATION SOCIETY) (Reuters)

During the Rutgers College Republicans event, a student asked Bovino about the deaths of Good and Pretti. He replied, "Poor decisions come with consequences," then said the circumstances were "still being sorted out." Bovino called ICE agents the "real victims" and added, "I love them and salute them."

Asked after Monday’s event whether he stood by the deaths of Pretti and Good, Bovino said, "I didn’t stand by anybody’s death."

He clarified that his earlier comment about going "harder" referred to mass deportation operations, not the shootings of Good or Pretti. Bovino said he would rejoin the Border Patrol "in an instant" to continue those operations and called the end of enforcement activity in Minnesota "the great surrender." He added that he hoped the administration would complete its mass deportation efforts but feared it would "surrender" its aggressive deportation agenda.

Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.
