articles.title: Robert Pattinson is the new James Bond. Can he become the hero the West needs?
articles.excerpt:
The 'Fox News @ Night' nightcap panel reacts to Robert Pattinson being chosen as the next actor to play James Bond, debating their top picks for the role.

So, Amazon MGM Studios announced that it cho...
articles.body_text:
The 'Fox News @ Night' nightcap panel reacts to Robert Pattinson being chosen as the next actor to play James Bond, debating their top picks for the role.

So, Amazon MGM Studios announced that it chose the British actor Robert Pattinson to be the new James Bond. This could be bigger than mere new films in the franchise, as Ian Fleming’s creation was never more important for the Western psyche than now — in this time of political division in America and a weak and troubled Europe, the West needs its myths and heroes.

Bond is an old-school ultimate man’s man. He dresses above occasions, is cool under pressure, is a lady’s man, a secret agent and spoiler of the plots of terrorist masterminds. At 40, Pattinson is the right age to play the long-running and, arguably, the most iconic man’s man in film history. Sean Connery was just 32 years old when his first Bond film, "Dr. No," came out. But Pattinson is no Connery.

IDRIS ELBA REJECTS 'WOKE' JAMES BOND CASTING PUSH, WARNS AUDIENCES 'WON'T GO FOR A BLACK MALE' IN THE ROLE

Pattinson has the looks, almost, but he is more emblematic of a weak Timothy Dalton than the unforgettable Sean Connery or even of Roger Moore. Still, he is more of a Bond than Daniel Craig, an actor never stately or commanding enough to carry the role.

Robert Pattinson has earned early Oscar buzz after the first trailer for "Primetime" showcased his uncanny performance as Chris Hansen. (Stephane Cardinale/Corbis)

Disappointingly, like Craig, Pattinson has expressed anti-gun sentiments. In interviews promoting the 2014 film, "The Rover," (in which his character uses a gun), Pattinson said he was "quite anti-gun." But that was a long time ago and Pattinson has since been careful not to express political positions. This is good, as we don’t need more divisive political rhetoric from actors who are seemingly embarrassed by their roles.

Pattinson’s casting followed screen tests and competition from actors reportedly including Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor and Jack Lowden. Given those choices, it is not hard to see why Pattinson stood out, even though his roles in "Harry Potter" and the "Twilight" films were boyish, not Bond-like.

Sean Connery’s Bond set the standard of the tall, dark-haired, impeccably tailored agent who could effortlessly go from a tuxedo to a wetsuit. This character is supposed to be both suave and understated, and very few can carry both off at once. Bond’s lines are supposed to be dry and straightforward. He is never weak, though he can be captured and beaten.

WHAT DO YOU THINK? NEW JAMES BOND IS ROBERT PATTINSON

The official teaser for the next 007 film to come does not include a single word, just Pattinson, gun in hand, emerging from blackness with the iconic Bond theme strumming. This tells us nothing, but it is on theme.

Pattinson shares key physical attributes with Connery — he is tall, has dark hair and an ability to look sharp in a tux. But can Pattinson look cool under pressure while emanating the danger of a lion in the tall grass?

JAMES BOND LEGEND ROGER MOORE'S SON CALLS OUT TIKTOK CULTURE, HOLLYWOOD'S RECYCLED COMIC BOOK MOVIES

I am hopeful, but previous roles never showed that Pattinson has the acting range or the manly bearing needed to pull this off.

In "The Batman" (2022), Pattinson showed he can carry himself in a larger-than-life role, and he had the poise to make the part believable, but again the strength was not there. He is too weak-chested and never quite gives the impression he is as sure of himself as Bond must be — Frank Sinatra, for example, had this quality.

'PRIMETIME' STAR ROBERT PATTINSON SHOCKS FANS WITH CHRIS HANSEN TRANSFORMATION IN 'UNSETTLING' TRAILER

So, OK, there can never be another Connery; therefore the comparison is not quite fair. Then, can Pattinson carry the part forward into something this generation needs? So many today prefer to apologize for or ignore the Western canon that produced a fictional hero like Bond — a man willing and able to risk his life to save us.

The official teaser for the next 007 film to come does not include a single word, just Pattinson, gun in hand, emerging from blackness with the iconic Bond theme strumming. This tells us nothing, but it is on theme.

James Bond, at his best, is sophisticated, but hardly a snob. He has what the Spanish call duende, a characteristic author James Michener said is almost indefinable, as it means something with taste, refinement, beauty, perfection and elegance all in just the right proportion and with no showiness at all. He is what the Japanese mean when they use the word shibui, which is something a samurai tried to embody, but only could manage in fleeting moments when life and art meet before again separating with a bad gesture or misstep.

JUDI DENCH BLASTS 'TRIGGER WARNINGS' RUINING STORIES, 'DRIVES ME WILD'

In other words, James Bond is an archetype of what men wish they could be in the moments they are needed. Cool under pressure, not afraid to act or to fail and confident they are fighting for something good. This, again, is not something Hollywood has given us enough of today.

Maybe, just maybe, if Pattinson is given the right script and if Hollywood does not try to apologize for his part, 007 could again be what Odysseus was once to the Greeks. He could be a hero representing an ideal showing the way again to the well-rounded man of action.

Perhaps he can do it. The English, in particular, need Bond to be a clean hero again standing strong against those who would imperil their civilization.

CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM FRANK MINITER

Frank Miniter is a New York Times’ bestselling author. His soon-to-be released book is "Cool Heroes for Boys."

articles.title: The FBI is changing how it fights crime and protects Americans in their communities
articles.excerpt: An FBI investigation was opened after an explosive device was found near an Illinois ethanol plant. Former DHS deputy assistant secretary Jonathan Fahey analyzes the threat and subsequent evacuation o...
articles.body_text:
An FBI investigation was opened after an explosive device was found near an Illinois ethanol plant. Former DHS deputy assistant secretary Jonathan Fahey analyzes the threat and subsequent evacuation on 'America Reports.'

When President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, America faced one of the highest threat environments in its history. Years of open borders, soft-on-crime policies and a government that turned its back on law enforcement had left our communities vulnerable and our law enforcement officers without the support they deserved.

Under Trump’s leadership, we set out to reverse that tide. We rebuilt the FBI around its core mission: protecting the American people. We changed our priorities, revitalized partnerships, overhauled our technology and transformed the Bureau into a more aggressive, effective crime-fighting organization.

The results: Over the last 21 months, this FBI made 71,650 violent crime arrests, a 114% increase compared to the final 21 months of the previous administration. We seized 4,616 kilograms of deadly drugs, up 32%, including enough fentanyl to potentially kill more than 350 million Americans.

FBI REPORTS 114% JUMP IN VIOLENT CRIME ARRESTS UNDER TRUMP COMPARED TO BIDEN’S FINAL MONTHS

We identified or located 5,801 child victims, up 25%, many of whom were trafficked, exploited or abused. We made 6,744 arrests tied to foreign terrorist organizations, an increase of 1,057%, and disrupted more than 1,300 terrorists. We arrested 10 fugitives from the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list, including alleged murderers, rapists and other violent criminals. That is 2.5 times the number arrested during the previous four years combined.

FBI Director Kash Patel with FBI agents in Washington, D.C. on Aug. 11, 2025, outside the Park Police Station, the command center for the Trump administration's new crackdown on crime in the nation's capital. (Courtesy: FBI, exclusively provided to Fox News Digital)

And through the historic, first-ever Most Wanted Fraudsters list, led by Vice President JD Vance and the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, we arrested six alleged fraudsters in three-and-a-half months who were collectively responsible for $2.1 billion in alleged fraud.

WHITE HOUSE LAUNCHES INTERACTIVE MAP TRACKING BILLIONS IN SUSPECTED FRAUD

These results were no accident. They were the product of deliberate decisions to change how the FBI operates, where we deploy our resources and how we work with our law enforcement partners.

On my first day as director, we made crushing violent crime a top priority. Previously, it barely ranked among the Bureau’s top 10 priorities. We changed that immediately. Today, "Crush Violent Crime" is more than a slogan. It drives our operations, our resource decisions and our commitment to the American people.

FBI TOUTS 6,000 ARRESTS, 44% HOMICIDE DROP ONE YEAR INTO TRUMP'S DC CRIME CRACKDOWN

We then put our people where they could make the greatest impact. This FBI moved nearly 2,000 personnel out of Washington and back into the field. Agents, analysts and FBI teams solve cases in the field, in neighborhoods and alongside local officers who know their communities, not from conference rooms at headquarters. We shifted our focus away from Pennsylvania Avenue and back to Main Street America.

The FBI cannot succeed alone. Our greatest strength comes from working shoulder to shoulder with the men and women of state, local, tribal and federal law enforcement.

FBI ANNOUNCES 305 ARRESTS, 24 MISSING CHILDREN RECOVERED IN CHICAGO DURING OPERATION NEW DAWN

Through our 59 Homeland Security Task Forces, 200 Joint Terrorism Task Forces, 30 Safe Trails Task Forces and other partnerships, we have strengthened coordination across agencies and delivered major joint operations.

Operation Summer Heat, our three-month violent crime surge, brought law enforcement together to target dangerous criminals nationwide with more than 9,000 violent crime arrests, a 3% increase from the record number of arrests in summer 2025. Operation Steadfast Promise deployed 500 FBI personnel to combat violent crime on tribal lands, representing the largest commitment to Indian Country in Bureau history — with surges like Operation Not Forgotten, where this FBI executed 118 arrests with Indian Country partners — up 123% from last year’s operation and bringing us to over 1,000 Indian Country arrests in 2026.

KASH PATEL TOUTS FBI 'FULL-THROTTLE MISSION' AFTER OPERATION SPRING CLEANING YIELDS 615 INDICTMENTS/COMPLAINTS

We added 2,770 Task Force Officers across the country by eliminating wasteful administrative bureaucracy that saw a 14-month onboarding process shrink to less than 30 days, allowing our agents to partner directly alongside state, local, tribal or other federal law enforcement officers.

We then put our people where they could make the greatest impact. This FBI moved nearly 2,000 personnel out of Washington and back into the field.

We also expanded our capabilities to confront emerging threats. Through our first-of-its-kind counter-unmanned aircraft systems (counter-UAS) school at the FBI’s Redstone arsenal, we equipped local law enforcement partners to detect, track and respond to dangerous drones. During the 2026 FIFA World Cup, those efforts helped lead to the seizure of more than 700 drones.

EXCLUSIVE: FBI EXTRADITIONS SOAR AS PATEL RAMPS UP FOREIGN OUTREACH, VOWS 'NO SANCTUARY'

And our reach extends beyond America's borders. We increased foreign transfers of custody to 84, up 71%, and extraditions to 157, up 121%. These are dangerous fugitives and alleged criminals who can no longer evade American justice simply by crossing an international border.

FBI OVERHAULS TECH BACKBONE TO COUNTER AI THREATS FROM FOREIGN ADVERSARIES, REDUCE RESPONSE TIMES, PATEL SAYS

For too long, outdated technology and bureaucratic processes slowed the Bureau's ability to deliver results. We changed that. The FBI increased its use of superintelligence by 605% compared to 2024, putting this FBI on a course to save nearly 640,000 labor hours, the equivalent of about 79,000 workdays, by synthesizing data and streamlining administrative paperwork. In less than two years, our Laboratory Division eliminated a four-year DNA backlog involving 1.8 million samples.

We transformed our headquarters’ operational command and control center, standing up the first-ever "Director’s Strategic Information Group" — cutting DNA processing and producing finalized reporting in just 20 minutes, compared to what took hours in the old system. We also achieved compliance with mandatory insider threat requirements for the first time since the policy took effect in 2021.

And through Operation Blackout, our campaign against transnational scam centers, we are dismantling sophisticated criminal networks that prey on Americans. Our efforts have resulted in shuttering dozens of scam compounds overseas, more than $17 billion in seizures and prevented over 11,000 Americans from being scammed out of nearly $700 million in cyber-enabled fraud schemes.

These changes are delivering results where they matter most: in American communities. The nationwide murder rate has fallen 30%. Violent crime is declining across American cities. And during a historic summer that included America 250 celebrations and the 2026 FIFA World Cup — 6.8 million fans, with most of those at the 11 venues throughout America, the equivalent of 78 Super Bowls in 39 days — the country had zero major security incidents at those events.

This is what happens when law enforcement has clear priorities, the right resources, strong partnerships and leadership willing to put the mission first. None of this would be possible without the extraordinary men and women of the FBI and our law enforcement partners who put themselves in harm's way every day. They deserve the credit for turning our priorities into results.

Americans have a fundamental right to feel safe in their homes, on their streets and in their communities. Under President Trump, we have restored the FBI's focus on delivering that security.

We have made tremendous progress, but our work is far from finished. Criminals will continue to adapt. Threats will continue to evolve. And this FBI will continue to meet them head-on.

CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM FBI DIRECTOR KASH PATEL

Kash Patel serves as director of the FBI, bringing a distinguished record of leadership across national security, law enforcement, and congressional oversight. He began his career as a public defender before joining the Department of Justice, where he prosecuted high-level terrorism cases and worked alongside U.S. special forces to disrupt threats around the globe. As senior counsel to the House Intelligence Committee, Patel led a landmark investigation into foreign interference and exposed serious failures within the FBI’s Crossfire Hurricane probe.

articles.title: Aging means learning how to prevent costly scams targeting older Americans
articles.excerpt:
U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro joins ‘Saturday in America’ to break down the task force taking down alleged Chinese-run scam centers in Southeast Asia.

Getting older comes with some unpleasant ...
articles.body_text:
U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro joins ‘Saturday in America’ to break down the task force taking down alleged Chinese-run scam centers in Southeast Asia.

Getting older comes with some unpleasant consequences — aches and pains, worsening vision and even some forgetfulness. But one of the downsides of aging that isn’t discussed enough is that it also puts you at a higher risk of being targeted by scammers and losing money to fraud and scams.

A recent report by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) to Congress stated that the cost of consumer fraud targeting older adults (60 and older) could have been as high as $119.5 billion last year. Plus, the risk of higher median losses also occurred with older adults, with a large disparity for those 80 years old and older.

When it comes to preying on older adults, scammers come from far and wide. The types of schemes and scams are varied, from romance schemes to tech support scams to fake sweepstakes and lotteries, investment scams and all kinds of impersonation scams, whether the scammer is impersonating a financial institution, government personnel or even a family member.

MEDICARE AND SOCIAL SECURITY SCAMS: WARNING SIGNS AND TIPS

Experts say that there are very concrete reasons that scammers focus on the aging population. Some of those have to do with having lived for decades in a high-trust society, which takes people at their word and generates a culture of being polite and even obedient to authority.

Senior citizens are increasingly the victims of scams. (iStock)

Another reason is that, in the U.S., more wealth has accumulated with the older generations, so the scammers are just following the money.

DATA BROKER OPT-OUT: HOW RETIREES CAN PROTECT THEIR DATA

Other factors include preying on loneliness, exploiting cognitive issues and even a lack of familiarity with technology.

So, given that scammers are trying to manipulate and scam those who are aging, how can you protect yourself or your aging family members from these schemes?

CYBERCRIME LOSSES NEAR $21B: 5 WAYS TO PROTECT YOUR MONEY

One of my late father’s favorite sayings was, "If it sounds too good to be true, it is." This is a great mantra to remember when it comes to scams. If a young, gorgeous person approaches you for a romantic liaison, be careful, and if they ask you to send them money, you can feel confident that it is a scam. If an investment is promising an outsized return, it’s also likely a scam. Be on high alert for any "luck" that seems to have befallen you and consider consulting some trusted sources for a second and third opinion before making any decisions on these special "offers."

Building on my dad’s mantra, I have created my own — if it sounds weird, it probably is. Details that don’t add up in the real world are a red flag. You are not James Bond, and therefore, you should not be asked to do anything that puts you in the middle of a spy thriller plot. This includes working with government officials, police, the FBI, major companies like Amazon or financial institutions to catch a criminal. None of the above would ever ask a citizen to do that. And, if you are told you need to keep a secret because someone in an authority position may be in on the plot, that is Hollywood writing, not reality!

FAKE FEDERAL AGENTS PUSH SENIORS TO TURN SAVINGS INTO GOLD BARS FOR COURIERS TO COLLECT

The same mantra applies to someone instructing you to move money to be "safe" or directing you to change your funds into another form of currency, whether that be gift cards, cryptocurrency or something else. No legitimate law enforcement, financial services or other entities need your help to catch criminals and if your own accounts were actually at risk, no one should or will ask you to undertake spy-level activities. Again, consider consulting some outside sources, including trusted family members or authorities, before you take any action.

Another tactic to keep scammers at bay is to defuse their urgency. Creating urgency is key for scammers. They make you worried and that causes you to panic. You can diffuse the urgency by not picking up calls you aren’t expecting and not replying to any urgent calls to action. Do your research at your own pace and on your timeframe and don’t fall for pressure to act immediately, even if threatened with a bad outcome.

So, given that scammers are trying to manipulate and scam those who are aging, how can you protect yourself or your aging family members from these schemes?

Also, if you have trusted family members or friends, have them check up on aging relatives and, with their permission, their accounts frequently to make sure there aren’t any scammers circling. I say trusted because scams can come from family members too, unfortunately.

And always have a family code word or phrase. This is something known only to family members that isn’t accessible to anyone else. If there is an urgent situation that involves a family member, you can be sure that it is really them by asking for the code phrase for verification. Otherwise, it’s just another scam.

Being aware of scammers’ techniques and anticipating them can help anyone avoid becoming a victim. With so much at stake and increasingly sophisticated techniques, it’s time well spent to go over these prevention measures yourself and with your family.

Carol Roth is a former investment banker, entrepreneur and author of the new book "You Will Own Nothing" Broadside Books. Her previous books are "The War on Small Business" and the New York Times bestseller "The Entrepreneur Equation."

articles.title: House Dems target Trump family, JD Vance in sweeping new investigation push
articles.excerpt: White House counsel Will Scharf joins 'Fox News Sunday' to address incoming Democratic investigations targeting the Trump administration. Scharf warns that the Department of Justice will push back agg...
articles.body_text:
White House counsel Will Scharf joins 'Fox News Sunday' to address incoming Democratic investigations targeting the Trump administration. Scharf warns that the Department of Justice will push back aggressively if lawmakers use their oversight powers to threaten or intimidate administration staffers.

The likely next chairman of the House Oversight Committee is officially taking the first steps to launch a wide array of investigations before Democrats take control in the new Congress.

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., is sending document preservation letters to 12 figures in President Donald Trump's orbit on Wednesday morning, including Vice President JD Vance, Donald Trump Jr., Eric Trump, Jared Kushner, former U.S. ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle, and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller.

House Oversight Committee Democrats are looking to investigate the Trump family's business deals, alleged misconduct at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), and the federal government's handling of Jeffrey Epstein's case, they said in a release.

Garcia said the probes "will lay the groundwork for legislation which helps all Americans."

THE TOP TRUMP OFFICIALS DEMOCRATS ADMIT ARE ON THEIR HIT LIST FOR INVESTIGATIONS IN THE NEW CONGRESS

Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump look on as President Donald Trump and President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen announce a U.S.-EU. trade deal after a meeting at Trump Turnberry Golf Club on July 27, 2025, in Turnberry, Scotland. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

The California Democrat is all but guaranteed to hold the Oversight gavel in the next Congress and has already signaled that he intends to kick off the new year with an aggressive investigation schedule.

‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH

His committee will also be key to any potential impeachment efforts House Democrats take on in the next term.

Other investigatory targets include former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, former DHS senior advisor Corey Lewandowski, former White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, Attorney General Todd Blanche, Federal Bureau of Prisons director William K. Marshall III, and Trust for the National Mall CEO Catherine Townsend.

"Oversight Democrats have been investigating the potential corruption, self-dealing, and abuses of power that have funneled billions of dollars to the Trump family as Americans struggle with rising costs," letters to the president's two eldest sons read.

"While the Trump Administration’s failed policies have made life increasingly unaffordable for the public, you have engaged in business pursuits that appear to have allowed you to personally profit from your father’s presidency on a massive scale and at the expense of the American people."

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., gives remarks to media outside the House Democratic Caucus meeting in the Longworth House office building on Nov. 10, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images)

The letter to Miller reads in part, "Oversight Democrats have heard directly from the victims of the lawless conduct of President Trump’s mass deportation campaign and from whistleblowers appalled by agency behavior. There must be accountability for those responsible for orchestrating, carrying out, and covering up these abuses, at all levels of the agency."

DEMS PIVOT FROM ‘AFFORDABILITY’ PITCH TO DHS PROBE THREATS AFTER MIDTERM WINS

Democrats have positioned their investigative efforts as accountability measures long-sought by the American public. But Republicans have argued that it shows Democrats are more interested in political retribution than working on solutions to lower issues like the high cost of living that millions of Americans are dealing with.

Trump and his family have long denied any wrongdoing when it comes to their business interests.

And while Miller and Noem did face bipartisan criticism over the administration's crackdown on illegal immigration, the majority of Republicans have lined up behind the White House and maintained that it is what Americans voted for.

White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller addresses the audience during opening remarks at the Ministerial on the Resurgence of Political Terrorism at the State Department on July 16, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

It's not immediately clear whether the investigatory targets will comply with House Democrats' demands to preserve documents and communications.

Republicans selected House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, as their leader in the new Congress and de facto top spokesman against Democrats' partisan activity.

Garcia's counterpart on the House Oversight Committee remains to be seen, but both Reps. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, and Pat Fallon, R-Texas, have expressed interest in the role.

Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

Follow on Twitter at @liz_elkind and send tips to elizabeth.elkind@fox.com

Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump look on as President Donald Trump and President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen announce a U.S.-EU. trade deal after a meeting at Trump Turnberry Golf Club on July 27, 2025, in Turnberry, Scotland. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

The California Democrat is all but guaranteed to hold the Oversight gavel in the next Congress and has already signaled that he intends to kick off the new year with an aggressive investigation schedule.

‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH

His committee will also be key to any potential impeachment efforts House Democrats take on in the next term.

Other investigatory targets include former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, former DHS senior advisor Corey Lewandowski, former White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, Attorney General Todd Blanche, Federal Bureau of Prisons director William K. Marshall III, and Trust for the National Mall CEO Catherine Townsend.

"Oversight Democrats have been investigating the potential corruption, self-dealing, and abuses of power that have funneled billions of dollars to the Trump family as Americans struggle with rising costs," letters to the president's two eldest sons read.

"While the Trump Administration’s failed policies have made life increasingly unaffordable for the public, you have engaged in business pursuits that appear to have allowed you to personally profit from your father’s presidency on a massive scale and at the expense of the American people."

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., gives remarks to media outside the House Democratic Caucus meeting in the Longworth House office building on Nov. 10, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images)

The letter to Miller reads in part, "Oversight Democrats have heard directly from the victims of the lawless conduct of President Trump’s mass deportation campaign and from whistleblowers appalled by agency behavior. There must be accountability for those responsible for orchestrating, carrying out, and covering up these abuses, at all levels of the agency."

DEMS PIVOT FROM ‘AFFORDABILITY’ PITCH TO DHS PROBE THREATS AFTER MIDTERM WINS

Democrats have positioned their investigative efforts as accountability measures long-sought by the American public. But Republicans have argued that it shows Democrats are more interested in political retribution than working on solutions to lower issues like the high cost of living that millions of Americans are dealing with.

Trump and his family have long denied any wrongdoing when it comes to their business interests.

And while Miller and Noem did face bipartisan criticism over the administration's crackdown on illegal immigration, the majority of Republicans have lined up behind the White House and maintained that it is what Americans voted for.

White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller addresses the audience during opening remarks at the Ministerial on the Resurgence of Political Terrorism at the State Department on July 16, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

It's not immediately clear whether the investigatory targets will comply with House Democrats' demands to preserve documents and communications.

Republicans selected House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, as their leader in the new Congress and de facto top spokesman against Democrats' partisan activity.

Garcia's counterpart on the House Oversight Committee remains to be seen, but both Reps. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, and Pat Fallon, R-Texas, have expressed interest in the role.

Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

Follow on Twitter at @liz_elkind and send tips to elizabeth.elkind@fox.com

articles.title: Fears grow over US sanctions on ICJ judges ahead of Myanmar genocide ruling
articles.excerpt:
A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza

Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, inc...
articles.body_text:
A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza

Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.

The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

Lawyers representing Rohingya survivors say patterns of behaviour by Myanmar’s military, including killing people as they fled, show clear attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state in 2016 and 2017.

It is the role of independent judges to interpret the genocide convention. However, judges at the court have taken advice on how to protect their assets from potential US sanctions, as a genocide ruling could be interpreted by Washington as lowering the “legal threshold” for the crime.

The Foundation for Defense of Democracies, an influential thinktank close to the White House, has predicted a genocide ruling will lead to the US imposing sanctions on the ICJ.

The US and Israel fear the final judgment may clarify how to establish a government’s intent to commit a genocide, and so set a precedent that makes it more likely the court will later rule that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.

Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising by insurgents.

The ICJ, sometimes described as the UN’s top court, is responsible for settling interstate disputes, unlike the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecuties individuals accused of war crimes and other international crimes.

The US has already imposed crippling sanctions on judges at the ICC after the court issued arrest warrants against the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. The US has also announced sanctions against the entire ICC as an institution, which it described as a “rogue court”. Washington fears the ICC could go after US troops.

The Gambia, as a litigant, was entitled to appoint an ad hoc judge in the case against Myanmar and chose the South African lawyer Pillay, who in October was awarded the Nobel peace prize. She is required to act as a jurist and not an advocate for the Gambia.

Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, has sent a warning shot to Pillay and the 15 ICJ judges, saying Washington “will not allow globalist, faux judges to weaponise the law against our troops”.

Waltz asserted last month: “The ICJ ad hoc judge Navi Pillay is tipping the scales on the ICJ’s current proceedings on Myanmar, intending to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide so that weakened and false standard can later be weaponised against American and allied soldiers whenever they raise a finger against terrorists that hide behind civilians”.

In remarks addressed to Pillay, he said: “We see your agenda and we’ll be watching the ICJ’s handling of these proceedings very closely.”

In a speech last Friday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said: “For this global elite, international law … is an instrument to advance their interests under the pretence of universal principles.”

He warned the ICC against quoting laws to “men with swords”.

Israel has previously criticised adverse advisory opinions issued by the ICJ and refused to implement 2024 orders requiring Israel to admit more aid into Gaza, and to cooperate with Unrwa, the UN relief and works agency.

In the Myanmar case, a 24-page submission jointly filed by the UK and five other mainly European states, argued that the ICJ, in judging intent to commit genocide, should examine a range of “facts and circumstances” assessed “comprehensively and holistically.”

It also stressed that genocide was not solely defined by killings, and that the treatment of children, gender-based violence and forced displacement were also relevant.

The US until recently had taken a relatively more benign view of the Hague-based ICJ, and under Antony Blinken as US secretary of state determined that Myanmar had committed genocide.

The 15 ICJ judges are elected for nine-year terms by the UN security council and the UN general assembly.

Rubio has given the ICC until April to respond to his criticisms before he imposes sanctions.

On Friday, the ICC formally decided to drop plans to prosecute US soldiers and intelligence agents for potentially unlawful acts in Afghanistan. The shelving of the near-dormant inquiry came after it was agreed evidence would be hard to obtain, but one side-effect may be a greater US willingness on the part of the US to abandon its plan to impose sanctions on the ICC.

articles.title: What do Deutsche Bank leaks reveal about Trump, Epstein and Russia?
articles.excerpt: A leak of more than 15 million internal records from Deutsche Bank has shed new light on its dealings with United States President Donald Trump, the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and other powerfu...
articles.body_text:
A leak of more than 15 million internal records from Deutsche Bank has shed new light on its dealings with United States President Donald Trump, the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and other powerful figures.

The Inside Deutsche Bank investigation, published on Tuesday by a consortium of international news outlets, has put Germany’s biggest bank back in the spotlight after years of trying to rebuild its reputation following its failures to prevent money laundering.

Files containing millions of emails, minutes of meetings and internal reports were leaked by two whistleblowers whose identities and links to the institution have been withheld for their protection, according to Le Monde, one of the participating news outlets. The pair told the media groups they believed the bank was engaging in criminal activity and that releasing the documents was in the public interest.

An Indian journalist and a South African journalist obtained the cache, then shared it with more than 230 reporters from about 50 news organisations, including Der Spiegel, the Financial Times and The New York Times, in an internationally coordinated effort.

The material includes some nine million emails, as well as meeting minutes, due diligence reports and financial crime reports dating back to the early 2010s, many of them from the bank’s internal investigations.

The whistleblowers also passed the data to US prosecutors and financial crime authorities, and could be eligible for a reward if Washington prosecutes the bank based on their leaks. Le Monde said the whistleblowers were not paid by the journalists and placed no conditions on how the material was used.

Deutsche Bank said concerns raised by the investigation “date back many years” and that it had since strengthened its controls, adding that it did not expect any meaningful financial impact. The bank’s chairman reaffirmed the board’s support for chief executive Christian Sewing, who has run the institution since 2018.

“Deutsche Bank is a different bank today,” the bank said in a statement.

The files identify more than $3m in transactions involving Trump-owned companies, including payments linked to suspected Russian and Azerbaijani money-laundering networks.

Deutsche Bank extended loans to Trump for years, even after a string of bankruptcies and defaults at his businesses from the early 1990s. By January 2021, it was his biggest creditor, with about $340m in loans to his company outstanding.

That month, following the January 6 assault on the US Capitol by protesters wanting to stop the certification of Democrat Joe Biden’s win in the presidential election, the bank ceased doing business with him, according to The New York Times. Trump had claimed the election had been rigged against him, of which there has never been any proof.

The Financial Times reported that the bank inadvertently sent a Trump tax document to another client’s accountant in 2017, during his first term in office, and never told him about the error. Asked about the disclosure during his visit to Manila for the ASEAN summit on Tuesday, Trump said the bank should not have released that information.

“They shouldn’t have done it. It’s illegal for them to do it,” he said. Deutsche Bank declined to comment on his remarks.

The leaked records also reveal special monitoring that the bank applied to Trump’s accounts, and its handling of them has drawn scrutiny before.

In 2019, The New York Times reported that Deutsche Bank had failed to alert US authorities to suspicious transactions linked to Trump. The bank said at the time that none of its investigators had been prevented from escalating such concerns.

The leaked files list about $582m in transactions linked to Epstein, which were flagged internally as suspicious. That is more than double the amount previously identified as being overlooked or not reported by banks during US Senate investigations. When the Senate findings were released in August, a Deutsche Bank spokesperson said the bank regretted its “historical connection” with Epstein.

Epstein, who was a US financier, became a Deutsche Bank client in 2013, five years after pleading guilty in Florida to procuring a minor for prostitution, and remained a client until 2018. He died in a New York jail in 2019 while awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges.

Internal emails in the newly leaked cache indicate that senior executives approved Epstein as a client despite his conviction, and kept his accounts open even after warnings about the activities of Ghislaine Maxwell, his former girlfriend and associate. Maxwell was convicted in 2021 of helping Epstein sexually abuse teenage girls. She is currently serving a 20-year prison sentence.

The files also reveal information about payments linked to wealthy Epstein associates such as private equity billionaire Leon Black and Wall Street financier Glenn Dubin.

A review commissioned by Black’s firm previously found he had paid Epstein $158m between 2012 and 2017 for tax and estate planning advice. Black has sought to distance himself from Epstein, repeatedly denying wrongdoing or any knowledge of his abuse of girls and young women.

The leak comes years after the bank paid fines and settlements of more than $200m over its handling of Epstein-related finances. In 2020, regulators fined it $150m for compliance failures linked to Epstein and other high-risk clients, finding that he had held more than 40 accounts at the bank. In 2023, it agreed to pay $75m to settle a suit brought by women who alleged they had been abused by him.

The documents also detail Deutsche Bank’s business dealings in Russia up until Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, despite concerns raised by some managers.

They include previously undisclosed internal warnings about the bank’s continued dealings with wealthy Kremlin-connected clients despite sanctions and money laundering concerns.

Those named include Russian billionaires Roman Abramovich, the former owner of English football club Chelsea, and aluminium tycoon Oleg Deripaska. Both men were sanctioned by the United Kingdom in 2022. Suleiman Kerimov, another billionaire whose name appears in the files, was sanctioned by the US in 2014 and 2018.

Transactions associated with Rifaat al-Assad, the uncle of former Syrian President Bashar al-Assad, also appear in the files. Rifaat, who died in January, was convicted in France in 2020 of acquiring millions of euros’ worth of property with funds diverted from the Syrian state.

Other files concern figures connected to the Sarkozy-Libya affair, in which former French President Nicolas Sarkozy was convicted in 2025 of criminal conspiracy over efforts to secure funding for his 2007 campaign from the government of late Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi.

articles.title: Why Democrat Mary Peltola’s US Senate win in Alaska matters
articles.excerpt:
Democrat Mary Peltola has won the United States Senate seat in Alaska, unseating two-term Republican Senator Dan Sullivan. It is the Democrats’ first US Senate win in the state in more than a decade.
...
articles.body_text:
Democrat Mary Peltola has won the United States Senate seat in Alaska, unseating two-term Republican Senator Dan Sullivan. It is the Democrats’ first US Senate win in the state in more than a decade.

As of early Wednesday, The Associated Press news agency’s count gave her 50.1 percent of first-choice votes against Sullivan’s 45.8 percent, with an estimated 99 percent of votes counted.

Clearing the 50 percent mark matters. Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, so a candidate who wins a majority of first-choice votes is elected outright, with no further rounds of counting.

The vote has been closely watched, not just because it is the last Senate race to be called in the midterm elections, but because of a Republican legal challenge to the election over the listing of two candidates with nearly the same name – Republican Dan Sullivan and independent Daniel Sullivan. The legal challenge was thrown out just days before the election.

The Trump administration alleged that Peltola’s campaign had deliberately recruited the second Dan Sullivan to divide Republican votes in the state – a practice known as “ballot stacking“.

But on Tuesday, it was clear that even if the “official” Dan Sullivan had received all the votes of his namesake, he would not have gained enough to beat Peltola.

Peltola’s win brings Democratic control of the Senate to 56 seats, against the Republicans’ 44.

Peltola, a Yup’ik Alaskan, became the first Alaska Native to be elected to Congress when she won a special election for the state’s sole House of Representatives seat in 2022. She served from September 2022 to January 2025, losing her re-election bid in 2024.

On the Senate campaign trail this year, she played down her Democratic label, which remains unpopular in the state, and focused on local issues such as energy jobs, border security and gun rights.

Scott Lucas, a professor of international politics at University College Dublin’s Clinton Institute, told Al Jazeera that Peltola is viewed as a “safe pair of hands”.

“Alaska is a very small population, with a very, very large landmass, so it’s very important that you try to build up, across that large landmass, ties and community ties,” he said. “Peltola was seen as someone who had represented Alaska’s interests very well.”

Lucas described her as “a pragmatist, very much in that centre line of Democratic politics”. “Not too provocative, doesn’t really play identity politics,” he said. “She didn’t play on the idea this is all about Native Americans, even though she happens to be a Native American.”

Sullivan, by contrast, “was tarnished because he was there on Trump’s ticket, as it were”, Lucas said, though “he was very much a local candidate”. “Had the Trump administration done a better job on the issues, then I suspect Sullivan holds his seat,” he added.

For one, it was the last Senate seat to be counted.

But also, there were two Dan Sullivans on the ballot.

In late May, Dan J Sullivan, a retired teacher from Petersburg, entered the race. On June 15, the state elections division removed him from the ballot. It said he had chosen the name to cause confusion with the senator, and pointed to his use of a political consultant who had previously worked for Peltola.

The courts reversed that decision. A superior court judge ruled he was eligible, and the Alaska Supreme Court upheld that ruling on June 29. The two candidates appeared on the ballot as “Daniel J Sullivan Jr”, with no party affiliation, and “Dan S Sullivan”, Republican and incumbent. The retired teacher finished in the top four of the August primary, earning a place on the November ballot.

Republicans claimed he was a decoy. The New York Times later reported that Peltola campaign staff and Democratic operatives had worked to get him to contest. At Trump’s urging, the Department of Justice (DoJ) sued to delay certification if Senator Sullivan lost and to separate ballots cast for his namesake. Federal Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed the case on November 1. The DoJ said it would appeal.

Lucas said this kind of “ballot stacking” – backing a minor candidate to pull votes from a rival – is not uncommon, and both parties have engaged in it in the past. If the second Sullivan had taken 2 percent of the vote, he explained, he could have pushed the incumbent below the 50 percent mark and forced a ranked-choice count. “You drain enough support from the Republican that you give yourself a better chance of winning,” he said.

In the end, he said, “I don’t think it made that much of a difference.” AP’s count gave Daniel J Sullivan Jr 1.7 percent, and Peltola won more than 50 percent of the vote.

Peltola is the first Democrat to represent Alaska in the Senate since Sullivan unseated Mark Begich in 2014. Her win is not a deciding factor in which party controls the chamber – Democrats already had enough seats to control the Senate – but Lucas said it is “significant in a wider context”.

Alaska is the latest in a string of Republican strongholds to switch to Democrats.

On election night, Democrats flipped seats in North Carolina, South Carolina, Ohio, Texas, Kansas, Iowa and Maine. Later-arriving counts then confirmed that Mississippi had flipped, electing its first Black senator in 150 years, and now Alaska has taken the tally to nine.

Texas went Democratic for the first time since 1988, and Kansas for the first time since 1932.

“Alaska was one of the seats that it was thought that the Democrats might win,” Lucas said. “So that in itself is not as surprising as, say, Mississippi, which is really, really surprising. South Carolina was quite a surprise as well. But still, it reaffirms the extent of this Democratic surge.”

Those wins also give Democrats a buffer. Senators serve six-year terms, with about one-third of the 100 seats contested every two years, so the seats won this month will not be on the ballot again until 2032. By holding seats in states they would not normally carry, Democrats can make it much harder for Republicans to retake the Senate in 2028.

Finally, the win brings Democrats closer to the magical two-thirds majority. They now hold 56 seats, which Lucas called “a pretty good majority when even the most optimistic analysts regarding the Democrats were looking at 53 seats at most”. They will still need Republican support on issues to secure the two-thirds majority needed to overturn a presidential veto in both chambers.

A two-thirds vote in the Senate is needed to convict an official in an impeachment trial. The more seats Democrats hold, the fewer Republicans they need to win over to reach that threshold. For now, Lucas said, “They cannot pass legislation because Trump can veto it. So they still have to try to work with Republicans if they want to get any legislation across.”

Lucas expects the new Democratic majorities to propose legislation and hold hearings on accountability, “whether that be with respect to AI and technology, whether it be with respect to the Epstein case”, or the wealth of Trump and his family, including through cryptocurrency. “Meanwhile, the Republicans are a fractured party,” he said.

In North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas, Trump’s inner circle imposed candidates on the party, and all three were lost. Democrats, by contrast, “went for more organic candidates, and Mary Peltola was one of them”, Lucas said.

“Diversity has become a bad word with the Trump camp,” Lucas said. “It’s interesting that in this very diverse election, you have your first US Muslim senator, you have your first US openly gay man in the Senate, and you have two Native American women who have won: Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota, and then Peltola. In this case, it was the party with the diversity of candidates that did better.”

Lucas predicts “a fairly chaotic couple of years, primarily because of the executive”, with Democrats needing to “show that they can provide some at least potential for stability” before the 2028 presidential race. Rising health insurance premiums and disputes about data centres, which have proved unpopular in part because of the drain they impose on local resources, are among the next tests.

“This isn’t really a right-versus-left issue any more,” he said. “This is an issue of who governs effectively when they’re in office.”

articles.title: Piecemeal wars: A new kind of world war is already under way
articles.excerpt:
Jordanian politician and former interior minister.

Many commentators in the Middle East and the West warn that the world is witnessing the early stages of another world war. I disagree, at least if w...
articles.body_text:
Jordanian politician and former interior minister.

Many commentators in the Middle East and the West warn that the world is witnessing the early stages of another world war. I disagree, at least if we are talking about a war on the scale of the two world wars fought in the last century. Nuclear deterrence makes such a conflict all but impossible.

The United States, Russia, China, the United Kingdom and France, the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council (UNSC), all possess nuclear weapons, as do India, Pakistan, North Korea and Israel. Iran may yet join them. An all-out war involving these powers would produce neither victors nor vanquished, but destruction on a scale that could threaten civilisation itself.

Yet while a world war in the traditional sense may be impossible, a different kind of global conflict is already under way. Some longstanding disputes and rivalries have already erupted into war, while others threaten to do so. Much as in the years preceding World War II, competing national interests are driving countries into opposing camps.

The alliances that emerged during World War II were shaped by the ambitions and strategic interests of the countries involved. Hitler’s Germany sought territorial expansion and revenge for its defeat in World War I. Mussolini’s Italy pursued imperial ambitions, while Japan sought to expand its dominance over China and Southeast Asia. Together, they formed the core of the Axis powers. Britain and France stood against them, later joined by the Soviet Union following Germany’s invasion in 1941 and the US after Japan’s attack on Pearl Harbor. Despite their different political systems and objectives, these countries were ultimately brought together by their interests and the threats they faced.

The question today is whether we are witnessing a similar alignment of interests among the world’s major powers, particularly among nuclear-armed states. Could Russia, China, North Korea and Iran form a bloc capable of confronting the US and its allies, and could their regional conflicts become part of a wider global war fought with different weapons and methods?

After the collapse of the Soviet Union, it appeared that US-led capitalism had triumphed. But under President Vladimir Putin, Russia has sought to rebuild its economic and military strength and reclaim its position as a global power. Despite abandoning communism, Moscow has once again emerged as a rival to the West.

The war in Ukraine is therefore far more than a conflict between two neighbouring countries. It is a confrontation between Russia and Europe, while Washington’s position has shifted from President Joe Biden’s efforts to weaken Moscow to the reluctance of his successor, Donald Trump, to regard Ukraine as a vital US interest or Russia as a principal adversary.

This is already one front in a wider global conflict. On one side stand Ukraine and Europe; on the other, Russia, supported by China, Iran and North Korea, which see its defeat as a threat to their own interests and regional standing.

China’s economic and military might represents the greatest challenge to the US and the West. Its economy is already the world’s second-largest, and many expect it to overtake that of the US within a decade or so. China has successfully used the tools of free-market capitalism championed by Washington to its own advantage, flooding US and global markets with its products and securing a major commercial victory.

Although Beijing has largely avoided direct military involvement in international conflicts, preferring diplomatic support for Russia and the Palestinian cause, as well as engagement on trade, development and climate change, Taiwan remains a major unresolved objective.

The principle of “one China” and the goal of bringing Taiwan under Chinese control, much as Hong Kong was returned to China, remain central to Beijing’s ambitions. If China decides to make this objective an immediate priority, it could trigger a major political and potentially military confrontation between China and its allies on one side and the US and its allies on the other.

North Korea’s nuclear arsenal makes the Korean Peninsula another potential flashpoint in a wider global conflict. Despite its economic superiority, South Korea faces a serious military threat from the North.

Any confrontation between the two Koreas could quickly become an international crisis. Historically, Korea was a battleground for competing powers. Following Japan’s defeat in World War II, the peninsula was divided into Soviet and American occupation zones, which subsequently became two states: one backed by China and the Soviet Union, and later Russia, and the other by the West. A renewed conflict could therefore draw in these powers and become another front in a wider global confrontation.

Iran’s far-reaching ambitions are rooted partly in the legacy of the Persian Empire. Since the 1979 Islamic Revolution, Tehran has also sought to export its sectarian ideology, fuelling divisions and conflict among Muslims.

More importantly, Iran’s pursuit of nuclear capabilities is regarded by the US and Israel as a direct threat, particularly to Israel. The continuing cycle of military confrontation, diplomatic brinkmanship and economic sanctions is pushing Tehran towards an increasingly clear alignment with China, Russia and North Korea.

Although other rising powers, including Brazil and India, must also be considered, the clearest emerging alignment places China, Russia, North Korea and Iran on one side, and the US and Europe on the other, despite the weakening of political and ideological ties between Washington and its European allies.

As for Japan, despite its longstanding tensions with China, I doubt it would be prepared to participate directly in a regional or global conflict, given its bitter experience of World War II and the atomic bombings it suffered.

I therefore do not believe we are heading towards an all-out world war in the traditional sense. Instead, we are witnessing what might be called “piecemeal wars”: a series of regional conflicts, some already raging, such as the war in Ukraine and the confrontation involving Iran, the US and Israel, and others that remain unresolved, such as the Taiwan question and the tensions between the two Koreas.

Taken together, however, these seemingly separate conflicts amount to a global war, one being fought piecemeal rather than through a single, openly acknowledged confrontation between opposing blocs.

There is another factor making the current international situation particularly dangerous: the declining authority of the UN, including the UNSC.

Throughout the Cold War, these institutions helped contain crises that might otherwise have escalated into wider wars. The leaders of that era also understood the devastating consequences of a global conflict, particularly given advances in conventional and nuclear weapons.

Unfortunately, the UN’s authority has steadily eroded. Its weakness became glaringly apparent when the US invaded Iraq in 2003 on the spurious pretext that Iraq possessed weapons of mass destruction, disregarding the UNSC and proceeding without its authorisation.

Today, the UNSC has effectively surrendered its authority over the Palestinian question to President Trump and his so-called Board of Peace. Yet this body has failed to implement even one of the 21 provisions intended to restore peace to Gaza. Instead, under its watch, what was a Palestinian-Israeli war in Gaza has given way to continuing Israeli aggression against civilians in the enclave, the occupied West Bank, Jerusalem, Lebanon and Syria, without any meaningful deterrent.

In my view, the paralysis of the UN today resembles that of the League of Nations on the eve of World War II. Perhaps the clearest illustration of this failure is the disregard for the decisions of the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court. Those responsible for genocide in Gaza face none of the accountability imposed on war criminals in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo or conflicts in Africa.

The international community must therefore strengthen the institutions and mechanisms designed to protect international peace, giving them the authority and effectiveness they need to prevent a wider collapse of the international order.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: ‘Phantom forests’ in Australia’s arid outback used to create carbon credits meant to offset emissions, report claims
articles.excerpt:
Carbon credit companies reject research that found only small increase in forest and canopy cover in regeneration areas despite wet conditions

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news po...
articles.body_text:
Carbon credit companies reject research that found only small increase in forest and canopy cover in regeneration areas despite wet conditions

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

A fight over the legitimacy of Australia’s climate change policy has reignited after researchers claimed “phantom forests” in the semi-arid outback are being used to create offsets that allow fossil fuel companies to keep pumping out pollution.

A group of academics, including professors from the Australian National University and the University of New South Wales, said they had examined 50 forest regeneration projects used to create carbon credits.

Led by Prof Andrew Macintosh, the former federal government carbon credit scheme integrity chair and the director of ANU’s Centre for Environmental Markets, the researchers said they found only a small increase in forest and tree crown cover in the areas over the past five years despite wet conditions.

They said the conclusions were consistent with their previous peer-reviewed studies that found Australia’s method for creating carbon credits from forest regeneration was doing little to nothing to help address the climate crisis.

The research was published in a report released on Wednesday by the Australian Conservation Foundation. Prof David Eldridge, one of the report’s authors and a former principal research scientist with the NSW environment department, said he was “gobsmacked” that “phantom forests” in outback areas north-west of the remote town of Bourke could earn carbon credits for forest regrowth.

“Some of these areas have never grown forests; they will never grow forests,” he said.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

The findings were rejected by companies that manage what are known as human-induced regeneration projects in north-western NSW. “These are some of the most closely examined carbon projects in the country, and the evidence on the ground shows they are working,” a spokesperson for Green Collar, a business that manages carbon credit projects, said.

Each carbon credit is said to represent one tonne of emissions that has been removed from, or prevented from being released to, the atmosphere.

Their use is contentious, in part, because industrial-polluting companies that are required to cut emissions under a federal policy known as the safeguard mechanism are allowed to buy an unlimited number of credits to count as their own cuts while continuing to pollute.

Scientists have warned limiting the climate crisis requires rapid direct cuts in emissions and that carbon credits – also known as offsets – should be used sparingly.

The Australian Conservation Foundation said it showed coal and gas companies should be banned from claiming offsets as their own emissions cuts.

Adam Bandt, the foundation’s chief executive and a former Australian Greens leader, said the safeguard mechanism was meant to “cut climate pollution and protect us from big coal and gas threatening our lives and livelihoods, but it’s not working”.

“Putting more climate pollution into the atmosphere now could push us past dangerous tipping points. It can’t be offset, and the science tells us to keep coal and gas in the ground,” he said.

Macintosh said the evidence showed the projects were by and large not regenerating forest, but had created more than 60m carbon credits worth up to $2bn.

The report said the safeguard mechanism was being “materially undermined” by poor-quality credits. It said a “flood of cheap, low integrity” credits was making it cheaper in many cases for big polluters to pay for offsets rather than make direct emissions cuts.

There have been more than 430 human-induced regeneration projects in Australia since 2013, covering an area of 38m hectares – larger than Japan. The federal government is now reviewing the safeguard policy, as required under legislation.

A spokesperson for the Clean Energy Regulator, which manages the scheme, said it took allegations about the integrity or efficacy of carbon credit projects seriously, and had confidence in the forest regeneration method.

It said projects were required to demonstrate every five years that canopy cover was increasing, and it had rejected non-complying areas that could have received 6.7m carbon credits.

Green Collar said it stood “firmly behind the integrity of its human-induced regeneration projects” and expressed frustration that the report had not been publicly released or published in a peer-reviewed journal. It said the researchers had “judged these carbon projects with satellite pictures and a single field visit”.

“Carbon is stored in stems, branches, leaves, roots and dead timber. Satellite canopy products see leaves from above. They do not measure the wood and roots where most of that carbon sits,” its spokesperson said.

Skye Glenday, the chief executive of Climate Friendly, another carbon credit project developer, said the criticisms of the carbon credit projects were “at odds with the facts and the extensive independent scientific and regulatory scrutiny that is applied to all projects”.

“Debate about the use of offsets is legitimate, but let’s have that debate on its merits rather than undermining the carbon drawdown Australia also needs,” she said.

articles.title: As Trump arrives in China, low expectations for breakthroughs in rivalry
articles.excerpt:
For more than a year, the United States and China have maintained an uneasy truce in their intense technological and economic rivalry.

As US President Donald Trump landed in Shenzhen on Wednesday for...
articles.body_text:
For more than a year, the United States and China have maintained an uneasy truce in their intense technological and economic rivalry.

As US President Donald Trump landed in Shenzhen on Wednesday for his third meeting with Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping since hitting pause on the US-China trade war last year, expectations for major breakthroughs are low.

At the Shenzhen airport, Xi greeted Trump — Chinese presidents rarely welcome visiting guests when they land — even as journalists travelling with the US president waited on Air Force One.

Yet despite the red carpet welcome, analysts expect few concrete agreements out of Trump and Xi’s meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday.

Instead, the two leaders are expected to focus on stabilising ties between Washington and Beijing at a time when their differences are in full view amid claims that chip giant Nvidia’s former CEO was targeted in a Chinese espionage operation.

Trump and Xi each benefit from “projecting a sense of having things under control in the US-China relationship,” said Ryan Hass, director of the John L Thornton China Center at Brookings.

“I do not expect that dynamic to change in the coming period,” Hass told Al Jazeera.

“Their ability to continue to guide the relationship will be challenged in the coming year, though, since they will not have as many opportunities for direct leader-level diplomacy as they did in 2026,” he added.

Ahead of the talks, Trump has sought to downplay the controversy surrounding Nvidia, which revolves around former CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with a Megaspeed executive accused of being a Chinese spy.

The scandal has highlighted tensions within the Trump administration over China’s access to AI chips amid suspicions that Megaspeed, a data centre company based in Singapore, diverted Nvidia GPUs to the country in violation of US export controls.

On Monday, US prosecutors confirmed that it had opened a criminal investigation into Megaspeed amid recriminations over the US Department of Commerce’s failure to place the firm on its export control list.

“We’re heading to China, and I don’t think you want to insult China just before you get there,” Trump, who will also join an unprecedented three-way meeting involving Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin at APEC, told reporters on Monday.

Beijing has denied the spying claims, calling them “entirely groundless” and “intended to smear and malign China”.

Rana Mitter, S T Lee Chair in US-Asia relations at the Harvard Kennedy School, said he expected “little mention” of Nvidia in public.

“China denies involvement, and Trump has stated that he doesn’t intend to raise it,” Mitter told Al Jazeera.

“Also, the US administration is still divided on the best course of action,” he said.

“Overall, the Trump administration will look to maintain the current detente, but the underlying competition remains strong.”

Trump and Xi have held three face-to-face meetings aimed at lowering the temperature in the US-China rivalry since the US president kicked off a renewed trade war against Beijing upon his return to the White House.

Amid tit-for-tat trade salvoes, tariff rates for Chinese and US goods rose as high as 145 percent and 125 percent, respectively, until Trump and Xi agreed to a trade truce in Busan, South Korea, in October last year.

The truce is currently set to expire on January 10, 2027, after Washington and Beijing agreed to extend the agreement beyond its original expiration date of November 10.

Speaking at the opening of the two-day APEC summit on Wednesday, Xi reiterated Beijing’s opposition to protectionism and unilateralism, urging countries to support “free and open trade and investment” and “inclusive and balanced development”.

“The primary focus of this meeting is the management of risks among major powers; it does not aim to produce any groundbreaking, sweeping agreements,” Wang Wen, dean of the School of Global Leadership at Renmin University of China in Beijing, told Al Jazeera.

“China’s primary expectation is to steer major power relations back toward a path of mutual respect and peaceful coexistence, preventing a slide into a Cold War-style bloc confrontation,” Wang added.

While Trump and Xi’s September meeting in Washington was heavy on pomp and ceremony, it produced only a handful of tangible outcomes, apart from the truce extension, including commitments to establish a communication channel for AI-related security incidents and lower tariffs on $60bn worth of goods.

Among the major outstanding areas of contention is China’s restriction of rare earth exports to the US, which remain about 75 percent below normal levels, according to the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies.

Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Singapore-based Hinrich Foundation, said the once “reasonably high” expectations for the talks had been dimmed by recent events.

“Now, particularly with the midterm election results and Nvidia fallout, if they manage to shake hands without incident, it will be viewed as a win,” Elms told Al Jazeera.

“Part of the issue on the US side is growing uncertainty about US positions. The Nvidia chip movement has broken open disagreements among Trump’s own team,” Elms said.

With a new crop of US lawmakers entering Congress in January, Elms added, “there is also no clarity on what the Democrats might want to see happen and I think the returning Republicans are also less clear about how closely to align with Trump on China”.

With Trump and Xi only expected to talk for about two hours, they will have much less time to hash out issues than during previous meetings and are unlikely to announce an extension of the trade truce at the summit, said Dennis Wilder, a former US national security official who is now an adjunct professor at Georgetown University.

“There are many protocol events, thus the time is very limited to a few topics,” Wilder, who worked on China at the CIA and the White House’s National Security Council, told Al Jazeera.

“The Chinese will voice their concerns over new export controls on high technology, the US will voice concerns that China is not lifting up to agreements on agricultural imports and rare earth exports,” Wilder said, adding that discussions would likely address AI generally but not touch on the Nvidia scandal.

“Trump’s goal is to continue the strategic stability that he and Xi announced at the Washington summit,” he added.

articles.title: Ghana's new $60m presidential jet sparks public outrage
articles.excerpt:
The French-made Falcon 6X replaces the ageing presidential jet, officials say

Ghana's government has defended its purchase of a new presidential jet amid criticism over its cost, as many citizens con...
articles.body_text:
The French-made Falcon 6X replaces the ageing presidential jet, officials say

Ghana's government has defended its purchase of a new presidential jet amid criticism over its cost, as many citizens continue to struggle with the high cost of living.

The $60m (£46m) French-made Falcon 6X has sparked a political row, with opposition politicians accusing President John Mahama's administration of misplaced priorities.

But the government says the purchase is justified, arguing that Ghana's improving economy makes the aircraft affordable and  is needed to replace an ageing presidential jet.

The controversy comes as Mahama's administration seeks to demonstrate an economic recovery after years of financial difficulties that forced Ghana to seek IMF assistance.

Can Ghana's new president meet the voters' high expectations?

Manufactured by French aerospace company Dassault Aviation, the aircraft was delivered to the Ghana Air Force on Monday at a reported cost of $61m.

Parliament approved its purchase last December as part of a broader programme to modernise Ghana's military aviation fleet, which also includes four helicopters from Airbus.

The jet was welcomed with a water salute on Monday, but its arrival triggered criticism online and among opposition politicians over the cost and timing of the purchase.

While in the opposition, Mahama himself opposed buying a new presidential jet, prompting questions about why his administration has now gone head with the purchase.

Opposition MP Samuel Abu Jinapor questioned the government's priorities, saying the expenditure came at a time when many Ghanaians continue to struggle with the cost of living and youth unemployment remained alarmingly high.

"What was unacceptable in opposition cannot suddenly become acceptable in government merely because the occupants of power have changed," Jinapor added.

He accused the governing National Democratic Congress (NDC) of hypocrisy, recalling how its senior figures had strongly opposed proposals for a new presidential aircraft when they were in opposition.

Jinapor also called for greater transparency over the procurement process, how the purchase was financed and the government's justification for the expenditure.

Defence Minister Kenneth Adjei welcomed and inspected the new jet on Monday

The purchase has also prompted sharp criticism on social media, with some users arguing the money could have been spent on more pressing public needs.

"This money can employ over 100,000 nurses and 200,000 teachers," an X user posted.

But the government has rejected the criticism, saying Ghana's economic circumstances have changed considerably since the NDC opposed a similar purchase.

Peter Lanchene Toobu, chairman of parliament's defence committee, said the party had never opposed acquiring a presidential jet in principle.

Its objection, he said, had been on the timing when Ghana was experiencing severe economic difficulties.

"We agreed in principle that we needed to purchase a new presidential jet," he said.

He argued, however, that Ghana could not justify the expenditure at a time when it was seeking a $3bn bailout from the IMF.

"The strength and macroeconomic stability of this country have enhanced our status in the sense that imports have become cheaper, and this is the right time," he added.

Toobu said the government had purchased the aircraft without borrowing, citing a stronger Ghanaian currency and improved economic conditions.

Government spokesperson Kwakye Ofosu also dismissed suggestions that the purchase was a misplaced priority.

He pointed to falling prices of construction materials and lower borrowing costs as evidence of the country's improved economic situation.

"When I was campaigning in 2024, and I was donating cement, it cost 115 cedis (£7.5) a bag. Today, for 80 cedis, you will get a bag of cement," he told JoyNews.

The controversy has also extended to the aircraft's interior, following claims that it has a dedicated bedroom and bathroom.

But Ofosu dismissed claims that the jet had such luxury facilities, saying the president has no intention of "bathing in the air".

"There certainly is no bathroom. President Mahama has no intention of bathing in the air," Ofosu said.

He explained that the jet has reclining seats that can be converted into sleeping arrangements but denied that it has a dedicated bedroom.

The government says the new jet will replace the 16-year-old Falcon 900EX, which has suffered recurring maintenance problems, including corrosion and leakages in its fuel tank.

The older jet was reportedly grounded in France for several months in 2025 while undergoing repairs.

Officials say the Falcon 6X has a longer flying range, reducing the need for refuelling stops on international trips and improving the reliability of presidential travel.

Professor Godfred Alufar Bokpin, an economist at the University of Ghana said that while the president's safety was paramount, the timing of the purchase was difficult to justify amid severe austerity measures, high unemployment and widespread infrastructure challenges.

"The timing makes it a bit difficult to understand," he told the BBC, adding that the government should provide a cost-benefit analysis explaining why buying the jet was preferable to leasing one and how the decision serves Ghana's interests.

Additional reporting by Thomas Naadi in Accra
